Start

@Graph Overview

@Graph is a macOS app for scientific data. It graphs recordings and other time series, measures and filters them, analyzes images, draws charts and runs statistics. It reads many recording, image and table formats (see Supported File Formats), and six toolkits add tools for particular fields. If you are new to @Graph, start with Getting Started.

The Five Workspaces

@Graph has five kinds of window to work in. Each has its own page in this guide.

WorkspaceWhat you do thereGuide page
Data LogCollect results as text. Measurements and fits from a graph are written here as tables, and statistics arrive when you click Send to Data Log. You can also type or paste data, then select a table and graph or chart it.Data Log & Text Editors
SpreadsheetsType, paste or open a table, tidy it, and send it to a graph, a chart or statistics. A graph and a chart each have a spreadsheet of their own data too.Spreadsheets
ChartsDraw summary figures of category data: bar, line, scatter, box, estimation and survival plots, with effect sizes and tests on the Statistics tab. The omics plots are chart types too.Charts; Statistics on a Chart; Omics Visualization
GraphsView recordings and other X-Y data as sweeps: zoom, filter, correct the baseline, measure, detect peaks and fit curves.Graphs; Measuring & Analysis
Image WindowView images, stacks and time series: set each channel's display, draw or detect ROIs, extract intensity traces over time, and export images and movies.Imaging

How Data Moves Between Windows

Results pass from one window to the next: import, look, measure, then chart and compare.

  • Recording file → Graph → measure → Data Log → select the table → Chart Selection… → statistics and a figure.
  • CSV or pasted table → Spreadsheet → Data to Chart → statistics and a figure.
  • Image file → Image Window → draw ROIs → Measure → Send to Graph → measure → Data Log → Chart Selection… → statistics and a figure.
  • Any Bar / Dot, Horizontal Bar or Box Plot chart → Statistics tab › Show Estimation Plot → the same chart as an estimation plot. Click the button again to switch back. A Line chart switches under Chart Type › Estimation Plot.

Getting Started walks through these steps once, with the sample files.

Toolkits

Six toolkits, each a set of tools for one field, come with @Graph and are shown by default: Electrophysiology, Pharmacology & Biochemistry, Biosignals, Spectroscopy, Flow Cytometry and Astronomy. Their tools are tabs in the inspector's Toolkits category, image tools in the image inspector's Toolkits tab, commands in the Toolkits menu (such as the Cytometry, Plate Map, Calibrate Frames and Stack Frames windows) and calculators in Lab Tools. Settings › Toolkits hides one you don't use. See Toolkits: Overview for what each holds.

@Graph Keeps Your Data Safe

While you work, @Graph keeps a recovery copy of each graph, chart, spreadsheet, Text Editor and image window with unsaved changes, and of the Data Log. If your Mac shuts down before you save, @Graph offers to bring those windows back the next time you open it.

  • Reopen brings the windows back as they were, still marked as unsaved. A window that came from a file saves back to it with ⌘S.
  • The Data Log comes back as a Text Editor window titled Recovered Data Log.
  • Image windows come back with their ROIs, overlays and settings, read again from the original image file. If @Graph asks for access to its folder, choose it.
  • Don't Reopen moves the copies to the Trash.
  • Recovery copies never change your own files, and they are removed when you save, close the window or quit.

VoiceOver and the Keyboard

@Graph works with VoiceOver.

  • Each chart and each graph panel reads as one item that says what it shows: the axes, and each group's n, mean (or median) and spread. Press VO-Shift-Return on it to hear the data as an Audio Graph.
  • Manhattan Plots, UpSet plots, spectrograms, histograms, the Spike Sorter's views and PSD, cross-correlation and coherence results have Audio Graphs too. On a Manhattan Plot, each point names its chromosome and position.
  • With Keyboard navigation turned on (System Settings › Keyboard), Tab moves between controls. Use the Step buttons to change sweeps. The Chart Type rows are buttons Tab reaches.
  • On a heatmap or dot plot, the Row labels and Column labels items let you pick a label with VO-Up and VO-Down Arrow and rename it with VO-Space.
  • In a New Spreadsheet window and a chart's table, each column header's Column Actions (and the toolbar's Column Actions button, for the selected cell's column) opens the column's menu: Insert and Delete Column and Sort, with Rename Column in a chart's table and Set as Header Column in a New Spreadsheet. Each row number's Row Actions opens the row's.
  • On a plate map, the arrow keys move between wells and VoiceOver reads each one. In the Cytometry window, each plot names its population, channels and events, and its gates are items to select.

Getting Started

This page takes you through a first session: open a file, look around a graph window, measure, make a chart, run a statistic, then save and export. Each part points to the page that covers it in full.

The Welcome Window

The Welcome to @Graph window opens at launch. It lists your recent files beside these buttons:

ButtonWhat it does
Open File / Import DataOpens the Data Importer, a drop zone that lists the kinds of file @Graph opens.
Open Data LogBrings the Data Log to the front.
New SpreadsheetOpens a blank spreadsheet to type or paste data into.
User GuideOpens this guide.
Sample Graph, Sample Chart, Sample T-SeriesOpen a generated recording, a small bar chart and a simulated calcium-imaging movie, so you can try @Graph without a file of your own.
More SamplesLists samples for microscopy and for each toolkit that isn't hidden. Each opens at the tool that analyzes it.
  • Drop a file anywhere on the window to open it, or click a recent file. To see which files @Graph opens, click "a file" in the line "Drop a file anywhere on this window to open it".
  • The window closes once a file opens. A file @Graph can't open is named in an alert, and a recent file that has been moved or deleted is taken off the list.
  • Every sample is made by @Graph, not recorded, and is the same each time. Each button's tooltip says what the sample holds.
  • To skip the window at launch, uncheck "Show this window at launch" (the same setting as Settings › General › Session › Show Welcome window at launch). To hide the sample buttons, turn off Show sample data buttons there.
  • Help › Welcome to @Graph… (⌘@) brings the window to the front, or hides it when it is already in front. Help › @Graph User Guide (⇧⌘U) does the same for this guide.
  • Help › Report a Problem… and Request a Feature… start an email to support in your mail app, with @Graph's version, the macOS version and the Mac's model filled in. Nothing is sent until you send it yourself.

Opening a File

To openDo this
Any supported fileDrag it onto the Dock icon or any @Graph window, or choose File › Open File… (⌘O) and select one or more. @Graph opens each in the right kind of window: a recording in a Graph window, an image in an Image Window, a table in a Spreadsheet.
A file you opened recentlyChoose it in File › Open Recent, or in the Welcome window's list. Open Recent › Clear Menu empties the list.
A file, after checking its typeChoose File › New Data Importer (⌘N). It lists the kinds of file @Graph opens by field; Formats and Extensions… shows each with its extensions. Drop a file on it or click Choose File….
Numbers you type or pasteChoose File › New Spreadsheet (⌥⌘N), enter the data, then click Data to Graph… or Data to Chart.
A table of text in the Data LogSelect the tab- or comma-delimited numbers, then choose File › Graph Selected Text… (⇧⌘G) or Chart Selection… (⇧⌘H).
A .txt or .rtf fileIt opens in a Text Editor window. Select the data in it and use its Text Tools menu to send it to a Graph, Chart or Spreadsheet.
ImagesImage files (.tif or .tiff, .czi, .lsm, .nd2, .lif, a Prairie View .xml) and a folder of TIFFs open the same ways, each in a new image window.

See Supported File Formats for every format and what is read from it.

Look Around a Graph and Measure

  1. Open a recording, or click Sample Graph in the Welcome window. A graph window opens with a toolbar at the top, a bar of sweep controls above the plot, a status bar at the bottom and the inspector on the right.
  2. Drag a rectangle on the plot to zoom in. Double-click the plot background to step back out.
  3. Choose which sweeps to show: type them in the "Review sweeps:" field above the plot (for example 1-10, 15) and press Return, or click the plot and press Tab to step through the sweeps one at a time.
  4. In the inspector, click a category icon (Display, Modify, Signal, Analyze or Toolkits), then a tab below it. Display sets how the graph looks, Modify and Signal process the data, Analyze measures it, and Toolkits holds the tools for one field.
  5. To measure, choose Analyze › Measure (⇧⌘M). Choose Full sweep or Between cursors A – B, check the measurements you want and click Measure.
  6. Press ⌘L to show the Data Log. The results are there as a table.

See Graphs for zooming, cursors and sweeps, and Measuring & Analysis for each measurement.

Every change to the data (filtering, smoothing, baseline, scale and offset) can be undone with ⌘Z and redone with ⇧⌘Z.

Make a Chart and Run a Statistic

  1. Click Sample Chart in the Welcome window. To use your own data, put it in a spreadsheet (File › New Spreadsheet, ⌥⌘N) with one column for each group and the group names in the first row, then click Data to Chart. To chart results from the Data Log, select their table and choose Chart Selection… (⇧⌘H).
  2. The chart opens with its inspector. On the Chart tab, click a type under Chart Type and set the chart's look.
  3. Click the Statistics tab. Under EFFECT SIZE, choose what to Compare, then click Compute Brackets. Each comparison is drawn on the chart as a bracket with its effect size and test. The Sample Chart opens with its brackets already computed, each group against Group 1.
  4. For the full tables, or for correlation, regression and categorical tests, click Open Full Statistics Window, set the analysis up and click Determine Effect.

See Charts › Make a Chart, Statistics on a Chart and Statistics: Overview.

Save and Export

  1. Press ⌘S (File › Save) to save a graph, chart or spreadsheet as a .@graph file, which keeps your analysis and the figure's look. Saving never changes your original recording.
  2. For a figure, click the Export button, the first tool button in a graph or chart window's toolbar, and choose Image… (PNG, JPEG, TIFF, GIF, PDF or SVG). Copy as PDF, in the same menu, puts it on the clipboard.
  3. For the numbers, choose a format under Data in the same menu.
  4. To print the front window, choose File › Print… (⌘P).

See Exporting Results.

The Data Log

The Data Log collects measurements, fits and other results as tables. It records from the moment @Graph starts but stays hidden until you ask for it.

  • ⌘L (View › Show Data Log) brings it to the front with everything logged so far. Pressing ⌘L again while it is in front hides it without losing anything.
  • Window › Data Log, which is checked while the log is on screen, and the Welcome window's Open Data Log button bring it forward too.
  • Each launch starts a new Data Log. Save one you want to keep with ⌘S; quitting asks first if it has unsaved results. After Clear, the next ⌘S asks for a new file, so the last one is never overwritten.
  • You can also paste numbers into it and graph or chart them, and type calculations (see Data Log & Text Editors).

Windows, Tabs and Sessions

  • Files open as tabs or as separate windows, as set in Settings › General › File Handling. Tabs keep each kind together: graphs with graphs, charts with charts, and images, spreadsheets and text editors each with their own kind.
  • Window › Merge All Windows gathers every kind at once, each into its own tabbed window (the Data Log, Welcome and the User Guide stay as they are). Window › Move Tab to New Window, or dragging a tab out of the tab bar, makes a tab a window again.
  • The Toolkits menu acts on the graph window you used most recently.
  • Windows aren't reopened at the next launch. To reopen your files, turn on Settings › General › Session › Restore last session on launch: each window's file comes back (for a graph, the .@graph file you saved it as, with your analysis, or else the original recording).

Where to Find Things

The sidebar groups the guide's pages under these headings:

  • Start: @Graph Overview, this page and Supported File Formats.
  • Workspaces: the windows you work in: the Data Log and text editors, Spreadsheets, Charts, Graphs and Imaging.
  • Graph Tools: Graph Display Settings, Modifying Graphs, Signal Processing, and Measuring & Analysis, for any graph.

  • Resources: Statistics, Omics Visualization, Batch Processing and Protocols, and the AI Assistant.
  • Settings & Helpers: Settings, Lab Tools & Calculators, Exporting Results and Keyboard Shortcuts.
  • Cited Works: every work this guide cites, in one list.

Supported File Formats

@Graph opens every format on this page directly, with no conversion step. The formats are listed by field, in the order the Welcome window and the Data Importer list them, and each entry says what the file opens as and what is read from it.

Open a File

  1. Choose File › Open File… (⌘O) and select one or more files, or drag them onto the Dock icon, the Welcome window or any @Graph window. File › New Data Importer (⌘N), also the Welcome window's Open File / Import Data button, opens a drop zone that lists these formats by field; its Formats and Extensions… link shows each with its extensions.
  2. If the file holds several parts (a workbook's sheets, a project's tables, a recording's series or streams, a microscope file's scenes), @Graph lists them. Check the ones you want and open them.
  3. The file opens in the kind of window its contents need: a graph, an image, a spreadsheet, a heatmap, a Text Editor, a plate map or a Cytometry window. The Data Log (⌘L) notes what was read and anything that was left out.

Where a file could open more than one way:

  • A table (.csv, Excel, Numbers, Prism and the like) opens as a spreadsheet. From there, click Data to Graph… or Data to Chart.
  • A plate reader's export opens as a plate map. To open it as a spreadsheet, click Open as Table Instead in its Read Values sheet.
  • A flow cytometry file opens in a Cytometry window. Open as Table there opens it as a spreadsheet, and it opens as a spreadsheet from the start while the Flow Cytometry toolkit is hidden.
  • Where two formats share an extension, @Graph tells them apart by what the file holds: .h5 (HDF5 or a 10x Genomics matrix), .mat (MATLAB or LabChart's export), .txt (plain text or a GEO series matrix), .hdr and .img (Analyze or ENVI), .dat (a recording, or ENVI with its .hdr beside it), and a plate reader's .csv, .txt or .xlsx export.
  • A recording or image kept in several files opens from the file its entry names, with the others beside it. @Graph asks for access to the folder when it can't already read them.

Formats @Graph Writes

File › Save (⌘S) writes the front window as a .@graph file (see @Graph Documents, below). A graph can also be exported, from its Export menu, to the data formats in this table, whatever format it was opened from, and an image window to TIFF. Exporting Results › Export a Graph's Data gives each export's choices and limits; this table adds what you need to read the file elsewhere.

FormatIn the file
ABF (.abf)The sweep start times, and the recording's date to the millisecond. pCLAMP, pyABF and neo read the file.
AxoGraph (.axgx)The same values, and the recording's date.
CSV (.csv)One column per visible sweep.
HDF5 (.h5)One float32 dataset per channel, [sweeps × samples]: in h5py, row k is sweep k, with NaN past a sweep's end. Each dataset carries its units, sample_rate and the channel's name, plus sweep lengths and start times when known. Each channel keeps its own rate, so nothing is resampled.
MATLAB (.mat)For each channel, a [samples × sweeps] matrix (NaN past a sweep's end) with <name>_sample_rate, <name>_units and, when known or needed, <name>_start_times and <name>_lengths, plus the recording's start (recording_start). A raster writes <unit>_spike_times vectors, with <unit>_spike_name (the unit's full name), <unit>_spike_win (the span recorded over) and <unit>_spike_t0 (its sweep's start). MATLAB and scipy.io.loadmat read the file.
NWB (.nwb)An NWB 2 file with the subject, session and electrode metadata you enter in the export sheet (see Exporting Results › Export to NWB).
TIFF (image windows)Export menu › Export Data as TIFF… saves every channel, Z slice and time point as OME-TIFF or ImageJ TIFF, with pixel size, Z step, frame times and channel names and colors, for Fiji or Python (see Imaging).

@Graph reads its own AxoGraph, HDF5, MATLAB and NWB exports back as they were.

Recording Times

Many formats record when each sweep started and when the recording was made. @Graph keeps both, saves them in .@graph files and writes them to its NWB, HDF5, MATLAB and ABF exports.

What is readFrom these files
Sweep start times, in seconds from the start of the recordingABF, ATF, HEKA, SutterPatch, NWB, Intan, Open Ephys, Neuralynx, Blackrock, Plexon, TDT, EDF+, Spike2, TDMS, SpikeGLX, BrainVision, WinWCP and LabChart (MATLAB export). The first sweep can start after 0 when the file says so.
The recording's date and timeABF, AxoGraph, HEKA, SutterPatch, NWB, Open Ephys, Neuralynx, Blackrock, Plexon, TDT, EDF, WFDB, Spike2, SpikeGLX, BrainVision, CFS, WinWCP (version 9 and later) and LabChart (MATLAB export). Files that store local time without a time zone are read in your Mac's time zone.
  • When a file opens, its Data Log line gives the date and time and the first and last sweep start times, or says the file records none.
  • Click a sweep to select it: the Plot Style tab of the inspector shows when it was recorded, below its name.
  • When a file records that a sweep's first sample isn't at time 0, the graph opens with its X axis at that true time. Set X = 0 works as usual, Reset returns to this time, and results made from the graph keep it (see Graphs › Cursors).
  • Synapse Detection's Results Over Time and time-binned summary can use the recorded sweep times instead of a typed interval (see Synapse Detection).

Plot Sweeps at Recording Time

View › Plot Sweeps at Recording Time draws each sweep at the time it was recorded, end to end along one time axis, instead of overlaid from 0. The X axis counts from the first sweep's start, and the time between sweeps shows as gaps. It is off by default, and the menu item is available only for a graph whose file records sweep start times.

  • It changes only the display: the data, and every analysis of it, stay the same. It is saved with a .@graph file and can be undone.
  • Zoom, pan and the hover readout work along the whole recording, and exported figures show the graph as the window does. Turning the option on or off returns the X axis to its full range.
  • Cursors, interval bars, trend lines, Export Visible and the panels that use cursors are unavailable in this view: turn the option off to use them.
  • A sweep with no recorded start time, such as a fit, isn't shown. The Data Log lists these sweeps when you turn the option on.

@Graph Documents

.@graph@Graph Files
File › Save (⌘S) writes the front window as a .@graph file: a graph, chart, spreadsheet, image or plate map. It reopens in the same kind of window with its settings and analysis. The file is HDF5, so h5py, MATLAB and HDFView can read a graph's sweeps (in the /acquisition/ group, one dataset per sweep, with unit and sample rate). It is not an NWB file: to share data as NWB, use the window's Export menu › NWB. A file saved by a later version of @Graph asks you to update before it opens.

Tables and Text

Tables open in a Spreadsheet window; from there, Data to Graph… or Data to Chart makes a graph or chart (see Spreadsheets). A file with more than one sheet or table asks which to open, and several open as tabs of one window (see Data Log & Text Editors › Opening Files from the Data Log). Text files open in a Text Editor window.

.arrow / .feather / .arrowsApache Arrow and Feather
Apache Arrow's file and stream formats, and Feather 2. The column names become the header row. Every flat column type is read; time-zone-aware timestamps show in UTC, a duration shows as a count (its column is named with the unit), and nulls and NaN are blank cells. Files compressed with LZ4 or Zstandard are read. Nested columns (lists, structs, maps) and Feather version 1 files report an error saying how to save a flat table.
.parquetApache Parquet
The column names become the header row. Every flat column type is read: integers, floating point, booleans (TRUE and FALSE), text, dates (2024-01-15), timestamps and times (time-zone-aware timestamps in UTC), exact decimals and category columns. Null and NaN values are blank cells. Snappy, gzip, zstd, LZ4 and Brotli compression are read. Nested columns (lists, maps, structs) and encrypted files aren't read: save a flat table first.
.csv / .tsvComma- and Tab-Separated Text
The first row becomes the column titles unless it holds only numbers. A .csv is split at commas, at semicolons (a European CSV with decimal commas) or at tabs, whichever its rows use; a .tsv is split at tabs. A table from R whose header row names every column but the first (the row numbers) gets an untitled first column, so each name stays over its own column. Data to Graph… asks for the delimiter, header row and X-axis mode. To write a graph as .csv, use its Export menu.
.xlsxExcel Workbook
Cells and formulas are read; charts, images and drawings are not, and hidden sheets aren't offered. Numbers, dates and formulas come in as described under How numbers, dates and formulas are read, below. A sheet whose cells span more than 25 million (usually a stray value far from the data) reports an error, and so does a password-protected workbook.
.xlsExcel 97–2003 Workbook
Workbooks saved by Excel 97 to 2003, and by programs that still save in that format (LibreOffice and much instrument software). Opens as an .xlsx does. Excel 95 and older workbooks and password-protected ones report what to do: open them in Excel or LibreOffice and save them as .xlsx. A text table saved with an .xls name, as some instrument software writes, opens as the text table it is, and the Data Log says so.
.json / .jsonl / .ndjsonJSON and JSON Lines
These layouts are read: an array of records ([{"dose": 1, "response": 2.3}, …]), an object of columns, pandas' split and table layouts, an array of rows under a first row of names, and JSON Lines (.jsonl, .ndjson: one record per line). An object holding arrays of records opens each as its own table. Columns follow the order their fields first appear, and a field a record lacks is a blank cell. Nested objects are flattened, their names joined with a period (visit.day), and an array inside a cell shows as its JSON text. Numbers keep every digit the file gives, null is blank, and true and false show as TRUE and FALSE. Row labels other than 0, 1, 2… come in as a first column, Row. A file of a single value, or of more than 25 million cells, reports an error.
.numbersNumbers Document (Apple)
Cells and formulas are read, as for .xlsx. Numbers show as Numbers shows them (2.6%, 290,000, $1,234.50), dates as 2024-01-15 or 2024-01-15 13:30:00, and a duration (1h 30m) as its number of seconds (5400). A document with more than one table asks which to open, listing each table's size. A document last saved by an old version of Numbers reports an error: open it in a current Numbers and save it again, or export it to Excel.
.txt / .textPlain Text
Opens in a Text Editor window named after the file, and Save (⌘S) writes back to it. Text in UTF-8, UTF-16, Windows-1252 or Mac OS Roman reads correctly, and a file over 20 MB asks before it opens. To plot a table in it, select the table and use Text Tools (Graph Selected Text…, Chart Selection…, Send to Spreadsheet… or Smart Visualization…). A GEO series matrix .txt opens as a heatmap instead (see Genomics and Cytometry, below).
.rtfRich Text Format
Opens in a Text Editor window, as a .txt file does, with its formatting removed. Save (⌘S) asks for a new file name, so the original keeps its formatting.

How numbers, dates and formulas are read

  • Number formats (Excel and Numbers): each number is its stored value, shown as the file formats it (percentages, decimal places, thousands separators, currency signs and scientific notation), with your Mac's decimal and grouping marks. A cell formatted as 45% shows 45% and holds 0.45, which formulas and Copy use; a chart made from it shows 45% or 0.45, as its Show percentages as switch says (see Spreadsheets › Number Formats).
  • Percentages in text: "45%" in a table or file is read as a percentage. A chart shows it as 45% or 0.45, as its Show percentages as switch says (see Charts). A graph of pasted data reads it as 0.45 (see Data Log & Text Editors › Graph Pasted Data).
  • Dates and times (Excel): cells formatted as dates or times show as 2026-10-05, 14:30:00 or both, with milliseconds when they have any (14:30:00.250). Elapsed times such as [h]:mm:ss stay numbers, a count of days (36:00:00 is 1.5).
  • Formulas (Excel and Numbers): a formula comes in live when @Graph computes the result the file saved; otherwise the cell keeps the saved value (see Spreadsheets › Formulas).
  • Error values (#N/A, #DIV/0!) show as Excel shows them and count as missing values.

Statistics

Files from statistics programs. Each table opens in a Spreadsheet window, and several tables open as tabs of one window.

.pzfxGraphPad Prism (XML)
Prism's XML project format. Each data table opens as its own table; a file with several asks which to open, listing each table's kind (XY, Column, Grouped and so on) and size. The columns are the X values, the row titles and every data set's subcolumns, named as the R package pzfx names them (Control_1, Control_2 for replicates; Control_MEAN, Control_SD, Control_N for entered means). Values excluded in Prism are left blank, as Prism leaves them out of its analyses. Graphs, results and layouts are not read. A table of more than 25 million cells reports an error.
.prismGraphPad Prism 10 and Later
Prism's current project format, read the same way as .pzfx, with the same column names. Entered CVs and high/low limits come in as Prism shows them. Graphs, analysis results, layouts and info sheets are not read. A damaged or incomplete file reports an error.
.xptSAS Transport File
Versions 5 and 8. Each data set opens as a table (a file holding several asks which to open), with the variable names as the header row. Numbers are read at full precision, missing values (., .A to .Z and ._) are blank cells, and numbers in a SAS date, date-and-time or time format show as dates (2024-01-15), dates and times (2024-01-15 08:30:00) or times (14:30:00). Variable labels aren't imported. SAS data sets (.sas7bdat) and CPORT files aren't read: in SAS, save a transport file (the XPORT engine or %LOC2XPT) or export CSV, then open that.
.sav / .zsavSPSS Data File
The variable names become the header row. Value labels show as their text (a value without a label as its number). System-missing and user-missing values (those a variable declares missing, such as 99 = Refused) are blank cells, as SPSS leaves them out of its analyses. Numbers in a date or time format show as dates and times. Variable labels and documents aren't imported. SPSS portable files (.por) aren't read: save them as .sav from SPSS or PSPP.
.dtaStata Data File
Stata 7 and later. The variable names become the header row, value labels show as their text, dates and times show as dates (weeks, months, quarters and half-years in Stata's own 2024w12 style), and missing values (., .a to .z) are blank cells. Variable labels and notes aren't imported. A file of more than 25 million cells (observations × variables) reports an error: keep the variables you need in Stata and save a copy. Files from Stata 6 or earlier: save them again from a newer Stata.

General Science

.h5 / .hdf5HDF5
Opens as a graph: every numeric 1-D or 2-D dataset in the file becomes a channel, wherever it is. The sample rate (sample_rate, fs, dt and the like), units and channel names are read from the datasets' attributes. A dataset with no rate is plotted at 1 sample per second, and the Data Log says so. A file another program still has open (an acquisition in progress) is read too. A Cell Ranger .h5 opens as a heatmap instead (see Genomics and Cytometry, below).
.pxp / .h5xpIgor Pro Packed Experiment
Each wave keeps its name, length, sample rate and units; X scaling in ms is converted to seconds. Waves named as a numbered series (RecordA0, RecordA1…) in one data folder become the sweeps of one channel, and a 2-D wave's columns are its sweeps. A SutterPatch experiment (.h5xp) opens one window per routine ("R1 VI_Ch1"): each of the routine's signals (Voltage1, Current1, AuxIN1…) is a channel at its own sample rate, and each sweep keeps its start time in its name ("Sweep 2 (2.210 s)"). Text waves, and waves that can't be read, are left out, and the Data Log counts them.
.ibwIgor Binary Wave
A single wave, with its sample rate and units from the wave header. A 2-D wave opens with its rows as samples and its columns as sweeps; a 1-D wave holding sweeps back to back, each ending in a NaN, opens as those sweeps.
.tdmsLabVIEW TDMS (National Instruments)
Files from LabVIEW, DIAdem and NI-DAQmx logging. Each group opens in its own window. Its numeric channels are timed by their waveform properties (a channel without them is counted in samples; when a group has both, those channels open in a window of their own, "group (by sample)") and shown in their units; raw DAQmx data are scaled with the file's linear, polynomial and table scales. A channel that needs a sensor scale (thermocouple, RTD, strain gauge or thermistor) is left out rather than shown in the wrong units, and the Data Log says which: export it scaled from LabVIEW or DIAdem to open it. Text and time-stamp channels are left out.
.matMATLAB
Level 4, level 5 (-v6 and -v7) and v7.3 files, Spike2's channel exports included. Numeric variables open as the channels of a graph, and spike-time vectors as a raster (see How MATLAB files are read, below). LabChart's MATLAB export is listed under Physiology.
.nc / .nc4 / .cdfNetCDF
Classic NetCDF and NetCDF-4. Variables open as Spreadsheet windows, and a file with several tables asks which to open: variables along one dimension together, the dimension's coordinate first (time, station, depth…); each 2-D variable as its own table, its rows and columns labeled by its coordinates; single values together. A column is named with its units (temp (K)). Fill values, missing values and values outside the valid range are blank, packed values are unpacked (scale_factor and add_offset), and times (days since 2000-01-01 and the like, on the standard calendar) show as dates; other calendars stay numbers. Variables of three or more dimensions aren't opened, and the Data Log names them: save a 2-D slice in Python (xarray) to open one.
.npy / .npzNumPy Array
Opens as a Spreadsheet window. A 1-D array opens as one column named after the array, a 2-D array as rows and columns (named 0, 1, …), and a structured array with a column per field. Every plain type is read, dates and times (datetime64) included; a time span (timedelta64) shows as a count of its unit, its column named with it, and NaN and NaT are blank cells. An .npz archive asks which arrays to open. Arrays of three or more dimensions report an error: save a 2-D slice. Object arrays are never read, because loading one runs code the file holds: save the array with a plain type, or as .csv.

How MATLAB files are read

In the fileHow it opens
Sample rateFrom a variable such as fs, srate or sample_rate, an interval such as dt, or an evenly spaced time vector. Without one, X is the sample number.
A matrixA [samples × sweeps] matrix is one channel of sweeps; a [channels × samples] matrix is one channel per row.
A 1×1 structIts fields are read, named struct.field.
Spike-time vectors (names such as spike_times or ts)A raster.
Variables on different time axesEach set opens in its own window; they are not forced onto one axis.
Cell arrays and sparse matricesSkipped, and the Data Log says so.

Microscopy and Imaging

Images open in a new image window (see Imaging). A file holding more than 4 images (scenes, positions or series) asks which to open, all checked to start. To write the pixel values back out, see Formats @Graph Writes, above.

.imsBitplane Imaris
Imaris 5.5 and later. Channels, Z planes and time points open at full resolution. Pixel size and Z step, each time point's time (kept frame by frame when they aren't evenly spaced) and channel names and colors are read. 8- and 16-bit data, in planes up to about 11,600 × 11,600 pixels. 32-bit and floating-point files, and files from before Imaris 5.5, are refused with a message saying how to convert them.
.bmp / .gif / .webpBMP, GIF and WebP
Pictures, opened as PNG and JPEG files are. An animated GIF opens as a time series, each frame at the time its delays give (see Imaging › Supported File Formats).
.xml + .tifBruker Prairie View
Prairie View 4 and 5 T-series and Z-series: the .xml and the TIFF files beside it. Drop the .xml file or its folder; @Graph asks for access to the folder if it can't already read it. Bit depth, pixel size, Z step, the time between time points and channel names are read from the XML. A bidirectional Z-series is put in one direction.
.hdr + .img / .dat / .raw / .bsq / .bil / .bip / .sliENVI Rasters
Images from hyperspectral cameras and imaging spectrometers, and spectral maps. The bands open as Z slices, with the header's band wavelengths as their spectral axis. Open the .hdr, or its binary file with the header beside it; a binary file without one says so. A .dat without an ENVI header beside it opens as a recording, such as HEKA PatchMaster's. An Analyze .hdr still opens as NIfTI (see Imaging › Supported File Formats).
.heic / .heifHEIC and HEIF
iPhone photos, opened as PNG and JPEG files are and turned as their orientation says. A HEIC holding several pictures opens its main one.
.jp2JPEG 2000
Opened as PNG and JPEG files are. A JPEG 2000 deeper than 8 bits is refused: open it in Fiji, or convert it to TIFF.
.lifLeica Image File
Leica LAS X files. Every image series in the file opens in its own window, titled with the file and series names: multi-channel images (color camera images included), Z-stacks, time-lapse and combined T×Z, 8- to 16-bit, in planes up to about 11,600 × 11,600 pixels (export a region of a larger merged tile scan from LAS X). Channel names (the dye, when the file records one), colors, pixel size (X, Y and Z) and frame interval are read. FLIM acquisitions add the images LAS X computed as extra channels, hidden at first: Intensity, Fast Flim (ps), Standard Deviation (ps) and Phasor Intensity. Spectral (λ) scans, floating-point series and the raw photon data are not read.
.nii / .nii.gz / .hdr + .imgNIfTI and Analyze
NIfTI-1 and NIfTI-2 volumes and time series, and Analyze 7.5 .hdr/.img pairs, gzipped or not. A pair opens from either file, and @Graph asks for access to the folder if it can't already read the other one. Slices open as Z, volumes as time points, and a fifth dimension or RGB samples as channels. Voxel sizes and the time between volumes are read, and the file's scaling (slope and intercept) is applied. Images show with the first row at the bottom, as ImageJ shows them; the orientation matrix isn't applied.
.nd2Nikon ND2
NIS-Elements 3 and later. Each XY position of a multipoint acquisition opens as its own image, named as in NIS-Elements. Multi-channel, multi-Z and multi-T images, 8- or 16-bit, in planes up to about 11,600 × 11,600 pixels (export a region of a larger stitched image from NIS-Elements); a full Z-stack at every time point gets separate Z and T controls (see Imaging). Channel names, emission wavelengths, recorded colors and pixel size (X, Y and Z step) are read when present. A color camera's exposure of one stain (DAPI, GFP, DIC…), recorded in red, green and blue, opens as one channel, their sum, in the color that holds its signal (gray when none does); for a stained brightfield image, Settings › Imaging can keep the three colors as channels. Lossy (JPEG 2000) and floating-point files are refused with a message.
.oib / .oifOlympus FluoView
FluoView FV1000, FV1200 and FV10i images: an .oib file, or an .oif with its .oif.files folder beside it (@Graph asks for the folder). Channels, Z planes and time points open as one image, at the bit depth FluoView records (12-bit, say). Pixel size, Z step and the time between time points are read; channels are named by their dye and open in their emission wavelength's color. A line or point scan is refused, and FV3000's .oir files aren't read: export either from FluoView as OME-TIFF.
.zarr folderOME-Zarr
OME-NGFF images (versions 0.1 to 0.5): open the image's .zarr folder from File › Open File…, or drop it. Channels, Z planes and time points open at full resolution. When a full-resolution plane is too large (more than about 11,600 × 11,600 pixels), the first lower level that fits opens instead, with its own pixel size, and the Data Log says so. Pixel sizes, the Z step, the time between time points and channel names and colors are read. A bioformats2raw folder opens each of its images. For a plate, open one field's folder inside it. Only 8- and 16-bit data are read, and images on a server (URLs) aren't.
.png / .jpg / .jpegPNG and JPEG
Photos of gels, blots, plates and tissue. The pixels are the values the file stores, not values adjusted for the display. A grayscale image opens as one channel; a color image as Red, Green and Blue channels, or as one channel when its three values are equal everywhere. Transparency isn't shown. 8-bit images stay 8-bit and 16-bit PNGs 16-bit. A JPEG from a camera or phone opens turned the way it was taken. The pixel size is read from the file only when it is a microscope's (50 µm or smaller); otherwise set it in the ROIs tab. JPEG compression changes pixel values slightly, so for measurements use a TIFF or PNG from the instrument. A CMYK (print) JPEG is refused with a message.
.tif / .tiffTIFF, ImageJ and OME-TIFF
8-, 16- and 32-bit integer and 32- and 64-bit floating-point images, a camera's 10- and 12-bit stills, and BigTIFF, uncompressed or with LZW, Deflate or PackBits compression. An RGB image opens as three channels, without its transparency. ImageJ hyperstacks and OME-TIFF open with their channels, Z and T and their calibration. For plain stacks, colors and pixels with no value, see How TIFF files are read, below. 1-bit, 16-bit floating-point, JPEG and zstd TIFFs are refused with a message.
folderTIFF Folder
A folder of TIFF files opens as a T-series, in natural name order (img2 before img10); check Treat T-series as Z-stack in the Channels panel to make it a Z-stack. Files holding several pages each open with every page, in file then page order. A folder of ImageJ Z-stacks, one per time point, opens as a Z-stack over time, and a folder holding an OME-TIFF set opens as that set. Files with their own channels are refused: open one of them instead. A folder saved by Fiji takes its pixel size from the first file.
.cziZeiss CZI
Files from LSM 800, 900 and 980, Axioscope and Airyscan systems: multi-channel, multi-Z and multi-T images, combined T×Z included, 8- or 16-bit, uncompressed or with ZEN's lossless (zstd) compression. Each scene opens as its own image, and tile scans are stitched at their recorded positions. A line scan along Z (an XZ scan) opens as one image per time point with Z down the vertical axis. Channel names, recorded colors and voxel sizes (X, Y and Z) are read. A color camera's exposure opens as one channel, as for Nikon ND2, above. JPEG XR, JPEG and LZW compression, and floating-point pixels, are refused with a message saying how to save the file instead.
.lsmZeiss LSM
LSM 510, 710, 780 and 880 files: multi-channel Z-stacks, time series and T×Z, 8-bit, 12-bit or floating point, including files over 4 GB. Channel names and colors, voxel sizes (X, Y and Z) and the time between time points are read. Line scans open as one image with time down the vertical axis, X-Z scans with Z down it. Only the first position of a multi-position file opens, and the Data Log says so.

How TIFF files are read

  • A plain multi-page TIFF opens as a T-series, and the Data Log says so. Check Treat T-series as Z-stack in the Channels panel to make it a Z-stack.
  • A plain ImageJ stack opens as a Z-stack, unless it records a frame interval and no Z spacing. Treat Z-stack as T-series switches it.
  • A stack saved by tifffile (Python, napari) opens with its channels, Z and T.
  • An OME-TIFF's per-plane times are read, and an OME-TIFF describing several images opens each in its own window.
  • ImageJ composites open in their saved channel colors, and ImageJ and Fiji TIFFs with their saved display range. A palette (indexed-color) image opens as its red, green and blue, except an ImageJ image with a lookup table, which keeps its values as one channel in the table's color.
  • NaN and infinite floating-point pixels (a ratio image's background) hold no value. They show black, read NaN under the pointer, and are left out of every ROI measurement, trace, Z projection and Auto range; the ROI statistics and the Data Log say how many there are. A 32-bit export writes them back as NaN.

Electrophysiology

Recordings from patch-clamp, multi-electrode array (MEA) and extracellular acquisition systems. Continuous data plot as waveforms, and spike events as a raster of spike trains.

  • A file with parts that don't belong in one graph (streams at different rates, spikes beside continuous data, events) opens each part in its own window, titled with the part. A file with more than 4 parts (SutterPatch routines, HEKA series, streams) first asks which to open, all checked to start.
  • A pause or gap in a recording starts a new sweep, named by its start time ("from 12.500 s"). It is never joined up as if continuous.
  • A very large recording loads from its start, and a warning says how much was loaded.
  • Formats that keep a recording in several files (Open Ephys, TDT, Intan's info.rhd and info.rhs, a HEKA .dat with a separate .pul, a Blackrock spec 2.1 .nsX with its .nev) ask for access to their folder when @Graph can't already read it.
.axgx / .axgdAxoGraph
AxoGraph X files and AxoGraph 1 and 2 files. Channels and episodes are read from AxoGraph's trace groups, or else from the column titles, and a time column in ms is converted. A file without a time column (a table of measurements), or whose time column isn't evenly spaced (0, 1, 2, 5, 10 min), opens as X-Y data with that column as X; the Data Log says so. Tags and interval bars marked during the recording are listed in the Data Log. @Graph also writes AxoGraph files.
.abfAxon Binary File (ABF1 and ABF2)
Clampex and pCLAMP recordings. Each recorded channel opens as its own channel, with its name and its samples scaled to their recorded units. Episodic, gap-free and event-driven recordings are read; event-driven sweeps keep their own lengths. The amplifier's telegraphed whole-cell Rₛ and Cₘ, filter and mode are read when the file stores them, for voltage-clamp Rₛ correction and its clamp-mode check. The Data Log lists the protocol name, the file comment and the tags (comments typed during the recording) with their times. @Graph also writes ABF files.
.atfAxon Text Format
Tab-delimited text exported from Clampex; a file saved with commas instead of tabs opens too. One time column (in s or ms), then one column per signal per sweep. Several signals ('Trace #1 (mV)', 'Trace #1 (pA)', …) open as separate channels, each with the unit in its column header. A file whose first column isn't evenly spaced (uneven times, or a results table) opens as X-Y data with that column as X; the Data Log says so.
.ns1 – .ns6Blackrock NSx
Continuous multi-channel recordings, file specs 2.1 to 3.0, each channel scaled to its units from the header. Each pause in recording starts a new sweep. Spec 2.1 files hold no calibration: it comes from the recording's .nev beside them, and without it the samples are raw ADC values.
.nevBlackrock / Ripple / Neuralynx NEV
Spike times, as a raster: one train per electrode and unit (unsorted, sorted units, noise). Digital-input events open as a second raster, one train per input value, for use as trial markers. A restarted recording's runs open separately. A Neuralynx .nev opens as a raster with one train per event string, and the events are listed in the Data Log.
.cfsCED Signal (CFS)
Files from CED's Signal and its older sweep programs. Each data section opens as a sweep (blank, named "(no data)", for a channel with no samples in that section), and channels sampled at different rates open in windows of their own. Values are scaled to each channel's units. When every section starts at the same X offset (before its trigger, say), the X axis starts there; sections that start at different offsets, or an X axis that isn't time, open as X–Y data, which Align, Baseline and the ABF, MAT and NWB exports don't take, and the Data Log says so. The file's comment and variables go to the Data Log. Matrix (X–Y) and text channels aren't read, and the Data Log names them.
.datHEKA PatchMaster
PatchMaster and PatchMaster NEXT data files, bundled (the usual) or with a separate .pul file. Each series opens in its own window, titled with its label; a file with more than 4 series asks which to open. Each sweep is an episode, and each trace (Imon, Vmon…) is a channel with its own length and sample rate, with leak traces as their own channels. The clamp command is rebuilt from the file's stimulus (see HEKA command waveforms, below).
.rhdIntan RHD2000
Every signal Intan records, each at its own rate: amplifier channels (µV), auxiliary inputs, supply voltage, board ADC, digital inputs and outputs and, in single-file .rhd recordings, temperature. For the "one file per signal type" and "one file per channel" formats, open their info.rhd. In files before version 3.0, the amplifier data are stored without the notch filter named in the file header.
.rhsIntan RHS2000 (Stimulation/Recording Controller)
Amplifier channels (µV), DC amplifier channels when saved (V), board ADC and DAC (V), and digital inputs and outputs (0 or 1), all at the amplifier rate. Each channel that delivered stimulation also shows its current in µA ("A-000 stim"). The onsets of stimulation, compliance limit, charge recovery and amp settle open as events in a raster window; each start of current is an event, so a biphasic pulse with an interphase delay gives one per phase. For the "one file per signal type" and "one file per channel" formats, open their info.rhs. The header's settings, electrode impedances and notes are listed in the Data Log, and the notes become the experiment description for NWB export.
.ncs / .cscNeuralynx
One continuous channel per file, in µV from the header's scale (and sign, for an inverted input). Each stretch between gaps in the record timestamps is a sweep. Continuous channels are timed from the session's start, as the spike and event files are.
.nse / .nst / .nttNeuralynx Spikes
Single electrode, stereotrode and tetrode spike files. The spikes open as a raster, one train per classified cell (cell 0 is unsorted), and their waveforms as a recording with one sweep per spike and one channel per wire, in µV. Times count from the session's .ncs files when @Graph can read their folder.
.nwbNeurodata Without Borders (NWB) 2
The time series in /acquisition/, including those inside containers such as LFP (or, when /acquisition/ has none, those in /processing/), open as channels with the file's rate and units: patch-clamp or extracellular, a 2-D series giving one channel per column. Spike times from /units open as a raster. See How NWB files are read, below. @Graph also writes NWB files.
.continuousOpen Ephys (Legacy Format)
One file per channel. Opening one loads every channel of its processor in the folder: neural channels in µV, ADC and AUX inputs in V. Lost data and acquisition restarts start new sweeps. TTL events and messages open as an Events raster, one train per line and direction ("TTL 1 on") followed by one per message, and .spikes files as a Spikes raster; messages are also listed in the Data Log. Each .spikes file's waveforms open as a recording too, one sweep per spike and one channel per wire, in µV.
.oebinOpen Ephys (Binary Format)
Open the recording's structure.oebin. Each stream (a probe's AP and LFP bands, an NI-DAQ board…) opens in its own window, with sweeps split where the sample numbers jump. A Neuropixels SYNC channel opens on its own. The recording's TTL events and Message Center text open as an Events raster, and the Spike Detector's spikes as a Spikes raster, one train per electrode and unit. Each electrode's waveforms open as a recording, one sweep per spike and one channel per wire, in µV.
.plxPlexon
Continuous channels (one window per rate: wideband at 40 kHz, field potentials at 1 kHz…), sorted spike times as a raster, and events (including strobed values) as another. If the header's gains give an implausible input range (placeholders left by a file converter), the load warning says so and JP Correction is off for the file.
.pl2Plexon PL2 (OmniPlex)
Not read directly, because Plexon hasn't published this format. Convert the file to .plx with Plexon's free PlexUtil, or to NWB with NeuroConv, and open the converted file. Opening a .pl2 shows these steps.
.smrSpike2 (CED)
Spike2 data files from every Spike2 version. Waveform and RealWave channels open in a window per rate, scaled to their units; a recording with pauses opens each stretch as a sweep at its own start time. Event, marker and text-mark channels open as a raster in an Events window (one train per marker code or text), and WaveMark spike channels as a raster by unit in a Spikes window; the spike waveforms themselves aren't drawn. 64-bit .smrx files aren't read: in Spike2, use File › Save As to save a .smr file, or File › Export As to save a MATLAB file, then open that.
.bin + .metaSpikeGLX (Neuropixels)
Neuropixels probe, NI-DAQ and OneBox recordings from SpikeGLX: open the .bin, or its .meta, with the other beside it (@Graph asks for the folder). Probe and NI-DAQ channels are scaled to volts by each channel's gain and named as SpikeGLX names them (AP12, LF12, XA0). A probe type @Graph doesn't know the gain of, whose .meta gives none, opens in ADC counts, and the Data Log says so. The sync channel and digital words open in a window of their own, as their 16 bits. Each file starts at its place on the acquisition clock, so a probe's AP and LF bands and the NI-DAQ of one run line up.
.tsqTDT Block
Open a block's .tsq. Stream stores (from its .tev, or their own .sev files) open one window per rate, float stores in volts and integer stores as recorded; snippets open as a raster of spike times by channel and sort code, and epocs as another. One block opens per file.
.wcpWinWCP (Strathclyde)
Each record opens as a sweep at its recorded time, named with its type (LEAK, say) and marked when it was rejected. Values are as WinWCP shows and exports them: each channel's zero level subtracted, and scaled by the record's A/D range and the channel's calibration. Records sampled at another rate open in a window of their own.
.edrWinEDR (Strathclyde)
Continuous recordings: each channel as one long sweep, scaled to its units with its zero level subtracted, as WinEDR shows it. Markers open as a raster in a Markers window, one train per marker text.

HEKA command waveforms

  • The clamp command (constant, ramp and continuous segments, with every increment mode) is rebuilt for each sweep from the file's stimulus tree, in mV or pA. It shows as a "Stim-DA-0" channel when no trace records it, and VI and IV plots, Rₛ correction and the membrane test use it as they use an ABF protocol.
  • Sine, square and chirp segments aren't drawn. The Data Log lists each series' protocol, its segments and increments, and why a command wasn't drawn.
  • Each Imon or Vmon trace uses the command from the amplifier that recorded it, or that amplifier's holding potential or current when the protocol doesn't use its D/A output. The Data Log notes a protocol that links an input to a different output.
  • An input no HEKA amplifier drives (a second amplifier wired to Adc5, say) shows as "Adc5 input", in volts at the input, with a Data Log note. Opening the file offers Channel Gain… to set its gain (see Modifying Graphs).

How NWB files are read

  • Scaling: each value is data × conversion × channel_conversion + offset, from the file's own conversion, offset and per-channel conversion.
  • Patch-clamp stimuli: each stimulus (in /stimulus/presentation) opens as a channel beside its recorded response, such as "Current stimulus (elec0)".
  • Patch-clamp sweeps are lined up by sweep number. Sweeps with no sweep number in common (voltage-clamp seal tests before current-clamp protocols, say) open in their own window.
  • A series timed by unevenly spaced timestamps (a behavioral measure, say) has no sample rate. It opens in its own window as X-Y data plotted against its timestamps, and the Data Log says so. To analyze it as a recording, resample it to an even rate (Modify › Graph Tools › Resample…).
  • A window of one time series (a photodiode, a pupil area) titles its Y axis with the series' name and unit.
  • A Units table without spike times isn't read as a raster.
  • The metadata of an NWB file you open fills the NWB export sheet when you export it again.

Physiology

Recordings from physiology and clinical acquisition systems: EEG, ECG, sleep, respiration and other body signals.

.acqBIOPAC AcqKnowledge
AcqKnowledge 3 to 5 files, from Windows or a Mac. Each channel is scaled to its units. Channels recorded at a lower rate than the others open in a window of their own, one window per rate. Event markers open as a raster in an Events window, one train per marker text. Channels that share a name get their channel number after it.
.vhdr + .eegBrainVision
EEG and other recordings from Brain Products' Recorder, and the EEG-BIDS standard's format: open the .vhdr, with its .eeg data and .vmrk markers beside it (@Graph asks for the folder). Each channel is scaled by its resolution to its unit (µV unless the header names another). Markers open as a raster in a Markers window, one train per type and description (Stimulus/S 1); a recording with several segments opens each as a sweep at its own time. Text (ASCII) data report an error: export the recording as binary.
.edf / .bdfEuropean Data Format (EDF, EDF+, BDF, BDF+)
EDF and EDF+, and BioSemi's BDF and BDF+. Each signal is scaled to its physical units. Signals recorded at the same rate open together, one window per rate. An EDF+ recording with pauses opens each stretch as a sweep at its own start time. Annotations open as a raster in an Annotations window, one train per distinct text, each annotation at its onset; an annotation's duration, such as a sleep stage's 30 s epoch, isn't kept, and the Data Log says so. The recording's date and time are read; the patient field isn't shown.
.matLabChart (MATLAB Export)
LabChart's MATLAB export. Each channel opens with its title and units, each block as a sweep at its start time, and comments as a raster. Channels at different rates open in separate windows: a block recorded at another rate opens in that rate's window, and a channel with no data in a block has a blank sweep there, named "(no data)", as the Data Log says. LabChart's firstsampleoffset isn't applied; the Data Log says so when a file has one. For other .mat files, see General Science › How MATLAB files are read.
.hea + .datPhysioNet WFDB
Open the record's .hea header; @Graph reads the signal files it names, asking for access to the folder if it can't already read it. Each signal is scaled to its units by its gain and baseline, and signals at different rates open in separate windows. In a multi-segment record, a gap between segments is left blank. Annotation files beside the record (atr, qrs and the like) open as rasters, one train per beat or rhythm label. FLAC-compressed records (formats 508, 516 and 524) aren't read: convert them first with WFDB's xform or wfdb-python.

Genomics and Cytometry

Expression matrices open as a Heatmap window (see Omics Visualization), and flow cytometry files in a Cytometry window.

.h5 / matrix.mtx10x Genomics and Matrix Market
Cell Ranger's feature-barcode matrices open as a heatmap, genes as rows and cells (barcodes) as columns: from the .h5 file (Cell Ranger 2 and later), from the filtered_feature_bc_matrix folder, or from its matrix.mtx or matrix.mtx.gz with features.tsv (or genes.tsv) and barcodes.tsv beside it, gzipped or not (@Graph asks for the folder). Genes are named by their symbols, repeats made unique with -1, -2. A file that counts several kinds of feature (Gene Expression, Antibody Capture, CRISPR guides) or several genomes asks which to open. Any other Matrix Market file opens with numbered rows and columns; complex values report an error.
.h5adAnnData (H5AD)
Single-cell matrices, dense or sparse, with their gene and cell names. A file holding several matrices (X, raw/X, layers such as counts) asks which to open, with X, the main one, selected; raw counts are usually in layers/counts or raw/X.
.clsCLS Class Labels
Sample class labels for a .gct file. Select the .cls file with the same name together with the .gct and open both: each sample's class is added to its name. A .cls file on its own has no values to plot.
.fcs / .lmdFlow Cytometry Standard (FCS)
FCS 2.0 to 3.2, and Beckman Coulter's .lmd. Opens in a Cytometry window with every event, compensated with the file's own matrix (see The Cytometry Window). With Open as Table, or with the Flow Cytometry toolkit hidden, it opens as a Spreadsheet window: one row per event and one column per parameter, named by its stain and detector (CD4 (FL1-A)); a file with several data sets asks which to open. Values are made linear as the FCS standard says: log-amplified parameters converted, gain divided out of linear ones, and Time in seconds. Compensation is not applied to the table: when the file holds a spillover matrix, the Data Log says so, and the values are as the instrument recorded them. A file with more events than a sheet holds (25 million cells) opens its first events, and its name and the Data Log say how many. Histogram and ASCII data sets report an error.
.wspFlowJo 10 Workspace
The workspace's samples, compensation matrices, transforms and gating tree open in a Cytometry window, with its FCS files found where the workspace says (see The Cytometry Window). It opens there even with the Flow Cytometry toolkit hidden, since a workspace has no table form.
.gctGCT Expression Matrix (Broad Institute)
Gene Cluster Text, versions 1.2 and 1.3. Opens as a heatmap with row and sample names (version 1.3's row and column fields aren't shown). The file must have as many rows and samples as its header declares. For sample class labels, open its .cls file with it (the CLS Class Labels entry, above).
.txtGEO Series Matrix (NCBI)
A GEO series matrix file (…_series_matrix.txt) is recognized by its content and opens as a heatmap, with the samples named by their titles. GEO serves it compressed (.txt.gz): decompress it first.
.loomLoom
A single-cell expression matrix. Opens as a heatmap, genes as rows and cells as columns. For a sparse matrix, check Hide all-zero rows and Hide all-zero columns in the Plot Style panel.

Heatmap size limits

  • A heatmap is built from at most 100 million values, and a table of more than 3,000 rows asks before it is drawn. A single-cell file of tens of thousands of genes by tens of thousands of cells is over the limit.
  • A 10x matrix over the limit leaves out the genes detected in no cell, then keeps the genes with the most counts, as many as fit, and says how many it left out. A raw matrix (raw_feature_bc_matrix), which holds every barcode, is usually too large even so: open the filtered one.
  • For other files, save a subset first, such as the highly variable genes or a sample of the cells.
  • Loom and h5ad files compressed with gzip (the usual) or LZ4 are read; LZF or Blosc compression isn't.

Plate Readers

A plate reader's export opens as a plate map when @Graph recognizes it by what the file says: a new Plate Map window named after the file, with the Read Values sheet up to choose its reads, or Open as Table Instead (see Plate Maps). Other plate-shaped tables and plater CSV files open as tables; read them into a plate map with Read Values from File….

.txt / .csvGen5 (BioTek, Agilent)
Text and CSV exports, with each well's reads named as Gen5 names them, its layout's well IDs and its kinetic tables.
.xlsxMagellan (Tecan)
Workbooks, each label named by its wavelength, the plate sized by its definition file.
.csvMARS (BMG LABTECH)
Exports, with the test's name and date.
.txtSoftMax Pro Text Export (Molecular Devices)
Each Plate section's endpoint, kinetic and spectrum reads at several wavelengths, and its Group tables' standards and samples as the layout.
.xlsx / .csvSparkControl and i-control (Tecan)
SparkControl's kinetic exports, and i-control's exports by label.

Chemistry and Spectroscopy

.jdx / .dx / .jcampJCAMP-DX
Infrared, UV-visible, Raman, NMR and mass spectra in JCAMP-DX (versions 4.24 and 5.x). Each spectrum opens in a Graph window named by its title, with its X and Y units from the file (cm⁻¹, nm, ppm, m/z and others). Peak tables, and mass spectra stored as X–Y pairs, are drawn as sticks: each peak from zero to its height. A file of several blocks opens each block in a window of its own, and an NMR file's real and imaginary parts each open as one. A data form @Graph doesn't read reports an error naming the form.
.mzMLmzML (Mass Spectrometry)
Mass spectrometry runs in mzML 1.1. The chromatograms (the total ion current and any others) open in a Graph window against retention time in minutes. The spectra open in a window for each MS level (MS1, MS2 and so on), each spectrum a sweep of intensity against m/z, named by its scan number, retention time and precursor m/z; centroid spectra are drawn as sticks. A run larger than the memory budget opens its first spectra, and the Data Log says how many; the chromatograms are read whole. Vendor raw files and mzXML aren't read: convert them to mzML with ProteoWizard's msconvert. To extract ion chromatograms or compare isotope patterns, see Mass Spectrometry.

Astronomy

.fits / .fit / .fts / .fits.gz / .fits.fzFITS
Telescope and survey images, spectra and tables, uncompressed, gzipped (.fits.gz) or tile-compressed as fpack writes them (.fits.fz). A file opens by what it holds: images and cubes in an Image window, one-dimensional spectra in a Graph window, and a file of tables only as a Spreadsheet. See How FITS files are read, below.
folderFITS Frames (Folder or Chosen Files)
A folder of FITS files (with no TIFF beside them), or several FITS files chosen or dropped together, opens as one time series, a frame per file (its first image). Frames are sorted by when they were taken (DATE-OBS, else MJD-OBS, else JD). The time axis is each frame's own time in seconds from the first, mid-exposure when every frame gives its exposure, else the start. If a frame gives no time, the series is in file-name order and the time axis counts frames. Frames must have the same size, Z and channels and no time axis of their own: the others are left out and named in the Data Log. Each frame keeps its own header, saved with the image; the sky coordinates and pixel scale shown are the first frame's.

How FITS files are read

  • Images show x across and y up, as ds9 and ImageJ show FITS. A third or fourth axis opens as Z slices, as time points when its type is TIME, or as channels when it is STOKES. A file of several images asks which to open.
  • Pixel values are the physical ones (BZERO and BSCALE applied), with BLANK and NaN pixels missing.
  • A sky image's pixel scale is shown in arcseconds, and its sky coordinates show under the pointer when the header gives a World Coordinate System @Graph reads (see Sky Coordinates and Regions).
  • The image is shown, and measured by ROIs, on 65,536 levels, which hold 8- and 16-bit integer data exactly. Floating-point and wider integer values are also kept at full precision, and Aperture Photometry measures those.
  • Spectra: wavelength (or frequency) on the X axis comes from the file's linear scale, or IRAF's log-linear one.
  • Tables: binary and ASCII tables, with units after the column names, null values blank, and a column holding several values a row (up to 100) as a column each.
  • Every header card is kept with the image and saved in its .@graph file.
  • Tile compression: Rice, GZIP 1 and 2 and none, with floating-point values quantized or kept exactly (32- or 64-bit). HCOMPRESS and PLIO compression aren't read: uncompress the file with funpack first.

Back to Contents

Workspaces

Data Log & Text Editors

The Data Log is a plain-text window that collects the results of your analyses. You can also type and paste into it, do arithmetic in it, and send any table in it to a Graph, a Chart, a Spreadsheet or Statistics. Text Editor windows work the same way but collect nothing: use them for notes and for tables of your own.

Use the Data Log

  1. Choose View › Show Data Log (⌘L), or Window › Data Log. There is one Data Log, and it keeps collecting while its window is closed.
  2. Run an analysis. Its results are added at the end of the log; nothing is overwritten.
  3. To use a table in the log, select its rows, click the blue Text Tools button and choose an action, such as Chart Selection… (⇧⌘H) or Send to Spreadsheet… (see Text Tools, below).
  4. Choose File › Save (⌘S) to keep the log as a text file.
  • ⌘L hides the Data Log when it is the window in front (the menu item then reads Hide Data Log), and brings it forward otherwise. Window › Data Log is checked while the log is on screen.
  • Paste (⌘V) brings text in as plain text. ⇧⌥⌘V pastes it with its formatting.
  • Wrap Lines (toolbar, or View › Wrap Lines; on by default): notes and messages wrap to the window's width, while each row of a logged table stays on one line with its columns lined up. Scroll sideways to read a wide table. Turn it off to keep every line whole.
  • Edit › Find › Find… (⌘F) searches the text; Find and Replace… is ⌥⌘F.
  • File › Save As… (⇧⌘S) saves the log under a new name, File › Print… (⌘P) prints it, and File › Duplicate (⇧⌘K) copies it into a new Text Editor window.
  • ⌘= and ⌘− make the text larger or smaller, and ⌘0 returns to the default size set in Settings › General › Data Log (13 pt by default).
  • Clear, in the toolbar, empties the log after asking.
  • When the log grows past about 5 MB, @Graph offers Save and Clear…; the log is cleared only after the file is saved. When you quit, @Graph asks about unsaved Data Log text.
  • Drop a supported file onto the Data Log to open it (see Opening Files from the Data Log, below).

What Is Logged

  • The analysis tools (Measure, Peak Detection, AP Detection, curve fits, synapse detection and the rest) write their results to the Data Log as they run, in order.
  • The Statistics window adds its result when you click Send to Data Log.
  • The log also gets short notes, such as how a pasted table was read, or how many formulas came in from an Excel or Numbers file.
  • Show Sweep Names (toolbar; off by default): result tables include a Sweep column only when the measured sweeps aren't an evenly spaced run (such as sweeps 1, 2, 5). For a run such as 1–10, or every 2nd sweep, the column is left out. Turn the button on to always include it.
  • Settings › General › Data Log has "Timestamp each log entry" (off by default), which adds the time to each entry; "Include filename header on file open" (on), which adds a line with the file's name and sweep count; and "Log routine file and window activity" (on), which records files opened, saved or exported and similar activity. Analysis results and errors are always logged.

Text Editors

  • File › New Text Editor (⇧⌘N) opens a separate text window, a new one each time, with the same Text Tools, Find, text size keys and Math Evaluator as the Data Log.
  • Every line holding a tab is a table row: it stays on one line with its columns lined up, whether it was typed, pasted or opened from a file. Other lines wrap to the window's width.
  • View › Wrap Lines (on by default) is each Text Editor's own: turn it off to keep every line whole. A new Text Editor starts with the last choice made.
  • Save (⌘S) saves the text as a plain-text file. A Text Editor opened from a .txt file writes back to that file. Text from an .rtf file is saved as a new file, so the original keeps its formatting.

To keep separate notes for separate experiments, open a Text Editor for each with File › New Text Editor (⇧⌘N).

Text Tools

The blue Text Tools button, in the Data Log and in every Text Editor, acts on the selected text. The first seven items open the selection in a new window; the last four work on the text itself.

ItemWhat it does
Graph Selected Text… (⇧⌘G)Opens the selection as a graph of traces or X-Y data (see Graph Pasted Data, below).
Chart Selection… (⇧⌘H)Opens the selected table as a new chart. Its columns can be separated by tabs, commas or semicolons.
Send to Spreadsheet…Opens the selected table in a new Spreadsheet window, its first row as a header row when it names the columns. Rows are split at tabs, or else at commas or semicolons, and blank lines are left out.
Omics PlotA submenu: Volcano Plot (⌥⌘L), Heatmap (⌥⌘M), Dot Plot, Cluster Scatter, GSEA Bar, Grouped Diverging Bar, Venn Diagram, UpSet Plot and Manhattan Plot, each "from Selected Text…", and Compute GSEA (Permutation)…. See Omics Visualization for what each needs.
Kaplan-Meier Curve from Selected Text…Builds a survival curve from a selected Time, Status and Group table (see Charts).
Smart Visualization… (⇧⌘V)Chooses the window that suits the data (see Smart Visualization, below).
Statistics… (⌘T)Opens the Statistics window on the selection, without making a chart.
Convert Lists / Table (⇧⌘L)Turns a tab-delimited table into lists separated by blank lines, or lists into a table. The direction is taken from the selection.
Transpose Table (⇧⌘X)Swaps the rows and columns of the selected table. The table must be rectangular; a short row is reported by number.
Reverse List Order (⇧⌘R)Reverses each selected list, or the row order of a selected table.
List Stats (⇧⌘T)Adds the mean, SD, SEM and count of each column of a selected table, or of each list of numbers, just below the selection. Decimal commas (1,5) are read, and NA or other text cells are left out.
  • ⇧⌘X transposes only while text is selected in a text window; elsewhere it opens a graph's Data Transform panel. ⌃⇧X always transposes.
  • Graph Selected Text…, Chart Selection…, the Omics Plot items and Kaplan-Meier Curve from Selected Text… are also on the File menu.

Smart Visualization

Smart Visualization… (⇧⌘V) weighs the selection's shape, values and headers and opens it as a Graph, a Chart, a Scatter (X,Y) chart, a Kaplan-Meier curve or one of the omics plots. When the evidence doesn't clearly favor one, it asks "What Kind of Data Is This?", names its best guesses and offers a menu of every destination with the best guess chosen, so Return opens it.

SelectionOpens as
A recording, or one column of samples that follow on from one anotherGraph
One column of separate measurementsChart of their spread
Two measures on different scales (height and weight)Scatter (X,Y)
Two groups on one scaleChart
A time and status table with such headings (Time, Event, Group)Kaplan-Meier curve
Long-form data with two factors and replicates (Site, Treatment, Response)Grouped Chart
A long table with a group column, a value column and a column naming where each row came from (Subject, Batch, Site…)Chart read One Row per Value

For the last kind, the chart's Statistics tab suggests the source column under Values from the same, and applies it only when you choose. The omics plots, Scatter, Manhattan and Kaplan-Meier read tables separated by tabs, commas or semicolons.

Graph Pasted Data

  1. Type or paste numbers into the Data Log or a Text Editor, with columns separated by tabs, commas, semicolons or spaces.
  2. Select the numbers, with their column titles if they have them.
  3. Choose Text Tools › Graph Selected Text… (⇧⌘G).
  4. In the Graph Data window, read the Preview. It names the delimiter, decimal mark and title row found, shows the first rows of values as read, and follows every change you make.
  5. If the preview is wrong, change Delimiter, Header Row or X-axis Data (below).
  6. Click Graph Data. The graph opens in a new window, and the Data Log records how the text was read.
SettingWhat it does
DelimiterAuto-detect (the default), Tab, Comma, Semicolon, Space, or Other with a character you type.
First row has column titlesStarts as the text suggests. Checked, the first row is read as titles even when it holds numbers (concentrations or wavelengths, say); unchecked, no row is. Units are taken from titles such as "Voltage (mV)".
Mode: Automatic (a time column if there is one)The default. Column 1 is the time axis when its title has a time unit, such as "Time (ms)", and its values are evenly spaced. Otherwise every column is Y, spaced by X sample interval.
Mode: Y columns only (use X interval)Every column is Y. Enter the time between samples in X sample interval, with its unit (such as 0.05 ms or 50 µs); the sample rate is worked out from it.
Mode: Y vs X column, or X,Y column pairs (X₁,Y₁,X₂,Y₂,…)One column, chosen by number, is X for all the others; or columns pair up left to right, each pair a series with its own X values.
  • Columns in different units ("Vm (mV)" and "Im (pA)") become separate channels, each with its own unit, in the order they come.
  • A label column, headed Group, Set, Batch, Block, Cohort or Replicate and holding a few whole numbers that repeat down the rows, isn't plotted as data. It becomes a group of its own that starts hidden; show it from the Grouping panel.
  • A row of missing values (NaN, NA or empty cells) keeps its place in time.
  • The preview says when a column or row is set aside: the untitled column of row numbers that R's write.table and write.csv add, or a row whose X cell is text, such as "Vehicle", which has no place on the X axis until you enter a number there.
  • Values copied as a spreadsheet shows them are read as numbers: "45%" is 0.45, and "$1,234.50" or "1 234,5" is 1234.5. Error values such as #N/A and #DIV/0! are missing values.
  • A cell marked with a limit, such as <0.5 or >29, says only that its value lies past that limit. Every analysis treats it as missing, and the data checks, the result and the figure legend say how many there are. Only the mixed model for profiles can fit it instead (Fit values past a limit).

To enter data in a grid instead, choose File › New Spreadsheet (⌥⌘N), paste the table into it, then click Data to Graph… or Data to Chart.

Math Evaluator

The Data Log and Text Editors work as a calculator.

  1. Type an expression followed by = (such as 88*3= or "The total is 37*81="). The result appears in blue after the =, and you can keep typing on the same line.
  2. Or type an expression on a line of its own, such as sqrt(144), and press Enter on the numeric keypad. The result appears in blue on the next line. Return just starts a new line.
  • Operators: + − * / % (remainder) and ^ (power), with parentheses. You can paste the signs × · ÷ and −. Use a period for decimals, and write every multiplication: 2*x, not 2x.
  • Functions: sqrt, cbrt, abs, exp, exp2, expm1 (eˣ − 1); ln and log (both the natural log), log10, log2, log1p (ln(1 + x)); sin, cos, tan, asin, acos, atan, sinh, cosh, tanh, asinh, acosh, atanh, with angles in radians; erf, erfc, gamma, lgamma; floor, ceil, round, trunc, sign; and with two values atan2, pow, hypot, min, max, mod and fmod.
  • Constants: pi (or π), tau (2π) and e, written in lowercase.
  • Results: whole numbers below 10^15 show in full; other results show 13 significant digits.
  • Order and rounding: ^ groups from the right (2^3^2 is 512) and binds tighter than a leading minus (−2^2 is −4), where Excel gives 64 and 4. % and mod give the remainder with the sign of the divisor (−7 % 3 is 2); fmod keeps the sign of the first value. round takes halves away from zero (2.5 gives 3).
  • A lone number or a date (2024-05-01) gets no result, so you can type a column of numbers on the keypad. If no result appears, start the expression at the beginning of the line or after words, as in "Total: 37*81=".
  • Formula fits use the same operators and functions (see Measuring & Analysis › Curve Fitting).

Opening Files from the Data Log

Drag a supported file onto the Data Log window to open it. A drop, File › Open File… (⌘O) and the New Data Importer window (⌘N) accept the same files. Supported File Formats lists them, with what is read from each.

FileOpens as
Recordings (such as .abf, .dat, .nwb or .edf)A new Graph. Spike-event files open as a raster of spike trains.
Images, and folders of imagesAn Image Window.
Omics matrices (.gct, a GEO series matrix .txt, .loom, .h5ad)A Heatmap window, with row and column names filled in.
Workbooks and data tables (.xlsx, .xls, .numbers, .csv, .tsv, .dta, .pzfx, .prism, .npy, .npz and others)A Spreadsheet window for each table. A file with several sheets or tables asks which to open (below).
Flow cytometry files (.fcs)A Cytometry window, while the Flow Cytometry toolkit is shown (see The Cytometry Window).
Text files (.txt, .text, .rtf)A Text Editor window named after the file, with an RTF file's formatting removed. A text file over 20 MB asks before it opens.
@Graph documents (.@graph)The kind of window they were saved from: Graph, Chart, Spreadsheet or Image.
  • Opening a file that's already open brings its window forward.
  • With Settings › General › Open files set to "Open as tabs (same window)", each kind of window tabs with its own kind: a recording opened over an image opens as a window of its own.
  • Workbooks bring in cells and formulas (see Spreadsheets › Formulas), not embedded charts or images.
  • Files dropped onto the Dock icon or any other @Graph window open the same way, except onto an empty spreadsheet, which loads a dropped table or recording into its own cells.

Choosing sheets and tables

When a workbook or Prism file holds several sheets or tables, @Graph lists them with a checkbox each, with the table's size and kind when the file states them. The first is checked, so Return opens it right away.

  1. Check the ones you want, or click Select All (⌘A). Select All shows a dash when only some are checked; clicking it then checks them all.
  2. Click Open. Its title counts them, such as Open 3 Sheets. One opens as its own Spreadsheet window; several open as tabs of one window, in the file's order.
