  • Space checks or unchecks the highlighted row (move with the arrow keys), Return opens, and Escape cancels.
  • Double-click a row to open just that one.
  • Opening many shows a small progress panel; Stop keeps the ones already open. Any that can't be opened (an empty sheet, say) are listed together at the end.

How omics files are labeled

  • .gct: open it together with its .cls file for sample classes. When the Name column holds database IDs and the Description column, or a version 1.3 symbol field, holds gene symbols, rows are labeled with the symbols; a symbol shared by several probes is shown as "symbol (ID)".
  • GEO series matrix: columns are named by sample title. An RNA-seq series matrix holds no expression values; @Graph says so and names the supplementary files the series lists, so you can download the counts table and open it.
  • .h5ad: when the file holds several matrices, @Graph asks which to open: X, the main matrix (the default); raw/X, which often has every gene; or a layer such as layers/counts, usually raw counts. Gene names come from a gene-symbol column when the file has one, otherwise from the gene index. A note after opening says which matrix and which name column were used.
  • .loom: gene names come from the Gene row attribute, or Accession when there is no Gene.

Back to Contents

Spreadsheets

A spreadsheet holds a table of cells that you type, paste or open from a file, and sends it to a Graph, a Chart or Statistics. @Graph has three: the New Spreadsheet window, which stands on its own; the Graph Spreadsheet, which edits a graph's data; and the Chart Spreadsheet, which edits a chart's data.

New Spreadsheet

  1. Choose File › New Spreadsheet (⌥⌘N), or click New Spreadsheet in the Welcome window. A blank 20 × 20 grid opens, titled Spreadsheet 1, Spreadsheet 2 and so on until you save it.
  2. Type your data, paste it with ⌘V, or drop a data file onto the empty grid. Put column titles in row 1 and row labels in column A: both start out marked as headers.
  3. To use only part of the table, select a block of more than one cell.
  4. Click Data to Graph… for traces or X-Y data, Data to Chart for groups, or Data Statistics.

Edit cells

  • Double-click a cell to edit it, or select it and start typing to replace its contents. Return commits and moves down; Tab commits and moves right. Option-Return starts a new line in the cell.
  • Shift-click or drag to select a block of cells; Command-click adds or removes one cell. Click a column header or row number to select the whole column or row; Shift-click adds more, and Command-click a row number adds or removes that row.
  • Delete clears the selected cells. Copy (⌘C) copies them as tab-separated text, or the whole table when nothing is selected.
  • Paste (⌘V) pastes at the selected cell, or at A1 when nothing is selected, and the grid grows to fit. Tab-separated text keeps its columns. Text without tabs is split at semicolons or commas when its lines have them, so put tabs or semicolons between columns of decimal-comma numbers.
  • Fill: point at a cell that holds something and drag one of the dots on its edges to copy it into the cells you drag over. Edit › Fill Down (⌘D) copies the top row of a selected block into the rest of it, and Fill Right (⌘R) its left column. Formulas move their references ($ parts stay fixed); values are copied as they are, without continuing a series.
  • Transpose Table swaps rows and columns. Clear All empties the sheet, back to a blank 20 × 20 grid.
  • Undo (⌘Z) and Redo (⇧⌘Z) step through up to 50 changes (fewer for a very large sheet). While you are typing in a cell, ⌘Z undoes the typing first.

Rows, columns and sorting

  • Point at a column header or row number and click the arrow that appears. The menu has Insert Column Before, Insert Column After and Delete Column, or Insert Row Above, Insert Row Below and Delete Row.
  • With several rows or columns selected, the menu reads Delete Selected Rows or Delete Selected Columns, and the Insert items add that many at once, such as Insert 3 Columns Before. One Undo brings them all back. Delete is dimmed when it would leave no row or column.
  • Header rows and columns are shaded and bold, and are always the first rows and columns of the sheet. To change them, choose Set as Header Row, Set as Header Column or Remove Header Status from the same menus.
  • Sort (toolbar, or Sort Ascending and Sort Descending in a column's menu) sorts the rows by the selected column. Whole rows move, header rows stay put, numbers come before text, and blanks go last. If a formula reads another row, @Graph asks before sorting, since the formula would then read different cells.
  • Drag the line between two column headers to make the column on its left wider or narrower, or double-click the line to fit the column to its contents. This works in all three spreadsheets.

Open a file in a spreadsheet

  • Drop a text table (.csv, .tsv, .txt, .rtf) onto an empty spreadsheet to load its cells as they are, text columns included. The first row becomes a header when it names the columns.
  • Drop a recording onto an empty spreadsheet to load one column per sweep, beside a Time column. The sheet holds up to 5 million cells; @Graph says when a recording has more rows than it shows.
  • Workbooks and statistics files (.xlsx, .xls, .numbers, .prism, .pzfx, .dta) ask which tables you want and open them in a new window. Other files, and any file dropped onto a spreadsheet that already has data, open in their own windows (see Supported File Formats).

Make a graph or chart, or run statistics

  • Data to Graph… opens the Graph Data window for the table. Check its preview, then click Graph Data (see Data Log & Text Editors › Graph Pasted Data).
  • Data to Chart opens a chart window named after the spreadsheet, such as Spreadsheet 1 Chart. A column title typed over several lines keeps its lines: the chart stacks them under the bar.
  • Omics Plot is a menu: Volcano Plot, Heatmap, Dot Plot, Cluster Scatter, GSEA Bar, Grouped Diverging Bar, Venn Diagram, UpSet Plot and Manhattan Plot, each built from the table (see Omics Visualization for the columns each needs). Compute GSEA (Permutation)… opens its own setup window and doesn't read the table.
  • Kaplan-Meier builds a survival curve from columns in this order, under a row of column titles: Time, Status (1 = event, 0 = censored), and optionally Group and Stratum (see Charts).
  • Data Statistics opens the Statistics window with the table. @Graph detects whether groups are in rows or columns and asks if unsure.
  • All of these use the selection when it is a block of more than one cell, and the whole sheet otherwise. Header rows and columns are always included, so the data keeps its labels. Right-click the selection for Chart Selected Cells, Statistics on Selected Cells and Graph Selected Cells.
  • A chart or Statistics window made from the sheet follows the sheet as you edit it. One made from a selection keeps reading the same range of cells, by position: after inserting or deleting rows or columns, make it again.

Column titles in row 1 such as "Voltage (mV)" and "Current (pA)" give the channel names and units when you use Data to Graph…. Leave row 1 blank if your data has no titles.

Save and export

  • Save (⌘S) saves the spreadsheet as a .@graph file, with its header rows and columns, formulas and number formats. Save As… (⇧⌘S) chooses a new name or location. The file reopens as a spreadsheet window.
  • The Export menu, beside Data Statistics, has Copy as PDF and Send to Keynote…, which draw the sheet or the selection as a table with bold headers and grid lines. Both are also on the right-click menu. They warn first when the table has more than 60 rows or 15 columns, since its text would be too small to read on a slide.
  • Export Data… in the same menu (also File › Export…, ⇧⌘E) writes the sheet or the selection as CSV, TSV or Excel (.xlsx). The Excel file keeps numbers as numbers, with the header row in bold and kept in view. Values are exported, not formulas.
  • With Numbers installed, check Open in Numbers after exporting to open the exported file there too, or click Open in Numbers to open the table there without saving a file.

Graph Spreadsheet

Click the spreadsheet button in a graph window's toolbar to see and edit the graph's data as a table. The first column is time, and each other column is one sweep. There is one table for each graph: clicking the button again brings it back, and it closes with the graph.

  • Edits change the graph's data directly. ⌘S saves the graph, and ⌘Z here and in the graph window undo the same changes.
  • With several channels, pick one with Channel, or turn on Show all channels. Channels recorded at different sample rates then each get a Time column of their own, titled with the rate ("Time (s), 1000 Hz"), followed by the sweeps recorded at that rate.
  • A graph of X-Y data whose sweeps have X values of their own (X,Y column pairs, a fitted curve) shows each sweep after its own X column, as Export › CSV writes it. Sweeps that share their X values share one X column.
  • Double-click a cell to edit it. Return commits and moves to the next row. A decimal comma is read. Text that isn't a number is refused, and the cell keeps its value. An empty cell is a gap in the trace.
  • Click a column header to select the column, or a row number to select the row. Shift-click extends the selection, and Command-click adds or removes one cell. Delete clears the selected cells.
  • Right-click a column header for Copy Column, Paste Into Column (one value per line; a heading on the first line is skipped) and Clear Column. A Time column's header has Copy Time Column.
  • Copy (⌘C) copies the selected cells as tab-separated text, or everything when nothing is selected, with the column headers and each value exactly as stored.
  • For 10,000 cells or more, Copy Options asks first: "Include column headers in first row" and "Round to a fixed number of decimal places". Edit › Copy with Options… shows it for a selection of any size, and later copies use the options chosen last. Copy handles up to 20 million cells.
  • Paste (⌘V) pastes tab-separated text at the selected cell. A single value fills every selected cell. A block larger than the grid adds sweeps (columns) and samples (rows) to fit. @Graph says what a paste left out: cells that aren't numbers are pasted blank, and columns can't be added while one channel of several is shown.
  • A spike-train raster's table has one column of spike times for each train and can't be edited. Copy gives the times in full.

Chart Spreadsheet

Click the spreadsheet button in a chart window's toolbar to edit the chart's data as a grid. Its window is titled "Data:" and the chart's name. The grid has the orientation the data was pasted or typed in: usually each column is one category (group) and each row one replicate. The chart redraws as you edit.

  • Edit cells, fill, sort, and insert or delete rows and columns as in a New Spreadsheet window (above). The toolbar's Column Actions button opens the selected cell's column menu, which here also has Rename Column….
  • Double-click a column header to rename it. Option-Return starts a new line, which the chart stacks under the bar.
  • The Paste button replaces the whole table with the copied data, growing the grid to fit. For more than one row, @Graph first asks whether the first copied row holds column titles: Use as Titles or Paste All as Data. ⌘V pastes into the selected cells instead.
  • The Copy button copies the whole table as tab-separated text. ⌘C copies the selected cells.
  • Undo (⌘Z) and Redo (⇧⌘Z) step through up to 50 changes.
  • Export… (also File › Export…, ⇧⌘E) writes the table as CSV, TSV or Excel, as for a New Spreadsheet.
  • A chart's table holds values only: no formulas and no number formats.

How the table is read

  • Transpose swaps rows and columns in this table view only. The chart's data doesn't change.
  • Columns Are Conditions, for a label column followed by several number columns. Off (the default): each row is a group and its numbers are replicate values. On: each column is a condition and each row is one subject (repeated measures). When the column titles look like condition names, @Graph asks once when the chart first opens and remembers your answer for that chart.
  • Each Column Is a Category, for all-number data with no row of column names. On: each column is its own group. Off: the first column labels each row, and the other columns are that row's replicate values.
  • Both switches rebuild the chart from the data as first pasted.
  • A first column that numbers the rows (1, 2, 3…) under a name such as Subject or ID is read as a label column, never as a group.
  • Charts whose data isn't a table of groups (Volcano, Dot Plot, Cluster Scatter, GSEA Bar, Grouped Diverging Bar, Stacked Bar, Kaplan-Meier, Manhattan and Scatter) show neither Transpose nor the two switches. Heatmap and PCA Plot show a simpler matrix table.
  • A Volcano Plot's rows are tied to its points, so its table has no Sort, and its rows and columns can't be added, deleted or renamed. Only the names in its first column can be edited: type them, or paste with ⌘V.
  • In a Dot Plot, Cluster Scatter, GSEA Bar, Grouped Diverging Bar, Stacked Bar, Kaplan-Meier or Manhattan table, the columns are the chart's fields, so they can't be inserted, deleted or renamed.

Formulas

Formulas work in New Spreadsheet windows. To compute a new column from the others:

  1. Click the first empty cell beside your data, in the first row of values.
  2. Type = and the formula, such as =B2*1000 or =AVERAGE(B2:D2), and press Return. The cell shows the result.
  3. Select that cell and the cells below it, then choose Edit › Fill Down (⌘D), or drag the cell's bottom dot down. Each row's formula reads its own row.
  • A formula starts with =, as in Excel or Numbers: =SUM(B2:B20), =AVERAGE(B:B), =B2/$B$1, =IF(C2>0,"up","down"). The cell updates when the cells it uses change. Double-click it to edit the formula.
  • Use $ to keep a row or column fixed when the formula is copied or filled. Copy and Paste move references as Excel does, and inserting or deleting rows and columns keeps them pointing at the same cells. A reference to a deleted cell shows #REF!.
  • Charts, Statistics and exports use the results, and a cell showing an error counts as missing. Formulas are saved with the spreadsheet.
  • Text starting with = in an opened text file stays text. To type text that starts with =, begin with an apostrophe ('=).
  • Formulas in Excel (.xlsx, .xls) and Numbers (.numbers) files come in as live formulas when @Graph gets the same result the file saved. Otherwise the cell keeps its saved value. So does a formula that uses a function @Graph doesn't have (such as VLOOKUP, NOW or RAND), refers to another sheet or table, uses a named range, or is an array formula. Window › Data Log lists how many formulas came in live and how many as values, and why.

Functions

Operators: + − * / and ^ (power); % after a number is a percent (50% is 0.5) and between two values the remainder; & joins text; = <> < > <= >= compare. A range is written B2:B20, or B:B for a whole column. Where a range goes, a list of numbers can be typed in braces instead: {2,3,4} is a row and {2;3;4} a column. SUM, AVERAGE and the other summary functions skip blank and text cells in a range, and an error cell makes their result that error; COUNT skips errors too.

  • Totals and averages: SUM, PRODUCT, AVERAGE, MEDIAN, MIN and MAX. MIN and MAX of no numbers are 0, as in Excel.
  • Counting: COUNT (cells holding numbers), COUNTA (cells that aren't empty) and COUNTBLANK(range) (empty cells).
  • Spread: STDEV or STDEV.S and VAR or VAR.S for a sample (n − 1); STDEV.P or STDEVP and VAR.P or VARP for a whole population (n); SEM, the standard error of the mean (SD / √n).
  • Lines and correlation: SLOPE(y range, x range) and INTERCEPT(y range, x range) of the least-squares line, RSQ (r²) and CORREL or PEARSON (Pearson's r). The two ranges must be the same size, or the result is #N/A. Cells are paired by position, and a pair is left out when either cell is blank or text, as in Excel. The x values can be typed as a list: with nine time points in columns C to K, =SLOPE(C2:K2,{1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9}) is row 2's change per time point, and the list stays the same when the formula is filled down. For unevenly spaced times, type the times themselves, such as {0,5,15,30,60}.
  • Rounding: ROUND(x, digits); ROUNDUP and ROUNDDOWN (away from and toward zero); TRUNC(x, digits); INT (down to a whole number); CEIL(x) (up to a whole number); CEILING(x, step) and FLOOR(x, step) (up or down to a multiple of step, 1 if left out).
  • Arithmetic: ABS, SIGN, SQRT, CBRT (cube root), POWER(x, y) or POW, HYPOT(x, y) (√(x² + y²)), MOD(x, y) (the remainder, with the sign of y, as in Excel) and FMOD(x, y) (the remainder with the sign of x).
  • Exponentials and logarithms: EXP, EXP2 (2 to the x), EXPM1 (eˣ − 1, accurate for small x), LN, LOG(x) (base 10) or LOG(x, base), LOG10, LOG2 and LOG1P (ln(1 + x), accurate for small x).
  • Trigonometry, in radians: SIN, COS, TAN, ASIN, ACOS, ATAN, ATAN2(x, y) (the angle of the point (x, y), in Excel's order), SINH, COSH, TANH, ASINH, ACOSH, ATANH and PI().
  • Special functions: ERF(x), or ERF(lower, upper) for the integral between two limits; ERFC; GAMMA or TGAMMA; LGAMMA or GAMMALN (the log of the gamma function).
  • Logic: IF(test, then, else), AND, OR, NOT, TRUE(), FALSE() and IFERROR(value, value if error).
  • Checks: ISBLANK, ISNUMBER, ISTEXT and ISERROR, each TRUE or FALSE; NA() gives #N/A, to mark a value as missing.

Number Formats

Numbers keep the format their file gives them: a cell Excel shows as 2.6%, 290,000, 1.50 or $1,234.50 shows the same here, and so does its editor, with your Mac's decimal and grouping marks. A format changes only how the number looks. The cell holds the value the file stored (0.025974… for 2.6%), and formulas, sorting, Copy and Data to Graph… use that value.

  • Data to Chart and Data Statistics read a percent cell as the percentage it shows (2.6 for 2.6%). On the chart, Show percentages as (Chart tab) switches between 45% and 0.45.
  • Type or paste a percentage, such as 3% or 12.5%, and the cell holds 0.03 or 0.125 and shows 3% or 12.5%.
  • Edit a formatted cell as it's shown, with or without its unit or parentheses: 1.6 mV, (1,240). Left unchanged, it keeps every digit; 5 typed into a percent cell is 5%. Text that isn't a number, typed over a number, is refused: the cell keeps its value, and a line in the window says why; NA and limits such as <0.5 are entered as typed. To enter other text, start it with an apostrophe ('). Entering text, or clearing the cell, removes its format.
  • Formats move with their cells when you insert or delete rows and columns, sort or transpose. Copy and Paste between spreadsheets, and Fill, carry them too, and Undo restores them. Header rows and columns show their text.
  • Formats are saved with the spreadsheet, and an export to Excel (and Open in Numbers) keeps them, so the workbook looks the same in Excel. CSV and TSV exports hold the plain values. A sheet whose numbers have decimal commas is exported as CSV with semicolons between the cells, as Excel writes CSV in those regions.
  • Print, Copy as PDF and Send to Keynote… show the cells as they look.
  • Formats are read from Excel (.xlsx, .xls) and Numbers (.numbers) files: fixed decimals, thousands separators, percentages, scientific notation, currency and other text before or after the number, and separate formats for negative numbers and zero. Dates come in as dates, and any other format (fractions, for example) shows the plain value.

Back to Contents

Charts

A chart draws a table of values as a figure, with the data points, error bars and, from its Statistics tab, statistics. Brackets, the Estimation Plot and the mixed model for profiles are on the Statistics on a Chart page, and the omics chart types on the Omics Visualization page.

Make a Chart

  1. Put the data in a Spreadsheet window (File › New Spreadsheet, ⌥⌘N): usually one column per category and one row per replicate, with the column names in the first row.
  2. Click Data to Chart in its toolbar. Or select a table in the Data Log or a Text Editor window and choose Chart Selection… (⇧⌘H) from the Text Tools or File menu.
  3. If the table can be read in more than one way, a "How Should This Table Be Read?" dialog asks.
  4. A Chart window opens, usually as Bar / Dot. To change the type, click another under Chart Type in the inspector's Chart tab.
  5. Style the chart in the Chart tab's Plot Style, Axes & Labels and Range panels (see Chart Settings), and add statistics on the Statistics tab.
  • A first column of row numbers or labels (such as Cell, Subject or ID) labels the rows and is not charted. A chart holds up to 2,000 data points.
  • A chart made from a spreadsheet follows the sheet as you edit it (see Spreadsheets); one made from text keeps its own copy of the data.
  • File › Duplicate (⇧⌘K) opens an unsaved copy of the front chart. The Statistics window's Make Chart, the AI Assistant and Text Tools › Smart Visualization… (⇧⌘V) also open charts.

Double-click the chart's title, an axis title or a category label to edit it, and an axis's tick values to set its range. Click a data point to see its value.

Chart Types

Chart Type, in the Chart tab, lists the types under Basic, Statistical and Omics Visualization; click a heading to show its types. A type that can't show the chart's data is grayed out; point at it to see what it needs. Switching type keeps the data.

TypeWhat it shows
Bar / DotEach category's values as points over a bar or mean marker, with an error bar. It can also draw violins (Plot Style › Mean / Bar › Display).
Horizontal BarBar / Dot on its side, for ranked comparisons or long category names.
LineEach series' mean at each category, joined by a line, with error bars.
Scatter (X,Y)Points on two numeric axes, each series with its own X values. Needs at least two number columns.
PieEach category (or each series, when there are several) as a wedge. Negative values are left out, and the inspector says how many.
Estimation PlotThe data beside the differences between groups and their CIs (see Statistics on a Chart).
Box PlotEach category's median, quartiles, whiskers and outliers.
Kaplan-Meier CurveOne survival curve per group, from its own table of times and events. Grayed out for an ordinary chart.
Ridge PlotEach category's distribution as a density curve, stacked down the chart.
Omics typesVolcano Plot, Heatmap and the others, built by the File › Omics Plot commands (see Omics Visualization).

Data Layouts

Data Layout, under Chart Type, sets how the table's columns and rows become categories and series. Most tables never need it changed.

Change the Data Layout

  1. In the Chart tab's Data Layout box, choose a layout from the menu. The table is read again at once.
  2. If your groups run down the rows instead of across the columns, check Switch Row/Column.
  3. If the layout can't read the table, a note under the menu says why.
  • Auto (detect from data), the default, lets @Graph work out the layout.
  • One Category (All Values Are Replicates), Each Column Is Its Own Category (its rows are replicates) and Each Column Is Its Own Series (Grouped Bars), where each row is a category.
  • Scatter Plot (X,Y Column Pairs) and Scatter Plot (First Column Is X): see Make a Scatter (X,Y) Chart.
  • One Row per Value (Group Column and Value Column) and Nested (Subcolumns under Each Category): see below.

Long and Nested Tables

When a table looks like one row per value or like a nested table, the Data Layout box offers Read as One Row per Value or Read as Nested; nothing changes until you click it. With either layout, the Chart Data window shows and edits the table as typed.

  • One Row per Value: a column naming each row's group (Control, Treated; or codes 1, 2) and a column of values. Choose them with Groups and Values, under the menu. Other columns, such as the batch, plot or classroom each row came from, stay in the table.
  • Nested: a heading row of categories, each name over its subcolumns (the cells after it left blank), an optional second heading row titling each subcolumn (Batch 1, Batch 2…), then the values. Each category's values are its subcolumns' values together, and Values from the same (Statistics tab) is set to the subcolumns; a title used under two categories is the same source. A table with a heading over every column can't be read as Nested, and the box says so.
  • Where each row came from: when a column's labels repeat beside 2 or more columns of measurements (a Batch column beside one column per treatment), Data Layout asks what the column is: Data (a category of its own) or Names (each row its own category), as it was read, or Where each row came from. The last leaves the column out of the chart and sets Values from the same to it. With Paired / Repeated on, each row also becomes a second level, so the brackets fit (1 | source/row).

Statistics on a Chart › Values from the Same (Clustered Data) says what this does to the statistics.

Means with Error Values

A table of means can carry its own error values, drawn as given: a label column, then each value column followed by its error column and, if you like, an n column, as in "Group | Mean | SD | N" or "Day | Control | Control SEM | Drug | Drug SEM". The error column's header says what the errors are:

HeaderRead as
SEM or SESEM.
SDSD.
CI or 95% CIA confidence interval's half-width. The Chart Legend states the level the header names (99% CI, CI90), whatever the level in Settings, or says that none was stated.
Error or ±Drawn as supplied; the Chart Legend says their type wasn't stated.
N or nEach mean's count.

Two value columns whose headers name no error, such as "Subject | Pre | Post", are read as each row's values, and @Graph asks how the table should be read. The Chart Data window and CSV export include the error columns.

How Numbers Are Read

  • Numbers may use a decimal point or a decimal comma. The convention is read from the table's own number cells, not from the Mac's region setting, and a semicolon-separated table is split at its semicolons.
  • A sheet opened from an Excel, Numbers, Stata or Prism file is read with a decimal point, as those files store numbers: "12.345" there is twelve point three four five, never twelve thousand.
  • "$1,234.50" is read as 1234.5, and "45%" as a percentage (see Range).
  • A blank or non-numeric cell (such as NA, N/A, NaN, NULL, None, ".", "-", "--" or a spreadsheet error such as #N/A or #DIV/0!, in any capitalization) is a missing value that keeps its row, so each row stays one subject in a paired design.

Repeated Measures by Group

For subjects in 2 or more groups, each measured at several conditions. The table has one row per subject, a column of groups (codes 0, 1, 2…, or labels that repeat, such as Control and Treated) and one column per condition. The chart puts the conditions across, with each group's mean ± error bars joined in its own color and each subject's line faint behind them. Its brackets come from a linear mixed model (see Statistics on a Chart › Repeated Measures by Group).

  1. Chart the table, then find the Repeated Measures by Group box. When the group column comes first or is named like a grouping (Group, Treatment), the box is under Data Layout and at the top of the Statistics tab, with a note; otherwise it is in Plot Style.
  2. Choose the Group column and, if several subjects come from one source (a batch, plot or site), the column naming it under Values from the same.
  3. Click Make Repeated Measures Chart.
  4. To go back, choose Edit › Undo, or click Back to One Column per Category in Plot Style › Subjects and Means; that box is shown while the chart type is Bar / Dot, so on another chart type set it to Bar / Dot first. Until then the Data Layout box offers no other layout.

A Statistics window set to the Split-plot or Mixed model design makes the same chart with Make Chart.

Work with a Chart

Edit the Data in the Chart Data Window

  1. Click the spreadsheet icon in the chart's toolbar. The Chart Data window opens, titled "Data:" and the chart's name; it closes with the chart.
  2. Edit the cells as in a Spreadsheet window: Undo, Sort, Copy, Paste, Fill and Export… work the same way. The chart, its brackets and a linked Statistics window follow each edit, and ⌘S saves the chart.
  3. If the chart came out the wrong way round, click Columns Are Conditions (each column a condition, each row one subject) or Each Column Is a Category (for numbers with no header row). Transpose changes this window's view only.
  • Undo here undoes only the table's edits. In the chart window, ⌘Z takes back changes to the chart's settings and leaves alone a data edit made since.
  • When an edit leaves rows out of the chart, a note in the window says how many and why. When the table can no longer be read as a chart, the chart keeps the data from before.
  • A Kaplan-Meier table's columns are its fields (Time, Status, Group, Stratum), so they can't be inserted, deleted or renamed. To add a Stratum column, paste the whole table with the Paste button.

Make a Scatter (X,Y) Chart

Use a scatter when series were measured at different X values, such as two calibration curves sampled at different concentrations.

  1. Arrange the data as X,Y column pairs (column 1 is the X for column 2, column 3 the X for column 4, and so on), or with the X values in the first column and one Y column per series.
  2. Chart the table. If it doesn't open as a scatter, click Scatter (X,Y) under Chart Type, or set Data Layout to Scatter Plot (X,Y Column Pairs) or Scatter Plot (First Column Is X).
  3. In Plot Style › Scatter (X,Y), set the points' Size and Opacity and each series' color, and check Connect Points to join each series' points.
  4. To fit a line to a series, see Fit a Regression Line, below.
  • X,Y column pairs: each series is named after its Y column's header, and the X axis after the first X column's. Pairs may differ in length, and a leftover unpaired column is dropped.
  • First column is X: a table whose first column plainly holds an X opens this way by itself, with Connect Points on.
  • A first column plainly holds an X when the table has a header row, the column's values increase down the rows, and it is named like an X (time, age, day, dose, concentration, voltage) or evenly or geometrically spaced. A column named like an identifier (Subject, ID, Sample) is never taken as X.
  • Connect Points joins the points in table order, not sorted by X, so a loop that doubles back keeps its shape. Curved lines smooths the line; where X values double back the curve can swing past the points, and a note says so.
  • Switch X and Y, in the Data Layout box, swaps the axes and their titles. It removes any fit lines, since a fit of Y on X does not describe X on Y.
  • A chart switched to Scatter (X,Y) and back has its original data.
  • A chart switched to Scatter (X,Y) plots columns that are X,Y pairs as pairs, and otherwise every other column against the first.
  • Graph windows take the same layout: Import Data's "X,Y column pairs" mode builds a Graph whose sweeps have their own X values, and Graph Utilities' Combine and Concatenate keep them.

Fit a Regression Line

On a Scatter (X,Y) chart, the Statistics tab fits a straight line to each series by ordinary least squares, with Pearson correlation. Series are never pooled, and each line is drawn in its series' color.

  1. Open the Statistics tab of a Scatter (X,Y) chart.
  2. Click Linear Regression under a series' name. The line appears dashed, as a preview, with its numbers below.
  3. Click Keep Fit to make the line solid, or Remove to discard it. A kept fit has a Remove Fit button.
  4. To shade a band around the fit lines, check Show band around the fit, then choose the band and its Level.
  5. Click Copy Chart Legend for sentences that state each kept fit.
  • The line spans the range of your X data, never beyond. A line from Connect Points is not a fit.
  • A preview is saved with the chart too, and stays dashed in print and exports. The Chart Legend describes a fit only once it is kept.
  • Reported: the equation, with the slope's CI (t-based); Pearson's r with its CI (Fisher's z-transform); r²; and p, from the two-sided test of slope ≠ 0. The CIs are at the Default confidence level in Settings › Statistics.
  • Values the data can't support show as n/a. p needs at least 3 points; with 2 the line is still drawn. When Y doesn't vary, r, r² and p are n/a. With fewer than 2 points that differ in X there is no fit, and a note replaces the button.
Band and options
  • Show band around the fit (off by default) shades a band around every fit line. Confidence band (mean response), the default, is where the true line lies. Prediction band (new observations) is where a new single point would fall, so it is wider. Level is 95% by default (50 to 99.99%).
  • The band is ŷ ± t·s·√(1/n + (x − x̄)²/Sxx), with 1 more under the root for prediction, and t on n − 2 degrees of freedom. It spans the same X range as the line.
  • Standardized slope (β) adds the beta weight, B × SD(X) / SD(Y), which equals Pearson r.
  • Robust (heteroscedasticity-consistent) SEs replaces the slope's CI and p with sandwich ones (HC3 by default), named in the panel and the Chart Legend. r's CI is unchanged. A confidence band then uses the same robust covariance, ŷ ± t·√(x₀ᵀV̂x₀); a prediction band stays the ordinary one.
  • Residual diagnostics adds a Residual Diagnostics… button to each fit, with the number of rows flagged. It opens the four residual plots and the influence table (Row is the point's number in the series) in a window of their own, which follows the data and has Send to Data Log, Export Table… and Export Plots.
  • The three options are off by default, apply to every fit on the chart and appear, with the band, once a series has a fit. The Other Analyses page describes them, with Simple Linear regression.
  • Open Full Statistics Window sends the X,Y columns to the Statistics window's Correlation and Regression analyses, where you choose one X and one Y.

Make a Kaplan-Meier Chart

  1. Arrange a table with a header row and 2 to 4 columns in this order: Time, Status, Group, Stratum.
  2. In a Spreadsheet window, click Kaplan-Meier in the toolbar. Or select the table in the Data Log or a Text Editor window and choose Kaplan-Meier Curve from Selected Text… from the File or Text Tools menu.
  3. The chart opens with one step curve per group, starting at 100% and dropping at each event. The legend gives each group's n and median survival and, with 2 or more groups, the log-rank test.
  4. Choose what is shown, and the tests, in Plot Style › Kaplan-Meier Curve. To cut the curves at a fixed follow-up time, type a Max under Range › Time Axis Range, such as 60 for five years in months.
ColumnWhat it holds
TimeFollow-up time, 0 or more. Its header becomes the time axis's title.
Status1/0 (1 = event), event/censored, dead (or death)/alive, yes/no or true/false, in any capitalization. A column coded 1 and 2 is read as in R's survival package: 2 = event, 1 = censored.
Group (optional)Each subject's group. Without it, everyone is one group called "All".
Stratum (optional)A stratum, such as a study site, used only by the stratified tests. Blank cells form a stratum of their own.
  • The first row is always the header: if it looks like a subject (a time and a status), the Data Log says it was left out. Rows that can't be read are skipped, and the Data Log says how many.
  • A chart holds up to 5,000 subjects; above that it shows a message instead.

Smart Visualization opens a table as a Kaplan-Meier chart when its header names the time or status column (Time, Months, OS, Event, Status, Censored…) and its second column holds two status codes.

Make a Ridge Plot

  1. Make a Bar / Dot or Box Plot chart of the data.
  2. Click Ridge Plot under Chart Type (in Statistical), or ask the AI Assistant for a ridge plot. Each category becomes a density curve, stacked and slightly overlapping.
  3. In Plot Style › Ridge Plot, set Overlap (1.5 by default): at 1.0 the tallest peak just touches the row above, and higher values let the curves flow into it. Show rug marks (on by default) puts a small tick at each data point along the ridge's baseline, and Ridge colors sets each ridge's color.
  • All ridges share one height scale, as in R's ggridges: the tallest density peak sets it, so a narrow distribution stands taller than a spread-out one and heights can be compared between ridges.
  • A category needs at least 2 values; categories with fewer are skipped. A chart of two or more series draws one at a time: the first, or the one chosen with Series.
  • Category names run down the left side and serve as the legend; Show legend hides them. Switching to or from Ridge Plot swaps the X and Y axis titles, since the axes swap roles.

Copy and Paste a Chart's Style

  1. In the chart whose look you want, choose Copy Style (⌥⌘C) from the Graph Utilities menu or the chart's right-click menu.
  2. Click the target chart and choose Paste Style (⌥⌘V) from the same menus.
  • The style is the chart's fonts, colors, sizes, axis styles, error bar type and point style. The target keeps its data, category labels, axis ranges, chart type, title, axis titles and brackets, and every choice that changes its results: each series' Center (Mean or Geometric mean) and a Volcano Plot's thresholds and adjusted-p choice.
  • Text, line and arrow annotations come along and replace the target's, in the same positions. To copy one annotation within a window, click it and use Duplicate in its editor (see Imaging › Text & Shape Annotations).
  • A Volcano Plot's color, size, shape or opacity mapping travels only to a column the target has.
  • ⌥⌘C and ⌥⌘V act on whichever window is in front: chart, graph or image. Pasting onto a Graph window brings the look (symbols, lines, colors, fonts, axes, ticks, the scale bar's look and the legend) and the annotations; values in data units (the X tick spacing, scale bar lengths, logarithmic axes) and hidden legend entries stay the target's own, and a sweep with its own line or symbol shape, such as kept AP markers or a fit's line, keeps its whole style.

Chart Settings

In the Chart tab, the three icons under Data Layout choose a panel: Plot Style (how the data are drawn), Axes & Labels (titles, fonts, grid and legend) or Range. Controls that don't apply to the chart's type are hidden, and an Estimation Plot's own settings are on the Statistics on a Chart page. To give another chart the same look, see Copy and Paste a Chart's Style.

Plot Style

Data Points is shown for Bar / Dot, Horizontal Bar, Box Plot and Estimation Plot charts; Mean / Bar for Bar / Dot and Horizontal Bar; Error Bars for those two and Line.

Data Points
  • Style: Beeswarm, the default, moves each point sideways just enough to clear the others; where a group is too crowded for its column, the extra points overlap and a note on the chart says how many. Jitter gives a small random sideways spread, Strip puts all points in one line, and None hides them (the default for 0/1 data).
  • Symbol and Point color: see Data Point Symbol. Size is 12 by default.
  • Opacity: strip points, and an Estimation Plot's, start out lighter the more of them share a column. Moving the slider sets the opacity exactly; Automatic Opacity brings the thinning back.
  • Mark possible outliers (off by default) rings in orange each point outside its column's box plot fences.
Mean / Bar
  • Display: Bar, the default; Violin; Mean line; Mean symbol, in the shape chosen under Data Points; or Points only.
  • Bar opacity (50% by default), Bar width (64%) and Bar gap, the space between bars (35%). With 2 or more series, Bar gap is the space between the bars of a group (8%) and Category gap the space between groups.
  • For violins: Median and quartile lines (on by default), Violin width, the widest violin's share of each group's space (90% by default), and Violin opacity.
  • Mean offset, with Mean line or Mean symbol, moves the mean marker sideways, away from the data points.
Error Bars
  • Center: Mean, the default, or Geometric mean, for log-normal data such as concentrations or titers. Copy Geometric Means then copies each group's numbers.
  • The menu under it: None, SD, SEM or CI (see Methods). A new chart starts with Settings › Statistics › New Chart Defaults › Default error bar type (SD unless changed). With Points only there are no means, so no error bars.
  • Color: Chosen color, the default; Same as line or bar; or Same as points. With data points hidden, Same as points follows the line.
  • Show caps (on by default), Cap width, and Bar width, the error bars' line width.
Connection Lines

Checking Paired / Repeated shows this box, turns on Show connection lines and shows bars as mean lines. The lines join each subject's points, the values in one table row; a subject missing a value has its line broken there. Hide data points, Hide mean marker and the lines' opacity, width and color are here too.

Lines and Category Spacing
  • On a Line chart, Lines sets each series' line color, point color and Solid or Dashed line, and the Point size. A missing value breaks the line, and a Line chart draws no brackets.
  • Category gap is the space at each end of the X axis (15% by default; at 0% the first and last points sit on the edges).
  • Curved lines (off by default) joins the points with a smooth curve through every point. It never rises above or falls below its neighbors, so it shows no peak the data don't have.
  • Offset the series slightly (off by default) moves each series a little to the side of the category, so overlapping error bars stay readable.
Box and Wedges
  • Box (Box Plot): the boxes' color, Box opacity and Box width; Notches (off by default); and Copy Box Statistics, which copies each box's n, whiskers, quartiles, median and notch ends as a table. Mean / Bar and Error Bars are hidden; Data Points can draw the values over the boxes.
  • Wedges (Pie): set each wedge's color, rename it (the label, legend and data table all follow), or click ↺ for its default color. Check Explode on a wedge to pull it out of the pie; Axes & Labels › Shape › Explode sets how far, and pulls out every wedge when none is checked.
Kaplan-Meier Curve
  • On by default: Show censor marks (a tick where a subject left the study or was event-free at last follow-up), Show median survival lines, Show log-rank test result, Show confidence band and Show numbers-at-risk table.
  • Band scale: Log-log (recommended), the default; Log (R's default); or Plain (linear).
  • Weighting: Log-rank, the default; Gehan-Breslow (Wilcoxon); Tarone-Ware; or Fleming-Harrington, with its ρ and γ (0 and 1 at first).
  • HR reference is the group the hazard ratios are relative to: the first, unless you pick another. A group named like a control is offered with a Use button, never picked for you.
  • Off by default: Stratify by the Stratum column (needs the 4th column), Show Cox model, Firth-penalized Cox and Show pairwise tests (Holm). Methods › Kaplan-Meier Estimates and Tests defines each result.
  • Line width, Median line width and Group color overrides set the curves' look. The survival axis is always 0 to 100%.
Subjects and Means

For a Repeated Measures by Group chart: Each subject's line, Group means ± error bars (with Join the means across conditions), Offset the groups slightly and Data points show or hide each part. With Each subject's line on, you can set the lines' opacity, width and colors.

Data Point Symbol

Symbol, in the Data Points box, sets the shape of the data points and of the Mean symbol marker: Circle, Square, Diamond or Triangle, each filled or open, or Cross or Plus. A new chart starts with Settings › Appearance › Charts › Default data point symbol (Circle unless changed). With several series, each is listed with its own color and symbol. The AI Assistant can also change the point shape and a chart's fonts; name a font family as Font Book lists it, or say System for the default.

Axes & Labels

  • Title, Axis Labels and Tick Values hold each text and its font, size and color. An axis title starts as the table's column header ("Dose (mM)"); a title you typed is never overwritten when the data are read again.
  • Rescale units automatically (Tick Values; on by default): when an axis title ends with a unit in parentheses or brackets, such as "Current (nA)", the axis switches to the prefix that avoids long decimals or long numbers, and the title changes to match: 0.02 nA reads 20 pA. It works for V, A, s, Ω (or ohm), M, mol, g, L, Hz, S, F, W and m; other units are left alone. Only the axis changes: the data, the Range fields and all statistics keep the unit you typed.
  • Axes & Grid: the axis, tick and grid colors and sizes, Dashed grid, Grid lines (5 by default) and Show grid. Show sample size (n) (on by default) writes each group's number of data points by its label.
  • Labels and Shape (Pie): Labels sets what each wedge shows (None, Name, Value, Percent, Name + %, the default, or Name + Value) and the labels' look. Shape sets Inner radius (for a donut), Explode and the wedges' stroke.
  • Appearance: the legend (see Legend); Legend font, also the font of the text a chart adds itself, such as brackets; Size, which also sets a Venn Diagram's counts (Text size when its legend is hidden); and Background. If a new background crosses from dark to light or back, @Graph offers to invert the foreground colors.
  • Category names too long to sit side by side are turned 45° (on a Horizontal Bar, wrapped onto two lines) or shortened with an ellipsis (…). In a category label, Option-Return starts a new line.
  • The Add Overlay menu at the top right of the chart adds a movable text label, line or arrow (see Imaging › Text & Shape Annotations).

Range

  • Y Axis Range (Value Axis Range on a Horizontal Bar) has a Min and a Max. Scatter (X,Y), Volcano and Cluster Scatter charts have X Axis Range too, and Kaplan-Meier has only Time Axis Range. Pie, Ridge Plot and, apart from Volcano and Cluster Scatter, the omics types have no range settings.
  • Type a plain number in the data's units, or add a unit to convert it: on an axis titled in mV, -0.08 V is kept as -80. A unit can be typed only when the axis title names one, as in Vm (mV). Editing the axis title or its unit later never moves the range. Marks beyond a typed range are cut at the axis.
  • The panel flags a Min or Max that isn't a number (the axis treats it as blank) and a Max that isn't above Min. If a bar chart's range leaves out zero, a warning explains that bar lengths then mislead.
  • Automatic range: a chart with filled bars always includes zero, because a bar's length is its value. Other marks show a value as a position, so zero is included only when it is close to the data. Line charts pad around the data.
  • Close means that zero costs no more than half again the height the data need: a box plot of values between −25 and −5 gets its zero line, and one over −90 to −60 does not.
  • Show percentages as appears for a chart of values written as percentages, such as 45% or a spreadsheet's percent cells (in the Data Layout box for a pie or ridge plot; on a scatter it applies to both axes). 45%, the default, plots them as percentages (45) and adds (%) to the value-axis title once; 0.45 plots them as fractions. Only values written with % change: plain numbers plot as typed, and editing the axis title or its unit never changes the data.

Logarithmic Axes

Logarithmic scale, in the Range panel, draws the value axis, or a scatter's X axis, on a base-10 log scale. It is offered for Bar / Dot, Horizontal Bar, Box Plot, Line and Scatter (X,Y) charts.

  • A log axis can't show zero or negative values, so they are left out, and the Range panel and the Chart Legend say how many. A typed Min or Max must be above zero.
  • Bars are shown as mean symbols, since a bar's length from zero means nothing on a log axis. Your bar setting comes back when you turn the log scale off.
  • Error bars are the mean ± SD, SEM or CI as computed, so they look longer below the mean. One that reaches zero or below is cut at the axis with no cap.
  • Violins are drawn from a density of the log of the values. Box plot quartiles and whiskers come from the values as they are.
  • A scatter's fit line is the least-squares line of the values as they are, so on log axes it curves. For a straight line on log axes, fit the log10 of your values instead.

Legend

Show legend (on by default) and Size, under Axes & Labels › Appearance, apply to every chart's legend. The legend names a chart's series, so a chart with one series has none. Drag a legend to move it; Reset Position puts it back.

  • A Bar / Dot, Horizontal Bar, Line or Box Plot chart of two or more series, and a Pie, also have Layout: Side by Side (the default) or Top to Bottom. A pie moves to make room for its legend.
  • Scatter, Cluster Scatter, Kaplan-Meier, GSEA Bar, Grouped Diverging Bar and Stacked Composition Bar charts list their legend one entry per line, at the right of the plot; when you drag it away, the plot widens into the space it leaves. A Kaplan-Meier legend starts inside the plot instead, when a corner the curves leave empty has room for it.
  • The other charts keep their legend in one place: in a row above a Volcano Plot or under a Venn Diagram, and at the right of the plot as the color scale of a Heatmap and the size and color keys of a Dot Plot. PCA, Manhattan and UpSet plots have no legend.

Methods

Error Bars and Centers

  • SD is the standard deviation of a category's values (n − 1 in the denominator). SEM is SD / √n. CI is SEM × the t critical value for n − 1 degrees of freedom, at the confidence level in Settings › Statistics (95% unless changed).
  • In a table of means, an SEM with its n gives the same t-based CI, and an SEM without n a CI from the normal distribution. An SD without n gives no CI, and the Error Bars box says so.
  • The geometric mean is exp of the mean of ln x. Its error bars are × / ÷ the geometric SD factor, exp(SD of ln x), or its confidence interval, the t-interval of ln x back-transformed. They look longer above the mean on a linear axis and symmetric on a log axis. SEM has no geometric counterpart, so it isn't offered.
  • Values at or below zero have no logarithm, so they are left out of a geometric mean, and the panel and the Chart Legend say how many. Geometric mean needs individual values: it isn't available for charts made from means with SD, SEM or n, for 0/1 data, or for violins.
  • Tests and effect sizes still use the values as entered. To compare geometric means, take LN of the values in a spreadsheet and test those: the difference of log means, exp(Δ), is the ratio of geometric means.

Box Plot

  • The box runs from the first to the third quartile, with a line at the median. Quartiles use the (n + 1) rule (Hyndman–Fan type 6), as in GraphPad Prism and Excel's QUARTILE.EXC; R's ggplot2 and NumPy default to type 7. The rule decides which points count as outliers, so state it in your methods: Copy Chart Legend (Statistics tab) writes the sentence.
  • Whiskers reach the most extreme value within 1.5 × IQR (the interquartile range) of the box, Tukey's convention. Points beyond them are drawn as outliers. A category with a single value is drawn as a flat tick.
  • Notches narrow each box at median ± 1.58 × IQR/√n (McGill, Tukey & Larsen 1978), using the IQR of the box drawn. Boxes whose notches don't overlap suggest that their medians differ, at roughly 95% confidence: an informal guide, not a test. With small samples a notch can reach past its box; it is then drawn folded outward, as R's boxplot draws it, and a note says so.

Violins

A violin is a kernel density estimate of each group's values (Gaussian kernel), cut off at the smallest and largest values and scaled to its own widest point, so violins compare in shape. The bandwidth is Silverman's rule, 0.9 × min(SD, IQR/1.34) × n^(−1/5), as in R: because it uses the smaller of the SD and the IQR, an outlier or a second peak does not smooth away the real shape. The solid line marks the median and the dashed lines the quartiles, the same quartiles as Box Plot. A Ridge Plot's curves use the same kernel and bandwidth, but each runs a little past the data.

Kaplan-Meier Estimates and Tests

The tests and models give the results of R's survival package (survdiff, coxph, cox.zph), of coxphf for Firth's method and of survminer's pairwise_survdiff.

Curves, bands and medians
  • Each curve drops at each observed event, not at a censoring. The numbers-at-risk table counts the subjects whose time is at or after each tick.
  • The band is a pointwise confidence interval for each curve (Greenwood's variance), at the confidence level in Settings › Statistics. Band scale sets how the band and the median's interval are computed: Log-log stays within 0 to 100% and covers best in small samples (as in SAS and Stata); Log matches R's survfit; Plain is linear.
  • Median survival is the first time the curve drops to 50% or below, or "not reached". Where the curve sits exactly at 50% over an interval, it is that interval's midpoint.
  • The median's confidence interval is read off the band (Brookmeyer & Crowley 1982): from the first event time whose band contains 50% to the last. An upper limit the band never reaches is shown as NR, and a lower limit the band leaves undefined (the curve drops straight to 0) as NE, not estimable.
Tests between groups
  • With 2 or more groups, the log-rank test compares all groups at once. Its p is a large-sample approximation that runs too small with few events, so with fewer than 10 events in all the legend adds "Approximate p".
  • Weighting: Log-rank is the most powerful test when the hazards are proportional. Gehan-Breslow (Gehan 1965; Breslow 1970) and Tarone-Ware (Tarone & Ware 1977) give early times more weight. Fleming-Harrington (Harrington & Fleming 1982) weights each event time by S(t−)^ρ · (1 − S(t−))^γ, for the pooled survival S just before it: ρ = 1, γ = 0 is R's survdiff(rho = 1), and a γ above 0 stresses late differences. Choose the weighting before looking at the curves: trying several and reporting the smallest p inflates false positives.
  • Stratify by the Stratum column compares the groups within each stratum (such as a study site) and combines the results. It also stratifies the Cox model; the curves stay pooled.
  • A group with nobody at risk at any event time, or alone in every risk set it is in (the only group in its stratum, say), is left out of the test, which then has one fewer degree of freedom.
  • Show pairwise tests (Holm), for 3 or more groups, tests every pair with the same weighting and strata and adjusts the p-values by Holm's method (Holm 1979). A pair that can't be tested reads "not testable" and counts as p = 1 in the adjustment.
Hazard ratios
  • With exactly 2 groups, the legend shows a hazard ratio with its confidence interval, labeled with its direction: "HR (B vs A)", where A is the HR reference. It comes from a Cox proportional-hazards model (Cox 1972) with group as its only covariate, Efron's handling of tied times (Efron 1977) and a Wald confidence interval.
  • Show Cox model gives each group's hazard ratio against the reference with its CI, the likelihood-ratio test of all groups at once, and the Schoenfeld-residual test of proportional hazards (Grambsch & Therneau 1994): global, plus one per group with 3 or more groups. A note appears when a proportional-hazards p is below α (0.05 at the default 95% level): the hazard ratio may change over follow-up, so it is an average.
  • When a ratio has no finite estimate (one group has no events, or every event in one group comes after the last subject of the other has left follow-up), the legend shows Firth's penalized estimate instead, labeled "Firth-penalized", with a line saying why. With strata, where Firth's method is not available, the legend says the ratio is not estimable.
  • Firth-penalized Cox fits every hazard ratio by Firth's penalized likelihood (Firth 1993; Heinze & Schemper 2001), with coxphf's defaults. The penalty keeps an estimate finite and reduces small-sample bias, so it also suits small studies. Each ratio has a profile penalized-likelihood CI (not a Wald interval) and a penalized likelihood-ratio p, for up to 11 groups; with more, the legend gives the ratios alone. Tied times use Breslow's method, where the ordinary fit uses Efron's, and the legend says so. The proportional-hazards test is not computed for Firth fits.

Back to Contents

Graphs

A graph window shows a recording, or a table of X-Y data, as traces. It has a toolbar at the top, the sweep controls above the plot, the plot itself, a status bar at the bottom and the inspector on the right. Every window keeps its own inspector settings. For zooming, cursors and moving through sweeps, see Navigating Graphs, below.

Toolbar Buttons (left to right)

  • Export: save the graph as an image (PNG, JPEG, TIFF, GIF, PDF, SVG), copy it as PDF, send it to Keynote, or save its data as @Graph, ABF, AxoGraph, HDF5, MATLAB, NWB or CSV. File › Export… (⇧⌘E) opens the image export panel directly.
  • Drag (hand): drag the graph into Keynote, Pages, Word, Mail or the Finder, as Copy as PDF makes it.
  • Spreadsheet: shows the sweeps in an editable grid, one channel at a time (check "Show all channels" to see them all). See Spreadsheets.
  • Cursors (⌘K): show or hide cursors A and B. Chart windows have no cursors, so no Cursors button.
  • Window Size: set the window's exact size (see Window Size, below). Chart windows have no Window Size button; for the size of a chart's figures, see Exporting Results.
  • Inspector (⌘I): show or hide the inspector.

Export Visible…, at the right of the bar above the plot, copies just the sweeps you're showing into a new window, a new .@graph file, or both. With the X axis zoomed, check "Only the X range on screen" to cut each sweep to that range.

The status bar shows the number of channels and sweeps, the samples per sweep and the duration. On its right, while the Electrophysiology toolkit is shown or one of its corrections is on, are JP Correction, for a graph with a membrane-potential channel, and the Rₛ button, for a recording with two or more channels or with an Rₛ correction applied (see Rₛ and Junction Potential Correction).

The Inspector

The inspector opens when a file is loaded. Click a category icon at the top, then a panel's icon below it:

CategoryPanels
DisplayPlot Style, Axes & Labels, Range, Groups. See Graph Display Settings.
ModifyData Transform, Graph Tools, Filter/Smoothing, Baseline. See Modifying Graphs.
SignalAverage, Normalize, Align at Peak, Spectrum. See Signal Processing.
AnalyzeMeasure, Peaks, Curve Fitting. See Measuring & Analysis.
ToolkitsTools for one field. Choose the toolkit from the row of toolkit icons, then a panel. See Toolkits: Overview.

The magnifier at the right of the category's name is Find a Tool: type a tool's name or what it does to find it in any category, toolkit, menu or calculator (see Toolkits: Overview › Finding a Tool).

Typing numbers in a panel

  • Press Return (↩) in a number field to run the panel's main action (Apply Filter, Measure, Fit and so on).
  • A number you have typed counts as soon as you click anything else, so you can type a value and click the panel's button straight away.
  • A field kept in a unit, such as Window (ms) or Frequency (Hz), takes a value typed with a unit of the same kind and converts it (0.5 s in an ms field is 500). A unit of another kind, or any unit in a field that has none (a count, a percentage, a factor), is refused with a beep.

What a panel remembers

  • Each panel keeps its settings when you switch panels and when you quit and reopen @Graph: one set per panel, for every graph.
  • A setting that belongs to one recording (a threshold in the trace's own unit, a window on its sweeps, a frequency range, a formula's starting values) is kept for that recording only, while @Graph stays open.
  • The graph's own settings (its display, and the filters, baselines and other changes applied to its data) are saved in its file. A panel's memory never changes them.
  • @Graph › Settings… › General › Reset Panel Settings… puts every panel back to its original settings, and each tool's cursors back to their starting place.

Graph Title and Axis Labels

  1. In the inspector, choose Display › Axes & Labels.
  2. For a title above the plot, check "Show title", type it, and set its Size, Font and Color.
  3. Check "Show axis labels" and type the X label and the Y label: the name, then the unit in the parentheses (Voltage and mV, say). A time axis picks its unit for you.
  4. To change one axis's label on the plot, double-click the label.

Editing a label or its unit changes the text only: the numbers on the axis and the data stay as they are. To convert the values to another unit, see Modifying Graphs › Data Transform.

Window Size

  1. Click Window Size in the toolbar, just left of the Inspector button.
  2. Type the Width and Height in points (1/72 inch, the unit of PDF and SVG export), from the window's minimum up to 10,000.
  3. Click Apply.

Match window (in the export panel), Copy as PDF and Send to Keynote use the size of the graph area inside the window, so windows given the same size, with the inspector shown or hidden alike, export as figures of the same size.

Navigating Graphs

Zooming

ToDo this
Zoom into a regionDrag a rectangle on the plot.
Set one axis's rangeDrag along a Y axis's tick area (left of the plot) for that panel's Y range, or along the X axis's tick area (below the plot) for the shared X range.
Type exact limitsDouble-click an axis's tick area. Or choose Display › Range, uncheck "Auto-range (fit data)" and type Min and Max.
Zoom X in or out⌘= or ⌘→, and ⌘− or ⌘←.
Zoom Y in or out⌘↑ and ⌘↓.
Pan a zoomed axisThe arrow keys.
Step back one zoomDouble-click the plot background. Repeated double-clicks retrace each zoom until the plot fits the data again.
Reset the zoom⌘0, or Reset to Auto in the Range panel.
Give groups with the same unit the same Y rangeMatch Y Ranges in the Range panel.
  • Each group's panel has its own Y range, and all panels share the X range.
  • A panel on Y auto-range fits the data in the X range shown, and follows as you pan or zoom X. To keep Y still while you scroll, zoom Y or uncheck Y's "Auto-range (fit data)"; every panel then keeps its current range, and typing a limit for one panel leaves the others as they are.
  • Limits can be typed with a unit, such as -80 mV, -0.08 V or 2 min, and are converted to the axis unit.
  • On a logarithmic axis, zooming works in decades, and values of zero or below are left out (see Logarithmic Axes under Graph Display Settings).

Cursors

  1. Click Cursors in the toolbar (⌘K). Cursors A and B appear as two dashed vertical lines over the middle 25% of the view, labeled in the X axis's unit.
  2. Drag each cursor, or type its position in the A and B fields of an inspector panel. Positions round to the nearest sample.
  • Panels with a "Full sweep" / "Between cursors A – B" choice follow the cursors: choosing Between cursors shows them, and Full sweep hides them.
  • Each tool with cursors (Measure, Peaks, Curve Fitting, Baseline and the others) keeps its own: switch from Measure to Curve Fitting and back, and Measure's cursors return to where you left them in that graph. In another graph, or after you quit @Graph, they return at the same relative place in the view.
  • A saved graph opens with the cursors it was saved with.
  • A result that keeps the graph's time axis (Decimate, Interpolate, Resample, Integrate, Differentiate, Average, Normalize, Delete Sweeps, Export Visible) opens with the same X shift, cursor positions and zoom. Results with a new X axis, such as Align at Peak, a spectrum or a histogram, start from their own.
  • The Cursors button is dimmed while View › Plot Sweeps at Recording Time is on.

Sweeps

  1. Type which sweeps to show in the "Review sweeps:" field above the plot, for example 1-10, 15, 20-25. ⌥⌘R jumps to this field.
  2. Press Return or click Apply. The All, Odd and Even buttons beside the field are quick choices.
KeyWhat it does
Tab / Shift-TabShows the next or previous sweep on its own, as the Step buttons above the plot do.
Comma / periodShows the first or last sweep.
Space / Shift-SpaceAdds the next sweep to those shown, or removes the last one added.

Click the plot first, so these keys go to it rather than to a text field.

Multi-channel Files

Files with more than one channel open with one panel per channel. In the Groups panel, "Split by channel" gives each recorded channel its own panel, Y axis and unit, and "Single group (all sweeps)" overlays everything in one panel. See Grouping Modes under Graph Display Settings for all the choices.

Back to Contents

Imaging

The Image window shows and measures images: single images, time series (T-series), Z-stacks and files that hold both, from Leica, Nikon, Prairie View and Zeiss microscopes, TIFF and FITS files, and ordinary pictures. Draw regions of interest (ROIs), measure each one's intensity over time, and send the traces to a Graph window.

The image is on the left, with its playback controls below it. The inspector on the right has a tab for each kind of work; the sidebar button at the top right shows or hides it. After Measure, the traces appear in a graph below the image.

TabWhat it holds
ChannelsEach channel's display, Frame avg, the frame Interval and the Z and T options.
ROIsMicroscopy Setup (the pixel size), the scale bar, the list of ROIs, Auto-Detect ROIs and Find Spots.
AnalyzeHow traces are measured, the Measure button and Image Info. For a Z-stack, also Spectral Cube or Profile Along Z.
CorrectShading, Debayer, Background, Frame Quality, Registration, Channel Alignment and Average Frames.
ToolkitsThe image tools of the toolkits that are shown (see Toolkits Tab, below).

Open and View Images

Open an Image

  • Drag an image file onto the Data Log, any open @Graph window or the Dock icon, or choose File › Open File… (⌘O). File › New Data Importer (⌘N) opens a drop zone that lists the file types by field.
  • Prairie View: drag the .xml file. If @Graph asks for access to the folder of TIFFs beside it, click Open Folder.
  • Folder of TIFFs: drag the folder. It opens as a T-series; for a Z-stack, check Treat T-series as Z-stack in the Channels tab.
  • FITS frames: drag a folder of FITS files, or choose several together with File › Open File…; they open as one time series in observation order.
  • A file holding more than 4 images (CZI scenes, ND2 positions, LIF or OME-TIFF series) shows Choose What to Open, which lists each image with its size, channels, Z and T. Uncheck the ones you don't need, then click Open. A file with 4 or fewer opens a window for each.

Supported File Formats

The Supported File Formats page lists every image format and what is read from each. For what you see and measure:

  • True values: signed, 32-bit integer and floating-point images open with Min, Max and every measurement in the file's own values. ImageJ's straight-line value calibration (value = c0 + c1 × stored) is applied to every measurement; the Data Log names it, or says when a calibration isn't applied (a non-linear function).
  • Pixels with no value (NaN or infinite pixels of a floating-point image, a FLIM pixel with no photons) are left out of every measurement.
  • FITS frames: a folder of FITS frames, or several chosen together, opens as one time series in the order the frames were taken (by DATE-OBS, else MJD-OBS, else JD). Each frame keeps its own header and is timed at the middle of its exposure.
  • Pictures open as stored, without color management: gray as one channel, color as Red, Green and Blue. An animated GIF opens as a time series, each frame at the time its delays give.
  • ENVI (.hdr with its binary file): the bands open as Z slices, with the header's band wavelengths as their spectral axis (see Spectra and Profiles Along Z, below). An Analyze .hdr still opens as NIfTI.

What Is Set When an Image Opens

  • Display range: an ImageJ or Fiji TIFF opens with the display range it was saved with (each channel's own, for a composite). A two-dimensional FITS image opens with Auto Stretch of its first frame (see ZScale and Auto Stretch, below). Other images open spanning the first time point's lowest to highest value.
  • Colors: files that record channel colors (CZI, LIF, LSM, ND2, OME-TIFF) open in them. Otherwise a single-channel image opens in Grayscale, and channels 1 to 4 of a multi-channel image get the default emission colors.
  • Scale bar: shown when the file records a pixel size.

Image Canvas

ToDo this
ZoomPinch on the trackpad, or press ⌘= and ⌘−. The zoom is around the pointer. ⌘0 fits the image again.
Go between Fit and 100%Double-tap with two fingers. At 100%, one image pixel is one screen point.
PanScroll with two fingers, or use the arrow keys.
RotateClick Rotate 90° in the toolbar (Option-click turns the other way). ROIs, text and arrows turn with the image.
Read a pixelHover over the image. The top-left corner shows the position in pixels (and in µm when the pixel size is known) and each visible channel's value, in the image's true values. The readout never appears in exports.
See what the file recordsClick Metadata in the toolbar.
Copy the image or its styleRight-click the image: Copy Image, Copy as PDF, Copy Style and Paste Style.

⌘Z undoes and ⇧⌘Z redoes changes to ROIs and overlays, and also to the display and measuring settings: a channel's LUT, color, Min, Max, Z proj and name, rotation, the scale bar, Frame avg, the frame Interval and Z step, the trace graph's axis labels, Microscopy Setup and the drift correction. Changes made in quick succession, such as a slider drag, undo as one step.

Move Through Time and Z

A badge next to the frame counter says what is loaded: "T-series: N", "Z-stack: N", "T×Z series: N×N" or "Single frame".

  • Time: the transport below the image has Play/Pause (Space), step buttons, a scrubber, a Speed menu and a Loop button, which makes playback start again at the end.
  • Z: when the file has more than one Z slice, a second transport appears above the first, with its own Play/Pause and Speed. The two can play separately or together. When the file records a Z step, it shows the current slice's depth from the first (z = 2.5 µm).
  • Speed: 1 to 30 fps. For time, the menu also offers Real time when the file has a frame interval: playback keeps the recording's own rate, skipping frames of a fast recording. When the frames were taken at uneven times, it offers Median rate instead: one frame per tick at the median interval.

Set the Pixel Size and Scale Bar

ROI sizes, the scale bar and spot sizes need the pixel size. Most microscope files record it; a plain TIFF or a picture usually doesn't.

  1. Open the ROIs tab. Microscopy Setup, at its top, shows the Pixel size read from the file.
  2. If it reads "Not in metadata: enter below", type the size in Manual (µm/px).
  3. To work the size out from the optics instead, uncheck Use metadata pixel size and choose the Objective, Coupler, Camera and Binning. For a laser-scanning microscope, leave Objective or Camera at None and type the size in Scan pixel (µm/px).
  4. Check Scale bar, or click Scale Bar in the toolbar. Choose the bar's corner from the menu below the checkbox.
  • From the optics, pixel size = camera pixel × binning ÷ (objective × coupler). When the image is the camera's sensor size divided by 2, 3, 4 or 8, Microscopy Setup asks whether the camera was binned.
  • Bar length: a round number (1, 2 or 5 × a power of ten, such as 20 µm), about 15% of the image width. Zoomed in, the bar on screen takes a round length for the part in view; exported and copied images keep the bar chosen for the whole image.
  • Bar color: Auto (on by default) picks white or black on every frame from the image behind the bar. Uncheck Auto to choose the color yourself with White.
  • Non-square pixels: when the file records different X and Y pixel sizes, each is used for its own axis, and the scale bar uses the size of the axis that is horizontal on screen. When Y isn't a length (a line scan, where Y is time), only widths are given.
  • Sky images: for a FITS file with sky coordinates, the pixel size is an angle and the bar reads in arcseconds (″), arcminutes (′) or degrees (°).
  • Plain TIFFs: the file's resolution is used as a pixel size when it is given per centimeter, or per inch at 508 dpi or more (50 µm or smaller). 72, 96 and 300 dpi are screen and print settings and are not used.

Set the Frame Interval and Z Step

  • Interval (Channels tab): the time between frames, in seconds, read from the file when it records one. It sets the time axis of the traces, the time readout, Real time playback and the movie clock. Type a value to set or correct it.
  • A file with no interval (such as a plain multi-page TIFF or a folder of TIFFs) shows "not set". Its traces are plotted against frame number, counted from 1. There is no time readout, Time Window baselines and Real time playback are unavailable, and movies play at 10 fps.
  • Uneven frames: when a file records each frame's time and the frames are not evenly spaced (cycles with a pause between them, or phases at different rates), each time point keeps its own recorded time for the time readout, baselines, traces, Send to Graph, CSV export and movies. The Interval field then shows the median interval, marked "median". Typing another Interval replaces the recorded times with even spacing.
  • Treat T-series as Z-stack (Channels tab, for a plain time series): makes every frame a Z slice of one time point, for a Z-stack saved without Z information, such as a folder of TIFFs.
  • Treat Z-stack as T-series (for a Z-stack of one time point): the reverse, for a time-lapse saved as a plain stack. Set the Interval above it.
  • Z step: every Z-stack has a Z step field, read from the file when it records one. Enter the real slice spacing when it doesn't; otherwise the Orthogonal Views draw each slice as tall as one pixel is wide.

Display

Everything in this part changes only how the image looks. Measurements, traces and Export Data as TIFF always use the values the file holds.

Channels Panel

The Channels tab has a set of controls for each channel. With two or more channels, an All Channels row follows them.

  1. Open the Channels tab. Check or uncheck a channel's box to show or hide it, and edit its name in the field beside the color swatch.
  2. To show a channel in color, uncheck Grayscale and choose a LUT (color table), or click the swatch and pick a color.
  3. Click Auto to fit Min and Max to the data, or type them.
  4. To bring out faint detail, choose a Stretch, or click Auto Stretch.
  5. For a Z-stack, choose how the slices are combined in Z proj (see Z-Stacks and Z Projection, below).
ControlWhat it does
GrayscaleOn by default for single-channel images. Shows the channel in grays from Min (black) to Max (white), with its stretch, instead of its LUT.
LUTUsed when Grayscale is off. Emission λ gives the hue of the fluorophore's emission wavelength: drag the spectrum slider or type 380–700 nm (defaults: Ch1 520 nm, Ch2 610 nm, Ch3 670 nm, Ch4 460 nm). Channel Color runs from black to the swatch's color. Grays, Green, Red, Blue, Cyan and Magenta are single-color ramps. Fire and Hot bring out detail in bright areas. Viridis looks even to the eye, but its darkest color is a dark purple, which tints a composite's background.
SmoothingOff by default, and one setting for the whole image. Off, each pixel is a sharp square, exactly as recorded. On, neighboring pixels are blended when the image is enlarged, on screen and in exports; this adds no real detail.
SubtractWith two or more channels: subtracts another channel from this channel's measured traces (see Background and neuropil subtraction, below). The image is not changed.

Leica FLIM channels are hidden until you check Show FLIM channels, and then each channel's own box. A FITS sky image leaves out Smoothing, Frame avg and Treat T-series as Z-stack, which are meant for microscopy, unless one is already on. A finished color picture made by Stack Frames shows a note in place of the controls: its stretch is already in its values.

Display range: Min, Max and Auto
  • The range from Min to Max is cut into 256 equal steps, one per color. Pixels at or below Min are black; pixels in the top step and above take the LUT's top color (white in Grayscale). For a floating-point, signed or calibrated image, Min and Max are in the image's true values.
  • Auto sets the range so that 0.35% of the pixels are saturated, half shown black and half at the top color (ImageJ's Enhance Contrast). It reads the whole series: every time point and, for a Z-stack, what the image shows (the Z projection with Show Z Projection on, otherwise every slice).
  • On a two-dimensional FITS image, Auto uses zscale of the frame shown instead, so that a few bright stars don't set Max.
  • Auto and ZScale set Min and Max only. A Midtones stretch goes back to Linear, since it belongs to the range Auto Stretch found.
Stretch

Stretch (Linear by default) sets how the values from Min to Max are spread over the colors. In the table, x is a value's place between Min (0) and Max (1). Gamma, Log and Asinh follow astropy's definitions; Midtones is PixInsight's midtones transfer function. Each stretch keeps its own value, shown in a field beside Auto Stretch.

StretchA value at x is shown atIts value
Linearx—
Square Root√x—
Gammax^γγ from 0.05 to 20 (0.5 by default). Below 1 brightens faint detail.
Loglog(a·x + 1) / log(a + 1)a = 1,000 by default. Larger is stronger.
Asinhasinh(x / a) / asinh(1 / a)a = 0.1 by default. Smaller is stronger. The gentlest on the brightest values.
Midtones(m − 1)·x / ((2m − 1)·x − m)The value at x = m is shown halfway up the colors. m = 0.5 is linear; smaller brightens.
Histogram EqualizationThe frame's values between Min and Max, spread evenly over the colors.Pixels below Min stay black, pixels above Max take the top color, and pixels with no value are left out.
ZScale and Auto Stretch
  • ZScale sets Min and Max from the frame shown, with the zscale algorithm that DS9 and astropy use. It suits images where a few pixels are far brighter than the rest, such as sky images.
  • Auto Stretch sets Min, Max and a Midtones stretch from the frame shown, as PixInsight's Screen Transfer Function AutoStretch does. The channel's values are scaled to 0–1 by the range they are stored in (255 for 8-bit data, otherwise 65,535; a floating-point image by its own range). From their median and MAD (median absolute deviation, × 1.4826 to estimate the noise SD), Min goes 2.8 of those below the median (to 0 if that falls below 0, or when the MAD is 0), Max stays at the top, and m is chosen so that the median lands a quarter of the way up the colors. An image with a bright background (median above half the range, such as brightfield) is stretched from the top instead: Min stays at 0 and Max goes 2.8 of them above the median.
