  • Auto Stretch reads the background from the median, so it suits images that are mostly background, such as sky frames and sparse fluorescence. Where the subject fills most of the frame, the stretch comes out mild; use Auto, or set Midtones yourself.
All Channels

With two or more channels, the All Channels row has its own Auto, Auto Stretch and, for a Z-stack, Z proj. They apply to every channel still following them; using a channel's own Auto, ZScale, Auto Stretch or Z proj makes that channel stop following. With Link channels on, Auto Stretch gives every channel one stretch, from their averages, so that a color image keeps its balance. Link channels is on by default when the channels are Red, Green and Blue.

Show Native Image

Show Native Image shows the data as the camera recorded them: linear from 0 to the detector's full scale, with no stretch, color table or smoothing. Click Native in the toolbar, or choose View › Show Native Image; click again to go back. Hold N on the image for a quick look at the other view.

  • Full scale: the file's bit depth (255; 4,095 for a 12-bit camera in a 16-bit file; 65,535). For FITS integer data, its SATURATE value or the largest value BITPIX and BZERO allow. Data with no known ceiling (floating-point frames, ratio images) are shown over their own minimum to maximum, and the label says "data range".
  • With several channels shown, the first visible one is shown alone, in grays (hide it to see the next). A color picture, or an RGB photo (a PNG, JPEG or RGB TIFF whose channels are Red, Green and Blue), is shown in its own colors: its stored red, green and blue values.
  • A label in the image's corner gives the range, such as "Native · 0–4095 · linear". Rotation and drift correction are kept.
  • It is temporary: turning it off brings back the channels' own display exactly, and it is never saved and never an undo step.

Z-Stacks and Spectral Cubes

Z-Stacks and Z Projection

For a Z-stack, the image shows one Z slice. To show the whole stack combined, check Show Z Projection in the Channels tab; each channel is combined by its own Z proj setting. Z proj also sets how the slices are combined when ROIs are measured: Measure takes each frame's value from the channel's Z projection, not from the slice shown.

Z projWhat each pixel shows
Max IntensityThe brightest value through the stack. Shows the full extent of labeled structures.
MeanThe average through the stack. Less noisy, but dimmer.
SumThe total through the stack. When the largest possible sum doesn't fit 16 bits, the image shows the sum divided by a whole number, the same at every time point and channel, and the Channels tab says by how much ("Sum shown ÷ 2"). ROIs measure the true sum.
Min IntensityThe dimmest value through the stack, for dark objects on a bright background.
Standard DeviationHow much each pixel varies through the stack (the sample SD, n − 1). The image shows it rounded to whole counts; ROIs measure the exact value.
  • Changing Z proj re-runs Auto while the projection is shown, since each kind of projection has a very different range.
  • While the image shows the projection with Orthogonal Views off, the Z slider and its buttons are dimmed: there is no slice to step through.

Orthogonal Views

Show Orthogonal Views (XZ/YZ) in the Channels tab, on by default for a Z-stack, shows side views of the stack below the image. XZ and YZ each have two panes: on top, the whole stack projected with the XZ/YZ proj setting; below, the slice at the current Y (for XZ) or X (for YZ). The panes are drawn at true proportions, from the X and Y pixel sizes and the Z step.

  • To move the position, use the X, Y and Z steppers above the panes, drag in an XZ or YZ pane, or drag the crosshair on the image (with any tool). Grabbing near one line moves that axis only; near the crossing, both.
  • The slice panes use the channel's LUT and display range. The projected panes are shown over their own range (their 0.175th to 99.825th percentile), since a projection is far brighter than one plane.
  • Scale bars, beside XZ/YZ proj, adds a scale bar to each pane.

Spectra and Profiles Along Z

Some images hold a spectrum at every pixel: a FITS cube whose third axis is wavelength, frequency or velocity, a hyperspectral image (ENVI), a Raman map or a confocal lambda stack. Their planes open as Z slices. When the file says what each plane is, the Z transport shows the plane's value (λ 656.28 nm, v −12.4 km/s), and Go to shows the plane nearest a value you type. A microscope's Z-stack uses the same tools along depth.

Read a spectrum or a depth profile
  1. Open the Analyze tab. Its first section is Spectral Cube (Profile Along Z for a Z-stack).
  2. With the pointer tool, click a pixel in the image. The plot shows its values along Z, with the plane shown marked. Hold ⌥ to follow the pointer instead. Click the plot to go to a plane.
  3. To add each visible ROI's spectrum, check Include ROIs and choose Mean or Sum.
  4. Click Open Spectrum Graph. The spectra open as an X–Y graph with the spectral axis as X, at Spectroscopy › Peak Fitting.
Make a band map or a moment map
  1. Under Band Map (Range of Planes for a Z-stack), choose the Map: Sum, Mean, Maximum, or Moment 0, 1 or 2.
  2. Set the Band's first and last planes. Use Plane sets both to the plane shown.
  3. To take off a baseline first, check Subtract the continuum and set the Left side and Right side bands. At each pixel, a straight line through the means of the two side bands is subtracted.
  4. Click Make Band Map. The map opens as a new image, with the cube's sky coordinates, its unit in BUNIT and how it was made in its HISTORY.
MapWhat each pixel holds
Sum, Mean, MaximumThe sum, mean or maximum of the chosen planes.
Moment 0The integrated intensity, Σ I Δx, in the image's unit × the axis's (such as K km/s).
Moment 1The intensity-weighted mean position along the axis: a velocity field for a cube; for a Z-stack, a depth map in the Z step's unit.
Moment 2The intensity-weighted variance of that position: a line width, or a spread of depths, squared.

The moments follow the spectral-cube package's definitions. Missing values are left out. In a T×Z stack, the time point shown is used.

ROIs

Draw and Edit ROIs

  1. Pick a tool in the toolbar: Rectangle, Ellipse, Polygon, Freehand or Line. Pointer selects and moves.
  2. Draw on the image. Rectangle, Ellipse and Line: drag. Polygon: click each corner and double-click to close. Freehand: drag around the region and release to close it. Escape cancels a polygon or freehand ROI in progress.
  3. To move an ROI, drag it, with any tool (the pointer turns into a hand over an ROI). Hold Option while dragging to duplicate it. Hold ⌘ to draw a new ROI starting inside an existing one.
  4. To delete the selected ROI, press Delete, or right-click it and choose Delete ROI. The menu also has Duplicate ROI.
  • ROIs are named ROI 1, ROI 2 and so on, each with its own color, which its trace takes in the sweep graph.
  • At the image's edge, a rectangle is cut to the image. An ellipse, polygon or line keeps its shape and direction as drawn, and only its part on the image is measured. An ROI drawn wholly outside the image is not kept, and a moved ROI stops before it leaves the image.
  • Clear ROIs in the toolbar and Clear All in the ROIs tab remove every ROI, after asking. The measured traces are kept, and the trace graph's header marks them as out of date.

ROIs Panel

Under Regions of Interest, the ROIs tab lists every ROI with its color, its name, a BG button, a show/hide (eye) button and a delete (−) button. When the pixel size is known, each row also gives the ROI's size (a line's length) and, for an area ROI, the number of pixels it measures and their area.

  • Rename: edit the name and press Return.
  • Hide: a hidden ROI isn't drawn or measured. Its eye button shows it again.
  • BG makes an ROI the background reference, which Subtract background in the Analyze tab uses. The row turns orange and the button reads Background; on the image and in exports the ROI has a dashed border and a ◆BG label. Only one ROI can be the background, and it gets no trace of its own.
  • Save ROIs saves every ROI's position and name as a .atgroi file. Load ROIs adds a file's ROIs to those on the image, so one set can be used on other recordings. On an image of another size, the ROIs are rescaled to the same relative positions. At the edge, loaded ROIs follow the same rule as drawn ones; an ROI with no part on the image is left out.
  • DS9 (for sky images) loads and saves SAOImage DS9 region files; see Sky Coordinates and Regions.
ROI statistics

Select an ROI to see its statistics below its row, for each visible channel on the plane shown (the current frame and Z slice, or the Z projection when one is shown). They update as you move through the image.

  • Mean, SD (the sample standard deviation, n − 1), min and max of the ROI's pixels, defined as in ImageJ's Measure, with the pixel count and area.
  • IntDen (integrated density): the ROI's area × its mean, with the area in µm² when the pixel size is known and in pixels otherwise.
  • NaN and infinite pixels of a floating-point image hold no value. They are left out, and the line says how many.

Auto-Detect ROIs

Auto-Detect ROIs finds bright regions, such as cells, in a channel and adds a polygon ROI around each. Treat the result as a starting point: every detected ROI can be edited by hand.

  1. Open the ROIs tab and click Auto-Detect ROIs. The defaults are usable, so you can click it straight away. The ROIs appear on the image, and a line says how many were added.
  2. To change how regions are found, click Detection Settings below the button and adjust the settings.
  3. Click Detect Again. It replaces the ROIs the last run added; ROIs you drew or loaded are kept. ⌘Z undoes each run.
SettingWhat it does
ChannelThe channel to search. On a Z-stack, its Z projection is used.
Detect fromCurrent Frame, or Mean of All Frames (the default for a time series). Three activity images find cells that are active but dim at rest, and are offered for a series of two or more frames: SD over Time (each pixel's sample SD through the series), Max − Mean (how far it rises at its peak) and Correlation with Neighbors (the mean Pearson correlation of each pixel's time course with its eight neighbors', as in CaImAn and Suite2p).
Smoothing (σ, px)A Gaussian blur applied before thresholding, so that noise isn't picked up as cells (1 px by default; 0 turns it off; up to 10).
Background radius (px)0 (off) by default. Removes the background before thresholding: at each pixel, the brightness that a square of this radius fits under (a grayscale opening), so that uneven illumination doesn't decide which cells pass. About 3 times the cells' radius suits.
Split touching cellsOn by default. Cuts a region where cells touch, along the narrow neck between them (a watershed). An oval cell stays whole.
Auto threshold (Otsu)On by default. Picks the threshold from the image's brightness histogram (Otsu 1979), taken over the 0.1st to 99.9th percentile so that one hot pixel can't stretch it. Turn it off to set Threshold yourself, as a percentage of the channel's Min to Max display range (50% to start). With a Background radius, the percentage counts up from 0; on an activity image, it is a percentage of that image's own range.
Min Area and Max Area (px²)9 and 5,000 by default. Regions outside this range are discarded. With a pixel size, the panel gives the range in µm² too.
Min Circularity0.5 by default, which keeps round and oval cells; 0 turns it off. Circularity is 4π × area ÷ perimeter² of the region's outline, with holes filled: about 1 for a round cell, 0.84 for an oval twice as long as wide, 0.66 for one three times as long, and lower for a crescent or a streak. Regions below the setting are discarded.
Exclude regions touching the frame edgeOn by default: a region cut off by the border has an unknown true size.
  • Outlines are found on the smoothed image; traces are always measured on the raw data.
  • Each outline is the line where the smoothed image crosses the threshold, traced between pixel centers. The pixels inside it are exactly the detected region, holes filled, and two ROIs never share a pixel.

Find Spots

Find Spots finds beads, puncta and other bright spots with TrackMate's LoG detector (Tinevez et al. 2017) and measures each one's size and intensity. Use it to count spots, or to check a microscope's point spread function on a bead slide.

  1. Open the ROIs tab and go to Find Spots. With several channels, choose the channel.
  2. Set Radius, the spots' estimated radius (2.5 by default), in the image's pixel-size unit (µm for a microscope image), or in pixels when it has none.
  3. Set Quality ≥ (50 by default): the detector's response at a spot's center must reach this. Raise it to leave out faint or noisy spots.
  4. Check Median filter to run a 3 × 3 median filter first, against shot noise and hot pixels. Leave Sub-pixel on to refine each position.
  5. Choose where to look: This Plane, Every Frame (each time point, at the Z shown) or Z-Stack (3-D), which finds the spots in 3-D in the time point shown.
  6. To measure the spots' traces afterward, check Add the spots as ROIs.
  7. Click Find Spots. A table of every spot opens, and the Data Log gets the count and the medians.
MeasurementHow it is measured
QualityThe detector's response at the spot's center.
Local backgroundThe 3σ-clipped median of a ring from 2 to 3 radii out.
PeakThe spot's peak above that background.
Net intensityThe sum in a circle of the radius, less the background.
FWHM (major and minor) and roundnessFrom a 2-D Gaussian fitted to the background-subtracted box around the spot: the full width at half maximum along its long and short axes, and their ratio, short ÷ long (1 is round).
Axial FWHM (Z-Stack)From a Gaussian plus a constant fitted to the values along Z through the spot's center.
  • The detector filters the image with a Laplacian of Gaussian of σ = radius ÷ √2 (√3 in 3-D), as TrackMate does, so a spot of about the radius gives the strongest response.
  • Add the spots as ROIs adds a circle ROI of the radius at each spot of the time point shown (at most 500), as one step to undo.

For a bead slide, set the radius to about the bead's apparent radius (0.1–0.2 µm for sub-resolution beads), use Z-Stack (3-D), and compare the median FWHM with the objective's expected resolution.

Measure Traces

Measure Intensity Traces

Measure takes each ROI's mean intensity in every frame and plots it as a trace: raw, or as ΔF/F₀, ΔF or a z-score.

  1. Draw or detect the ROIs (see ROIs, above).
  2. Open the Analyze tab and choose the Sweep Mode (ΔF/F₀ by default).
  3. For ΔF/F₀, ΔF or a baseline z-score, choose the Baseline (F₀) and its frames.
  4. Under Background, choose what to subtract: a background ROI, a ring around each ROI, the neuropil, or nothing.
  5. Under Photobleaching, choose a correction if the signal fades over the recording.
  6. Click Measure. Every visible ROI except the background ROI is measured in every frame, for each visible channel, and the traces appear in the sweep graph below the image.
  7. After you change a setting or an ROI, click Measure again. The graph's header says when the traces are out of date.

With more than one channel, each trace is named by ROI and channel. An image whose intensities a correction changed shows a warning in the tab (see Intensities and ΔF/F₀, below).

Sweep Mode
Sweep ModeWhat the trace shows
Raw IntensityThe ROI's mean pixel value, in camera counts (ADU), or in a.u. for a calibrated file such as a 32-bit float or ratio image.
ΔF/F₀(F − F₀) / F₀, the fractional change from baseline.
ΔFF − F₀, the change from baseline.
Z-score(F − mean) / SD. Under Mean and SD of, choose Whole Trace (every measured point, with the SD ÷ n) or Baseline (the mean and sample SD of the baseline frames, before frame averaging).

A Whole Trace z-score compares the shapes of traces of very different brightness, but every transient raises the SD and lowers every z-score. To judge how far an event stands above the noise, use Baseline.

Baseline (F₀)
BaselineF₀ is taken from
First N FramesThe first N frames (10 by default).
Frame RangeThe frames from one number to another, inclusive, numbered from 1 as in the frame counter.
Time WindowThe frames whose time lies between two times in seconds, ends included, with the first frame at 0 s. Unevenly spaced frames use their recorded times. It needs a frame interval.
Sliding PercentileFor each frame, a low percentile (the 8th by default) of the frames within half the Window (30 s by default; in frames when there is no frame interval) on either side. F₀ then follows slow drift and photobleaching (Dombeck et al. 2007).
  • F₀ from the: the Mean (the default) or the Median of the baseline frames. The median, with 1.4826 × the median absolute deviation as its spread, is barely moved by a transient that falls inside the baseline.
  • Frame counts and numbers are acquired frames, even when Frame avg is above 1×: F₀ is taken from exactly those frames, before averaging.
  • Sliding Percentile: a low percentile of noisy frames sits below the baseline itself (1.41 noise SDs at the 8th), so F₀ is raised by that amount, from the trace's frame-to-frame noise. Keep the window several times longer than a transient and well under the bleaching time constant. With a baseline z-score, the scale is the robust SD of the trace about F₀.
  • When ΔF/F₀ is blank: if F₀ is not more than three standard errors above zero, as happens when background subtraction removes almost all the signal, ΔF/F₀ is not computed. The trace (with Sliding Percentile, the point) is drawn as a gap, and the Data Log names the ROI and channel. Use ΔF or Raw Intensity for such traces.
  • A baseline that holds no frame gives no F₀; an orange note under the fields says why.
Background and neuropil subtraction

These are applied to each ROI's mean, frame by frame and in this order, before Sweep Mode. Nothing is clipped at zero: near the background level, noise swings both ways, and clipping would bias F₀ and every ΔF/F₀ upward.

  • Subtract background: the background ROI's mean. Mark one ROI as BG in the ROIs tab first; the panel names the one in use.
  • Local background (a ring per ROI): in place of a background ROI, each ROI's own background, the 3σ-clipped median (or mean, or SExtractor's mode) of a ring around its outline that starts Gap pixels out (2 by default) and is Width pixels wide (4 by default), leaving out every other ROI but the background ROI. It is better than one background ROI when the background is uneven.
  • Subtract neuropil: F − r × Fneuropil, with r = 0.7 by default (the usual two-photon value; 0 to 2). The neuropil is a ring around each ROI from 2 px out, widened 5 px at a time until it holds 350 pixels (up to 50 px), leaving out every ROI's pixels. With a background too: (F − B) − r·(Fnp − B). A line ROI has no ring and isn't corrected.
  • Subtract (Channels tab, two or more channels): another channel's trace of the same ROI, for example to remove bleed-through or a reference signal. Each channel has its own background and neuropil taken off first.
Photobleaching

Off (the default), Single Exponential or Double Exponential. An offset plus one or two exponential decays is fitted to each trace, after the subtractions above and before Sweep Mode. The fit is robust (iteratively reweighted with Tukey's bisquare), so transients barely pull it. The decay is then undone, F' = C + (F − C)·g(0)/g(t), so the trace keeps its starting brightness and a constant offset isn't scaled. A trace with no clear decay is left as it is, with a note, and the correction is capped at 20×. For ΔF/F₀, a Sliding Percentile baseline already follows bleaching.

Frame averaging

Frame avg (Channels tab; 1× to 10×, 1× by default) averages this many consecutive frames into each point of the measured traces, which lowers noise at the cost of time resolution. Each point is plotted at the mean time of its frames, and frames at the end that don't fill a whole group are left out. The image and exported movies are not averaged.

How an ROI is measured
  • Each frame's value is the mean of the pixels whose centers lie inside the ROI. An ROI too small to hold a pixel center takes the pixels it touches, and a line takes the pixels along it. Parts of an ROI outside the image are left out.
  • The ROIs tab gives the number of pixels each area ROI measures and their area, which is what the trace averages.
  • With a drift correction applied, the values are taken from the corrected frames (see Live Drift Correction, below).
  • A frame whose plane, or any Z slice of it, can't be read is a gap in the trace, and the Data Log counts them.

The Sweep Graph

After Measure, the graph below the playback controls shows one sweep for each ROI, in the ROI's color. With more than one channel, each channel of an ROI has its own dash pattern (the first solid). The Y axis follows the Sweep Mode: F (ADU), ΔF/F₀, ΔF (ADU) or Z-score, with a.u. in place of ADU for a calibrated file. The X axis is time, or the frame number when the file has no frame interval.

ToDo this
Step through the sweepsPress Tab or Shift-Tab, or use the buttons in the graph's header; All shows every sweep again. The others stay in the legend, dimmed.
Go to the first or last sweepPress the comma or the period key.
Show one more sweepPress Space, in an image with one time point. In a T-series, Space plays the movie.
ZoomDrag in the plot area to zoom both axes to the rectangle. Drag on the Y-axis strip or on the X-axis tick numbers to zoom one axis.
Type exact limitsDouble-click the Y-axis strip or the X-axis tick numbers.
Fit the dataDouble-click the plot area.
Rename an axis labelClick the X or Y pencil button above the graph. Only the label changes, not the numbers. Reset brings back the default label.
Remove the tracesClick Clear in the header. The ROIs are kept.

Send to Graph, Spreadsheet and CSV

  • Send to Graph (in the sweep graph's header) opens all traces on one graph in a Graph window, with the Y unit of the Sweep Mode they were measured in, for grouping, statistics and export. If the window from the last Send to Graph is still open, it is reused.
  • Spreadsheet (in the toolbar, after Measure) opens the traces in a new spreadsheet window: a Time(s) column (Frame when the file has no frame interval), then a column for each sweep, labeled with the ROI name, the channel when there is more than one, and the Sweep Mode's unit. After measuring again, click Spreadsheet again.
  • Export Sweeps as CSV… (in the toolbar's Export menu) saves the same table as a CSV file.
  • All three hold exactly the values in the sweep graph, with the Sweep Mode applied, against the same X: time, or frame number. With frame averaging, each point sits at the center of its frames.
  • Unevenly spaced frames are sent to a graph as X-Y data, each point at its own time. Filters, spectra and other analyses that assume evenly spaced samples will be wrong on them, as the Data Log notes.

After sending to a graph, use the Grouping panel to arrange the sweeps, or Groups mode to compare ROIs side by side.

Correct Images

The Correct Tab

The Correct tab's sections are in the order corrections are made: Shading, Debayer, Background, Frame Quality, Registration, Channel Alignment and Average Frames. Click a section's title to open it. Every tool but Frame Quality and Live Drift makes a new image, named for what was done (such as Corrected ·, Debayered · or Registered ·), and leaves the original unchanged. The Data Log says what each did.

  • Frame Quality, Registration and Average Frames appear for a time-lapse, Channel Alignment for an image with several channels, and Debayer for a one-channel image.

Intensities and ΔF/F₀

Some corrections keep intensities that measure the light; others change them. Each section of the Correct tab ends with a line that says which: Intensities: kept, or changed.

CorrectionIntensities
Dark and flat shading, BaSiC's flatfieldKept. They scale each pixel and take out the camera's offset. The dark subtraction even makes ΔF/F₀ more accurate, since an offset left in F₀ shrinks it.
BaSiC's time-lapse baseline removalChanged. A level is taken out of each frame, which changes F₀.
Debayer, Registration, Channel AlignmentKept. Values are interpolated between pixels; no light is added or taken away.
BackgroundChanged, not for ΔF/F₀. The background is fitted under each object, frame by frame, so it takes away part of a large or bright object's own light, and more of it when the object brightens. F₀ and ΔF shrink by different amounts, and ΔF/F₀ is biased (Waters 2009).
Average FramesKept, unless Match backgrounds is on, which shifts each frame's level.
  • An image whose intensities were changed says so: the Analyze tab shows a warning, and the Data Log repeats it when traces are measured.
  • Copy ROIs to Original (in the ROIs tab of such an image) adds a copy of its ROIs to the image it was made from, in the same places, and brings that image to the front: find or segment the objects on the background-subtracted image, then measure ΔF/F₀ on the original. It is offered when the new image keeps the original's pixels where they were (not after Registration or Channel Alignment).

Shading Correction

Uneven illumination makes the edge of a widefield image dimmer than its center, and the camera adds its own dark level. Shading corrects both, from dark and flat images or, without them, from the image itself.

Correct with dark and flat images
  1. Open the dark and the flat as images of their own, the same size as the image to correct. The dark is taken with no light at the same exposure; the flat is an evenly lit field, such as a fluorescent slide, for each channel.
  2. In the image to correct, open Correct › Shading and leave the method on Dark & Flat Images.
  3. Choose each channel's Dark and Flat from the menus; either can stay at None. Use This Dark for Every Channel gives the first channel's dark to the channels without one.
  4. Choose the arithmetic: Exact (32-bit) or Same as @Cam (16-bit). For Exact, choose how the Masters are combined.
  5. To repair hot pixels, check Repair hot pixels at and set the limit.
  6. Click Make Corrected Image.
  • corrected = (raw − dark) × mean(flat − dark) / (flat − dark), the textbook correction (Model & Burkhardt 2001). Every plane of the image chosen as a dark or flat is averaged into its master. A pixel whose flat holds 5% of the flat's mean or less (dust, the edge of the field) is left as it is.
  • Exact (32-bit), the default: ccdproc's arithmetic, in double precision. The result keeps its full precision, and noise below zero isn't clipped. Masters: Average (the default); Average, 5σ clipped (the CCD Data Reduction Guide's recipe, which leaves out a spike; for 10 or more frames); or Median (for a flat made from many fields of the sample).
  • Same as @Cam (16-bit): @Cam's own arithmetic, with the masters averaged in whole numbers and the result rounded and clamped to the camera's range, so the numbers match an image that @Cam corrected while it was taken. It needs camera counts (whole numbers from 0).
  • Repair hot pixels at (off by default; 5 MAD-std): pixels whose dark current (mean) or noise (standard deviation) in the channel's dark planes lies beyond this many robust SDs above the median are replaced by the median of their good neighbors. It needs a dark; with one dark plane, only hot pixels are found. The Data Log counts them.
  • If @Cam already corrected the image when it was taken, the section says so: correcting again would apply the correction twice.
Correct without flat images (BaSiC)
  1. In Correct › Shading, choose BaSiC (No Flat Images).
  2. Check Estimate the darkfield too only if the image has had no dark subtraction.
  3. For a time-lapse, decide on Time-lapse: take out each frame's baseline (on by default). It removes the background's slow change from photobleaching, which changes intensities: uncheck it if you will measure ΔF/F₀. With Keep the mean level on, the baselines' mean is added back; off, the background goes to about 0.
  4. Click Make Corrected Image. With Also open the flatfield on, the fitted profiles open too, so you can check them.

BaSiC estimates the flatfield, and optionally the darkfield, from the image's own planes (Peng et al. 2017): corrected = (I − darkfield) / flatfield. It needs several images of the channel (tiles, time points or Z planes); a few dozen work best. With more than 300, the profiles are fitted on 300 of them, evenly spaced, and applied to every plane.

Debayer

A color camera's sensor sees through a mosaic of red, green and blue filters, one over each pixel, in a 2 × 2 pattern (the Bayer pattern). A raw frame holds that mosaic as one gray channel, which looks finely checkered. Debayer estimates the two colors each pixel didn't see from its neighbors and makes a new image with Red, Green and Blue channels.

  1. Correct the mosaic's shading first (see Shading Correction, above), since each filter color has its own dark level and flat.
  2. Open Correct › Debayer and choose the Pattern. From the File uses the pattern the file records (the Channels tab says when it records one). Otherwise choose RGGB, BGGR, GRBG or GBRG: the colors of the top-left 2 × 2 pixels, row by row, as the image is shown. The camera's manual gives it; a wrong pattern swaps red and blue, or gives a checkered green.
  3. Choose the Method, and Whole Numbers or Exact (32-bit).
  4. Click Make Color Image.
MethodHow the missing colors are found
Malvar–He–Cutler (the default)Interpolation corrected by the gradient of the color the pixel saw: sharper, with fewer color fringes (Malvar, He & Cutler 2004).
MenonGreen is estimated along rows and along columns, and at each pixel the direction whose color differences vary less is kept, for sharp edges with few color fringes (Menon, Andriani & Calvagno 2007).
BilinearEach missing color is the mean of its nearest samples.
Super-PixelEach 2 × 2 cell becomes one pixel (red, the two greens' mean, blue). Nothing is interpolated. The image has half the width and height, and its pixels are twice the size.
  • Whole Numbers (the default): values are rounded and kept in the camera's range (0 to 4,095 for a 12-bit camera). Malvar–He–Cutler can overshoot at a sharp edge, and the Data Log counts the values clamped. It needs camera counts. Exact (32-bit) keeps full precision, for a mosaic already corrected for shading.
  • No white balance is applied: the colors stay the camera's own, linear, for measuring.
  • Registration, alignment and averaging come after debayering.

Background Subtraction

Background takes an uneven background out of the whole image: out-of-focus haze, autofluorescence, a glow around a bright region, or a gradient across the field. Use it for finding, segmenting and showing objects. It changes intensities, so measure them on the original (see Intensities and ΔF/F₀, above).

  1. Open Correct › Background and choose the Method: Rolling Ball, Sliding Paraboloid or Mesh (SExtractor).
  2. For Rolling Ball and Sliding Paraboloid, set Radius (50 pixels by default): at least the radius of the largest object that isn't background, such as a cell or a nucleus. From ROIs sets it to half the largest ROI's longer side. For Mesh, set Box (64 pixels by default) and Filter (3 × 3 by default).
  3. For dark objects on a light background (brightfield, a stained section), check Light background.
  4. Choose what to Make: Subtracted Image, Background Image or Both. For an 8- or 16-bit image with either ImageJ method, also choose 32-bit Values or Same as ImageJ.
  5. With several channels, tick the Channels to process. The others are copied unchanged.
  6. Click Make Background-Subtracted Image. Every Z plane and time point is processed on its own.
MethodHow the background is found
Rolling BallImageJ's Subtract Background (Sternberg 1983). A ball of the radius is rolled under the image, and whatever it can't reach is kept. A smaller ball takes away part of the objects; a larger one leaves more of the background's unevenness.
Sliding ParaboloidImageJ's alternative: a paraboloid of the same curvature slid along the rows, the columns and both diagonals. It follows the background closer to the image's edges and corners. @Graph follows ImageJ 1.54t (April 2026), which corrected it, so earlier ImageJ and Fiji versions give somewhat different backgrounds.
Mesh (SExtractor)The background map astronomers use (Bertin & Arnouts 1996), with photutils' defaults. The image is cut into boxes. In each box, values beyond 3 SDs of the median are set aside, repeatedly, and the background is 2.5 × median − 1.5 × mean (the median in a crowded box). A median over neighboring boxes (Filter) takes out boxes a bright object spoiled, and a smooth spline joins the boxes. It suits large, smooth gradients under many small objects.
  • Disable smoothing: ImageJ normally finds the background from a 3 × 3 mean of the image, so that noise doesn't pull it down. This turns that off.
  • 32-bit Values (the default): value − background at full precision, so noise around the background stays around 0, some of it below. Same as ImageJ (8- or 16-bit): ImageJ's own result on an 8- or 16-bit image, rounded and clamped at 0, with a light background made white.
  • Background RMS image (Mesh) also makes an image of the background's noise, for setting thresholds.
  • Debayer a raw color mosaic first.

Frame Quality

Frame Quality measures every frame of a time-lapse, to find where the focus drifted or the sample moved.

  1. Open Correct › Frame Quality. To count spots in each frame as well, check Count spots and their FWHM.
  2. Click Measure Frame Quality. A table of every frame opens, and the flagged frames are listed in the section and in the Data Log.
  3. Average Frames can leave the flagged frames out. Clear Flags forgets them.
  • It measures the Registration Channel (set under Registration › Live Drift): two sharpness scores, normalized variance (Groen et al. 1985) and Tenengrad (the mean squared Sobel gradient), which fall when a frame is less sharp; the background (median) and the noise; optionally the spot count and the spots' median FWHM, which widens with blur; and the drift, when a drift correction is computed.
  • A frame is flagged when a measure is more than 3 robust SDs (1.4826 × MAD) from the series' median the bad way: sharpness lower, FWHM larger, fewer spots, or a brighter background. The drift is reported, not flagged. A series of fewer than 5 frames isn't flagged.

Live Drift Correction

Live Drift corrects slow XY drift that would move cells out from under their ROIs during a long time-lapse. Each frame is shifted, without rotation or warping, to line up with a reference frame. No new image is made: the correction applies to the display, exports and measurements, and can be turned off. For rotation or scale, use Registered Copy (below).

  1. Open Correct › Registration and choose Live Drift.
  2. Choose the Registration Channel: a bright channel with steady structure, rather than a sparsely active indicator.
  3. Set the Reference Frame (Use Current takes the frame shown) and Average, the number of frames around it that are averaged into the reference (10 by default; 1 for none).
  4. Set Max Drift Search (50 px by default) comfortably above the largest drift you expect.
  5. Click Compute Drift Correction. It turns the correction on and reports the largest shift found.
  6. Uncheck and check Apply Correction to compare the image without and with the correction. Clear discards it.
  • With Average above 1, the reference is the mean of that many frames centered on the reference frame, each first aligned to it, and every frame is then registered to that mean. This makes the reference less noisy, which helps at low photon counts.
  • Max Drift Search is a distance in pixels, not per axis, from 5 px to half the image's short edge.
  • A frame is accepted only when its best match stands out clearly and lies inside the search distance. Frames that could not be registered are counted in the status line and listed in the Data Log; their shift is interpolated in time from the nearest registered frames.
  • On a Z-stack, the channel's Z projection is aligned.
  • Changing the channel, its Z projection, the reference frame, the averaging or Max Drift Search clears a computed correction; compute it again.
  • The correction also applies to Auto-Detect ROIs' Mean of All Frames. Export Data as TIFF saves the pixels as recorded.
  • Measure takes each ROI's values from the shifted frame, interpolating between pixels. Pixels shifted in from beyond the frame's edge were never imaged, so an ROI that drift moves partly out of view is measured, in every frame, on the pixels that stay in view in all of them. The Data Log says how many frames this affected.

Registered Copy

Registered Copy aligns every frame of a time-lapse to the reference frame with rotation and, optionally, scale, and resamples every channel and Z plane into a new image. Use it when the sample turns, or when every later tool should read aligned frames.

  1. Open Correct › Registration and choose Registered Copy. It uses the Registration Channel, Reference Frame and Max Drift Search set under Live Drift.
  2. Choose By Image or By Spots.
  3. Choose the transform: Shift, Rigid (shift and rotation; the default) or Similarity (shift, rotation and scale).
  4. Choose the Interpolation (Lanczos-3 by default).
  5. Click Make Registered Image. A table gives every frame's rotation, scale and shift.
  • By Image finds the transform that best matches each frame's pixels to the reference's, by least squares, coarse to fine, as Fiji's StackReg does (Thévenaz et al. 1998), with the frame's brightness free to differ (bleaching). It works on any structure. With Start each frame from its neighbor's on (the default), a slow turn is followed across a long recording.
  • By Spots finds the spots Find Spots would find (its Radius and Quality), matches them to the reference frame's by the triangles they form, and fits the transform to them by least squares. It is best for beads, puncta or nuclei.
  • Rotation and scale are about the image's center. On a Z-stack, the channel's maximum over Z is registered.
  • Interpolation: Lanczos-3 is the sharpest and keeps a spot's total intensity. Lanczos-3, Clamped damps the faint dark rings Lanczos can leave around very bright points. Bicubic, Bilinear and Nearest are the others. Keep total intensity (on by default) scales values by the change of area when the scale changes.
  • A frame that can't be registered takes the nearest registered frame's transform, and the Data Log lists it.

Channel Alignment

Objectives focus colors slightly differently, so the channels of one image are shifted and magnified relative to one another (lateral chromatic aberration), enough to skew colocalization. Channel Alignment measures this on an image of multicolor beads and corrects other images with it.

  1. Open an image of multicolor beads, and open Correct › Channel Alignment.
  2. Choose the reference channel in Onto, and the Transform: Similarity (shift, rotation and scale; the default) covers chromatic aberration, Affine adds shear, and Shift only moves.
  3. Click Measure From This Image. The Data Log gives each channel's beads matched, its RMS residual, shift, rotation and scale. The alignment is kept, also after you quit @Graph.
  4. On the image to correct (the same size and number of channels), click Make Aligned Image. Every channel but the reference is resampled onto it, in a new image.

The beads are found in every channel at the frame shown (the maximum over Z for a stack), with Find Spots' Radius and Quality, and matched to the reference channel's. Each channel's transform is fitted to them by least squares.

Average Frames

Average Frames averages a time-lapse's frames, pixel by pixel, into a new image: every N frames into one, for a cleaner recording at a lower frame rate, or all of them into one clean image. Frame avg in the Channels tab, by contrast, averages the measured traces only.

  1. Open Correct › Average Frames and choose Every with a number of frames (5 by default), or All Frames.
  2. Choose Mean or Median. With Mean, choose a rejection, which sets outliers aside at each pixel first (Winsorized Sigma Clipping at 3σ by default), and optionally check Weight by noise.
  3. If the frames bleach, check Match backgrounds (bleaching).
  4. Click Make Averaged Image.
  • Rejection sets aside a camera spike or a passing particle, by the same definitions as Stack Frames. With fewer than about 6 frames per group, it has little to go on.
  • Weight by noise: cleaner frames count more (weights 1 / noise²).
  • Match backgrounds: each frame's background level is matched to the group's first, so that bleaching between frames isn't taken for outliers. It changes intensities.
  • Leave out frames Frame Quality flagged (on by default) is offered once Frame Quality has flagged frames.
  • A last group that isn't full is left out. Each new frame is timed at the mean time of the frames its group keeps, so with even frames and none left out, the new interval is N times the old.

Toolkits Tab

Part of the Pharmacology & Biochemistry toolkit.

Part of the Spectroscopy toolkit.

Part of the Astronomy toolkit.

The Toolkits tab appears while a toolkit with image tools is shown. Choose a tool from the menu at the top of the tab, which lists each one as toolkit › tool. Show or Hide Toolkits… in that menu opens Settings › Toolkits. A FITS image opens the tab on Aperture Photometry, and other images on the tool chosen last. Each tool has its own page:
