Annotate, Save and Export

Text & Shape Annotations

The Add Overlay menu at the top right of the image adds movable text labels, lines and arrows, separate from ROIs. It works the same way on Graph and Chart windows.

  1. Choose Add Text, Add Line or Add Arrow from Add Overlay.
  2. Drag the overlay into place. Drag the middle of a line or arrow to move it whole, keeping its length and angle; drag an end to change them.
  3. Click the overlay to open its editor, for font, color, size and style. Duplicate there makes a copy with the same style. Delete an overlay from its editor.
  • While dragging an end: hold ⇧ Shift to snap to horizontal or vertical; hold ⌥ Option to rotate around the other end at a fixed length; hold both to do both.
  • Drag the editor by its ≡ handle if it covers something.
  • On a Graph or Chart window, Position by data value in the editor pins a label, or both ends of a line or arrow, to X and Y values, typed in the units the axes show. On a Bar, Box or Horizontal Bar chart the category axis has no unit: it counts the categories from 0, so 0 is the first category's center, 1 the second's, and 0.5 halfway between them. An image window and a spike-train raster place overlays on the canvas only.
  • Overlays stay in place when the window is resized, appear in every export (image files, clipboard, PDF, movie) and are saved in the .@graph file. Every change to an overlay can be undone with ⌘Z.

Copy and Paste Image Style

Copy Style and Paste Style carry display settings and ROIs from one Image window to another without touching the pixel data, to give a set of recordings the same look and ROI layout.

  1. In the source window, press ⌥⌘C, click Copy Style in the toolbar, or right-click the image and choose Copy Style.
  2. In the target window, press ⌥⌘V, click Paste Style, or right-click and choose Paste Style. ⌘Z undoes the whole paste.
  • What is copied: each channel's LUT, color, display range, stretch (with its value), emission wavelength, Grayscale, Smoothing, Z projection and Subtract channel; Sweep Mode, baseline, Subtract background, neuropil subtraction, photobleaching correction and the scale bar; and all ROIs.
  • Pasted ROIs replace the target's ROIs; a style copied with no ROIs leaves them. If the images differ in size, the ROIs are rescaled to the same relative positions.
  • If the source has more channels than the target, the settings go to the first channels and an alert says so. Extra channels in the target are left unchanged.

Saving and Reopening Image Sessions (.@graph)

File › Save (⌘S) saves an Image window as a .@graph file that recreates it: the pixel data, ROIs, display settings and analysis settings. The file holds the pixel data, so it doesn't need the original image files.

  • What is saved: all pixel data, losslessly, with the original bit depth; the ROIs; each channel's name, display and Subtract setting; the frame interval, pixel size and microscope setup; the measuring settings (Sweep Mode, baseline, subtractions, photobleaching correction, frame averaging); drift correction; the scale bar, overlays, axis labels, smoothing and rotation; the Auto-Detect ROIs settings; for a FITS image, every frame's header and Aperture Photometry's apertures and settings; and the toolkit tools' work (gel lanes and bands, plate grids, colony counts, spectrum traces, plate solutions).
  • Reopening: double-click the file or drag it onto @Graph. The window reopens with its ROIs and settings; click Measure to extract the traces again.
  • Save (⌘S) saves to the window's file without asking once it has one; the first save asks where. Save As (⇧⌘S) saves to a new name or place, and the window then belongs to the new file.
  • Unsaved changes show as a • in the window title, display changes included; moving through frames, playing or opening Orthogonal Views doesn't count. Closing such a window (⌘W) asks whether to Save, Don't Save or Cancel, and quitting (⌘Q) offers Review Changes…, Cancel, or Discard Changes and Quit.

Export Image, Movie and Data

The toolbar's Export menu has two parts. As Shown (for figures and talks) has Export Image… and Export Movie…, which save what the window shows. Raw Data (for analysis) has Export Data as TIFF… and, after Measure, Export Sweeps as CSV…, which save values. File › Export… (⇧⌘E) also opens Export Image.

Export an image
  1. Choose Export Image… from the Export menu.
  2. Choose the format: PNG, TIFF, JPEG, GIF, PDF or SVG. PNG or TIFF is best for figures. JPEG and GIF lose detail or colors, so the panel marks them with a warning.
  3. Choose the Scale and the Resolution (300 dpi by default). Click Export… to save the file.
  • As Shown exports look as the window does: the colors and display range, the Z slice or projection shown, rotation and drift correction, ROIs, overlays, the scale bar if shown, and Smoothing. Text, outlines and the scale bar keep the size they have against the image in the window, whatever the export size.
  • Scale: 1× keeps native pixels; 2×, 3×, 4×, 6× and 8× draw each image pixel as a sharp square block (blended when Smoothing is on). A large image is offered only the scales whose output stays within about 268 million pixels (6,000 × 6,000 pixels: 1× and 2×). The panel shows the output size in pixels.
  • Resolution sets only the print size stored in the file; the pixels stay the same. For PDF and SVG it sets the size of the page. PDF and SVG hold the picture as pixels, not vector shapes.
Export a movie
  1. Choose Export Movie… from the Export menu.
  2. For a file with both time and Z, choose Time Points or Z Slices under Animate. A time movie shows the Z slice or projection on screen; a Z movie flies through the slices of the current time point.
  3. Choose the format: MP4 (H.264), small and playable everywhere; ProRes 4444 (.mov), visually lossless, for editing; or TIFF Stack, every frame exactly as shown, which Fiji opens with the frame interval or Z step set.
  4. Choose the Frame rate (1 to 60 fps, or Real time when the file has a frame interval; Median rate when its frames are unevenly spaced) and the Scale (as for Export Image, a large image is offered fewer scales). To burn in each frame's time since the first frame, check Show the elapsed time on each frame (for a Z movie, Show the Z position on each frame; for a spectral cube, Show each plane's value on each frame, its wavelength, frequency or velocity).
  5. Click Export… to write the movie. It holds every acquired frame (Frame avg doesn't apply). Cancel Export stops it and leaves no file.
Export the pixel values

Export Data as TIFF… saves the measured pixel values of every channel, Z slice and time point, for analysis in Fiji, napari or Python. Colors, contrast, rotation, drift correction, ROIs and annotations are not applied.

  • Format: OME-TIFF (written as BigTIFF above 4 GB) or ImageJ TIFF (limited to 4 GB).
  • The file keeps the pixel size, Z step, frame interval, and channel names and colors. An ImageJ TIFF also keeps each channel's display range; an OME-TIFF keeps each frame's own time when the frames are unevenly spaced.
  • 8- and 16-bit values, signed ones included, are saved exactly. A 12-bit camera's image records its true bit depth, and a raw color mosaic keeps its Bayer pattern, so it can be debayered after it is opened again.
  • For a floating-point or calibrated image, choose Calibrated values (32-bit floating point, as the measurements use them) or Stored levels (16-bit). An image with pixels that hold no value is saved as calibrated values only, with those pixels as NaN.

For figures, turn Grayscale off and choose a LUT (Emission λ recommended). To analyze the pixels elsewhere, use Export Data as TIFF, not an image or a movie.

Back to Contents

Graph Tools

Graph Display Settings

How a graph looks is set in the Display category of the inspector, and the plot updates as you change a setting. Plot Style holds symbols, lines, colors and the legend; Axes & Labels holds the title, axes, ticks, scale bars, interval bars, error bars and trend/base lines; Range sets axis limits and log scales (see Graphs › Zooming); Groups sets how sweeps are grouped into panels. None of these settings changes the data.

Plot Style

  1. In the inspector, choose Display › Plot Style.
  2. Click a sweep or a group's panel on the graph to style it alone. With nothing selected you style every sweep, and the top of the panel reads "All sweeps (global)".
  3. Set the Symbol and the Line.
  4. To give the style shown to more sweeps, click Sweep, Group or All beside "Apply current style to:". Clear returns the selection to the global style.
  • Symbol: Type (None, the default, for lines only; Dot, Circle, Square, Triangle, Diamond, Cross, Plus, Tick, and filled circles, squares and triangles), Size (1–20 pt) and Color. A raster always draws ticks.
  • Line: Type (Solid, Dashed, Dotted, Dash-Dot or None), Width (0.5–5 pt) and Color.
  • Curved joins the points with a smooth curve that never passes its neighbors, for sparse X-Y data. Traces of more than 2,000 samples stay straight. If the X values double back, the curve can swing past the points; the panel says so, and sorting the table by X avoids it.
  • Wavelength color: beside each color well, type a wavelength from 380 to 700 nm in the λ field, or drag along the spectrum, and @Graph picks the matching color.
  • Palette colors: "Use rainbow spectrum for overlaid sweeps" (on by default, and named for the palette chosen in Settings › Appearance) gives each sweep its own color, which it keeps when other sweeps are shown or hidden. Choosing a line color for all sweeps turns it off. "Color by position within group" restarts the colors in each group.
  • Apply current style to: Group also clears the per-sweep styles in that group; All clears every per-sweep and per-group color, symbol and line. Y ranges, ticks, scale bars, error bars, trend lines and visibility stay per group.
  • Rename a sweep: click it on the graph, then edit the Name field at the top of the panel. The name ("Sweep N" by default) appears in the legend and wherever else the sweep is listed, and is saved in the .@graph file.

Legend

  1. In the Plot Style panel, check "Show legend". A key appears on the plot with one row per sweep: its name and a sample of its line and symbol.
  2. Optionally type a heading in "Legend title (optional):" and set the text Size (until you do, it follows the axis labels' size).
  3. Drag the legend on the plot to move it.
  4. To rename a sweep or drop its row, double-click the row. Type a new name, or click "Remove from Legend" (or press Delete): the row goes and the sweep stays on the graph.

The key always matches what is drawn. It is included in every export as shown on screen, and removed rows are saved with the file and carried by Copy Style and Paste Style.

Axes & Labels

BoxSettings
Graph Title"Show title" adds a title above the plot, with its own Size, Font and Color.
Axis Labels"Show tick labels" (the numbers at the major ticks) and "Show axis labels" (the name and unit along each axis), with their fonts, sizes and text.
AxesShow X axis, Show Y axis, Show grid (grid lines fall on the major ticks), "Rescale Y units automatically", whether each axis crosses at zero, and Axis line width.
ColorsBackground, Axis lines, Axis text and Grid. When you switch between a dark and a light background, @Graph offers to invert the other colors so they stay readable.
Tick MarksMajor and minor ticks, their lengths, Minors per major, Direction (Outside, Inside or Symmetric), and the spacing: X interval and Y interval.
  • Tick spacing: leave X interval or Y interval on "auto", or type an exact major interval (a number in axis units, or a value with a unit such as 50 ms). X is shared by all panels; Y is set per panel. A logarithmic axis places its own ticks.
  • Automatic ticks step by 1, 2 or 5 times a power of ten, and the X axis picks the time unit that fits: a 3 ms zoom reads in ms, a long recording in min. A short panel gets fewer ticks and smaller labels, so they don't overlap.
  • "Rescale Y units automatically" (on by default) does the same for Y: when a small range would need tick labels with two or more decimals, the axis switches to a smaller prefix of the channel's unit, so 0.05 mV steps read 50 µV and the label reads Voltage (µV). Only the labels change: the data, the Y range fields and every measurement stay in the channel's own unit. A logarithmic Y axis, or a Y interval you typed, keeps the unit as it is.
  • Editing an axis label or its unit changes the text only, never the values (see Graphs › Graph Title and Axis Labels).

Logarithmic Axes

Check "Logarithmic scale" under X Axis or Y Axis in Display › Range, or in the box that opens when you double-click an axis's tick labels.

  • A log axis is labeled at powers of ten, with minor ticks at 2 to 9 times each. A narrower range is labeled at 1, 2 and 5 times a power of ten, so there are always at least three labels.
  • Values at or below zero, and samples at time zero or earlier on a log time axis, are not drawn, and the Range panel says how many. A Min or Max of zero or less is ignored, and that end fits the data.
  • A log time axis shows s, ms, µs or ns, chosen from its upper end.
  • Scale bars are hidden while an axis is logarithmic, and a log Y axis shows values without junction-potential correction.

Scale Bars

  1. In the Axes & Labels panel, check "Show scale bars". An L-shaped pair of bars appears on the plot.
  2. Type the X length and Y length: a number in the unit shown, a value with a unit such as 500 ms or 50 pA, or "auto" for a round length. When groups have different units, set each group's under "Per-group Y length:".
  3. Drag the corner of the bars on the plot to move them.
  4. For a figure without axes, also uncheck Show X axis and Show Y axis.

Scale bar and interval bar labels share one font and size, on screen and in every export. The X scale bar's label uses the X axis's unit. Scale bars aren't drawn while either axis is logarithmic.

Interval Bars

An interval bar is a horizontal bar that marks a stretch of X, such as the time a treatment was applied, at a height you choose, with an optional label.

  1. In the Axes & Labels panel, check "Show interval bars" and click Add Bar. Add as many as you like.
  2. Double-click a bar on the graph, set its Start, End and Y, an optional Label, and "Label above bar" or "Label below bar", and click Apply.
  3. To remove a bar, click Delete in that box, or the trash icon beside the bar in the inspector's list. ⌘Z undoes a deletion.
  • Start, End and Y are as the axes show them: X after Set X = 0, in the axis's unit, and Y junction-potential corrected when that is on.
  • Bars are drawn in the Axis lines color, with square ends, and are included in PDF, SVG and image exports.
  • In a graph with stacked panels, bars are drawn and edited on the top panel only, using its Y scale.

Error Bars

These error bars take their size from another sweep, such as an SD or SEM loaded as its own column: at every visible point a vertical bar with caps is drawn, ± that sweep's value at the same point.

  1. In the Axes & Labels panel, under Error Bars, check "Show error bars" ("Show for" and the group's name when there are several groups).
  2. Choose the Source sweep that holds the ± values.

Values are paired sample by sample, so the source sweep should have the same number of samples and the same sample rate as the sweeps it is drawn on.

Trend/Base Line

A reference line for a group, computed from the group's average trace over an X range you choose and drawn across the full width of the panel.

  1. In the Axes & Labels panel, under Trend/Base Line, check "Show trend/base line" ("Show for" and the group's name when there are several groups).
  2. Choose the Mode: Trend (regression), a fitted straight line, or Base (average), a flat line at the mean Y value.
  3. Type Fit start and Fit end, the X range of the data used, as the X axis reads them.
  4. Optionally set the line's Color and Style (by default the axis color, dashed).
  • Under Mode the panel shows the line's equation, which you can select and copy: Y = Slope·t + Intercept (X for X-Y data), or Y = Mean for a base line.
  • For a group of several sweeps, the fit uses their sample-by-sample average.
  • On a logarithmic axis the fitted straight line is drawn as the curve it becomes there.

Grouping Modes

A group is a set of sweeps drawn together in one panel, with its own Y axis. Choose the grouping under Sweep Grouping in Display › Groups:

ChoiceResult
Single group (all sweeps)All sweeps overlaid in one panel (⌥⌘G).
Split by channelOne group per recorded channel, with its own Y axis and unit. Offered when the file has more than one channel.
Combine groups of NEach run of N consecutive sweeps forms one group (sweeps 1–4, 5–8 and so on).
Combine every NN groups, with the sweeps dealt out in turn (sweep 1 → group 1, sweep 2 → group 2…), for example for interleaved channels.
Separate all sweepsOne panel per sweep (⌥⌘S).

"Clear all style overrides", in the same panel, removes every per-sweep and per-group color, symbol and line. Each group keeps its own Y range, ticks, scale bar, error bars, trend line and visibility.

Group Order & Visibility

  • Order: with more than one group, the Groups panel lists them under Group Order & Visibility. Click a group's ↑ or ↓ to move it; "Reset order" restores the original order. The order is saved in the .@graph file.
  • Hide or show: click a group's Hide or Show button in that list ("Show all" brings every group back), or right-click a panel on the graph. The Groups button above the plot (the eye) lists every group with its sweeps, such as "Sweeps 1, 4, 7", and shows or hides each with a click.
  • Panel heights: drag the gap between two stacked panels up or down (the pointer shows ↕ over it) to make one taller and its neighbor shorter. Double-click a gap, or right-click a panel and choose Reset Panel Heights, to make all panels equal again. Only the heights change, not the Y ranges; they are saved with the graph and used in every export.

Match Y Ranges, in the Range panel, gives all groups with the same unit the same Y range, so figure panels can be compared by eye.

Back to Contents

Modifying Graphs

The panels of the inspector's Modify category change the values in a graph: filter or smooth them, subtract a baseline, scale them, shift the X axis, or make a resampled, integrated or differentiated copy. They change the graph, never the recording file it was read from. Each change can be undone with ⌘Z and redone with ⇧⌘Z.

  • Apply to: Filter, Smoothing and Baseline each have an Apply to menu: Selected group, All groups, All sweeps, Visible sweeps or Selected sweep. Filter and Smoothing start on Selected group, and Baseline on All groups.
  • Channel: when the sweeps come from more than one recorded channel, the Channel menu under Apply to limits the change to one channel, so that All sweeps need not change a command or stimulus channel. All channels is the default.
  • Fitted curves and AP markers on the graph are never changed: they are drawn from the data, not recorded.
  • Pressing Return (↩) in a number field runs the panel's main action.
  • Wait for the message under the button before you save. Undo, or another edit, made before it appears cancels the operation.

Filter / Smooth

  1. In the inspector, choose Modify › Filter/Smoothing (⇧⌘F).
  2. Under Filter, choose a Type (see the table below).
  3. Type its Frequency (Hz). Band-pass takes a Low cutoff and a High cutoff, Band-stop a Low edge and a High edge, and Boxcar and Median a number of Points.
  4. For a low-pass, high-pass, band-pass or band-stop filter, set the Order (4 by default), and leave Causal off unless you need it.
  5. Choose Apply to and, if offered, a Channel.
  6. Click Apply Filter. The message under the button says what was done.
TypeWhat it does
Low-passRemoves high-frequency noise. A Butterworth filter: the flattest passband and the steepest roll-off for its order, but it overshoots a step (by about 7% at order 4) and rings after it.
Low-pass (Bessel)The type many amplifiers have (their 4- and 8-pole settings). It barely overshoots a step (0.5% at order 4), so rise times and waveform shapes are kept, at the price of a gentler roll-off.
High-passRemoves slow drift.
Band-passKeeps the band between the two cutoffs.
Band-stop (notch)Attenuates the band between the two edges. Use it when interference covers a range; for one frequency, Mains hum and Single-frequency are more precise.
Mains hum (50/60 Hz)Removes power-line interference at the frequency measured in the data, and only where it is present. See Mains Hum, below.
Single-frequencySubtracts a fitted sine wave at one exact frequency, and its harmonics only if you ask (Harmonics: Fundamental only by default). Use it for a known, steady frequency, such as a pump or chopper. It does not test whether the frequency is there, so it also works on sweeps too short for Mains hum.
BoxcarA running average over Points samples. Fast, but it blurs edges.
Three-pointThe lightest smoothing: a ¼, ½, ¼ weighted average of each sample and its two neighbors.
MedianA running median over Points samples. It keeps sharp transitions better than Boxcar.

Filter settings

  • Order: 1–8. A higher order cuts more steeply but rings more after a sudden step; the roll-off far beyond the cutoff is 12 dB per octave per order. A band filter takes even orders only; its order is that of the whole filter, so each side of the band rolls off at 6 dB per octave per order.
  • Causal (one pass, forward only): off by default. Off, the filter runs forward and then backward (zero-phase), so nothing shifts in time, but each event's filtered edge starts slightly before the event itself, which can make an onset or latency read early. On, the filter runs once, as an analog filter does: nothing appears before an event, but the whole trace is delayed and the roll-off is half as steep. For a low-pass, the panel and the message give the delay; subtract it from measured times. A causal high-pass or band filter delays each frequency differently, so it changes event shapes.
  • Every cutoff and band edge you type is the −3 dB point of the filter as applied, both passes together. (Forward-backward filtering in MATLAB and SciPy puts the typed frequency at −6 dB.)
  • A cutoff or band edge must be below the Nyquist frequency (half the sample rate) of every sweep filtered; otherwise the panel says so and nothing is changed. The panel shows the Nyquist frequency. A low-pass cutoff or band-pass high edge left at its 5000 Hz default is lowered below a slower recording's Nyquist frequency, and the panel says so; a value you type is never lowered.
  • A low-pass filter leaves the baseline level unchanged (−70 mV stays −70 mV). Within about one filter time constant of each end of a sweep, the result is an estimate.
  • Points (Boxcar and Median): the window in samples, at least 3 and odd; an even value runs one point longer.

Smooth

  1. In the same panel, go to Smoothing, below the filters.
  2. Choose the Method: Boxcar (moving average), Gaussian or Savitzky-Golay (the default).
  3. Type the Window (ms) (2 ms by default). The line under the field shows the window in samples.
  4. For Savitzky-Golay, set the Polynomial order (2–6, 4 by default).
  5. Choose Apply to and click Apply Smoothing.

Savitzky-Golay fits a polynomial over the window, so it keeps peak heights better than an average; higher orders keep peaks closer to the data but smooth less. Gaussian's window spans ±3 standard deviations. Missing samples stay missing.

Mains Hum (50/60 Hz)

  1. In Modify › Filter/Smoothing, set Type to Mains hum (50/60 Hz).
  2. Type the nominal line frequency in Frequency (Hz): 60 in North America, 50 in most of Europe and Asia.
  3. Choose Harmonics: Those present (the default), Fundamental only, or First N.
  4. Choose Estimate from: Whole sweep (the default), Between cursors A–B or Outside cursors A–B.
  5. Choose Apply to and click Apply Filter. The message gives the frequency and harmonics removed, and the Data Log lists each sweep, with why any was left unchanged.

How hum is found and removed

  • Frequency: grid frequency drifts, so the filter measures the frequency actually present within ±0.5 Hz of the nominal value. If the strongest frequency in that range sits at its edge, there is no hum peak in the range (a real 59.4 Hz rhythm, say), and nothing is removed.
  • Test: each harmonic's power must exceed 20 times the background power 3 to 5 frequency bins either side. The fundamental is tested too, so a sweep without hum is left unchanged. Those present removes each harmonic that passes, up to the 40th; Fundamental only and First N remove what they name once the fundamental passes.
  • The test needs at least 8 cycles of the line frequency (133 ms at 60 Hz, 160 ms at 50 Hz). On a shorter sweep nothing is removed and the message says why; use Single-frequency if you know hum is there.
  • Fit: a straight line plus the sine waves is fitted to the data, and only the sine waves are subtracted, from the whole sweep. Almost no bandwidth is removed, so a real 58 Hz oscillation survives, and a resting level or slow drift is not mistaken for hum.
  • The fit is robust: samples that a line plus hum cannot explain, such as a response, are set aside (a Huber fit, then Tukey's bisquare). When more than 10% of a sweep was set aside, the message suggests fitting a quiet stretch instead.
  • A long sweep is fitted in overlapping two-second segments, so the removal follows the hum as it drifts.

Estimate from

Whole sweep suits recordings that are mostly baseline. When responses fill much of the sweep, as in a stimulus train or rhythmic activity, no fit to the whole sweep can tell them from hum: choose Between cursors A–B and place the cursors on a quiet stretch, such as the baseline before the stimulus, or Outside cursors A–B and place them around the response. The hum is always subtracted from the whole sweep; the longer the stretch it is fitted on, the more precisely its frequency and phase carry over.

Hum removal is a remedy, not a substitute for a clean recording. Grounding, shielding and moving the offending transformer or lamp away from the setup remove the hum at its source.

Data Transform: Scale/Offset Axes

The Data Transform panel (Modify › Data Transform, ⇧⌘X) rescales Y values, converts a channel through its gain, rescales X, and sets X = 0 (see Set X = 0, below). This is where values are converted to another unit: editing an axis label or its unit never changes the data.

Scale or offset the Y values

  1. Under Y Axis, type the Scale and the Offset. Each value becomes value × Scale + Offset.
  2. Under Scope, choose the sweeps. By default the visible sweeps of the selected group are changed ("Visible sweeps only" checked, "Apply to all groups" not).
  3. Click Apply.
  • Use it to convert units or to invert a trace (Scale = −1).
  • Scale must be a plain number (not 1/1000, 50% or 1.5k). Offset is in the sweeps' unit, and can be typed with a unit of the same kind (0.5 V is 500 on sweeps in mV).
  • It works on the values as the graph shows them, junction-potential correction included. Error bars scale with the values.
  • The unit is not changed. If the scale changes it (A to pA, say), edit the Y-axis label.

Convert a channel through its gain

Channel Gain is for a channel recorded in the wrong unit, such as a raw amplifier input in volts. It changes the values and the unit as if the channel had been recorded that way, so analyses and exports read the new unit.

  1. Click Channel Gain…, under Y Axis, and choose the Channel if the graph has several.
  2. Type the Gain as the amplifier states it (0.5 mV/pA, 10 mV/mV), the Unit to show, and an optional Offset.
  3. Click Apply. Remove Gain gives the input back.
  • For HEKA files, check "Use for every series of … opened later" (the checkbox names the file) to remember the gain on this Mac for that file and channel name. Forget This File's Gains clears it. When such a file opens with a raw input and no gain, @Graph offers Channel Gain once.
  • A graph made from this one (Delete Sweeps, Decimate, Interpolate, Resample, a duplicate) keeps the gain with its channel, so it can still be changed or removed there.

Scale the X values

  1. Under X Axis, type the Scale.
  2. Click Apply.
  • Every X value (time, or the X column of X-Y data) is multiplied by the factor, across the whole file, not just the sweeps in Scope. For evenly sampled data this rescales the sample rate, so the factor must be positive.
  • The cursors, the Set X = 0 shift, a fixed X range, X error bars and the sweeps' recorded start times scale too.
  • The unit is not changed. Edit the X-axis label if the scale changes it.

Set X = 0

Set X = 0 shifts the X axis so that a time you choose (or an X value, on X-Y data) becomes 0, for example to line the axis up with a stimulus. The data are unchanged; only the axis labels move.

  1. In the inspector, choose Modify › Data Transform (⇧⌘X). Set X = 0 is below X Axis.
  2. With the cursors showing, drag cursor A to the new zero: the New zero field follows it. Or type the value as the axis shows it.
  3. Click Apply, or press Return (↩).
  • "Active offset" shows the current shift in the axis unit.
  • Reset removes the shift, back to the recording's own time: 0 at each sweep's start or, for a file whose first sample isn't at 0, that first sample's time (see Supported File Formats › Recording Times).
  • Measure and Peaks report times on the shifted axis.

Baseline Correction

  1. In the inspector, choose Modify › Baseline (⇧⌘B). The Start field is ready for typing.
  2. Choose a Method (Mean subtraction by default).
  3. Set the Baseline region: type Start and End in ms as the X axis shows them (or with a unit, such as 0.1 s), or drag cursors A and B onto a quiet stretch, such as the time before a stimulus. The fields follow the cursors.
  4. Choose Apply to and, if offered, a Channel.
  5. Click Apply Baseline.
MethodWhat is subtracted
Mean subtractionThe mean of the baseline region.
Median subtractionThe region's median, which an event or an artifact inside the region barely moves.
Linear detrendA fitted straight line, to remove slow drift.
Polynomial fitA fitted polynomial of the Polynomial order you set (1–8, 2 by default).
Line through two windowsThe straight line through the means of two windows, each mean placed at its window's middle: the first window before the response (the region fields) and the second after it (it starts on the last 10% of the sweep). A drift that runs straight across the response is removed without fitting the response itself.
  • Fit to (Linear detrend and Polynomial fit): The whole sweep (the default), Only the region below, or Everything except the region below. A fit to the whole sweep fits the response too and takes part of it away, so fit the stretches without a response. The fitted curve is always subtracted from the whole sweep.
  • Single point: set Start = End to zero the trace on the one recorded sample nearest that time. One sample's noise then sets the zero, so a short window is steadier on a noisy trace.
  • The line under the fields lists the samples averaged. A baseline and a Measure mean over the same times average the same samples.
  • A sweep that ends before the region starts is left unchanged, and the message says how many. A region that starts before the sweep's first sample is refused.
  • Polynomial fit: when a sweep or the region has too few samples for the order, a lower order is used, and the message names the sweeps and the order.
  • Missing samples are skipped and stay missing. Baseline correction works along a time axis, so X-Y data are refused.
  • After correction the Y axis fits the new data, even if you had set a range, and junction-potential correction is turned off, since both set the reference level. Undo restores both with the data.

Graph Tools

The Graph Tools panel (Modify › Graph Tools) opens each result in a new window; the original is unchanged. Each sweep is processed at its own sample rate and length. A result keeps the source's X shift, cursors and zoom (see Graphs › Cursors), and its groups, hidden groups, Review sweeps, colors and labels.

Change the sample rate

  1. Under Sample Rate, click Decimate…, Interpolate… or Resample….
  2. Set the options in the sheet.
  3. Click Decimate, Interpolate or Resample. If the tool can't run (the graph already has the rate asked for, say), the sheet stays open and says why.
ToolWhat it does
Decimate…Lowers the point count by a whole-number factor: "Keep 1 point every N points" (10 by default). Each sweep is low-pass filtered against aliasing (zero-phase, at 80% of the new Nyquist frequency) and every Nth point kept, which gives the same points as Resample to the same rate.
Interpolate…Inserts new points between each pair ("Points between each pair", 1 by default). Linear by default: it never overshoots, but flattens a peak that falls between samples. "Band-limited (windowed sinc) instead of linear" recovers such a peak, at the cost of ringing near steps and clipped samples.
Resample…Converts every sweep to the sample rate you type, with anti-alias filtering when lowering the rate and windowed-sinc reconstruction. A whole-number reduction, such as 20 kHz to 2 kHz, keeps every Nth filtered sample, as Decimate does. Each sweep keeps its duration. Near the source's Nyquist frequency, and within about 8 samples of each end of a sweep, the result is less exact.
  • Decimate by averaging: check "Average Y values within each bin" to make each new point the mean of N samples, placed at the center of its bin. Error bars (SEM, SD or None) also opens a second graph of each bin's SEM or SD, for use as error bars. A partial bin at the end of a sweep is dropped.
  • Averaging is only a weak anti-alias filter: content just above the new Nyquist frequency is only about 4 dB down and folds back into the result. Leave it off when the trace has content there.
  • Resample also puts X-Y data (a series with uneven timestamps, or a Y-against-X table) on an even grid, by straight lines between neighboring points, so that Align at Peak, Average and the other analyses work on it. X in a time unit becomes seconds; X of another quantity keeps its unit, and the rate is then in points per that unit. No anti-alias filter is used, so a rate lower than the points' own spacing skips what lies between grid points. X must increase from each point to the next.
  • Decimate and Interpolate don't run on X-Y data with its own X values; use Resample.

Integrate or differentiate

  1. Under Calculus, choose Full sweep or Between cursors A – B.
  2. For the derivative of a noisy trace, choose Pre-smooth (pts): None (the default), 3, 5, 9, 15 or 25.
  3. Click Integrate or Differentiate.
  • Integrate: the running integral of each visible sweep, by the trapezoidal rule. The Y unit becomes unit·s (such as mV·s). Between cursors, the final value equals Measure's Area for the same window.
  • A missing sample stays missing in the integral, and the intervals on either side of it add nothing to the total. On X-Y data the points are taken in increasing X, and points with a missing X are left out.
  • Differentiate: the first derivative of each visible sweep, as the three-point difference over the actual X spacing, so unevenly spaced X-Y data are differentiated as accurately as evenly sampled sweeps. The Y unit becomes unit/s (such as mV/s), and on X-Y data unit per X unit, labeled d/dX.
  • Pre-smooth applies a boxcar average of that many points before differentiating, because differentiating amplifies noise. The whole sweep is smoothed before a cursor window is cut.
  • Between cursors, a sweep with no sample between them is left out of the result and named.

The derivative of a raw, fast-sampled trace is large and noisy (thousands of mV/s for a voltage sampled at 25 kHz). That is correct. Pre-smoothing over 9–25 points brings out features such as a fast rising phase.

Back to Contents

Signal Processing

The tools on this page average, normalize and align sweeps, show which frequencies a signal holds, and compare two signals. Each opens its result in a new window and leaves the original unchanged. Average, Normalize, Align at Peak and Spectrum are panels in the inspector's Signal category; the rest are in the Graph Utilities menu. To filter or smooth a trace, see Modifying Graphs.

Average Sweeps (⇧⌘A)

Averages the visible sweeps, sample by sample, into one sweep per group, so a voltage + current recording gives one average of each. The average can show how much the sweeps spread around it.

  1. In the inspector's Signal category, choose Average.
  2. Under Variability, choose what to Show: None (the default), SD, SEM or Confidence interval. For anything but None, choose Shaded band or Mean + and − sweeps; for a confidence interval, type its Level (95% by default).
  3. Click Average Visible Sweeps. The average opens in a new graph window.

⇧⌘A runs the same average from any graph window without opening the inspector, with the Variability you chose last.

Average other sets of sweeps

The panel's other buttons ignore which sweeps are visible and give one average per recording channel. Sweep numbers count trials within each channel, as Review sweeps does: on a voltage + current file, All Odd averages trials 1, 3, 5… of each channel separately.

ButtonSweeps averaged
AllEvery sweep.
All Odd, All EvenSweeps 1, 3, 5… or sweeps 2, 4, 6….
Every NEach run of N consecutive sweeps separately: N = 3 on 9 sweeps gives averages of 1–3, 4–6 and 7–9. Type N in the N = field.
Every NthSweeps N, 2N, 3N….
Average CustomThe sweeps you list, such as "3, 5-7, 33-41".

Variability

Each measure is worked out at every sample from the sweeps that have a value there, so where sweeps have different lengths or gaps each sample uses its own n. A sample with fewer than 2 sweeps gets no error, and the band has a gap there.

MeasureDefinition
SDThe sample standard deviation, with n − 1 in the denominator.
SEMSD/√n.
Confidence intervalMean ± t(n − 1)·SEM. It is pointwise: an interval for each sample, not a simultaneous band for the whole trace.
  • Shaded band draws the spread around the mean, in the mean's color. It is saved in a .@graph file, drawn in every figure export, kept by Export Visible and Scale / Offset, and hidden if you change the mean in any other way.
  • Mean + and − sweeps adds two ordinary sweeps, such as "Mean + SEM" and "Mean − SEM", drawn dashed and thinner in the mean's color. Every file format, export and measurement sees them.
  • Each average is named for its group and gives the number of sweeps behind it, such as "Vm avg (n=30)", or a range, such as "n=24–30", where sweeps have unequal lengths or gaps. With a shaded band it also names the measure, such as "± SEM". The Data Log states the measure and the n.
  • A group whose sweeps are in different units (mV with pA) or have different X values is not averaged, and the panel gives the reason.
  • Sweeps at different sample rates are interpolated linearly onto the group's highest rate, never past a sweep's own last sample. The Data Log says so.

Normalize (⇧⌘R)

Rescales each sweep to a reference so that sweeps can be compared: to its own peak to compare shapes, to the largest peak of all to keep relative amplitudes, or to a baseline window (percent of baseline, ΔF/F₀, z-score).

  1. Press ⇧⌘R, or choose Normalize in the inspector's Signal category.
  2. Under Normalization Mode, choose Per sweep (the default) or Global (all sweeps).
  3. Choose what to normalize to (the choices are listed below).
  4. Under Measure from, choose A baseline window (the default) and type its From and to times, or click From cursors. Or choose Zero.
  5. Under Scope, leave both boxes checked to normalize the visible sweeps of every group.
  6. Click Normalize → New Window.

Per sweep

Each sweep is scaled by a value of its own, so differences in amplitude between sweeps are lost. Use it to compare shapes, such as AP waveforms across conditions.

Normalize each sweep to its ownThe sweep becomes
Auto-detect (largest absolute)Divided by its largest peak of either sign (the default).
Positive peak, Negative peakDivided by its largest positive or negative peak.
Amplitude at cursor ADivided by its value at cursor A.
User-defined valueDivided by the Value you type.
Percent of baseline100 × value / baseline mean, so its own baseline reads 100%, the way synaptic plasticity is plotted. A negative baseline, such as a field EPSP's slope, still reads +100%.
ΔF/F₀ (F₀ = baseline)(F − F₀) / F₀, with F₀ the baseline mean, for fluorescence traces. F₀ must be positive, so subtract background first.
z-score (baseline mean and SD)(value − mean) / SD of the baseline window, with n − 1 in the SD. Measured from Zero, the mean and SD of the whole sweep.
Min–max (0 to 1)Scaled from 0 (its smallest value) to 1 (its largest).

Percent of baseline and ΔF/F₀ need a baseline window. Peak points and polarity (below) don't apply to the last four choices.

Global

All sweeps of one unit are divided by the largest peak among them: Auto-detect (largest absolute) (the default), Largest positive peak or Largest negative peak. Relative amplitudes are kept and only the largest sweep reaches ±1, which suits a dose–response series or run-down. Each unit is scaled on its own, so a current sweep is never divided by a voltage peak.

Baseline, peak points and polarity

  • A baseline window (the first 5 ms of the sweep to start with): each sweep's own mean over the window is subtracted first, and the trace becomes (value − baseline) / (reference − baseline). A response is then scaled by its amplitude, not by the level it sits on. X-Y data start on Zero.
  • Zero: peaks are measured from 0. On sweeps that sit far from 0 (a membrane potential, a holding current) the "peak" is then mostly that level, and the panel warns you.
  • Peak = mean of N points (1 by default): the reference is the mean of N samples centered on the peak, or on cursor A. With one point, noise makes the normalized response read small; a few points spanning the top of the peak reduce that.
  • Keep polarity (a negative peak becomes −1) (on by default): each sweep is divided by the size of its reference, so a negative-going response stays negative. Off, a negative-going trace is turned upside down (peak +1).
  • A sweep with no usable reference (no positive peak above the baseline, cursor A missing) is left unchanged and named in the panel's message. The Data Log lists each sweep's reference.
  • Values are taken as the graph shows them, with junction-potential correction if it is on. Fit curves and AP markers are not normalized.

Align Sweeps at Peak (⌥⌘K)

Shifts each visible sweep in time so that its main peak falls at X = 0 in a new window. Use it to overlay action potentials, EPSPs or other repeated events and compare their shape.

  1. In the inspector's Signal category, choose Align at Peak.
  2. Under Peak direction, choose Largest absolute peak (the default), Positive peak or Negative peak.
  3. To keep a stimulus artifact or a spontaneous event from being taken as the peak, check "Search for the peak between cursors A and B only" and place the cursors around the event. Otherwise the whole sweep is searched.
  4. Choose Align on: The peak (the default) or Half-way up the rising phase.
  5. To drop the trace long before each peak, check "Trim the lead-in before each peak" and type the time to keep in "Keep before the peak (ms)" ("2 s" and "1 min" are accepted too).
  6. Click Align at Peak.

⌥⌘K aligns on the largest absolute peak right away, without opening the inspector.

How sweeps are aligned

  • Largest absolute peak: the polarity is chosen once for all sweeps, from their median excursion above and below rest, so a biphasic event aligns on the same phase in every sweep.
  • Half-way up the rising phase: the first sample before the peak's top that is half-way from the resting level (the median before the peak in the search window) to the peak. Noise barely moves it, whereas lining up single peak samples inflates an average of the aligned sweeps.
  • Sweeps are shifted by whole samples, so each peak lands on the sample nearest the common time. For brief events recorded below about 20 kHz this blurs an average of the aligned sweeps (its peak reads low and its half-width wide). Raise the sample rate first with Modify › Graph Tools › Interpolate… (band-limited), then align.
  • Unless you trim the lead-in, every sample is kept: each sweep is shifted, not cut. The tail is never cut. Where a shifted sweep has no data it has a gap, which Measure and the other tools skip.
  • Each sweep moves by its own amount, so the new window doesn't take the original's cursors, X shift or zoom.
  • Fit curves, AP markers and flat sweeps are left out; the panel's message and the Data Log name the flat sweeps. X-Y data have no time axis and can't be aligned: resample them to an even rate first (Modify › Graph Tools › Resample…).

Spectrum: Power Spectral Density / FFT (⌥⌘P)

The Spectrum panel shows which frequencies or rhythms a signal holds. For an evenly sampled recording it computes the power spectral density (PSD) by FFT. For X-Y data, whose X values may be unevenly spaced, it always computes the Lomb–Scargle periodogram instead (see Lomb–Scargle Periodogram, below).

  1. In the inspector's Signal category, choose Spectrum.
  2. Leave Method on FFT (Welch or multitaper).
  3. Set the options (below). The defaults give a power spectral density in units²/Hz on a linear scale.
  4. Click Compute PSD / FFT. The spectrum of each visible sweep opens in a new graph window, with frequency (Hz) on the X axis.

⌥⌘P runs it with default settings from any graph window (the periodogram, for X-Y data). A long computation shows a progress bar with a Cancel button, in the panel or, for ⌥⌘P, at the bottom of the graph.

Options

OptionWhat it does
Normalize to PSD (units²/Hz)On (the default): power density in units²/Hz (such as mV²/Hz), which doesn't depend on the sample rate or segment size. Off: the power spectrum in units², where a sinusoid of amplitude a peaks at a²/2 when its frequency falls on a bin (half a bin away it reads up to 1.4 dB low, so sum the bins around a peak for its exact power). Use it to size a line-noise or stimulus peak.
Amplitude (√ of power)Off by default. Shows the square root: the amplitude spectral density in units/√Hz (such as µV/√Hz), the way amplifier and electrode noise is usually quoted, or, with Normalize off, the RMS amplitude spectrum in units. Not for dB values.
Confidence intervalOff by default. Shades each spectrum's pointwise interval at the level you type (95% by default).
Remove from each segmentMean (the default), so a steady level such as a resting potential doesn't swamp the low frequencies. Linear trend removes each segment's least-squares straight line, so a slow drift doesn't raise the lowest few bins.
Y scaleLinear (the default); Logarithmic axis, which keeps the power values linear and draws them on a log axis, the way to see the wide range of a noise spectrum; or dB values (10·log₁₀), for export.
Segment size (Welch FFT window)Auto (the default), or a fixed size from 1024 points up to the largest power of 2 that fits in the shortest sweep. Each choice shows its frequency resolution in Hz/bin. Larger segments give finer resolution but a noisier spectrum.
Multitaper, sine tapers (reduces variance)Off by default. See Multitaper, below.
Max frequency (Hz)Limits the X axis. At 0 (the default) the spectrum runs up to the Nyquist frequency (half the sample rate), and the window opens zoomed to where the power is.

For a smoother spectrum, average the spectra of several sweeps: press ⇧⌘A in the spectrum's window. Average linear power, not dB values: a mean of dB values reads low. To compare spectra from several files, use Graph Utilities › Combine Open Graphs.

How the spectrum is computed

  • Welch's method (Welch 1967): each sweep is cut into segments that overlap by 50%; each segment has its mean (or linear trend) removed and is multiplied by a Hann window; and the segments' one-sided spectra are averaged. The two scalings are the "density" and "spectrum" scalings of Welch's method in SciPy and MATLAB.
  • Auto segment size: the largest power of 2 up to a quarter of the shortest sweep, so that at least 7 overlapping segments are averaged, but never below 64 points (a sweep shorter than 256 samples has fewer segments).
  • Sizes are powers of 2, so the samples after a sweep's last whole segment are left out. The Data Log says how many.
  • Confidence interval: from the χ² distribution on the estimate's equivalent degrees of freedom: 2 per segment (per taper with Multitaper), fewer for overlapping segments (Welch 1967), and half as many at 0 Hz and the Nyquist frequency. Seven half-overlapping Hann segments give about 13.4. The interval is for each frequency on its own, not a band for the whole spectrum at once. The Data Log gives the degrees of freedom.
  • Fit curves and AP markers are left out.

Multitaper

Multitaper is for a spectrum that still looks noisy after averaging every available segment (a short recording, or a large segment size chosen for fine resolution). In place of one Hann window, each segment is analyzed with several sine tapers (Riedel & Sidorenko 1995), and their spectra are averaged before the segments are. This trades some frequency resolution for less noise.

  1. In the Spectrum panel, check "Multitaper, sine tapers (reduces variance)".
  2. Type the Time-bandwidth product (NW), from 1 to 10 (3 by default, which gives 5 tapers). The ⓘ beside the field gives the resolution in Hz for the current segment size, and advice on choosing NW.
  3. Click Compute PSD / FFT.
  • The number of tapers is K = 2 × NW − 1, and the frequency resolution widens to roughly 2 × NW divided by the segment's duration. A lower NW keeps nearby peaks apart; a higher NW smooths more.
  • The Spectrogram's Multitaper uses Slepian tapers, so the same NW gives different tapers in the two tools. For smooth spectra the two kinds give nearly the same result.

Lomb–Scargle Periodogram

The Lomb–Scargle periodogram is the spectrum of unevenly sampled data, where an FFT can't be used: field series, measurements at irregular visits, imaging frames at irregular times, observations with gaps. For each frequency it fits a sinusoid (and the mean) to the points and reports how much of their variance it explains, so a rhythm stands out as a peak at its frequency.

  1. In the inspector's Signal category, choose Spectrum. X-Y data opens on the periodogram. For a recording, set Method to Lomb–Scargle periodogram (for series of up to 10,000 points).
  2. Set the options (below).
  3. Click Compute Periodogram. Each visible series gets its own periodogram, in a new graph window, and the Data Log lists its strongest peaks.
OptionWhat it does
PowerStandard (0–1) (the default): the share of the variance explained, comparable between series, with a false-alarm probability for each peak. PSD: half the reduction in squared deviations, in the data's units².
Harmonics fitted1 (the default) to 3. More than one fits the sinusoid's harmonics too, for rhythms that aren't sine-shaped, such as a sharp daily peak, so that their period stands out instead of splitting into harmonics.
Frequencies per peakHow finely the frequencies are spaced, as a number across each peak's width (1 ÷ the data's span). 5 by default; 10 locates the peaks more exactly.
FrequenciesThe range searched, in cycles per X unit (Hz for seconds). 0 is automatic: from half a peak's width up to 5 × the average Nyquist frequency (half the number of points ÷ the span).
Plot againstFrequency (the default), or Period (1 ÷ frequency, in the X unit: hours for a circadian series, days for a variable star), on a logarithmic axis.
Weight points by their error barsShown when the graph has Y error bars, and on by default: each point counts by 1 ÷ its error².

Reading the periodogram

  • The Data Log lists each series' strongest peaks: period, frequency and power.
  • False-alarm probability (given for one harmonic with Standard power): the chance that noise alone gives a peak this high at any frequency up to the highest one searched (Baluev 2008). A small value (0.01 or less) indicates a real rhythm; one near 1 is noise. Lowering the highest frequency lowers it; the lowest frequency doesn't change it.
  • The Data Log also gives the best-fitting sinusoid at the strongest peak, y = c + a·sin(2π·f·t) + b·cos(2π·f·t), and the same as an amplitude and phase, y = c + A·sin(2π·f·t + φ).
  • Method: the generalized Lomb–Scargle periodogram (Zechmeister & Kürster 2009), as astropy's LombScargle computes it.
  • X values are kept to about 7 significant digits, so times far from zero for their spacing (Julian dates, say) lose fine detail, and the Data Log says when. Subtract a start time before importing.

Histogram (⌃⌘H)

A histogram bins the values of a graph's sweeps to show their distribution: of membrane potential, noise or fluorescence, for example.

  1. Choose Graph Utilities › Convert to Histogram… (⌃⌘H). The Histogram Setup form opens.
  2. With several groups, choose Selected group (the default) or All groups.
  3. Under Values, optionally type limits (From and to), which keep one outlier from squeezing the rest into a few bars, and check "Only between the graph's cursors (A–B)". The bins span the limits, and values outside are counted and reported.
  4. Under Bins, choose Bins by, and type a Bin width or a Bin count.
  5. Under Y-Axis, choose Count (the default), Frequency (%) or Density.
  6. Click Generate. In the histogram window you can change the Y axis, add a curve, check Cumulative or Log axis, and click Copy as Table. ← Setup goes back to the form.

Bins

  • Width or Count: the histogram is built from the one you typed last. A width gives bins with edges at whole multiples of it (5 mV gives edges at …, −70, −65, …). A count gives that many equal bins from the smallest value to the largest. The form starts with a width that gives about 30 bins.
  • A rule works out the number of equal bins from the values, as numpy.histogram_bin_edges does: Sturges (width = range ÷ (log₂ n + 1)), Scott (3.49 · SD · n^(−1/3), for roughly normal data), Freedman–Diaconis (2 · IQR · n^(−1/3), robust to outliers and long tails) or Square root (range ÷ √n). The count it gives shows in the Bin count field, and the histogram window says which rule set the bins.
  • Log-spaced bins: bins equal in log₁₀ of the value, on a logarithmic X axis, for heavy-tailed positive data such as inter-event intervals. They are set by count or by a rule (which then works on log₁₀ of the values), and need every value above 0.
  • Same bins for every group (on by default; for All groups with a count or a rule): every group is binned over the range of all of them, so their bars and percentages line up. A width gives every group the same edges anyway.
  • Each bin holds values from its lower edge up to, but not including, its upper edge (R's hist() closes bins on the right by default). With a count, the last bin also holds the largest value.

Y axis, curves and table

  • Each histogram shows n, the values binned, and how many missing values were skipped or fell outside the limits. Frequency (%) is of n.
  • Density is count ÷ (n × bin width), so the bars' areas sum to 1. Use it to compare groups of different size or histograms with different bin widths.
  • Log axis shows the counts on a logarithmic scale, for heavy-tailed data. Empty bins have no bar on it.
  • Cumulative: each bar counts every value up to its bin's upper edge, as a running count, a running percentage of n, or, on the Density axis, the fraction of n (the empirical distribution function at the bin edges).
  • Curve: Normal draws a normal distribution with the binned values' mean and SD. Kernel density draws a Gaussian kernel density estimate with Silverman's bandwidth, 0.9 · min(SD, IQR/1.34) · n^(−1/5) (R's default, bw.nrd0). Either is scaled to the Y axis and has its parameters shown under the chart. Read it as a guide to the shape, not as a test of whether the data are normal.
  • Copy as Table copies one row per bin (center, edges, count, percentage, density and the cumulative values) as tab-separated text.
  • The values are those the graph shows: junction-potential corrected on a voltage panel, and without fit curves or AP markers.
  • Graph Utilities › Cumulative Probability plots the cumulative distribution (0 to 1) of the same values instead, as a graph.

For inter-event interval or dwell-time histograms, copy the event times from the Data Log into a Spreadsheet and use Data to Chart.

Spectrogram

A spectrogram shows how the power at each frequency changes over time, as a frequency × time heatmap. It works like the PSD, but keeps the spectra of successive windows separate instead of averaging them. Use it for power that changes over time, such as theta and gamma power during behavior or LFP power around a stimulus.

  1. Bring the graph to the front and choose Graph Utilities › Spectrogram…. The Spectrogram section of the LFP / Spike Train Analysis tab has the same controls for that tab's graph.
  2. Choose the Sweep.
  3. Choose the Method, Short-time FFT (the default) or Multitaper, and set its window (see the table below).
  4. To show only a low band, check "Restrict max frequency shown" and type the Max frequency (Hz).
  5. Leave "Log scale (dB)" checked (the default) to show power in dB.
  6. Click Compute Spectrogram. The result opens in a new heatmap window, and the status line gives the window used, in ms, and its frequency resolution. Cancel stops a long computation.
SettingWhat it does
Window size (samples)Short-time FFT. 256 by default, rounded down to a power of 2, at least 64. Shorter windows give finer time resolution but coarser frequency resolution.
Overlap (%)Short-time FFT. How far successive windows overlap (50% by default).
Window (s), Step (s)Multitaper. The length of each window, T (1 s by default), and how often a window starts (0.1 s by default).
NWMultitaper. The time–half-bandwidth product (3 by default). It sets the frequency resolution, 2W = 2·NW/T, shown under the settings.
TapersMultitaper. Automatic by default: 2NW − 1, the most that stay well concentrated.
DetrendMultitaper. What is removed from each window: Mean (the default), Linear (a fitted line) or None.
FFT paddingMultitaper. None (the default), ×2 or ×4. Padding gives finer frequency bins, not finer resolution.

How the spectrogram is computed

  • Short-time FFT: each window has its mean removed and is multiplied by a Hann window. Scaling is as in scipy.signal.spectrogram (window "hann", detrend "constant", density scaling).
  • Multitaper: each window is multiplied by several Slepian tapers and the results are averaged, which gives a smoother map (Thomson 1982; as in Chronux and Prerau et al. 2017).
  • Power is a one-sided density, in units²/Hz or in dB re 1 units²/Hz (the chart title gives the unit), scaled as the PSD is, so the two agree.
  • Frequency runs up the vertical axis, and times are as the graph's X axis shows them. The heatmap opens unnormalized; its inspector's z-score options show each frequency's change over time instead.
  • A window holding a missing (blank) sample is left out, and a time with no complete window shows as a gap.
  • Where there are more frequency bins or windows than a heatmap can draw (windows of 8192 samples or more, or a long recording), neighbors are averaged, so every sample still counts.

Cross-Correlation / Coherence

Compares two signals. Signal cross-correlation shows whether two continuous signals vary together, and with what delay. Coherence shows at which frequencies they are related. Spike-train cross-correlogram shows whether two spike trains fire together.

  1. Bring the graph that holds Signal A to the front and choose Graph Utilities › Cross-Correlation / Coherence…. The LFP / Spike Train Analysis tab has the same controls, with that tab's graph as Signal A.
  2. Choose the Analysis: Signal cross-correlation (the default), Coherence or Spike-train cross-correlogram.
  3. Choose Sweep A (Train A for spike trains).
  4. Under Signal B from, choose this graph or another open graph window, then choose Sweep B (or Train B).
  5. Set the analysis's options (below).
  6. Click Run. The result opens in a new graph window, with lags in s or frequencies in Hz.

Signal cross-correlation

  • The correlation between two continuous signals over a range of lags, after each signal's mean is removed. A positive lag means B follows A. Both signals must share a sample rate.
  • Max lag (ms) (200 ms by default): rounded to the nearest whole sample. The lag range stops at the record's length (and at 500,000 samples), and the result's name says when it was shortened.
  • Normalize (±1 scale) (on by default): divides by the square root of the product of the two mean-removed signals' sums of squares over the whole record (MATLAB's xcov "coeff"), so identical signals read 1 at zero lag. The overlap shrinks at longer lags while the divisor doesn't, so values taper toward the ends of the lag range.
  • No significance band is drawn: each signal's own autocorrelation makes chance peaks tall, so a peak alone doesn't show that the signals are coupled.

Coherence

  • Magnitude-squared coherence between two continuous signals, frequency by frequency, averaged over Hann-windowed segments that overlap by 50% (Welch's method, as in SciPy).
  • Segment size (samples, 0 = auto) (0 by default): rounded down to a power of 2, at least 64, so 1000 uses 512. Auto uses the largest power of 2 up to a quarter of the record, at most 8192 samples, which averages at least 7 segments for records of 256 samples or more. The result's name gives the size used, its frequency resolution and the segment count.
  • Coherence is biased upward with few segments: two unrelated signals read about 1 ÷ (number of segments), so 0.5 from 2 segments means nothing. With too few samples for 2 segments, the analysis stops with a message.
  • Significance level: a second trace marks the 95% level for two independent signals, 1 − 0.05^(1/(K − 1)), with K the effective number of segments (the count reduced for their 50% overlap). About 1 frequency in 20 crosses it by chance, so look for a band of adjacent frequencies above it, not a single bin. The line leaves out 0 Hz, the first frequency above it and the Nyquist frequency, where chance coherence runs higher.
  • Phase and time lag: two more panels show the cross-spectrum's phase, as B's phase lag behind A in degrees, and, at the frequencies whose coherence is above the significance line, the time lag that phase implies: phase ÷ (360° × frequency), in seconds (Bendat & Piersol 2010). Both are positive when B lags A.
  • A phase is known only up to whole cycles, so the lag shown is the one within half a period of zero. For a longer lag, a steady slope of phase against frequency across a coherent band is the more reliable estimate.

Spike-train cross-correlogram

Both signals must be spike trains, such as rasters from AP Detection (Extracellular) or spike-sorted units. Each bar counts the B spikes at that lag from an A spike (positive lag: B after A). Choosing the same train as A and B gives an autocorrelogram, with each spike's pairing with itself left out.

SettingWhat it does
Bin width (ms), Max lag (ms)The lag axis: 5 ms and 200 ms by default. Bins are centered on whole multiples of the bin width.
Y scaleCounts (the default), or Rate (Hz): B's firing rate around an A spike (counts ÷ number of A spikes ÷ bin width), which compares across bin widths and train sizes.
All trials of both unitsOff by default. Sums trial k of Train A's unit with trial k of Train B's unit over every trial. Units are found from Spike Sorter names ("<unit>: <sweep>"); a raster without them counts each train as a trial. The note under the checkbox shows which trials were paired.
Shift predictorWith All trials of both units: All shifts, averaged (the default), Next trial (k with k + 1) or None.
Jitter bandsOff by default. Set the Window (ms) (20 ms by default; typically 10 to 25 ms) and the number of Surrogates (1000 by default).
Preserve spike patterns shorter than R (ms)With Jitter bands: 10 ms by default. 0 is plain interval jitter.
  • Chance level: a second trace shows what each bin would hold if the trains were independent, from each train's mean rate over its recorded span (for a spike-sorted file, from its first to its last spike). It falls toward the ends of the lag axis, as the correlogram of two unrelated trains does on short sweeps, so compare a peak with the line, not with the outer bins. The line is a guide, not a significance test.
  • Shift predictor (Perkel et al. 1967): two units that both respond to a stimulus make a broad peak even with no connection between them (Brody 1999). The predictor is the same correlogram between different trials, which share the stimulus but no moment-to-moment coupling. All shifts, averaged sums A's trial j with B's trial k for every j ≠ k and divides by (trials − 1); Next trial pairs trial k with k + 1 (the last with the first). The result adds the predictor and the corrected CCG (raw − predictor), which is near 0 where only the stimulus links the two.
  • Jitter bands (Amarasingham et al. 2012) test for fine-timescale synchrony. Every spike of B is moved to a random time within its own window (the windows tile each trial from its start) while A stays as recorded, which keeps B's slower rate changes and destroys only its fine timing relative to A. The correlogram is recomputed for each surrogate. The random draws are seeded from the data, so the same trains always give the same bands.
  • Pattern jitter (Harrison & Geman 2009): spikes of B no more than R apart keep their exact intervals and move together, and every longer interval stays longer than R, so B's bursts and pauses survive. Set R to cover B's burst intervals (the max interval of ISI / Burst Detection is a good guide; see LFP / Spike Train Analysis). A larger R leaves less room to detect weak synchrony. R = 0 breaks B's bursts up, and two bursty trains then cross the global band by chance far more often than it allows, so use 0 only when B doesn't fire in bursts.
  • Reading the bands: the pointwise band is each lag's 2.5th to 97.5th percentile over the surrogates, and about 1 lag in 20 crosses it by chance. The global band (Fujisawa et al. 2008) is set from each surrogate's highest and lowest bin over all lags shown, so an unrelated pair crosses it anywhere only about 5% of the time: a bin beyond it is significant.
  • The result also shows the mean of the surrogates and the jitter-corrected CCG (raw − jitter mean; Smith & Kohn 2008), which is near 0 where the two trains aren't synchronized more finely than the window.

How the two signals are lined up

  • When both sweeps carry a recording clock (a recording date and sweep start times, as two graphs of one file, two files of one session or two sweeps of one graph do), they are lined up on that clock and only the time both cover is used. Without a clock they are compared from their starts. The result's name and the Data Log say which.
  • Two sweeps recorded at different times (sweep 1 against sweep 3, say) don't overlap on the clock. The panel explains this and offers a button, "Compare from each sweep's start (not simultaneous)", which lines them up from each sweep's start, as trials. The result's name, legend and Data Log entry then say "not simultaneous".
  • Channels of one sweep were recorded together and are compared as they are. Missing samples at either end (a blank tail some files carry) are left out of both.
  • Spike trains follow the same rule: B's spikes are moved onto A's clock and cut to the time both cover. Over trials, each pair of trials is lined up on its own sweeps' clocks.

Other Graph Utilities

The Graph Utilities menu also holds the commands below. Each works on what the graph shows: a hidden group, the sweeps outside Review sweeps, fit curves and AP markers are left out of Combine, Concatenate and the episodic conversions, and the Data Log says so.

CommandWhat it does
Copy Style, Paste Style (⌥⌘C, ⌥⌘V)Copies the look of one graph (colors, line widths, symbols, fonts) onto another, so your figures match; data and axis ranges stay as they are. Paste Style pastes onto the front window, a graph's style onto a graph and a chart's onto a chart. Both are also in the plot's right-click menu.
Combine Open GraphsOverlays the visible sweeps of all open graph windows in one window, keeping their colors, sample rates and lengths. Groups that measure the same quantity are pooled, one from each graph: two voltage + current recordings give one voltage and one current group. A pooled sweep in another prefix (nA beside pA) is converted to the group's first unit, and the Data Log says so.
Combine Selected Graphs…The same for the windows you check, in the order you set by dragging.
Concatenate Open GraphsJoins the visible sweeps of the open graphs end to end in time, such as a recording split across files: group by group and episode by episode, in window order. The pieces joined into one sweep must have the same sample rate and measure the same quantity (a piece in nA after one in pA is converted to pA). If not, nothing is joined and the message names the mismatch.
Continuous to Episodic…Cuts a long continuous sweep into equal episodes (length in s, ms or samples) in a new window. A channel recorded at a different rate is cut into episodes of the same duration. The last episode keeps whatever remains.
Episodic to ContinuousJoins each visible group's shown sweeps into one continuous trace, for example for LFP or EEG saved as episodes. The sweeps of a group must share a sample rate.
Delete Sweeps…Lists the visible sweeps by group. Check the ones to remove, such as sweeps with artifacts, and click Delete Selected. The result opens in a new window. Sweeps in a hidden group or outside Review sweeps aren't listed and are kept, and the sheet says how many.
Swap X and Y AxesExchanges the X and Y data, for example to show an I(V) curve as V(I).
  • With Single Group on a recording of several channels, the shown sweeps are still taken channel by channel.
  • Decimate, Interpolate and Resample are in the inspector's Graph Tools panel: see Modifying Graphs.
  • VI Plot, IV Plot, Firing Properties, Sag Analysis and Membrane Test are in the Toolkits menu, under Electrophysiology: see Electrophysiology Commands.
