Measuring & Analysis

The Analyze category of the inspector has three panels: Measure (statistics of a stretch of each sweep), Peaks (find peaks and measure their size and time course) and Curve Fitting. Each works on the sweeps of the front graph and writes its results to the Data Log. Action potentials have their own tool: see AP Detection.

  • Range: each panel works on the Full sweep or Between cursors A – B. Choosing Between cursors shows the cursors, and Full sweep hides them; ⌘K switches the choice to match. Drag the cursors, or type their positions in the panel's A and B fields.
  • Scope: by default a panel uses the visible sweeps of the selected group ("Visible sweeps only" checked, "Apply to all groups" not). Change either checkbox to include hidden sweeps or every group.
  • Press Return (↩) in any number field, including A and B, to run the panel's main action again.

Measure Panel

  1. In the inspector, choose Analyze › Measure (⇧⌘M).
  2. Under Measurement window, choose Full sweep or Between cursors A – B.
  3. Under Metrics, check what to report (Average amplitude is checked to start).
  4. Set the Scope and click Measure. The results go to the Data Log.
MetricHow it is computed
Average amplitudeThe mean of the samples in the window.
AreaThe integral of the trace (amplitude × time) by the trapezoidal rule, from the sample nearest cursor A to the sample nearest cursor B. It equals the last value of Integrate over the same window.
Maximum, MinimumThe largest and the smallest sample. "Location of maximum" and "Location of minimum" add where each is, on the X axis as shown (so it follows Set X = 0).
Number of pointsThe number of samples in the window.
VarianceThe sample variance (n − 1).
Standard deviationThe square root of the variance.
Std error of meanThe standard deviation divided by √n.
  • A single point has no spread: its variance, SD and SEM read N/A.
  • Gaps (missing samples, such as the edges Align at Peak leaves, or a missing Y value in X-Y data) are skipped: every statistic uses the real samples, and the area is not integrated across a gap.

Peaks Panel: Peak Detection

  1. In the inspector, choose Analyze › Peaks (⇧⌘D).
  2. Under Detection range, choose Full sweep or Between cursors A – B.
  3. Under Detection, choose the Direction and Which peaks. For First or All, set the Threshold.
  4. To measure from a baseline, check "Subtract baseline before threshold" and set "Baseline from … to …" (the first 10% of the sweep to start). The window is shaded on the graph.
  5. Under Output measurements, check what to report.
  6. Set the Scope and click Run Peak Analysis. The table goes to the Data Log, one row per peak; a sweep with no peak gets a "no peak" row, so the rows line up with the sweeps.

Detection settings

SettingWhat it does
DirectionAuto (the default), Positive or Negative. Auto takes, for each sweep, whichever direction swings further from the reference level: the baseline window's mean, or the resting level without one.
Which peaksMaximum (the default): the largest peak in each sweep, with no threshold. First: the first peak beyond the threshold. All: every peak beyond it.
ThresholdAbsolute: a level in the trace's unit. With a baseline subtracted, it is a signed distance from the baseline, so type it negative for downward peaks, or check "Threshold is a distance in the peak's direction". Relative %: that percentage of the way from the reference level to the largest peak.
Separate peaks by50% of threshold by default. A peak counts only if the trace falls back on both sides, before reaching a larger value, by this share of the threshold's distance from the reference level (a prominence, as in SciPy's find_peaks). Noise around the threshold then doesn't split one event into several peaks.
Min. spacing0 by default (off). Of two peaks closer than this, only the larger is kept.
Subtract baseline before thresholdOff by default. Each sweep's mean over the baseline window is subtracted, and each peak is then reported as an Amplitude from that baseline.
  • With First or All, a peak on the first or last sample of the window (an event cut by its edge) is not reported. Maximum reports the largest value wherever it is, the window's edge included.
  • The Data Log warns when the threshold is on the wrong side of the reference level to separate anything, and when a detected peak falls inside the baseline window. A sweep with no data in the baseline window gives N/A amplitudes.

What is measured

MeasurementHow it is measured
Peak or AmplitudeOn by default. Without a baseline, Peak: the trace's value at the peak. With one, Amplitude: the peak's size from the baseline.
LocationOn by default. Where the peak is, on the X axis as shown (so it follows Set X = 0).
Rise timeThe time the rising phase takes between two levels, 10–90% by default.
Width atHow long the trace stays beyond a level, 50% of the peak by default: the half-width.
Decay timeThe time the falling phase takes between two levels, 100–50% by default.
Onset atThe time when the rising phase reaches a level, 5% by default, counted from cursor A when detecting between cursors, otherwise from the start of the sweep.
Inter-event interval (IEI)The time from each peak to the next in the same sweep. Offered when Which peaks is All.
Area (Charge on a current)The trace minus the reference level, integrated by the trapezoidal rule from where the trace last crosses that level before the peak to where it first returns to it after. A current's area is reported as charge in pC; any other as the trace's unit × s (× the X unit on X-Y data). N/A when the trace doesn't return to the level before the neighboring peak or the window's edge.
Max rise and decay slopesThe steepest slope on each side of the peak, per ms, from central differences between neighboring samples.
  • Rise, width, decay and onset levels are percentages of the peak's height above a reference level: the baseline if one is subtracted, otherwise the resting level, not zero. A peak that rises from −70 mV therefore has its 50% level halfway up the peak, not halfway to 0 mV.
  • The resting level is the median of the first or the last 5% of the window, whichever lies on the resting side of the peak. If the two ends differ by more than a quarter of the peak, the Data Log suggests a baseline window.
  • Each level is timed where the trace crosses it, interpolated between samples. A phase only a sample or two long still reads long, so sample fast events densely.
  • With All, each peak is measured between its neighboring peaks, and a time reads N/A when the trace doesn't come back to its level between them.
  • With junction-potential correction on, a voltage trace's peaks are measured on the corrected values, and the Data Log says so. Amplitudes from a baseline and all the times are differences, so the correction doesn't change them.

Noise and drift (optional)

On a noisy trace the most extreme sample sits on a noise peak, so the peak reads high and the times read off. These options, all off by default, reduce that. With them off, the Data Log warns when peaks are under 30 times the baseline window's noise SD.

  • "Peak = mean of N points": the peak is the mean of N samples centered on it.
  • "Smooth kinetics over N points": rise, width, decay, onset and slopes are measured on a copy smoothed by an N-sample moving average. It lengthens a rise shorter than about 3 times its window.
  • "Local baseline for each peak": each peak is measured from the mean of a short stretch just before it ("Mean over … ending … before the peak"), for a drifting baseline. Detection still uses the sweep's baseline.

X-Y data

X-Y data (a spectrum, a current–voltage curve, a dose-response) is measured along its X axis: the cursors, the baseline window and Location are X values, and rise, width, decay, onset and the interval between peaks are spans in the X unit (a spectral peak's width in Hz, say). Points are taken in order of increasing X; if a sweep's X runs back and forth, its two branches are merged, and the Data Log warns.

Curve Fitting

The Curve Fitting panel fits a curve to each sweep in Scope and draws it over the data as a dashed curve. Its top part fits a line, a polynomial, exponentials or a power law; its lower part fits a preset function or a formula you type. The parameters, R² and goodness of fit go to the Data Log.

Fit a line, polynomial, exponential or power law

  1. In the inspector, choose Analyze › Curve Fitting.
  2. Under Fit type, choose Linear (y = ax + b), Polynomial (Degree 1–6, 2 by default), Exponential (Terms: Single, Double or Triple, A·e^(−t/τ) + C and so on) or Power (y = A · x^B).
  3. Under Fit range, choose Full sweep or Between cursors A – B.
  4. Set the Scope and click Fit. The model and the fitted equation appear under the button and in the Data Log.
  5. Click Keep to turn the fitted curves into regular sweeps you can style and save, or Remove to discard them.

Fit a preset function or a formula

  1. In the lower part of the panel, choose E-phys preset or Formula.
  2. For a preset, choose the Preset function (its name gives its equation) and a Weighting.
  3. For a formula, type it with lowercase x as the X variable, such as a * exp(-x / tau) + c. The panel lists the fitted parameters as you type.
  4. Choose the Fit range and Scope, and click Fit.
  5. Click Keep fits or Remove fits.
  • Presets: mono-, bi- and tri-exponential decay, mono-exponential rise, mono-exponential plus linear, alpha function, Boltzmann, Hill dose-response and dose-inhibition, Hill, Gaussian, double Gaussian, Lorentzian, and a line or parabola through zero.
  • Alpha function: A·(t/τ)·e^(1−t/τ) + C, an event that starts at t = 0, with peak amplitude A at t = τ. On a sweep, t = 0 is the start of the fit range, so place cursor A at the event's onset; on X-Y data it is X = 0. The form A·t·e^(−t/τ) + C is the same curve with A multiplied by e/τ.
  • Weighting (presets only): Least squares (unweighted), the usual choice, or Relative weighting (1/Y²), for data whose scatter grows in proportion to Y. The weights come from the fitted curve's Y, re-estimated until they settle (Carroll & Ruppert 1988); a program that weights by each point's own Y gives a different fit. Use least squares when the curve comes close to or crosses Y = 0, where a point would get a very large weight; the Data Log warns.
  • A fit is drawn in the panel of the sweep it was fitted to, and follows that sweep when you change it in place: Baseline moves it with the data, and Scale/Offset and Channel Gain scale it. Filter and Smoothing change the trace's shape, so they clear the fits drawn over it and say so; fit again.
  • A long fit shows its progress and a Cancel button beside Fit. Cancel leaves the graph and the Data Log as they were.

Writing a formula

  • Use lowercase x for the X variable: on a sweep, the time in seconds from the start of the fit range. Only pi (or π) and lowercase e (Euler's number) are constants. Every other name, including X, t, tau and E, is a fitted parameter.
  • Operators: + − * / ^ (power) and % (remainder). Write every multiplication (2*x, not 2x).
  • Functions (in any case): exp, exp2, expm1, log or ln (both natural log), log10, log2, log1p, sqrt, cbrt, sin, cos, tan, asin, acos, atan, sinh, cosh, tanh, asinh, acosh, atanh, erf, erfc, gamma, lgamma, abs, sign, floor, ceil, round and trunc; and with two values pow, atan2, hypot, min, max, mod and fmod. Angles are in radians.
  • ^ groups from the right (2^3^2 is 512) and binds tighter than a leading minus (−2^2 is −4). % and mod give the remainder with the sign of the divisor (−7 % 3 is 2); fmod keeps the sign of the first value (fmod(−7, 3) is −1). round takes halves away from zero (2.5 → 3).
  • Starting values come from the data, and Levenberg-Marquardt then refines the best candidates. To help a hard fit, or to choose between two fits, type starting values as name = value, separated by commas or semicolons (with a decimal comma: b = 0,005; c = 2).
  • A formula that can't be fitted is refused with the reason, such as a formula without x. A fit needs at least as many points as parameters. A sweep whose fit doesn't reach a minimum reads "did not converge" in the Data Log, with no values.
  • When two sets of values draw the same curve (a Boltzmann with A → −A, C → C + A and k → −k), the fit is reported with its slope factor positive, so the same data always give the same values. A Gaussian's width is reported positive too.

Reading a fit

  • The panel and the Data Log show the model ("Model: Y = A·e^(−t/tau) + C") and the same equation with the fitted values ("Fitted: Y = 42.3·e^(−t/0.0185) + 2.1 (Y in pA, t in s)"), one Fitted line per sweep. You can copy either line. Values are given to 4 significant digits (7 for polynomials of degree 3 or more).
  • Time constants (τ) are in the recording's own X unit, usually seconds, even when the axis shows ms. They are always positive, and a double or triple exponential lists its components fastest first.
  • On a time axis, exponential and polynomial fits take the start of the fit range as t = 0 (the Data Log says where that is). On X-Y data, an exponential's amplitude is the value at x = 0, as the equation is written. When X starts too many time constants from 0 for that, the fit is reported about the first X value, x₀: the equation is written in x − x₀, and the Data Log says so.
  • R² is 1 − (residual sum of squares) / (total sum of squares). With relative weighting both sums are weighted, and for a line or parabola through zero the total is taken about Y = 0. The Data Log notes both, since such an R² can't be compared with an ordinary one.
  • Goodness of fit, below the parameters in the Data Log: N, df, the sum of squares, Sy.x (the residual SD, √(SS/df)), Adj. R², and AIC, AICc and BIC, counting the residual SD as a parameter, as R's AIC() and BIC() do. Lower is better, and only fits of different models to the same points, with the same weighting, can be compared.
  • On a sweep, consecutive samples are correlated, so AIC, AICc and BIC tend to favor extra components. Keep an extra exponential only if it also removes a trend from the residuals.
  • "Parameters not identifiable" in the Data Log means the best fit leaves a parameter undetermined (a Boltzmann steeper than the spacing of the X values, two merged time constants, or parameters that can't be told apart, as b and c in a*x + b + c). No intervals or band are given: treat those values with caution.
  • Missing samples in the fit range are skipped.

Confidence intervals and bands (X-Y data)

  • Fits to X-Y data, such as a dose-response or a current–voltage curve, report each parameter's confidence interval beside its value, at the confidence level in Settings › Statistics. These are asymptotic intervals, which assume the points are independent; a straight line's are exact. With exactly as many points as parameters there are none.
  • Fits to a sweep (a decay, a rise) get no intervals and no band: consecutive samples of a recording are correlated, so the intervals would be far too narrow to mean anything. For the uncertainty of a value such as τ, fit each sweep, sample or experiment, and summarize the values across them, for example with a mean and its CI.
  • Show band, in either part of the panel, shades a band around each fitted curve: "Confidence band (mean response)", where the true curve lies (the default), or "Prediction band (new observations)", where a new single point would fall, so always wider. Set its Level (95% by default).
  • A line or polynomial gets the exact band. A nonlinear model gets the delta-method band, which is approximate and most trustworthy when the parameters are well determined.
  • The band is exported with the curve to PDF, PNG and SVG, and is saved with the file. Editing the curve in a way the band can't follow (a filter, say) hides the band; Scale/Offset keeps it in step.

Results in the Data Log can be graphed directly: select a column of numbers there and press ⇧⌘G.

Toolkits

Toolkits: Overview

A toolkit is a set of tools for one field. @Graph has six: Electrophysiology, Pharmacology & Biochemistry, Biosignals, Spectroscopy, Flow Cytometry and Astronomy. All six are free, come with @Graph and are shown by default. Everything else in @Graph is the core and is always there. Hide the toolkits you don't use to keep the inspector and menus short.

Where the Tools Are

PlaceWhat it holds
A graph window's inspectorThe Toolkits category (the last icon) holds each toolkit's tabs. Choose a toolkit from the row of toolkit icons (its name shows beneath), then a tab.
An image window's inspectorThe Toolkits tab holds the toolkits' image tools. Choose one from the menu at the top of the tab, such as Astronomy › Plate Solve.
The Toolkits menuBetween Graph Utilities and Lab Tools, with a submenu for each toolkit that has menu commands. Electrophysiology's commands act on the front graph window; those of Pharmacology & Biochemistry, Flow Cytometry and Astronomy open their own windows. Show or Hide Toolkits… at the bottom opens Settings › Toolkits.
The Lab Tools menuThe core calculators first, then each toolkit's under its name.
Settings › ToolkitsWhich toolkits are shown, then the settings of Electrophysiology, Biosignals and Astronomy.

What Each Toolkit Holds

Each table lists a toolkit's tools by where they are, with the guide page that describes them. The calculators are all on the Lab Tools & Calculators page.

Show or Hide a Toolkit

  1. Choose Toolkits › Show or Hide Toolkits…, or open Settings › Toolkits.
  2. Uncheck a toolkit to hide it. Its tabs, image tools, submenu, calculators and status-bar controls are then hidden.
  3. Check it to show it again, or click Show All to bring every toolkit back.
  • Hiding a toolkit only hides it. Nothing is removed or turned off: Find a Tool still finds every tool, and a hidden toolkit's Batch Processing and Protocol steps still work.
  • Two lists leave a hidden toolkit out. Statistics › Regression leaves out the Pharmacology & Biochemistry models. The AI Assistant leaves a hidden toolkit's tool group out of its Tools list and its requests, to keep them small (see AI Assistant › Choosing Tool Groups).
  • Hiding applies to windows opened afterward. A graph or image window that is already open keeps the toolkits it opened with. Lab Tools, the Welcome window's More Samples and the Regression list follow at once, and the Toolkits menu follows the graph window in front. Showing a toolkit adds it everywhere at once.
  • A graph that uses a toolkit's tools, such as one saved with an Rₛ or junction-potential correction, shows that toolkit even when it's hidden, so you can see and change what was applied.
  • The keyboard shortcuts of a hidden toolkit's tabs (⇧⌘J for AP Detection, ⇧⌘I for Rₛ Correction) do nothing until it's shown again.
  • A guide page that belongs to a hidden toolkit says so, with a button to show it.

Finding a Tool

  1. In a graph window's inspector, click the magnifier at the right of the category's name, under the category icons.
  2. Type a tool's name or what it does (for example "spike", "filter" or "Nernst").
  3. Press Return to open the first result, or click Open beside any result.

Find a Tool searches every inspector tab, every Graph Utilities and Toolkits menu command, every Lab Tools calculator and every image tool, including those of hidden toolkits, and says where each one lives. A tool of a hidden toolkit has a Show button in place of Open (Show E-Phys, for example), which shows the toolkit again and opens the tool. An image tool reads "In image windows": open an image and choose its inspector's Toolkits tab.

Electrophysiology

Rₛ and Junction Potential Correction

Part of the Electrophysiology toolkit.

Two corrections for patch-clamp and sharp-electrode recordings. Series resistance (Rₛ, the resistance of the electrode and its access to the cell) adds an error in proportion to the current through it; Rₛ Correction removes that error from a recorded voltage or current. Junction Potential Correction subtracts a liquid junction potential from membrane potentials. Neither changes your data: each can be removed or undone, and a saved graph keeps it.

Series Resistance Correction: Rₛ (⇧⌘I)

Open the Rₛ Correction panel in the inspector's Toolkits category (Electrophysiology › Rₛ Correction), with ⇧⌘I, or by clicking the Rₛ button in the status bar. It has two modes, chosen at its top. Current clamp removes the Rₛ voltage drop from a recorded voltage, as the amplifier's bridge balance does. Voltage clamp corrects a recorded current for the voltage error and the filtering that Rₛ causes (Traynelis 1998). The panel starts in the mode that matches the recording, judged from the amplifier's telegraphed mode when the file stores it and otherwise from how fast its voltage steps are, and warns when you choose the other one.

Correct a current-clamp recording

Injected current adds an instant voltage jump at the start and end of each current step (ΔV = I × Rₛ), which distorts resting potential, AP threshold, sag ratio and steady-state voltage. The correction needs a voltage channel (mV) and the injected current.

  1. Open the recording, show the Rₛ Correction panel (⇧⌘I) and choose Current clamp.
  2. Read the Injected Current box, which says where the current comes from: a recorded current channel (pA or nA, used whenever there is one), or the file's protocol (an episodic ABF file stores its current-clamp protocol, so a voltage-only recording still gives each step's timing and size).
  3. For a file with neither, or to override the protocol, check "Describe the current step" (or "Use a step I enter instead") and fill in Step starts at, Step ends at, Step on sweep 1 and Change per sweep.
  4. Under Correct, choose how much of the current the correction follows.
  5. To apply an Rₛ you measured another way, such as the amplifier's bridge-balance value, check "Use manual Rₛ instead of auto-detect" and enter the Rₛ value in MΩ.
  6. Click Apply Rₛ Correction. The message and the Data Log give the Rₛ applied: the mean over the measured sweeps and its range.
SettingWhat it does
A step you enterTimes are as the X axis shows them, and the step is relative to the resting current: −50 pA and +10 per sweep gives −50, −40, −30 … pA. The voltage jump is looked for within 2 ms of the start you enter, and the step is moved to it.
Post-onset windowHow long after the step's onset the voltage is fitted. It is set from the sample rate to hold about ten samples (1.0 ms at 10 kHz, 0.4 ms at 25 kHz and above). If you type your own value, keep it under about a tenth of the membrane time constant, or the fit measures membrane charging.
Baseline windowThe time before the step used for the pre-step voltage and current (5 ms by default).
Correct: Every current step, relative to the sweep's startThe default. Subtracts (I − I at the sweep's start) × Rₛ at every level of the current, so a multi-step or biphasic protocol is corrected throughout.
Correct: The measured step onlySubtracts ΔI × Rₛ during the one step Rₛ is measured on. A holding current, other steps and the second phase of a biphasic pulse stay uncorrected. Offered only with a recorded current.
Correct: The whole current, holding current includedSubtracts I × Rₛ throughout (2 mV for −100 pA at 20 MΩ). Use it only when the current channel reads 0 with no current injected.
Use manual Rₛ instead of auto-detectApplies the value you enter to every sweep. Zero and negative values are allowed. It needs no step: with a protocol of ramps or pulse trains it is applied along the whole command.
Log per-sweep Rₛ estimates to Data LogOn by default. Adds each sweep's step, jump, Rₛ and fit to the Data Log.

Typical Rₛ is 5–20 MΩ for whole-cell patch, 30–100 MΩ for perforated patch and 50–200 MΩ for sharp electrodes, and always smaller than the input resistance. If a computed Rₛ looks implausible, check the channel units first.

When Rₛ can't be measured

  • A sweep with no clear current step (such as the 0 pA sweep of a family), or whose jump is inside its own noise, has no Rₛ of its own. It gets the Rₛ pooled over the other sweeps, and the Data Log names it below the table.
  • An estimate that can't be Rₛ is refused with an explanation: a jump in the opposite direction to the current step, an Rₛ larger than the input resistance, or a voltage that jumps at once to 90% or more of its final deflection (a voltage-clamp command, or a pipette without a cell). Use a manual Rₛ in those cases.
  • When the electrode and amplifier take more than one sample to follow the step, as with an uncompensated pipette capacitance, Rₛ reads low and the panel warns. Neutralize the pipette capacitance when recording, or enter the bridge-balance value as a manual Rₛ.
  • Below 8 kHz the estimate is about twice as noisy, and the panel warns. When the post-onset window holds too few samples for a line, automatic Rₛ is refused.
  • After bridge balance at the amplifier, the remaining Rₛ may be zero or negative (over-compensated). Both are handled.

Correct a voltage-clamp recording

The current flows through whatever Rₛ the amplifier left uncompensated. The membrane then sits at Vₘ = Vcmd − I·Rₛ, not at the command potential Vcmd (500 pA through 20 MΩ moves it 10 mV), and the membrane capacitance Cₘ charges through Rₛ, which slows fast currents with a time constant of Rₛ·Cₘ. This mode corrects a recorded current (pA or nA) for both.

  1. Open the recording, show the Rₛ Correction panel (⇧⌘I) and choose Voltage clamp.
  2. Under Rₛ and Cₘ, choose a Source (Measure automatically is the default), then click Measure to see the Rₛ, Cₘ and membrane resistance Rₘ that will be used, and where they came from.
  3. Under Command and Erev, read the Vcmd line. If the file has no command waveform or voltage channel, enter the Holding potential (−70 mV by default).
  4. Enter Erev, the reversal potential of the current being corrected (0 mV by default, which suits AMPA and NMDA receptor currents), or check "Erev from the last IV Plot".
  5. Click Apply Rₛ Correction. The message gives Rₛ, Cₘ and Erev, and the details go to the Data Log.
SettingWhat it does
Source: Measure automaticallyMeasures Rₛ, Cₘ and Rₘ from a voltage-step test pulse in the same sweeps (a step of 0.5–25 mV, 2 ms or longer, that returns to the level before it), fitted as Membrane Test fits it. The pulse gives the Rₛ the amplifier left uncompensated, so no compensation % is needed.
Use each sweep's own test pulseOff by default: the sweeps' pulses are averaged first. On, each sweep is corrected with its own values, to follow an Rₛ that drifts. The Data Log warns when Rₛ changes by more than 20% across the sweeps.
Source: Measure in a window I setUses the test pulse that starts in the window you enter (times as the X axis shows them).
Source: From the last Membrane TestUses the last result of Toolkits › Electrophysiology › Membrane Test…, run on a recording made with the same amplifier settings.
Source: From the amplifier's telegraphsUses the whole-cell Rₛ and Cₘ dial settings that an ABF file stores. The Rₛ dial is the total, so enter the Online Rₛ compensation % set on the amplifier (0 if it was off); the remainder is corrected.
Source: Values I enterRₛ, Cₘ and, optionally, Rₘ, filled in from the file's telegraphs when it has them. Check "This Rₛ is the amplifier's dial reading (before compensation)" to enter the compensation % as well.
ErevEntered as the window shows potentials; with JP Correction on, the panel allows for the junction potential. The Data Log reports how much a 5 mV error in Erev changes the corrected peak.
Fraction to correct100% by default. A lower value applies part of the correction.
Choose the dV/dt low-pass automaticallyOn by default. Uncheck it to type the dV/dt low-pass in kHz: a lower one is quieter but slows fast rises.
Correct the leak separately (uses Rₘ)On by default. With Rₘ known, the resting leak is moved to the command potential on its own, and only the rest of the current is rescaled with Erev.
  • With whole-cell capacitance compensation on, the amplifier cancels the test pulse's transient, so there is nothing to measure. When the file's telegraphs say it was on, Measure automatically uses the telegraphed values (enter the compensation %). When a pulse has no transient that can be fitted, the panel asks for another source.
  • When the command is within 5 mV of Erev the correction is refused: there is too little driving force. Samples whose Vₘ comes within 10% of the command's distance from Erev, or crosses it, are left unscaled and listed in the Data Log.
  • For a very noisy recording, low-pass filter it first (Filter/Smoothing) or average sweeps.
  • The correction assumes a single-compartment cell (space-clamp errors in dendrites can't be fixed offline) and a current channel whose zero is right. It is exact for ligand-gated currents and approximate for voltage-gated currents, whose gating depends on the true Vₘ. For those, correct the IV Plot's voltage axis.
  • The AI Assistant can apply the correction too, with the same choices.

Correct the IV Plot's voltage axis

In the Voltage clamp mode's IV Plot box, check "Correct the IV Plot's voltage axis for Rₛ". The panel finds Rₛ from the Source chosen above, and IV Plot then plots and fits each point at Vₘ = Vcmd − I·Rₛ, the potential the membrane reached. This needs no Erev and is exact for steady-state currents, voltage-gated ones included. It is unavailable while a voltage-clamp trace correction is applied. See Electrophysiology Commands › IV Plot.

Re-apply, remove and save

  • With a correction applied, the button reads Re-apply Rₛ Correction. Re-applying replaces the correction and never adds to it. Applying one mode's correction replaces the other's.
  • Remove restores the uncorrected data, and ⌘Z undoes a correction too. Once something else has changed the data (a filter, baseline correction or scale/offset), Remove and Re-apply are unavailable: use ⌘Z to undo the changes in order.
  • The status bar's Rₛ button appears for recordings with two or more channels and whenever a correction is applied. It turns orange and shows the value applied, with (VC) for a voltage-clamp correction.
  • Saving keeps the correction. Re-apply and Remove work after reopening as before.

Junction Potential Correction

A liquid junction potential (LJP) between the pipette and bath solutions shifts every recorded membrane potential by a fixed amount. JP Correction subtracts it, on screen and in measurements.

  1. In the graph window's status bar, type the junction potential in the mV field beside JP Correction (12 mV unless you change the default).
  2. Click JP Correction to turn it on. Membrane-potential channels then show V(corrected) = V(recorded) − LJP, and measurements use the corrected values.
  3. Click it again to bring back the recorded values. Turning it on or off and changing the value can each be undone with ⌘Z.
  • Sign: the value is subtracted, so a positive value makes potentials more negative and a negative value makes them more positive.
  • New graph windows start with "Enable JP correction by default" (off) and "Default JP value (mV)" (12) from Settings › Toolkits.
  • Only channels that look like a membrane potential are corrected: a voltage channel that stays between −120 and +180 mV and whose typical level is at least 20 mV from 0, such as a cell at rest or a voltage-clamp holding potential. Current channels, extracellular recordings, TTL and trigger lines, and traces already relative to baseline are left alone.
  • A file with no such channel opens with correction off, and its status bar has no JP Correction button.

How the Corrections Are Computed

Current clamp

  • For each sweep, a straight line is fitted to the voltage over the post-onset window and extrapolated back to the step's edge, the clock tick of the last sample before the step. That jump, divided by the current step, is Rₛ. Extrapolating separates the instant jump across Rₛ from the membrane charging that follows it.
  • Each sweep gets its own Rₛ, so drift during a recording is followed. With a protocol, Rₛ is measured on each sweep's largest change of level; in a biphasic step, on the reversal between its phases. The step should last at least about 2 ms.
  • The pooled Rₛ, applied to sweeps without their own (scaled by each one's step), is the weighted least-squares slope of the measured jumps on their current steps, each sweep weighted by the inverse variance of its jump. A pooled Rₛ, or a sweep's jump, within 3 of its standard errors of 0 counts as zero.
  • A recorded current is read as constant levels between its steps, so the corrected trace has sharp edges and none of the current's noise.

Voltage clamp

  • The correction is made point by point (Traynelis 1998). The membrane potential is Vₘ = Vcmd − I·Rₛ. The ionic current is Iₘ = I − Cₘ·dVₘ/dt, which removes the Rₛ·Cₘ filtering. The corrected current is Icorr = Iₘ · (Vcmd − Erev) / (Vₘ − Erev), the current the cell would have passed at the command potential.
  • Vcmd comes from the file's protocol (an ABF's epochs), else from a recorded command or Vₘ channel (read as its constant levels), else from the holding potential you enter.
  • The derivative of Vₘ amplifies high-frequency noise, so it is taken through a zero-phase Gaussian low-pass. The automatic choice is the highest low-pass that at most doubles the sample-to-sample noise, starting from a quarter of the sample rate or the amplifier's filter. The Data Log gives the low-pass used and how much the noise grew.
  • With "Correct the leak separately" off, the whole current, holding current included, is rescaled as one conductance, as in Traynelis's original. The Data Log says how much the holding current was rescaled.

AP Detection

Part of the Electrophysiology toolkit.

AP Detection finds action potentials and measures them. The panel has two modes, chosen at its top: Intracellular, for whole-cell or sharp-electrode voltage recordings, and Extracellular, for spikes on a continuous extracellular recording. A raster (spike times only) opens in Extracellular. In the panel, the ⓘ beside a setting gives more detail about it.

Detect and Measure APs (Intracellular)

  1. Open the recording and, in the inspector's Toolkits category, choose Electrophysiology › AP Detection (⇧⌘J). Leave the mode on Intracellular.
  2. Under Detection range, choose Full sweep, or place cursors A and B and choose Between cursors A – B.
  3. Under Detection, choose a Method and set its dV/dt threshold (see Threshold methods, below).
  4. Choose Find: First AP (the first AP in each sweep, the default) or All APs.
  5. Under Measurements, check what to report.
  6. Click Detect APs. The table goes to the Data Log, and each threshold is marked on the graph. Then choose Keep markers or Remove markers.

Detection runs on the visible sweeps of every voltage channel, with junction-potential correction applied when it is on. Every sweep analyzed gets a row in the table, so the rows line up with a current-step family.

For rheobase, firing rates, adaptation and the F–I curve of a current-step family, use Toolkits › Electrophysiology › Firing Properties…, which finds spikes with the settings of your last AP Detection run.

Threshold methods

  • Derivative threshold (the default): the threshold is the first sample where dV/dt reaches the value you set (20 mV/ms, the Allen Institute IPFX's value, unless you change it in Settings › Toolkits). The rise must also be sustained: its average slope over the crossing step and the next two samples must be at least the Sustained-slope multiplier (2 by default) times that value. Lower the multiplier if real APs are missed; raise it if brief noise counts as APs.
  • Fractional derivative threshold: for each AP, the threshold is where dV/dt, followed back from the AP's steepest rise, falls to a percentage of that maximum (Fraction of max slope, 5% by default, as in IPFX). The dV/dt value becomes a floor that an upstroke must clear to count at all.
  • Second derivative threshold: the threshold is at the peak of d²V/dt², where the rise accelerates fastest.
  • Phase-slope threshold (Sekerli): the threshold is at the peak of (d²V/dt²)/(dV/dt), the slope of the phase plot: the "kink" where the spike takes off (Sekerli et al. 2004). It suits cells with a sharp onset.
  • Phase-plane curvature threshold (Sekerli): the threshold is where the phase plot (dV/dt against V) bends upward most sharply, the peak of d²(dV/dt)/dV² (Method II of Sekerli et al. 2004). Noise moves it less than the phase slope.

The last three methods find the same APs as Derivative threshold and differ only in where they place each threshold.

Min. amplitude from threshold (40 mV by default) applies to every method: a candidate counts as an AP only if its peak rises at least this far above its threshold. This leaves out subthreshold depolarizations and noise.

What is measured

MeasurementHow it is measured
ThresholdThe voltage where the fast rise begins, placed by the Method chosen.
LatencyThe time from the start of the sweep to the threshold. For latency from the onset of a current step, use Firing Properties.
PeakThe highest voltage before the trace falls back below the threshold.
AmplitudePeak minus threshold.
Rise time and Decay timeThe time between two levels you set, each a percentage of the amplitude above the threshold: 10–90% for the rise and 90–10% for the decay by default. The table's column headers show the percentages used.
Half-widthThe AP's width at half its amplitude above the threshold.
Max rise and decay slopesThe steepest rise between threshold and peak, and the steepest fall between peak and trough, in mV/ms (the fall is negative). These are IPFX's upstroke and downstroke.
AHPThreshold minus the trough, the lowest point between the peak and the next AP's threshold, and the time from the peak to that trough.
  • Rise, half-width and decay are timed where the trace crosses each level, interpolated between samples, so they aren't rounded to whole samples.
  • Recordings at 15 kHz and faster: the threshold and the maximum slopes are found on a filtered copy of the trace (a zero-phase 4-pole Bessel low-pass at 10 kHz, or at 0.4 of the sampling rate when that is lower, as in IPFX), so the same cell gives the same threshold at any sampling rate. Your data is never changed, and the threshold's voltage and every other measurement are read from the unfiltered trace.
  • Recordings below 15 kHz are not filtered, and the threshold falls on a whole sample. Check "Interpolate threshold between samples (below 15 kHz)" to place it between samples instead. Batch Processing and Protocol AP steps have the same checkbox.

When a measurement is blank

  • In a burst, when the trace doesn't fall far enough before the next AP, half-width and decay time are blank rather than timed on a later AP.
  • An AP still rising at the end of the sweep or at cursor B is counted, with its threshold and latency only. An AP already rising at the start of the sweep or at cursor A is skipped: its threshold isn't in the data.
  • For the last AP in a sweep, the search for the AHP stops at the end of the current step when the file records it. Otherwise choose Between cursors A – B, with B at the end of the step, so the fall back to rest isn't read as the AHP.
  • The Data Log lists the APs these apply to.

Phase Plot

A phase plot shows dV/dt against membrane potential, which brings out the shape of the AP and how it changes from sweep to sweep.

  1. In the AP Detection panel (Intracellular), go to Phase Plot (dV/dt vs V).
  2. Set Smoothing, the number of samples averaged to smooth dV/dt (an odd number; 1 = none), and Sweeps: Visible / selected (the default) or All sweeps.
  3. For one average trajectory in place of a trace for each sweep, check Average across sweeps (binned), and set Bin width (1 mV by default) and Error bars.
  4. Click Generate Phase Plot (Generate Average Phase Plot when averaging). The plot opens as a new graph.
  • Each sweep's trace takes the color the sweep has in the source window.
  • The average groups the points into voltage bins and averages them across sweeps, with error bars in both V and dV/dt. Each voltage is passed twice, so the rising phase (orange) and the falling phase (blue) are averaged separately, which keeps the loop's shape. Falling runs from each spike's peak to the trough after it; rising is the rest.
  • Error bars: SD is the spread of the sweeps around the mean in a bin. SEM (the default) is SD / √n. CI is SEM × the t critical value for n − 1 degrees of freedom, at the confidence level in Settings › Statistics (95% unless changed). A bin that only one sweep reaches has no error bar.
  • dV/dt is a central difference between neighboring samples, so it reads low on the fastest part of the upstroke at low sampling rates: for a fast spike (about 600 mV/ms), about 40% low at 10 kHz, 17% at 20 kHz and 4% at 50 kHz. Record at 50 kHz or faster when the maximum dV/dt matters.

Detect Spikes (Extracellular)

Extracellular detection needs a continuous extracellular recording, such as a multi-electrode-array or single-electrode recording (see Supported File Formats).

  1. Open the recording, show the AP Detection panel (⇧⌘J) and set the mode to Extracellular.
  2. Leave "Pre-filter to spike band before detecting" on (300–3000 Hz by default). It removes slow field potentials and drift before detection.
  3. Choose Polarity: Negative-going (the default) or Positive-going.
  4. Choose Threshold: Auto (× noise SD), with its multiplier (5 by default), or Manual value.
  5. Set Dead time (1.5 ms by default): the pause after each spike, so that one spike isn't counted twice.
  6. Choose Full sweep or Between cursors A – B, then click Detect Spikes → Raster. The spike times open in a new raster window, one train for each sweep, showing its LFP / Spike Train Analysis pane.
  7. To check the spikes' shapes, go back to the recording's window and click Amplitude/Width Report or Show Spike Waveforms…. Both use the last detection run.

How spikes are found and measured

  • Pre-filter: a Butterworth band-pass, 4th order overall, run forward and backward, so it doesn't delay the spikes.
  • Auto threshold: each sweep (usually each channel) gets its own threshold, the multiplier × that sweep's noise SD, estimated as median(|x|)/0.6745 of the filtered trace (Quiroga et al. 2004). The panel previews the threshold for the first visible sweep, and the Data Log records the range used.
  • Manual threshold: a value in the first visible sweep's unit. A channel shown in another prefix of that unit (mV beside µV) is converted, so the level means the same on every channel.
  • Spike time: the spike's peak, located between samples, on the recording's own time axis, so the raster and the recording read the same time for a spike.
  • Amplitude/Width Report: each spike's amplitude (from its peak to the opposite peak that follows), its trough-to-peak width and its half-width (the time spent beyond half the peak, measured from zero), all within ±1.5 ms of the spike. They are plotted as a scatter of amplitude against width, and each train's mean and SD of all three go to the Data Log. A wide spread can mean a train holds more than one unit.
  • Half-width assumes a trace centered on zero, so keep the pre-filter on. A spike band also reshapes the waveform, so widths can read short or long. Check "Measure widths on a wide-band copy" to measure amplitudes and widths on the unfiltered trace, high-passed at the frequency you set (100 Hz by default). Spike times still come from detection, and the report's title says which trace was measured.
  • Show Spike Waveforms…: overlays 3 ms of trace (±1.5 ms) around each spike.

These tools need the continuous waveform. LFP / Spike Train Analysis works from spike times alone, so it also runs on spike-sorted files (such as .nev and .plx) that have no waveform.

Synapse Detection

Part of the Electrophysiology toolkit.

Synapse Detection finds synaptic responses and measures them. The panel has two modes, chosen at its top. Evoked measures the response at each known stimulus time, for paired-pulse and train protocols. Spontaneous finds events anywhere in the trace, such as miniature excitatory and inhibitory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs and mIPSCs) or potentials (EPSPs and IPSPs). Both run on the selected group. Batch Processing, Protocols and the AI Assistant give the same results from the same settings. In the panel, hold the pointer over a setting for more detail about it.

Detect Evoked Responses

  1. Open the recording and select the group to analyze. In the inspector's Toolkits category, choose Electrophysiology › Synapse Detection, and leave the mode on Evoked.
  2. Under Evoked Event Timing, choose where the pulse times come from: Uniform Train, Manual Timings or From TTL / Stimulus Channel (see Pulse times, below).
  3. Under Expected response, choose Upward (e.g., EPSP, IPSC) or Downward (e.g., EPSC, IPSP), and set the Onset threshold.
  4. Under Detection window, choose the Stimulation type, which sets how long after each pulse a response is looked for.
  5. Under Measure each response, choose what a response in a train is measured from: From rest (before the first pulse) or From the previous response's decay.
  6. Under Measurements to Report, check what to report (see What Is Measured).
  7. Click Detect Evoked Events. Every sweep of the group is analyzed, and the tables go to the Data Log.
  • A pulse with no response in its search window is recorded as a failure (amplitude 0), not skipped, so the failure rate is meaningful.
  • When pulses scored as failures cross the onset threshold shortly after the window ends, the Data Log says how many and when. Lengthen the window if responses are expected that late.
  • While detection runs, Cancel beside the progress bar stops it, and nothing from that run is added.

Pulse times

SourceWhat to enter
Uniform Train (the default)Start time (550 ms by default), Pulses (2) and Frequency (20 Hz). The line below them gives the interval and the last pulse's time.
Manual TimingsA list of pulse times in ms, separated by commas or spaces, for irregular protocols. Use a period for decimals. Entries that aren't plain numbers (such as "10ms") are ignored and listed in the Data Log.
From TTL / Stimulus ChannelThe Stimulus channel (the group that holds the stimulus trace), its Threshold, Min. pulse separation (5 ms by default) and Polarity. Each threshold crossing is a pulse onset, found separately in each sweep, so sweep-to-sweep jitter is followed.
PolarityActive-high (rises at onset), the default, or Active-low (falls at onset) for a TTL that is high at rest. Set wrong, there is no error, but every pulse time is late by the pulse width.
Add extra manual pulse time(s)Adds typed times to a train or to TTL pulses, such as a train plus one late pulse.

Typed times are in ms as the X axis shows them, also after Set X = 0. The Data Log lists the pulse times each run used.

Evoked settings

SettingWhat it does
Expected responseThe direction looked for at every pulse. It starts Upward for a voltage channel and Downward for a current channel.
Onset threshold; Threshold in baseline SDsHow far past the level before its pulse a response must go. With Threshold in baseline SDs checked (the default, at 4), it is a multiple of the noise SD in the baseline window before the first pulse. Unchecked, it is a size in the channel's unit.
Stimulation typeFills in Search up to: 4 ms for Electrical (the default) and ChR2, 6 ms for Chrimson. Each is 1 ms past the usual latency, for the time the rise takes to reach the threshold. Choose Custom to set your own.
Ignore after pulse (ms)1 ms by default. Nothing in this stretch is taken as the onset, so the stimulus artifact isn't read as the response. Lengthen it for a large or slow artifact.
Search up to (ms after pulse)The response must cross the onset threshold by this time. It must be longer than Ignore after pulse.
Never search past the next pulseOn by default, so a response in a fast train isn't given to the wrong pulse.
Measure for (ms after onset)100 ms by default. The peak is searched for this long after the onset, and the half-width and decay are measured this far past the peak, never past the next pulse. Shared with Spontaneous mode's Measure for.
Baseline window (ms before each pulse)10 ms by default. Shared with Spontaneous mode's Baseline before each event.
Paired-pulse ratio: 95% confidence intervalOff by default. Adds Fieller's interval to each paired-pulse ratio (see Evoked results).

What each response is measured from

  • From rest (before the first pulse), the default: every response is measured from the resting level, the mean of the baseline window before the first pulse. A later response in a train then includes what remains of the earlier ones: the summed response the cell sees.
  • From the previous response's decay: each response's decay is fitted (with the Model chosen under Decay Time Constants) and subtracted, extrapolated under the responses after it. Each later response is then measured from that decay: the response to its pulse alone, as paired-pulse ratios usually intend. A decay needs a few milliseconds before the next pulse to be fitted. If it can't be, the pulses after it are measured from the level the tail has reached at each pulse, and the Data Log says how many.
  • Onsets are always found from the level just before each pulse: the baseline window's straight-line trend carried to the pulse. On a flat baseline that is the window's mean; on an earlier response's decay it is the level the tail has reached.

Evoked results

TableWhat it holds
Per-sweep tablesOne for each measurement checked (Latency, Amplitude, Rise, Half-Width, Charge, Decay τ), with a row per sweep and a column per pulse. A failure is 0 in the Amplitude table. With exactly two pulses, the Amplitude table adds each sweep's own paired-pulse ratio (PPR).
Per-Pulse SummaryFor each pulse across sweeps: the sweeps, failures and failure rate (%); the mean amplitude with its SD (n − 1) and CV (SD ÷ |mean|), failures counting as 0; the number of responses and their own mean amplitude (the potency); then the responses' mean latency, rise, half-width and decay τ, and the mean charge, each when checked. Batch Processing's evoked report is this same table.
Paired-Pulse RatiosFor each consecutive pulse pair, the ratio of the mean amplitudes across sweeps (mean₂ ÷ mean₁). With the confidence interval checked, Fieller's 95% interval, computed from the sweeps that hold both pulses and allowing for the two pulses' covariance. "unbounded" means the first pulse's mean is not clearly away from zero, so the ratio is undetermined.
Train Summary (3 or more pulses)Each pulse's mean amplitude divided by Pulse 1's.
Steady-state (6 or more pulses)The mean of the last third of the pulses (at least the last 3) divided by Pulse 1's mean.
Short-Term Plasticity (2 or more pulses)Each sweep's own Pₙ ÷ P₁, averaged across sweeps. A sweep counts only if its Pulse 1 is a real response, in the expected direction and past the onset threshold. The N sweeps column says how many counted.

Report the Paired-Pulse Ratios (the ratio of means). A mean of per-sweep ratios, as in Short-Term Plasticity, reads high whenever amplitudes vary from sweep to sweep: about 1.1 with no plasticity at an amplitude CV of 0.3 (Kim & Alger 2001).

Plot results over time

For time-course experiments (a drug application, LTP or LTD), where each sweep is a time point.

  1. Under Results Over Time, check "Plot results over time".
  2. Choose the Time axis: Sweep interval (s), the default, and type the interval (10 s by default), or Recorded sweep times.
  3. Click Detect Evoked Events. A graph opens with one panel per pulse for each measurement checked in Measurements to Report, charge excepted. "Short-Term Plasticity (Pₙ / P₁, per-sweep)" (on by default) adds each sweep's ratios.
  • Sweep interval: each sweep sits at its position in the group × the interval. A sweep where no pulse was found leaves a gap.
  • Recorded sweep times: each sweep sits at the start time the file records for it, with 0 at the group's earliest sweep. Choose it when the time between sweeps matters, for example a pause while a drug washes in. It is available when the file records sweep start times (see Supported File Formats › Recording Times). A sweep without one is left out, and the Data Log names it.

Detect Spontaneous Events

Spontaneous mode has three methods, chosen under Detection Method: From Threshold, From Template and Deconvolution. See Choosing a method, below.

Detect by threshold

  1. Show the Synapse Detection panel and set the mode to Spontaneous.
  2. Under Detection range, choose Full sweep, or place cursors A and B and choose Between cursors A – B. With several sweeps, also choose the Multi-sweep mode.
  3. Under Detection Method, choose From Threshold, then the Threshold Type: Amplitude or Derivative.
  4. Enter the Threshold: negative for downward events (EPSCs, IPSPs), positive for upward ones (EPSPs, IPSCs). For Derivative, also set the Regression interval.
  5. Under Measurements to Report, check what to report.
  6. Click Detect Synaptic Events. Three graphs open: a Detection Graph, Captured Events and Event Measurements (one group per measurement, plotted against event number). The Synaptic summary goes to the Data Log.

Detect by template

  1. Under Detection Method, choose From Template.
  2. Under Template Source, choose Function and set Rise τ (2 ms by default) and Decay τ (18 ms) close to your events'. Or choose From a Graph and pick the open graph window whose sweeps are the templates, one per sweep.
  3. Under Event Direction, choose Upward or Downward.
  4. Set the template's Baseline (5 ms) and Length (30 ms). Keep it short: its baseline plus one or two decay τ.
  5. Under Detection Threshold, set Threshold: noise SD × (4 by default).
  6. Click Detect Synaptic Events.
  • A template from a graph must be sampled at the recording's rate, and each sweep should start Baseline before its event. An average of the Captured Events graph starts Baseline before each event early (10 ms by default), so set Baseline to that.
  • Number of templates adds templates (a fast and a slow one, for example), so events of each shape are found. "Show templates in new window" plots them.

Detect by deconvolution

  1. Under Detection Method, choose Deconvolution.
  2. Set the template as for From Template, with its rise and decay τ close to your events'.
  3. Under Deconvolution, set Threshold: noise SD × (4 by default), Low-pass (100 Hz) and High-pass (0.1 Hz). Keep the default band for most recordings.
  4. Click Detect Synaptic Events.

If the recording was already filtered below the events' frequencies and events are being missed, raise Low-pass. In an unfiltered recording a higher Low-pass lets noise through.

Spontaneous settings

SettingWhat it does
Multi-sweep modeContinuous (concatenate), the default, searches the sweeps as one recording, for one set of results. Each join between sweeps is a break: nothing is measured across it. Episodic (per sweep) analyzes each sweep separately, with its own graphs. In Continuous mode a per-sweep table goes to the Data Log, and "Add per-sweep summary graph" plots it.
Threshold (Amplitude)An event starts when the signal moves this far from baseline, and is kept only if its measured amplitude reaches the threshold. It is in the channel's unit. Slow drift and the resting level are removed for detection, so enter a size, not a level such as −70 mV.
Threshold (Derivative); Regression intervalAn event starts when the slope, measured over the Regression interval (1 ms by default; set it close to the events' rise time), crosses the threshold, in the channel's unit per ms.
Separating valley (% of peak)50 by default. An event ends once the signal falls back to this fraction of its peak, so the next event can be counted before the trace returns to baseline. Each new event must itself rise by at least the threshold from the lowest point since the previous one.
Minimum amplitudeFor the Derivative, Template and Deconvolution methods. Drops every detection whose amplitude is smaller than this, sign ignored (0, the default, keeps them all). A few times the baseline noise SD works well.
Est. time to peak (ms)Shown for the Derivative and Template methods. For Derivative, the peak is looked for within three times this after each onset. For Template, it is the least time between two detections, and it follows the template's time to peak.
Reject overlapping eventsOff by default. On, events closer together than Min. event separation (10 ms by default) form a cluster. "Accept first event in an overlapping cluster" keeps the first; unchecked, the whole cluster is dropped. Rejected events are left out of the event count, the frequency and the inter-event intervals, which then read low, and the Data Log says how many. Leave it off to measure frequency.
Baseline before each event (ms)10 ms by default. The stretch before each onset whose mean is the event's baseline.
Measure for (ms after peak)100 ms by default. How far past the peak the half-width, the decay fit and charge reach, never past the next event.
Capture events (waveforms)On by default. Saves each event's waveform over the two windows above and opens the Captured Events graph. Turn it off to run faster; the measurements are the same. "Baseline captured events" subtracts each waveform's baseline. "Align captured events" (Template and Deconvolution) aligns them at their peaks; Threshold events are always captured from their onsets.

Choosing a method

MethodGood forLimits
Amplitude thresholdSimple and fast.The threshold is in the recording's unit, so set it from the noise (about 3 to 4 noise SDs). Smaller events are missed, and a threshold near the noise lets noise peaks through.
Derivative thresholdRecordings with slow drift.The slope of fast noise is large, so on its own it detects many noise events. Pair it with a Minimum amplitude.
TemplateThe most selective when the template's kinetics match the events. Its threshold carries between recordings.It misses the first of two events closer together than the template, and events whose shape differs from every template.
DeconvolutionEvents close together and high rates.It needs a template close to the events' kinetics: a slow template on fast events gives false detections. A lower Low-pass merges events closer than about 0.3 ÷ low-pass seconds (3 ms at 100 Hz).

No method has excluded regions. To leave out a stretch such as a stimulus or a seal test, analyze between cursors A and B.

Summaries and distributions

  • "Overall summary (Data Log)" writes one summary of the recording: the number of events, the frequency, and the mean, SD (n − 1), median and CV (SD ÷ |mean|) of each measurement checked.
  • "Cumulative distributions (amplitude, IEI)" opens two graphs: the cumulative distribution of event amplitude (absolute value) and of inter-event interval (IEI), each value against the fraction of events at or below it. Copy or export their data to compare conditions, for example with the two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test in Statistics.

Plot a time-binned summary

  1. Under Time-Binned Summary Graphs, check "Plot time-binned summary graphs" and set the Bin width (30 s by default).
  2. Choose the Time axis: Sweeps joined end to end (the default) or Recorded sweep times.
  3. For error bars, check "Show error bars" and choose SD, SEM or the confidence interval of the mean (SEM × the t critical value, at the confidence level in Settings › Statistics).
  4. Click Detect Synaptic Events. A graph opens with one panel for each measurement checked, averaged in each bin.
  • A Mean Frequency (Hz) panel is always included: the bin's event count ÷ the bin width. This is not Instantaneous Frequency, which is 1 ÷ the interval before each event.
  • With Recorded sweep times, each event sits at its sweep's start plus its time within the sweep, and a bin's frequency is its events ÷ the time sweeps covered in it, so gaps between sweeps don't count as silence. Sweeps without a recorded start time are left out, with a note in the Data Log.
  • The bins cover the whole analyzed recording, so a quiet stretch at the end shows as zero frequency. If the bin width doesn't divide the recording, the last bin is shorter and its frequency uses its own width.
  • The section is hidden in Episodic mode, which has no continuous timeline.

Synaptic Summary

Every Spontaneous run adds a Synaptic summary to the Data Log, one row for the group: the channel, the events' direction, the number of sweeps, whether they were joined or searched one by one, the time analyzed (s), the number of events, the frequency (events ÷ the time analyzed) and the mean of each measurement checked in Measurements to Report. The time analyzed is the time searched, less any gap of missing samples and, with template matching, the last template length of each stretch searched, where no template fits. Batch Processing and a protocol's Detect Events step write the same table, so the same sweeps and settings give the same numbers in all three.

What Is Measured

Both modes measure each event the same way, on the recorded trace. Check each measurement under Measurements to Report.

MeasurementHow it is measured
BaselineSpontaneous: the mean of the trace over Baseline before each event, before the onset. Evoked: as chosen under Measure each response.
Peak AmplitudeThe peak minus the baseline. With "Average over" checked (the default, 0.3 ms), the peak is the mean over that time centered on the peak sample. The amplitude is always measured, since the other measurements are read relative to it; unchecking it only leaves it out of the results.
Rise TimesThe time between 20% and 80% of the amplitude; the picker beside the checkbox chooses 10–90%. Crossings are interpolated between samples.
Half-Widths (50% peak)The width at half the amplitude, between the crossings on the rise and on the decay.
Decay Time ConstantsThe τ of an exponential fitted by nonlinear least squares (Levenberg-Marquardt) from where the event has fallen to 80% of its amplitude to the end of Measure for, or to the next event. Model: Single exponential (the default) or Double exponential, when the decay has a clear fast and slow phase. Decay τ (ms) is always one number: the single τ, or the amplitude-weighted average (A₁τ₁ + A₂τ₂)/(A₁ + A₂), with Decay τ1 (ms, fast) and Decay τ2 (ms, slow) reported beside it when at least one event fits two components. Use the same model for every group you compare.
Charge (area)Off by default; in pC, on current channels only. Spontaneous events: the trace minus the baseline, integrated (trapezoid rule) from the onset to where it first returns to baseline after the peak. Evoked responses: by default "Fixed window after each pulse", from the end of Ignore after pulse for the Window you set (50 ms by default), ending before the next pulse; a failure then reads about 0 and counts in the mean. Lengthen the window for slow NMDA or GABA-A responses. "Onset to return to baseline" uses the spontaneous rule; a failure then has no charge.
Onset Times (Latencies in Evoked)Unchecked at first. Threshold methods and Evoked: where the line through the 20% and 80% points of the rise meets the baseline, never later than the threshold crossing, so onsets don't depend on event size. Template: the fitted template's onset. Evoked onsets are in ms from the stimulus (the latency). Spontaneous onsets are from the sweep's start, from cursor A, or from the first sweep's start in Continuous mode; the checkbox says which.
Inter-Event Intervals; Instantaneous FrequencySpontaneous mode only. The time from the previous event's onset (ms), and 1 ÷ that interval (Hz).
  • The peak is looked for within Measure for after an evoked onset; up to the separating valley for an amplitude threshold; within three times Est. time to peak for a derivative threshold; and within the template's Length for the Template and Deconvolution methods. It is never looked for past the next event or pulse.
  • An event that starts on the previous event's decay is measured from where that decay would have been: each event's fitted decay is subtracted before the next is measured. Half-width, decay and charge stop at the next detected event's onset, whether or not Reject overlapping events keeps that event.

Fitted waveform

Read from the samples, a small event's peak is lifted by the noise (by about one noise SD when the noise is band-limited), its rise reads long and its half-width short. With Fitted waveform checked (off by default), amplitude, rise and half-width come from a least-squares fit of the event shape, exp(−t/τdecay) − exp(−t/τrise), with its onset, both time constants and its scale free, about the same baseline. Charge, when measured, is then the fitted event's integral. The decay τ and which events are kept are unchanged. It is slower, and an event whose fit fails keeps its sampled values; the Data Log says how many. With it off, the Data Log notes when the median event is under 20 times the baseline noise SD.

When a measurement is blank

  • Tables show NaN for a value that couldn't be measured, so that a spreadsheet's statistics skip it.
  • Decay τ is NaN when the fit doesn't describe a decay (a τ over 5 times the stretch fitted, as an event on a plateau or a step gives). With the Double exponential model, an event too short for two components is fitted as a single exponential and has NaN for τ1 and τ2.
  • Charge is N/A when the trace hasn't returned to baseline within Measure for or before the next event; the Data Log says how many. On a voltage channel the checkbox reads "Charge (current channels only)" and is unavailable: the area under a voltage event is not a charge.
  • Rise time or half-width is blank when a level crossing isn't found between the previous event's peak and the next event's onset.
  • The first event, and in Continuous mode the first event after each join between sweeps, has no interval or instantaneous frequency.
  • An evoked failure has amplitude 0 and no kinetics. A sweep's paired-pulse ratio is NaN when its Pulse 1 isn't a real response.

Method Notes

  • Detection runs on a copy of the trace with slow drift removed (a 0.2 Hz high-pass). Measurements are made on the recorded trace.
  • Samples a file leaves unrecorded, such as a short gap at the end of each sweep, are read as baseline, so in Continuous mode detection carries on into the sweeps after them.

Template method

The optimally scaled template of Clements & Bekkers (1997). The template is slid along the data. At each point it is scaled and offset to fit best, and the point is scored by the scale divided by the standard error of the fit, a signal-to-noise ratio. An event is detected where the score passes the threshold: 4, the default, gives very few false positives, and 3 finds more small events. Because the template is scaled, only its shape matters, and the same threshold carries between recordings. With several templates, each point takes the score of whichever fits best.

Deconvolution method

After Pernía-Andrade et al. (2012). The trace is deconvolved by the template (the first, with several): its spectrum is divided by the template's, which turns each event into a brief peak at its onset however much it overlaps the next. The result is band-pass filtered, 0.1–100 Hz by default as in the paper, with Gaussian filters that add no phase shift or ringing. Its noise SD is the SD of a Gaussian fitted to its all-points histogram, and every local maximum above the threshold (4 noise SDs by default; the paper uses 4 to 4.5) is an event, timed at its onset. A template that ends while still decaying is continued along its own exponential tail. Detected events are then measured on the recorded trace as with the other methods.

Back to Contents

LFP / Spike Train Analysis

Part of the Electrophysiology toolkit.

The LFP / Spike Train Analysis panel has tools for local field potentials (LFP: the slow extracellular signal of many cells) and for spike trains (the times of each unit's spikes). To open it, choose Electrophysiology › LFP / Spike Train Analysis in the inspector's Toolkits category. Each section has its own button, and the ⓘ beside a setting explains it.

Sections of the panelWork on
Spectrogram; Cross-Correlation / CoherenceA continuous recording (two spike trains for the cross-correlogram)
Band Power Over Time; Hilbert Envelope and Phase; Phase–Amplitude CouplingA continuous recording
Spike-Triggered LFP and Phase LockingA spike-train raster and a continuous LFP graph
PSTH (Firing-Rate Histogram); ISI / Burst Detection; Fano FactorA spike-train raster

Field Potentials

On a spike-train raster, Band Power Over Time, Hilbert Envelope and Phase and Phase–Amplitude Coupling show a note in place of their controls: they need a continuous recording. Toolkits › Electrophysiology › LFP Oscillations… opens those three and Spike-Triggered LFP and Phase Locking in a window for the front graph, with the same controls and results.

Spectrogram and Cross-Correlation / Coherence

These two sections hold the controls of Graph Utilities › Spectrogram… and Graph Utilities › Cross-Correlation / Coherence…, working on this window's graph. See Signal Processing › Spectrogram and Signal Processing › Cross-Correlation / Coherence.

Bands, Sweeps and Phase

The four sections for rhythms share these rules.

  • Band: type the two edges in Hz, or choose from Presets: Delta 1–4 Hz, Theta 4–8, Theta (rodent hippocampus) 6–10, Alpha 8–12, Beta 13–30, Low gamma 30–50, Gamma 30–80 and High gamma 80–150 Hz.
  • Sweep: one sweep, or All sweeps of one channel. Channels are never pooled together.
  • Every band-pass is the Filter panel's zero-phase Butterworth (4th order, both edges −3 dB).
  • Phase is 0° at each peak of the band-passed signal and ±180° at each trough.
  • Within a cycle or two of an end of the trace or a gap, results carry edge effects. Coupling and phase locking leave out data within two cycles of the phase band's low edge of an end or gap.

Band Power Over Time

Shows the power in one frequency band as a time series, to follow how a rhythm grows and fades.

  1. Choose the Sweep and set the Band (4–8 Hz by default).
  2. Choose the Method: Spectrogram (the default) or Band-pass + Hilbert.
  3. For Spectrogram, set Window (samples, 0 = auto) and Overlap (%) (50% by default).
  4. Optionally check Relative power (band ÷ total) and set the Total range (1–100 Hz by default), check Decibels (10·log10), and set Smoothing (s, 0 = none).
  5. Click Compute Band Power. The result opens as a new graph on the recording's time axis; with All sweeps, each sweep becomes a sweep of the result. The Data Log records the settings used.
SettingWhat it does
SpectrogramThe power spectral density of each short Hann window (mean removed), integrated over the band, with each frequency bin counted by the share of its width inside the band. This is the band's variance in that window, placed at the window's center.
Band-pass + HilbertHalf the squared amplitude envelope of the band-passed signal, at every sample. Its mean over time is the band's variance.
WindowRounded down to a power of 2, at least 64. Auto picks the shortest window whose frequency bins are at most a quarter of the band's width apart (for 4–8 Hz at 1 kHz: 1,024 samples). A window with a missing sample has no value.
Relative powerDivides the band's power by the power over the Total range, found the same way, so a change in overall signal size doesn't read as a change in the band.
SmoothingA centered moving average that shrinks at the ends. For relative power, the band and the total are each averaged before they are divided. Decibels are taken last.
  • Both methods estimate the same quantity: a steady sinusoid of amplitude A reads A²/2 by either. Band-pass + Hilbert follows changes sample by sample; Spectrogram averages over each window.
  • Relative power by Band-pass + Hilbert needs Smoothing of at least one cycle of the band's low edge, and the panel says so: a ratio of two unsmoothed envelopes is not a share of the power and can exceed 1.
  • The Data Log says when a window was cut to fit a short sweep, and gives the smoothing window used (a whole, odd number of points).

Hilbert Envelope and Phase

Band-passes the signal and gives the rhythm's amplitude envelope, its phase and, if you like, its instantaneous frequency.

  1. Choose the Sweep and set the Band (4–8 Hz by default).
  2. Check the outputs. Band-passed signal, Amplitude envelope and Phase (degrees) are on by default; Instantaneous frequency (Hz) is off.
  3. Click Compute Envelope and Phase. The outputs open as channels of a new graph on the recording's time axis.
  • The envelope and phase come from the analytic signal (the Hilbert transform by FFT, as SciPy's hilbert), after each end is extended by odd reflection for 10 cycles of the band's low edge. Blank samples stay blank, and each unbroken stretch is analyzed on its own.
  • Instantaneous frequency is the rate of change of the unwrapped phase ÷ 2π, by central differences. Where the envelope dips toward zero the phase is poorly defined, and the frequency can swing widely, even below 0.
  • Phase and instantaneous frequency describe one rhythm only for a narrow band. For a band wider than an octave the Data Log says so.

Phase–Amplitude Coupling

Measures whether the amplitude of a fast rhythm (such as gamma) depends on the phase of a slow one (such as theta), and tests the result against surrogates (time-shifted copies of the data).

  1. Choose the Sweep: one sweep, or All sweeps (pooled), which puts every sweep of the channel into one index.
  2. Set the Phase band (4–8 Hz by default) and the Amplitude band (30–80 Hz by default), which must lie above it.
  3. Choose the Measure: Tort MI (the default) or Canolty MVL.
  4. Set Surrogates (200 by default; 0 skips the test).
  5. Click Compute Coupling. The index and its test go to the Data Log. For Tort MI, the phase–amplitude plot also opens as a new graph.
ResultHow it is computed
Modulation index (Tort MI)The phase band's phase is divided into 18 bins of 20°, and the amplitude band's mean envelope is found in each. MI measures how far that distribution is from flat: (log 18 − its entropy) ÷ log 18, from 0 (no coupling) toward 1 (Tort et al. 2010).
Phase–amplitude plot and preferred phaseFor Tort MI. The plot shows the normalized mean amplitude in each phase bin over two cycles, with the flat 1/18 line for no coupling. The Data Log gives the center of the bin with the largest amplitude (so coupling at 0° reads ±10°) and the distribution's circular mean phase.
Mean vector length (Canolty MVL)The length of the mean of A·e^(iφ), with A the amplitude band's envelope and φ the phase band's phase, in the signal's unit; its angle is the preferred phase (Canolty et al. 2006). It is also given as a z-score against the surrogates and as direct PAC, from 0 to 1 (Özkurt & Schnitzler 2011).
Surrogate testEach surrogate circularly shifts the amplitude envelope against the phase by a random lag between 10% and 90% of the data's length, which keeps each signal's own rhythm and breaks only their timing (Canolty et al. 2006). The Data Log gives the surrogates' mean, SD and 95th percentile, z = (index − mean) ÷ SD, and p = (1 + surrogates at or above the index) ÷ (1 + surrogates), so 200 surrogates can show p down to 0.005.
  • Use p for significance, not z: the surrogate values are skewed, so z overstates it slightly. Running the test again gives the same result.
  • This p is right for a band pair you chose before looking at the data. For a pair picked from a comodulogram, use the whole-map p.
  • The Data Log warns when the amplitude band is narrower than twice the phase band's top frequency: coupling puts the fast rhythm's power in sidebands at ± the phase frequency, which a narrower band cuts off (Aru et al. 2015).
  • With fewer than 30 cycles of the phase band's low edge, the panel and the Data Log warn that p tends to be a little too small. Pooling sweeps helps.
Comodulogram

The comodulogram maps the chosen Measure for every pair of phase and amplitude frequencies, as a heatmap. Open Comodulogram in the section, set Phase (Hz) (from 2 to 14, step 1, width 2 by default), Amplitude (Hz) (from 20 to 200, step 5, width 20) and Whole-map test surrogates (200; 0 skips the test), and click Compute Comodulogram.

  • Amplitude bands are widened to at least twice the top edge of the highest phase band (15 Hz with the defaults, so 30 Hz wide). A cell whose amplitude band reaches down to its phase band is left empty.
  • Whole-map test: the brightest of hundreds of cells, tested alone, shows coupling in pure noise most of the time, so the map is tested as a whole. Each surrogate shifts the amplitude by one random time, the same in every cell, and gives the largest index anywhere on its map. A cell is significant when its index exceeds that maximum in all but 5% of the surrogates (a max-statistic test; Maris & Oostenveld 2007), so the chance of even one false cell on the map is 5%.
  • The significant cells open as a second heatmap, and the Data Log lists them with their whole-map p. Use that p for any pair you pick from the map.
  • The whole-map test costs power, most of all in short recordings and for cells whose index is naturally small. If you have a band pair in mind, test it on its own with Compute Coupling.

Read coupling with care. Sharp or non-sinusoidal waves (sawtooth-shaped theta, spikes, artifacts) give a significant index without any interaction between two rhythms, and so can a too-narrow amplitude band (Aru et al. 2015). Look at the raw traces and the phase–amplitude plot before drawing conclusions.

Spike-Triggered LFP and Phase Locking

Averages the LFP around each spike of a train, and measures how consistently the spikes fall at one phase of an LFP rhythm. It needs a spike-train raster and a continuous LFP graph, both open.

  1. In the panel of either window, choose the other one: Spikes from on the LFP graph, or LFP from on the raster.
  2. Choose the Train and the LFP sweep. When the raster has as many trains as the LFP graph has sweeps, you can instead check "Each train with the LFP sweep of the same number", which pools the trials.
  3. Set Window ± (ms) (250 ms by default), the time averaged on each side of a spike, and the Phase band (4–8 Hz by default).
  4. To filter the LFP before averaging, check "Band-pass the LFP before averaging" and set the Average band (1–100 Hz by default).
  5. Click Compute Spike–LFP. The spike-triggered average and a histogram of spike phases open as new graphs, and the statistics go to the Data Log.
ResultHow it is computed
Spike-triggered averageThe LFP from −window to +window around each spike's nearest sample, as the mean with mean ± SEM (the standard error across spikes). A spike whose window runs past an end or into a gap is left out, and the Data Log gives the count.
Spike phasesEach spike's phase in the phase band, interpolated between the samples either side of it. The histogram has 18 bins, with the flat level for no locking. The Data Log gives the resultant length R and the mean phase.
