PPCThe pairwise phase consistency (Vinck et al. 2010): the average cosine of the phase difference over all pairs of spikes. It is about 0 without locking and, unlike R, is not inflated when spikes are few. For von Mises-locked spikes it estimates R².
Rayleigh testThe test of uniform phases, by Zar's approximation from 10 spikes (as in CircStat; Berens 2009). Below 10 spikes, p is exact for 2 and found by simulation for 3 to 9.
PPC across trials (PPC₁)With each train paired with its sweep: the average over pairs of spikes from different trials only (Vinck et al. 2012). Spikes of one burst share a phase, which raises PPC but not PPC₁, so prefer PPC₁ for a unit that fires in bursts.
  • Spike times are lined up with the LFP on the recording clock when both carry one, and otherwise from their sweeps' starts (see Signal Processing › How the two signals are lined up). The result says which.
  • A train and an LFP sweep recorded at different times are refused, with a button, "Compare from each sweep's start (not simultaneous)". That result is labeled "not simultaneous".

Spike Trains

These sections work on a spike-train raster: one made by Detect Spikes → Raster in AP Detection (Extracellular) or by the Spike Sorter, or a file that stores spike times, such as Blackrock/Ripple .nev, Plexon .plx, an NWB file's units or TDT snippets (see Supported File Formats). They use spike times only. Amplitude, width and waveform analysis need the waveform and are under AP Detection (Extracellular).

Recorded Time and Gaps

  • A raster from Detect Spikes → Raster or the Spike Sorter knows the span each train was recorded over, so a silent stretch at the end counts as zero firing.
  • A spike-sorted file stores only spike times, so each train is taken as recorded from its first to its last spike. Every spike-train tool follows this rule.
  • Recordings with gaps (a paused Plexon or TDT recording, or an NWB unit with several observation intervals): every analysis uses only the time observed. Rates are spikes ÷ observed time, a PSTH bin wholly in a gap is left blank, and no interval, burst or counting window spans a gap.
  • A spike exactly on a bin edge, judged in whole samples, goes in the bin that starts there, and an interval equal to a limit counts as within it.

PSTH (Firing-Rate Histogram)

Shows firing rate over the recording's time axis. To align the histogram to stimulus events instead, see the next section.

  1. Leave Align to stimulus events off.
  2. Choose Output: Pooled average (the default, one trace for the population) or Per train.
  3. Set Bin width (ms) (10 ms by default), or click Suggest to fill in a width chosen from the data.
  4. To set the time covered yourself, check Custom time window and set Start (s) and End (s). Otherwise the PSTH covers the recorded span (for a spike-sorted file, the earliest first spike to the latest last spike).
  5. Click Compute PSTH. The firing rate in Hz opens as a new graph.
  • Each bin's rate is its spike count divided by the time actually recorded in that bin, summed over the trains when pooled. When sweeps differ in length, a late bin is averaged over only the sweeps that reach it. A bin that no train recorded shows as a gap.
  • For a spike-sorted file, each train counts only in the bins wholly between its own first and last spikes.
  • If the bin width doesn't divide the window, the last bin is shorter and its rate uses its own width. Spikes outside the window are left out.
  • Suggest chooses the width from this data's own spike counts (Shimazaki & Shinomoto 2007), among widths that divide the window into whole bins. When at no width the counts vary more than chance (Poisson) would make them, the spikes are too few to resolve a change in rate: Suggest says the data are insufficient and leaves the width alone. When the best width is the finest or coarsest it tries, a note says the best may lie beyond it.

PSTH Aligned to Stimulus Events

A peri-stimulus time histogram (PSTH; Gerstein & Kiang 1960): each trial's spikes are re-timed from its stimulus, and each bin shows the mean firing rate across trials.

  1. In PSTH (Firing-Rate Histogram), check Align to stimulus events.
  2. Choose Stimulus times from (see Where the event times come from, below).
  3. Leave "First event in each sweep only" on for one trial per sweep, or turn it off to make every event a trial.
  4. Set Before (s) and After (s) (0.5 and 1 by default), Bin width (ms) and, optionally, Smoothing SD (ms).
  5. Choose Curves: All trains (one population curve), Per unit (one curve for each unit of a Spike Sorter raster, over its own trials) or Per train (the events within each train, such as many stimuli in one long recording).
  6. Optionally check Also show ± SD, and "Baseline z-score and bins that differ from baseline".
  7. Click Compute Aligned PSTH. The mean rate with its ± SEM band opens as a new graph, and the aligned raster (one row per trial) as another. The table goes to the Data Log.
Where the event times come from
Stimulus times fromThe events
TTL / stimulus channelEach onset on a channel of the open recording, where it crosses the Threshold, found as in evoked synaptic detection.
Stimulus command in fileEach time the file's stimulus command leaves its holding level (ABF protocols): a step, a ramp, or each pulse of a train.
Typed timesEvent times (s) on the raster's time axis, as the graph shows it. The same times are used in every sweep.
Event rasterA train of an open event raster: a file's digital events (Blackrock), events and strobed words (Plexon), epocs (TDT), TTL lines and messages (Open Ephys, Neuralynx) or stimulation events (Intan RHS). Every event is a trial.
  • Channel and command events are timed on the recording's own time axis, as the raster's spikes are, and stimulus sweeps pair with the raster's trials in order. Keep the recording's window open.
  • Event raster: Min. interval (ms) leaves out an event that comes less than that long after the one before it, so a burst of TTL pulses gives one trial. "Only events from (s)" uses one stretch of the experiment. The two rasters must share a clock (the same file, or recordings started at the same moment); otherwise the panel says why it can't use them.
  • A trial whose window the train didn't record at all is left out, and the Data Log says how many.
How the aligned PSTH is computed
  • Bins are anchored at the event: one bin edge sits at 0, and the window is widened to whole bins.
  • A trial counts in a bin only if its sweep recorded the whole bin, so an event near the end of a sweep doesn't read as silence after it. The Data Log lists how many trials each bin used.
  • Each bin shows the mean rate across trials, with a band of ± SEM (the SD with n − 1, divided by √n).
  • Smoothing SD: when above 0, each trial's binned rate is smoothed with a Gaussian of that SD, cut off at 4 SD, before the trials are averaged (Nawrot et al. 1999), so the SEM describes the smoothed curve. At recording gaps and ends the kernel is rescaled over the bins that have data, so missing time isn't treated as silence.
  • Data Log: each curve's pre-event rate (spikes in the Before window ÷ its length) and post-event rate (the After window), both as mean ± SEM across trials; the peak; and every bin's mean, SEM and trial count.
Bins that differ from baseline

With "Baseline z-score and bins that differ from baseline" checked, set Baseline from (s) and to, in seconds from the event (the whole Before window by default), and α (0.05 by default).

  • z-score: (the bin's mean rate − the baseline bins' mean) ÷ the baseline bins' SD, on the curve as plotted, in a new graph. It measures size only; it is not a test.
  • The test: each bin outside the baseline is compared with the baseline's mean rate. Its p-value comes from shuffling each trial's bins within that trial 1,000 times (fewer on very large data; the Data Log gives the number) and taking the largest difference over all the bins tested (a max-statistic permutation test with step-down; Westfall & Young 1993). This holds the family-wise error rate at α: the chance of marking any bin when the stimulus has no effect.
  • The test uses unsmoothed rates and assumes that, without a stimulus, a trial's bins are interchangeable (a steady rate across the window). Each trial keeps its own spikes, so bursts don't cause false marks.
  • The bins that differ are marked on the z-score graph and on the PSTH's mean. The Data Log adds each bin's z and adjusted p and lists the periods that differ.

ISI / Burst Detection

Plots a histogram of inter-spike intervals (ISI: the time from one spike to the next) and writes a burst summary for each train to the Data Log.

  1. Choose the Method: Max Interval (the default) or Poisson surprise.
  2. For Max Interval, set Max intra-burst ISI (ms) (10 ms by default) and Min. spikes per burst (3 by default). For Poisson surprise, set Min. surprise (−ln P) (5 by default).
  3. Set the options (see Options, below).
  4. Click Detect Bursts. The ISI histogram opens as a new graph, and the summary table goes to the Data Log.
How bursts are found
  • Max Interval: a burst is a run of spikes, at least as many as Min. spikes per burst, in which every interval is at or below Max intra-burst ISI.
  • Max Interval options (NeuroExplorer), all 0 by default, turn that plain rule into NeuroExplorer's full method. "Max ISI within a burst" keeps a burst going, once started, on intervals up to a longer limit. Bursts closer than "Merge bursts closer than" (last spike to next first spike) are then joined. Last, bursts shorter than Min. burst duration or with too few spikes are dropped.
  • Poisson surprise (Legéndy & Salcman 1985, after Cotterill et al. 2016's implementation, with the stop interval taken at the burst's end): a burst starts at three spikes whose two intervals are both shorter than half the train's mean interval. Later spikes are added while that makes the burst more surprising, and early ones dropped while that does. Surprise is −ln P, with P the chance that a random (Poisson) train at the train's mean rate fires that many spikes that quickly. Bursts below Min. surprise are left out (5 is P below 0.7%), and the Data Log lists every burst.
Options
OptionDefaultWhat it does
Pool all trains into one ISI histogramOffOne histogram for the population in place of one for each train.
Log-scale ISI binsOffOff: about 100 equal-width bins. On: ten bins per decade (Pasquale et al. 2010) on the same edges every run, on a log axis, so short intervals within bursts and long gaps between them both show.
Bias-corrected ISI CV (jackknife)OffAdds a column with the jackknife-corrected CV: n·CV − (n − 1)·the mean CV leaving out one interval at a time. It is less biased than the plain CV, but varies more.
Poisson chance referenceOnMax Interval only. Adds, beside % spikes in bursts and the burst rate, what the same rule gives on average for a Poisson train with the same number of spikes and mean interval.
Mark bursts on a copy of the rasterOnOpens a copy of the raster with a bar under each burst.
The burst table
ColumnMeaning
Spikes; spanThe spike count, and the time the train was recorded over. With gaps, the time observed and the time spanned.
Bursts; burst rateThe number of bursts, and bursts ÷ span.
Spikes in bursts; %The spikes that belong to a burst, and their share of all spikes.
Mean spikes per burst; mean burst durationAverages over the train's bursts.
Mean intra-burst rateEach burst's (spikes − 1) ÷ duration, averaged over bursts.
Mean interburst intervalFrom the last spike of one burst to the first spike of the next (as in Cotterill et al. 2016).
ISI CV, CV2, LVThree measures of irregularity, each about 1 for random (Poisson) firing, below 1 for more regular and above 1 for burstier firing. CV2 (Holt et al. 1996) and LV (local variation; Shinomoto et al. 2003) compare neighboring intervals, so slow changes in firing rate affect them much less than CV.
  • The Pooled row sums spikes, bursts and spans, averages over every burst rather than over the trains' averages, and takes CV2 and LV from every pair of neighboring intervals within a train. It has no CV: intervals pooled from trains that fire at different rates look irregular even when each train is regular.
  • The CV reads low from few intervals (about 0.87 instead of 1 for a Poisson train with 5), and the Data Log says so for a train with fewer than 20. CV2 and LV have no such bias.
  • Poisson chance reference: random firing makes bursts too (at 20 Hz with the default 10 ms and 3 spikes, 8.5% of the spikes of a 100-spike Poisson train). The reference is exact, from the chance that an interval is at or below the maximum, 1 − exp(−maximum ÷ mean interval), and the lengths of the runs of such intervals. An observed % near it is what chance gives at that rate. With few spikes it reads a little high. It covers the plain rule only: with Max Interval options set, its columns are empty.

Fano Factor

The Fano factor F is the variance of spike counts divided by their mean (variance with n − 1): 1 for a Poisson train, below 1 for more regular firing, and above 1 for more variable or bursty firing.

  1. Choose Count spikes in: Consecutive windows (the default) or Across trials.
  2. Set Counting window (ms) (100 ms by default).
  3. For Across trials, set Window start (s). Optionally type Events (s), or check "Events from an event raster" and choose the Raster, the Train and Trials of.
  4. Optionally check "Also plot Fano factor against window length".
  5. Click Compute Fano Factor. The table goes to the Data Log.
Count spikes inWhat is counted
Consecutive windowsOne value for each train, from back-to-back windows over the span it was recorded. For a spike-sorted file that span is its first to its last spike, and those two spikes are left out: they are in the span by construction and, counted, would raise F.
Across trialsOne window per trial, at the same time in each: from Window start on each sweep's time axis, from each event you type, or from each event of an event-raster train. A Spike Sorter raster gives one value for each unit; any other raster counts all trains as trials of one unit. With an event raster, Trials of sets this: Per train, Per unit or All trains. A trial counts only if its sweep recorded the whole window.
  • The Data Log gives F with its confidence interval, at the confidence level in Settings › Statistics (95% unless changed), and the p-value of F = 1 from the index-of-dispersion test: (n − 1)·F against χ² with n − 1 degrees of freedom (Eden & Kramer 2010). The interval inverts the same χ². It is asymptotic, and conservative (wider than it needs to be) at low counts.
  • F depends on the window. It tends to 1 for windows much shorter than the interval between spikes and, for long windows, to the squared CV of the intervals, while slow changes in rate raise it. Compare Fano factors at one window length. "Also plot Fano factor against window length" plots F with its confidence interval at 25 window lengths on a log axis, with the Poisson line at 1.
  • A train needs at least two whole windows with a spike in them. When none has, the panel says so: use a shorter window.
  • Across trials, a Window start before every sweep's recording begins moves to where the recordings begin, and the Data Log says so.

Back to Contents

Electrophysiology Commands

Part of the Electrophysiology toolkit.

The Toolkits › Electrophysiology menu holds analyses that run on the front graph window straight from the menu. Each needs a particular kind of recording. The toolkit's inspector panels (Rₛ Correction, AP Detection, Synapse Detection and LFP / Spike Train Analysis) have their own pages.

CommandNeedsGives
VI PlotCurrent clamp: a family of current stepsA V–I graph; input resistance and membrane τ in the Data Log
IV PlotVoltage clamp: a family of voltage stepsAn I–V graph; input resistance and Erev in the Data Log
Firing Properties…Current clamp: a family of current stepsA table in the Data Log; an F–I graph
Sag AnalysisCurrent clamp: hyperpolarizing current stepsSag ratio and slope in the Data Log
Slow AHP Analysis…Current clamp: trains of spikesIts own window; a table in the Data Log
LFP Oscillations…Any graphIts own window
Spike Sorter…A continuous extracellular recordingIts own window; sorted units as a spike-train graph
Membrane Test…Voltage clamp: a small voltage stepRₛ, Rₘ and Cₘ in the Data Log
  • Every command except LFP Oscillations needs a sampled recording, not a spike-train raster.
  • VI Plot, IV Plot, Firing Properties, Sag Analysis and Membrane Test measure the episodes the window shows. A sweep hidden with Review sweeps, or a hidden group, is left out, and the Data Log says how many were. A hidden channel of the same episodes (the current, say) is still read. Fit curves and AP markers are never measured.
  • Times in the Data Log are as the X axis shows them, after any Set X = 0 shift. Each of those five tables ends with the definitions of what it reports.
  • If you edit the graph while a command runs, the Data Log says so. Run the command again to measure the edited data.
  • LFP Oscillations, Spike Sorter and Slow AHP Analysis keep one window for each graph: choosing the command again brings that graph's window forward.
  • Spectrogram and Cross-Correlation / Coherence are in the Graph Utilities menu (see Signal Processing).

VI Plot (Voltage–Current Relationship)

Plots the steady-state voltage against the injected current for a family of current steps, and reports input resistance (Rin) and the membrane time constant (τ). It needs current-clamp voltage sweeps with one step size per sweep.

  1. Bring the recording to the front and choose Toolkits › Electrophysiology › VI Plot.
  2. The current steps are read from the recorded current channel or, without one, from the file's stimulus protocol. If the file has neither, a dialog asks for them: First step (pA) and Increment per sweep (pA), or each sweep's step; the Holding level (pA); and Step start (ms) and Step end (ms) as the X axis shows them (left empty, the step is found in the voltage sweeps). Click Analyze.
  3. The V–I graph opens in a new window with the fitted line, and the table goes to the Data Log.
ReportedHow it is computed
Current step and steady-state voltage responseFor each sweep, the steady state is the mean over the last 20% of the step, ending 0.5 ms before the step's end. Both are measured from the baseline: the mean over the 100 ms before the step, ending 0.5 ms before it.
Baseline VmThe potential before the step, averaged over all sweeps, junction-potential corrected when correction is on.
Input resistanceThe slope of a line fitted to the steady-state responses over the linear range around 0 pA, with R². The Data Log gives the range and the sweeps it held, and the plotted line spans it.
Membrane τFor each sweep that didn't fire: V(t) = V∞ + A·e^(−t/τ), fitted by nonlinear least squares from where the response first reaches 10% of its peak deflection to that peak (the method of the Allen Institute's IPFX). V∞ is fitted, not taken from the end of the step. The reported τ is the mean over the hyperpolarizing sweeps, because depolarizing steps recruit active conductances that shorten it; all fitted sweeps are averaged only when no hyperpolarizing sweep was fitted.

The linear range

  • The range depends on the cell, so it is found from the data. Starting from the steps nearest 0, it grows one step at a time while the slope changes by no more than 10% (beyond the noise, with 7 or more steps).
  • A sweep that fired action potentials (a rise of more than 20 mV within 1 ms) is still plotted, but its steady state includes the spikes, so it is left out of input resistance and τ. The Data Log marks it with *.
  • A sweep that lies far off the curve the other sweeps trace is left out of input resistance and marked †.
  • A sweep whose response is too small (under 20 times the baseline noise SD) or too brief to fit has no τ, shown as a dash.
  • IPFX fits the peak deflection of its hyperpolarizing sweeps instead of the steady state, so the two input resistances can differ where Iₕ sags.
  • VI Plot and IV Plot stop with a message when the family looks recorded in the other clamp mode, judged from how quickly the voltage reaches its new level at each step. The check needs at least 2 sweeps.

Input-resistance settings

These are in Settings › Toolkits and apply to VI and IV Plots from the menu, Batch Processing, Protocols and the AI Assistant.

SettingDefaultWhat it does
Fit the line through the originOffFits the range's steps by a line through (0, 0); R² is then measured about 0. Off, the line has its own intercept, and (0, 0) is added as a point only when no step is near 0.
Allow for noise with 5 or 6 stepsOffEstimates the noise from the scatter about a quadratic through all the steps, so noise alone doesn't end the range early while real curvature still does. It doesn't apply to an IV Plot, which always allows for noise.
Flag outlier sweeps with a robust fitOnFrom 6 steps, leaves out sweeps more than 4 robust SDs (5 with 6 steps) off a robust (Huber) quadratic through all the steps. Off, a local rule is used from 7 steps, and the Data Log still names sweeps the robust fit would leave out.

IV Plot (Current–Voltage Relationship)

Plots the steady-state current against the voltage step for a family of voltage steps, and reports input resistance and the reversal potential (Erev). It needs voltage-clamp current sweeps with one step size per sweep.

  1. Bring the recording to the front and choose Toolkits › Electrophysiology › IV Plot.
  2. The voltage steps are read from the recorded command channel or the file's protocol. If the file has neither, enter them in the dialog, as for VI Plot: First step's command potential (mV) and Increment per sweep (mV), or each sweep's step; the Holding level (mV); and the step's times. Click Analyze.
  3. The I–V graph opens in a new window with the fitted line, and the table goes to the Data Log.
ReportedHow it is computed
Voltage step and steady-state currentX is the step, the change from the holding potential. The steady state and the baseline are measured as for VI Plot, so the capacitive transient at the step's edge stays out.
Baseline current and holding potentialThe holding potential is junction-potential corrected when correction is on.
Input resistance1 ÷ the slope of the current regressed on the voltage (the current is the measured variable), over the linear range around the holding potential.
ErevWhere the total current (holding current included) crosses zero: the zero of a line fitted to the two points either side of the first crossing, with a confidence interval by Fieller's method, at the confidence level in Settings › Statistics.

The linear range around the holding potential

  • The range grows from the 0 mV step and one step either side, a step at a time, while the slope (here a conductance) changes by no more than 10% beyond the noise. The holding potential is the center because it is commanded, so it is known exactly, and the baseline-subtracted current is 0 there.
  • The noise comes from the holding current: every sweep returns to the same holding command, so the scatter of its baseline current from sweep to sweep measures the noise whatever the curve's shape.
  • The Data Log gives the range in command potentials and as steps from the holding potential, how many steps it held, and the steps left out on each side and why: for example "nonlinear, the conductance rises (outward rectification)" above the range. A sweep beyond the range is reported there, not marked † as an outlier.
  • When even the steps nearest the holding potential bend by more than 10%, the Data Log warns that the value includes voltage-gated current: record smaller steps near the holding potential. It also says when the cell's zero-current potential lies outside the range.
  • Fitting through the origin, outlier flagging and the clamp-mode check work as for VI Plot. For a range of your own, run Linear Fit on the I–V graph over it: the slope is a conductance, and 1 ÷ slope is the input resistance.

Rₛ-corrected voltage axis and Erev

  • In the Rₛ Correction panel's Voltage clamp mode, check "Correct the IV Plot's voltage axis for Rₛ" (see Rₛ and Junction Potential Correction). IV Plot then plots and fits each point at Vₘ = Vcmd − I·Rₛ, as a step from the holding Vₘ, and the Data Log adds a Vcmd column.
  • The correction needs no Erev and is exact for steady-state currents, voltage-gated ones included: each current is plotted at the potential the membrane reached. Input resistance then excludes Rₛ; on the command axis it includes the uncompensated Rₛ.
  • The axis is not corrected while a voltage-clamp trace correction stands, which already scales each current to its command. The Data Log says so.
  • Erev is reported with or without the corrected axis. At zero current there is no Rₛ error, so for a single-compartment cell it is the reversal potential, and the Rₛ panel can use it ("Erev from the last IV Plot").

Firing Properties (Rheobase and F–I Curve)

Counts the action potentials each current step evokes and reports firing rates, adaptation, rheobase (the smallest current that makes the cell fire) and the F–I curve (firing rate against current). It needs current-clamp voltage sweeps with one current step per sweep.

  1. To choose how spikes are detected, run AP Detection once first: Firing Properties finds spikes with the settings of AP Detection's last run, or its starting settings before one.
  2. Choose Toolkits › Electrophysiology › Firing Properties…. The dialog names the AP Detection settings in use.
  3. Leave "Fit the F–I slope (steps at or above rheobase that fired)" checked to get the slope.
  4. If the file has neither a stimulus protocol nor a current channel, enter First step (pA) and Increment per sweep (pA), or each sweep's current, and Step start (ms) and Step end (ms) as the X axis shows them.
  5. Click Analyze. The table goes to the Data Log, and the F–I curve opens as a new graph.
ReportedHow it is computed
Step currentFrom the file's stimulus protocol when it has one (each step's change from the level before it), else from the recorded current channel (measured as in VI Plot), else as entered. In pA.
Spikes and mean rateEvery AP whose threshold falls within the step, its start and end included. Mean rate = spikes ÷ the step's duration.
First and last ISI frequency1 ÷ the first and the last inter-spike interval (ISI).
LatencyFrom the step's onset to the first AP's threshold.
ISI CVThe ISIs' sample SD ÷ their mean, from 3 spikes. IPFX's isi_cv uses the population SD: multiply by √((n − 1)/n), for n ISIs, to compare.
Adaptation indexThe mean of (ISIᵢ₊₁ − ISIᵢ) / (ISIᵢ₊₁ + ISIᵢ), as IPFX defines it: near 0 for regular firing and positive when firing slows.
RheobaseThe smallest positive step that fired at least one AP. It is only as precise as the steps, so the Data Log also gives the step below it that didn't fire (rheobase lies between the two), or says that the smallest positive step tested already fired (rheobase is then that step or less).
F–I slopeA least-squares line through the steps at or above rheobase that fired, in Hz/pA (IPFX's fi_fit_slope).
Maximum firing rateThe highest mean rate over a step, with its current.
  • A step within 1% of the largest step's size of 0 counts as 0. A sweep that fires at 0 pA or below is noted as spontaneous firing.
  • Steps above rheobase that fire no AP (depolarization block, or a cell running down) are plotted at 0 Hz, left out of the F–I slope and named in the Data Log. A rate that falls at the largest steps is noted too, since a line then fits only below it.
  • Batch Processing, Protocols and the AI Assistant run Firing Properties too.

Sag Analysis

Measures the sag in the voltage response to hyperpolarizing current steps: an initial hyperpolarization that partly recovers before the step ends, typical of HCN (Iₕ) channels. It needs current-clamp voltage sweeps recorded during negative current steps.

  1. Bring the recording to the front and choose Toolkits › Electrophysiology › Sag Analysis.
  2. Read the table in the Data Log: each sweep's sag peak, peak time and steady-state value, then the reference sweep's sag ratio and sag slope. To plot a column, select it there and press ⇧⌘G.
ReportedHow it is computed
Sag peakThe most negative point of a 4 ms running mean (so noise doesn't deepen it), measured from the baseline, the mean over the 100 ms before the step. The search ends once the trace has risen for 8 ms, and at most 400 ms into the step.
Steady state (SS value)The mean over the last 20% of the step, from the baseline.
Reference sweepThe sweep whose peak falls closest to 20 mV below its baseline. The ratio and the slope are reported for it.
Sag ratio (%)(peak − steady state) / peak × 100.
Sag slopeThe slope of a line fitted from the peak to 50 ms after it, ending within the step, in mV/s. It is not reported when less than 10 ms of the step is left.
  • Step timing comes from the current channel. Without one it comes from the file's protocol or, failing that, from the voltage sweeps themselves: each edge is where the sweeps first leave the level they held before it by more than three times that level's own 1 ms noise (usually within 1 to 2 ms of the real edge).
  • Only a sweep whose peak and steady state are both at least 1 mV below its baseline counts. A graph with none (depolarizing steps only, or a step edge found in the wrong place) gets a message in place of a ratio, and so does a graph that records only current.
  • IPFX instead uses the sweep whose peak potential is closest to −100 mV, and takes the steady state over the last 30 ms of the step.

Slow AHP Analysis

Finds each train of spikes and measures the afterhyperpolarization (AHP) that follows its last spike: the peak amplitude, the slow AHP at a fixed latency, the recovery time from an exponential fit, and the area. It needs current-clamp voltage sweeps with spike trains.

  1. Bring the recording to the front and choose Toolkits › Electrophysiology › Slow AHP Analysis…. A window opens for that graph.
  2. Under Spike Detection and Train Grouping, set how spikes and trains are found.
  3. Under Baseline, choose Before each train (the default), Time window or Manual value.
  4. Set the options under Peak AHP Search, Slow AHP at Fixed Latency, Recovery Search and Recovery Fit.
  5. Click Run Slow AHP Analysis. A row for each train goes to the Data Log, with times in ms from the sweep's start.
SettingDefaultWhat it does
Threshold (mV)0A spike is a peak above this voltage. Spikes are not found by slope, so capacitive artifacts aren't counted. Set it below the smallest late spike of an adapting train.
Min. separation between spikes (ms)5Peaks closer together count as one spike. Lower it for firing above 200 Hz.
Max. inter-spike gap (ms); Min. spikes per train500; 3Spikes closer than the gap form one train, and trains with fewer spikes are ignored.
Baseline: Before each trainLength 200 msThe median of up to this long, ending 2 ms before the train's current step starts (from the file's protocol). Without a protocol it ends where the trace starts rising toward the first spike.
Baseline: Time window or Manual value600–1000 msThe median over a time range, one baseline per sweep (Fixed values, or Live from cursors), or a value you type.
Start (ms after last spike peak)5Where the peak search starts. It never starts before the current step ends (from the protocol or, without one, where the trace falls at least 5 mV off a plateau), so an adapting cell's depolarized plateau isn't read as an AHP.
Peak search duration (ms)100The AHP peak is the lowest point, within this window, of the trace smoothed over ±10 ms.
Peak averaging window (ms)20The amplitude is the baseline minus the trace averaged over this window around the peak. 20 ms is one cycle of 50 Hz mains hum; 0 uses the single sample at the peak.
Slow AHP at Fixed Latency500–1000 ms after the stepThe baseline minus the mean voltage over this span after the current step ends (after the last spike when no step end is known).
Integral from the step to1000 ms after itThe area between baseline and trace over a fixed span. Unlike the peak-to-recovery integral, it doesn't depend on where recovery is placed, so it compares directly between cells.
Limit recovery search to a maximum durationOffOff, the search for recovery runs to the end of the sweep or to the next train.
ModelSingle exponentialThe recovery fit: Single exponential or Double exponential.
Fit start delay (ms after peak)400A single exponential skips the fast early part of the recovery. Choosing Double exponential sets the delay to 0, since it needs that part for its fast τ.
Recovery fraction (%)95Recovery time is when the fit reaches this fraction of the way back to baseline.
  • The peak found within 100 ms of the step's end is what many studies call the medium AHP (mAHP), and the fixed-latency value the slow AHP (sAHP). Both are measured from the baseline before the train, not from the spike threshold as AP Detection's AHP is.
  • The recovery is fitted on the trace averaged into 1 ms bins. A time constant shorter than two bins or longer than three times the fitted span is reported as "not determined", and fewer than 10 points give no fit.
  • If the fit is already past the recovery fraction where it starts, the recovery time is read from the trace smoothed over ±10 ms. If it never gets there, the result says "not reached" and how far it recovered.
  • Each train's windows (recovery, fit, integral and fixed latency) end before the next train's onset or the next spike of any kind.
  • The Data Log gives each train's baseline window and warns when it holds a spike, overlaps a train, was cut short or drifts by more than 0.5 mV.
  • When the peak is within 10 ms of the search window's end, or the trace keeps falling past it, the Data Log warns that the true peak may lie beyond: a slow AHP often peaks several hundred ms after the train, so lengthen the window or use the fixed-latency value. A trace above baseline at the peak is flagged too.
  • The analysis measures the selected group's visible sweeps. Voltages are converted to mV. Sweeps that aren't a voltage, or that are a command waveform (16 or fewer distinct levels), are skipped and listed in the Data Log. With more than one train, the Data Log also gives the mean, SD and n of each measurement across trains.

A "not reached" result with a high recovered percentage usually means the recovery window is too short for that trace, not that the cell failed to recover. If "Limit recovery search to a maximum duration" is on, raise the limit or turn it off. Otherwise record longer sweeps, or space the trains further apart.

LFP Oscillations

Toolkits › Electrophysiology › LFP Oscillations… opens a window with Band Power Over Time, Hilbert Envelope and Phase, Phase–Amplitude Coupling and Spike-Triggered LFP and Phase Locking for the front graph. These are the same controls as those sections of the LFP / Spike Train Analysis panel, with the same results: see that page. On a spike-train raster the window shows only Spike-Triggered LFP and Phase Locking.

Spike Sorter

Detects spikes on one channel, or on a group of channels you choose (such as a tetrode), groups them into clusters, lets you review and edit the clusters, and commits them as named spike trains. It needs a graph with at least one continuous extracellular channel. It is a semi-automated sorter for a few channels, not a replacement for probe-based sorters: @Graph knows nothing about electrode layout, so you choose which channels belong together.

  1. Bring the recording to the front and choose Toolkits › Electrophysiology › Spike Sorter…. A window opens for that graph.
  2. Choose the Primary channel. Under Channel Group, optionally check nearby channels, so that spikes are clustered by their shape on all of them together.
  3. Set the Detection and Clustering options (see Detection and clustering settings, below).
  4. Click Detect & Sort. Each run replaces the current result.
  5. Review the clusters in the Waveforms, PC Scatter, ISI and Drift tabs and in the Clusters list, and edit them (see Review and edit the clusters, below).
  6. Optionally click Refine via Template Matching, to find further spikes of each cluster's shape, and Resolve Spike Collisions, to find spikes hidden by an overlapping spike.
  7. Click Commit Sorted Units. A new spike-train graph opens with one named train for each cluster and sweep, ready for LFP / Spike Train Analysis. Clusters labeled Noise are left out.

Detection and clustering settings

SettingDefaultWhat it does
Detect onAll channels in the groupWith a channel group. All channels: each channel is thresholded at its own noise level, so a unit largest on any channel is found. Primary channel only: spikes must cross on the primary channel.
Pre-filter to spike bandOn, 300–3000 HzBand-passes the recording before detection.
PolarityNegative-goingThe direction of the spikes.
ThresholdAuto (× noise SD), 5Auto: the multiplier (3 to 8) × the noise level, median(|x|)/0.6745, taken as the median over up to 20 sweeps spread through the recording. One threshold serves every sweep, and the status line reports it. Manual value: a level in the primary channel's unit.
Dead time (ms)0.5The pause after each spike, so one spike isn't counted twice. Keep it shorter than Refractory, or no refractory violation could be seen.
Refractory (ms)1.5The unit's refractory period, used only for the quality measures: shorter intervals count as violations.
Snippet window (ms)2The length of waveform cut out, centered on each spike. A spike closer than half of it to a sweep's start or end is left out, and the status line counts those.
Auto cluster countOnOn: the number of clusters is chosen automatically, and the split, overlap check and merge steps run. Off: set K, and the clusters stay as k-means leaves them.
Auto-exclude amplitude outliersOnSets spikes with extreme amplitudes (usually movement or electrical artifacts) aside in an Artifacts cluster labeled Noise before clustering.
  • Each detected spike is re-centered on its true peak, searched for over 0.75 ms after the threshold crossing, and its time is refined between samples, so timing jitter doesn't blur the clusters.
  • Channel group: the channels must share the primary's sample rate and length, and every channel is read in the primary channel's unit, so thresholds and amplitudes mean the same on all of them. A spike that crosses on several channels counts once: of crossings closer than the dead time (at least 0.3 ms), the one largest relative to its channel's noise is kept, and the waveforms are cut on every channel at its time.
  • A channel with no signal adds no features, and a spike whose waveform window touches missing samples is left out. The status line names and counts them.

How spikes are clustered

Clustering runs these steps in order. Split, overlap check and merge run only with Auto cluster count on. The status line reports what each step moved.

  • Outliers: spikes with extreme amplitudes go to the Artifacts cluster, with every detection within 5 ms of one (a large artifact rings for a few milliseconds after band-pass filtering). Outliers whose amplitudes agree closely with each other (at least 20 spikes) are a large real unit, and are clustered like any other spikes.
  • Features: each waveform is reduced to 3 principal components, or with a channel group to 3 for each channel. The components are taken after noise whitening: the background noise is measured between spikes and divided out (Pouzat et al. 2002), so one unit forms a round cloud rather than an elongated one.
  • k-means: the spikes are grouped by the best of 5 k-means++ starts.
  • Split: a cluster is cut in two by k-means, and the cut is kept when its spikes, projected on the line between the two halves, form two peaks (Hartigan's dip test at the 5% level; Hartigan & Hartigan 1985). Each half is tested again.
  • Overlap check: a small cluster (under a tenth of the largest) may be other units' spikes landing on or next to each other. Each of its spikes is fitted with the other clusters' average waveforms (templates): one unit at the spike's time, or that unit plus a second spike at another lag (Pillow et al. 2013; Ekanadham et al. 2014; Pachitariu et al. 2016). If at least half the cluster's spikes fit that way, clearly better than the cluster's own template fits them, each spike goes to the unit fitted at its time and the cluster is removed. Spikes that nothing explains go to an Unresolved overlaps cluster labeled Noise. A small cluster with a consistent shape of its own, such as a rarely firing unit, is kept.
  • Merge: two clusters are merged when their spikes, projected on the line between the two cluster centers, form a single peak (the same dip test), as one unit cut in two does. A small cluster, under a tenth of the pair's spikes, is tested against only as many of the larger cluster's spikes as it has, those nearest to it. Clusters of under 10 spikes are left as they are. Split and merge together follow ISO-SPLIT (Magland & Barnett 2015).

Review and edit the clusters

  • Waveforms: each cluster's waveforms on each channel. Show templates draws each cluster's average waveform over them.
  • PC Scatter: the spikes' principal components. With a channel group, pick the channel and component for X and Y, or leave them on Auto (PC1 against PC2 of the selected cluster's best channel). To move spikes to the selected cluster, drag a rectangle around them.
  • ISI: the interval histogram in 0.5 ms bins, with intervals inside the refractory period in red. Intervals are measured within each sweep, never across sweeps.
  • Drift: spike amplitude against recording time, with the sweeps laid end to end.
  • The Waveforms, PC Scatter and Drift views are scaled to the spikes not labeled Noise, so a few huge artifacts can't shrink the real units into a corner.
  • In the Clusters list, rename a cluster, set its label (Unsorted, Good, MUA for multi-unit activity, or Noise), or select it and choose Merge with…, Split or Mark as Noise. A Noise cluster stays listed and is left out at Commit.
  • Every edit can be undone one step at a time with ⌘Z (Edit › Undo) or the Undo button under the list, and redone with ⇧⌘Z: the last 20 steps, including spikes added by template matching or collision resolution and a result that Detect & Sort or Load Sort State replaced.

Quality measures

Each row of the Clusters list gives these for its cluster. With a channel group, a cluster's best channel is the one where its average waveform is largest.

MeasureWhat it is
Spikes and rateThe spike count, and spikes per second over the whole recording searched.
SNR (p-p ÷ 2σ)The peak-to-peak size of the cluster's average waveform over twice the noise level, on its best channel. SpikeInterface divides the largest deflection by the noise level instead, which reads about 1.4 times higher.
ISI viol.The percentage of intervals shorter than Refractory.
ContaminationThe estimated share of the cluster's spikes that come from other neurons, from the violations, the dead time and the recording length (Hill et al. 2011, with the correction of Llobet et al. 2022 for violations between two contaminating spikes). It is shown with the number of violations it rests on, and with only a few it is very uncertain. It assumes the other neurons' spikes come at random times; more violations than that allows show as ≥100%.
Isolation dist. and L-ratioHow well the cluster is separated from every other spike of the sort, the Artifacts cluster included (Schmitzer-Torbert et al. 2005): a higher isolation distance and a lower L-ratio are better. They use 3 principal components (3 for each channel of a group), not the 8 features per spike the often-quoted marks (isolation distance above 20, L-ratio below 0.05) were set with, so compare clusters with each other rather than with those marks.
Amp. cutoffThe estimated fraction of the unit's spikes that were too small to cross the threshold, from how sharply the low end of its amplitude histogram is cut off (Hill et al. 2011): 0 to 0.5, lower is better (the Allen Institute keeps units under 0.1). It needs at least 500 spikes and assumes the amplitudes spread evenly around their middle, which drift breaks. Each spike's amplitude is the least-squares scale of the cluster's average waveform fitted to it.
PresenceThe fraction of 60 s stretches of the recording in which the unit fired at least once, so a unit lost partway through reads low (the Allen Institute keeps units above 0.9). It needs a recording of at least 60 s.

The presence ratio, amplitude cutoff, firing rate, violation count, L-ratio and isolation distance are computed as SpikeInterface's quality metrics compute them (Buccino et al. 2020).

Template matching and collision resolution

SettingDefaultWhat it does
Drift-tolerantOffLets each template change gradually along the recording. The recording is cut into Blocks (4 by default) of equal recorded time, each with its own template (a block with fewer than 5 of the unit's spikes is left out), and the template at any point is interpolated between the two nearest. Turn it on when the Drift tab shows a unit's amplitude changing slowly.
Match strength0.70How large an event must be relative to the template. The template is scaled to fit the event by least squares, and the event counts when that scale is at least this value. Lower finds smaller spikes but also more noise.
Shape checkOnRejects a match that lines up with a template but has the wrong shape, such as a spike of another unit. What is left after subtracting the scaled template may be at most Tolerance (1.5× by default) times as large as for a typical spike of the cluster. Clusters with fewer than 5 spikes aren't checked.
  • Refine via Template Matching builds an average waveform for each cluster and scans the recording for further spikes of that shape, which recovers spikes just below the threshold. Each match is aligned between samples before it is scored. Where two templates match the same event, only the better match is kept.
  • Resolve Spike Collisions uses the same Match strength. It subtracts the template of every spike already in a non-Noise cluster, scaled to fit, then looks within half a snippet of each one for another spike that matches any template. A recovered spike must be at least 0.4 ms from any other spike and at least the Dead time from another spike of the same unit, so two spikes less than 0.4 ms apart can't be separated.
  • Neither pass accepts a spike within 5 ms of a spike in the Artifacts cluster, where the filter's ringing can look like a spike.
  • Both passes use the channel group and band-pass filter of the last Detect & Sort run (or loaded sort state), not the current controls. To use new ones, run Detect & Sort again.

Automatic clustering and template matching are starting points. Review the waveforms, PC scatter and ISI histogram before committing, and check the ISI violations and SNR after each pass: a Match strength that is too low picks up noise, and one that is too high misses real spikes.

Save and commit

  • Save Sort State… saves the whole session (settings, clusters and every spike) to a .atgsort file, by default next to the recording, and Load Sort State… reopens one. Closing the window or quitting asks before discarding unsaved changes. A sort state saved from a different recording loads only after you confirm.
  • Commit Sorted Units makes one train for each kept cluster and sweep, including sweeps where the unit never fired, so a trial without spikes counts as zero in a PSTH. Spike times are on the recording's own time axis.
  • The Data Log records how the units were made (Detect & Sort's settings and counts, and each template-matching or collision pass), then a table of each unit's label, spike count, rate and quality measures.
  • The AI Assistant can run the sorter too. It opens its result in a new window as an unreviewed first pass; review and commit it in the Spike Sorter.

Membrane Test: Rₛ, Rₘ, and Cₘ

Measures series resistance (Rₛ), membrane resistance (Rₘ) and membrane capacitance (Cₘ) from the current response to a brief voltage step (typically 5–10 mV). It needs a voltage-clamp graph with that response.

  1. Bring the recording to the front and choose Toolkits › Electrophysiology › Membrane Test….
  2. If the graph has a voltage command channel, the step size (ΔV) is measured from it. Otherwise a dialog asks for the step's amplitude in mV: enter it and click Analyze.
  3. Read the table in the Data Log: each sweep's Rₛ, Rₘ, Cₘ, τ and R², then the three values and the inputs behind them.
ReportedHow it is computed
τOne exponential fitted by least squares to the transient's decay toward the new steady-state current, from just after the peak until the decay falls to 20% of it. The R² beside it is measured on the current itself.
RₛΔV ÷ the peak current change. The recording filter rounds off the transient's instant jump but keeps its area, so the peak is rebuilt from the charge Q the transient carries above the steady state: ΔI_peak = ΔI_ss + Q/τ, as pCLAMP's Membrane Test computes it.
RₘΔV ÷ ΔI_ss − Rₛ, where ΔI_ss is the steady-state current change: the mean over the step's last 20%, less what remains of the fitted decay.
Cₘτ × (1/Rₛ + 1/Rₘ).
  • Rₛ, Rₘ and Cₘ come from one fit to the averaged transient of all the sweeps, which leaves the fit much less noise than averaging per-sweep values afterward. Each sweep is also fitted on its own and listed, to follow the cell's stability. With a single sweep, or if the averaged transient can't be fitted, the per-sweep values (or their mean) are reported.
  • With a voltage channel, each current sweep takes the step and ΔV from its own voltage sweep, paired in order. Without one, the step is found in the current trace.
  • If the transient is cut short (by the step's end, say), the peak comes from the fit extrapolated back to where the transient's rise reaches half its height.
  • When the cell's τ approaches the recording filter's rise time (τ = 0.1 ms behind a 2 kHz filter, say), Rₛ and Cₘ read high. Record with a filter of 5 kHz or wider when they matter.
  • A graph of voltage alone (current clamp) is refused, with a pointer to the Rₛ Correction panel. So is a graph whose current carries the voltage-clamp Rₛ correction, which has taken out the transient the test fits: remove the correction first.

Cₘ is the least certain of the three. Capacitive transients often have a fast component followed by a slower one (from imperfect space clamp in cells with extensive dendrites, for example), which a single exponential can't separate. Use Cₘ as a relative measure, such as to track a cell's stability during an experiment, rather than as a precise absolute value.

Back to Contents

Pharmacology & Biochemistry

Curves on a Graph

Part of the Pharmacology & Biochemistry toolkit.

Six tabs in the inspector's Toolkits category, under Pharmacology & Biochemistry, fit and measure curves on an X-Y graph: Dose–Response, Schild Analysis, Kinetics & Binding, Initial Rates, Pharmacokinetics (NCA) and qPCR & Melt Curves. The toolkit's other parts have pages of their own: Gels and Blots, Plate Photos and Colonies, Plate Maps, its calculators in Lab Tools, and its Regression models in Other Analyses › Enzyme Kinetics, Binding and Assays.

What the Tabs Share

  • Data: an X-Y graph with doses, concentrations or times in X and responses in the other columns. Each visible sweep is one curve; hidden groups and sweeps outside Review sweeps are left out. Where a tab has a Curves choice, a group can be one curve with its sweeps as replicates (Display › Groups sets the groups).
  • Where a tab needs a concentration for each curve (an antagonist, inhibitor or substrate), it reads the first number in the curve's own name ("10 nM", "[I] = 5") into a field you can change.
  • Fitted curves are drawn on the graph: click Keep Curves to keep them or Remove Curves to remove them. Each tab shows a summary, and every full table goes to the Data Log. Confidence intervals use the confidence level in Settings › Statistics.
  • Changing a setting clears the tab's results until you fit again.
  • The curve fits are those of Statistics › Regression, so the same data give the same numbers there and here.
  • Batch Processing and Protocols run Dose–Response, Initial Rates, Pharmacokinetics and qPCR amplification on every sweep (see Batch Processing and Protocols).

Dose–Response

Dose–Response fits a sigmoidal curve to responses measured at several doses and reports each curve's EC50 (or IC50, or Kᵢ) with its confidence interval.

  1. Open the data as an X-Y graph, with doses in X, and in the inspector's Toolkits category choose Pharmacology & Biochemistry › Dose–Response.
  2. Choose Curves: Fit each data set (the default, one curve per visible sweep), Fit each group (its data sets pooled), or One curve from all data sets (replicates pooled).
  3. Choose the Model: 4PL (variable slope), the default; 3PL (Hill slope ±1); 5PL (asymmetric); or Competition binding (Kᵢ).
  4. Check "X is already log10(dose)" when X holds logarithms. The tab checks it for you when any X is negative.
  5. When the raw doses include 0, choose what they do under Dose 0 (see Doses of 0, below).
  6. To hold a plateau, type its value under Fix Bottom at or Fix Top at; blank fits it. For competition binding, type Labeled ligand [L] and Its Kd, in the unit of X.
  7. Choose Weighting: None (equal weights), the default; or 1/Y² (relative) or 1/Y, for responses whose scatter grows with their size.
  8. Click Fit Curves. The curves are drawn on the graph, and each curve's EC50, confidence interval, Hill slope and R² show in the tab.
  9. Click Log X Axis to show the doses on a log scale.
  • One curve from all data sets fits every value of every visible sweep at its dose. Use it for replicates laid out in columns (one column per subject or cell), where each column alone has too few values to fit. When data sets fitted one by one share their doses and most hold fewer than two values per fitted parameter, the tab suggests it.
  • A pooled or group fit treats every value as independent. When the same sources give values at several doses, use Values from the same (below).
  • Weights come from the fitted curve and are refitted until they settle.

Models

ModelEquation and notes
4PL (variable slope)Y = Bottom + (Top − Bottom)/(1 + 10^((LogEC50 − log X)·Hill slope)).
3PL (Hill slope ±1)The 4PL with its Hill slope fixed at +1 or −1, the sign the data take. Hill slope check: the Data Log tests the fixed slope against a free one (the extra-sum-of-squares F test for unweighted fits with every value independent; a likelihood-ratio test under Values from the same). When the free slope fits significantly better, the tab says so and suggests the 4PL.
5PL (asymmetric)The 4PL with an asymmetry S that tilts one end (Gottschalk & Dunn 2005). It reports the half-maximal EC50, which differs from LogXb when S ≠ 1, with a delta-method interval, and for unweighted fits an F test of whether the asymmetry is needed (5PL against 4PL). Its plateaus can't be fixed.
Competition binding (Kᵢ)The 4PL with its Hill slope fixed at −1. Kᵢ = IC₅₀/(1 + [L]/Kd) (Cheng & Prusoff 1973), from the relative IC50.

Doses of 0

A dose of 0 (a vehicle, or a group with nothing applied) has no logarithm. With raw doses, Dose 0 chooses what those values do. The 5PL always leaves them out, as does Schild Analysis. Compare curves fits them as the curves are fitted under Fit them; under Fix Bottom at their mean it leaves them out and fits that plateau free, and its summary says so.

Dose 0What it does
Fit them (dose 0 sets Bottom)The default. The 4PL on raw doses, in which a dose of 0 is the curve's low-dose plateau (Bottom when the curve rises, Top when it falls), as R's drc fits it (LL.4). LogEC50 and its CI are still on the log scale of the doses above 0.
Fix Bottom at their meanThe low-dose plateau is fixed at the mean of the dose-0 values, and the doses above 0 are fitted.
Dose-0 group responds to an endogenous agonist: estimate itSee Endogenous agonist, below. Not offered for competition binding.
Leave them outThe dose-0 values are not fitted; a note says how many.

A log X axis has no place for dose 0, so those points aren't drawn there: a note gives their mean ± SD, and the curve starts at the lowest dose above 0. On a linear axis, a curve whose doses of 0 were fitted runs from 0.

Endogenous agonist

When the group with no agonist applied responds anyway, because some agonist is already there (released by the tissue, or kept from breakdown), a plateau placed at that group's response puts the curve's foot in the wrong place. This model adds the applied dose X to an endogenous concentration ce, so the dose-0 group sits on the curve at ce: Y = Bottom + (Top − Bottom)·(X + ce)^Hill / ((X + ce)^Hill + EC50^Hill).

  1. Put the applied doses in X, with 0 for the group with none.
  2. Choose the Model: the 4PL fits the Hill slope, and the 3PL fixes it at 1.
  3. Under Dose 0, choose "Dose-0 group responds to an endogenous agonist: estimate it".
  4. Type the Baseline, the response with no agonist at all (0 by default, for a Y that is the change from a baseline taken before any agonist was present). Bottom is fixed at it.
  5. Click Fit Curves. Under each curve's row, the tab gives ce with its interval and the applied EC50.
  6. If the tab warns that ce and the EC50 aren't separated, and its F test finds no better fit with a free slope, choose the 3PL and fit again.
  • The EC50 is in total agonist (applied plus endogenous). The applied dose that gives half the response is EC50 − ce, the applied EC50; an absolute EC50 is an applied dose too.
  • The fit is unweighted least squares, with EC50 and ce fitted as log10. Both have profile-likelihood confidence intervals (Wald, from the covariance, only where a profile can't be found, and labeled so).
  • With the Hill slope free, ce and the EC50 are often not separately determined: a small ce on a steep curve and a large one on a shallow curve give the dose-0 group the same response. When either CI spans more than a decade or is open, or the two estimates correlate beyond ±0.95, the tab warns, suggests the 3PL, and reports the extra-sum-of-squares F test of the free slope against 1, with the slope-1 fit's EC50 and ce.
  • The model assumes no response at baseline other than Bottom, and that applied and endogenous agonist act as one concentration at the same receptors.
  • Batch Processing, Protocols and the AI Assistant give ce and its interval as columns of their summary.

Values from the same

With a group or pooled curve, the values in one data set often come from one source (a cell, a subject, a plate) measured at several doses: repeated measures, not independent values. Values from the same then fits the curve as a nonlinear mixed-effects model, with a random effect for each data set.

  1. Lay the table out with one data set per source, and blanks where a source has no value at a dose. Sources may hold different doses.
  2. Choose Curves: Fit each group or One curve from all data sets.
  3. Under Values from the same, choose Each data set. When a label column such as Group says which set of sources each row belongs to, choose Each data set, within Group: each data set's rows in each group are one source, and the label column is left out of the fit.
  4. Choose Varies between data sets: EC50 (the default) or, with the endogenous-agonist model, ce, each as a fold change; or Top or Bottom, in the response's units. A plateau the settings hold fixed isn't offered.
  5. Set Weighting to None and click Fit Curves. The fit runs in the background for a few seconds; Stop ends it.
  • It works with the 4PL, the 3PL and the endogenous-agonist model. The 5PL, competition binding, weighting and Compare curves are not offered with it.
  • The fit is by maximum likelihood, each source's random effect integrated out by adaptive Gauss–Hermite quadrature (30 nodes).
  • The EC50 is the typical source's (the median across sources), and the curve drawn is the typical source's curve, not the average of the sources' curves, which would be shallower. Check Draw each data set's own curve to draw each source's curve too.
  • The EC50, ce and a free Hill slope have profile-likelihood confidence intervals (Wald where a profile's end can't be found, as the Data Log then says). The parameter that varies has sources − 1 degrees of freedom; the others have N − sources − p + 1, the rule of R's nlme (N values, p fitted curve parameters). When that leaves them no degrees of freedom (too few data sets with repeated values), the tab says so and fits no curve.
  • Under the curve's row, the tab gives the SD between data sets and within them, and the EC50 with every value independent.
  • The Data Log adds every parameter with its SE, df and CI; a likelihood-ratio test of variation between data sets (half of χ²₁, as an SD can't be below 0); the likelihood-ratio test of a free Hill slope against ±1; the AIC of the other choices of what varies; each data set's own EC50; and a sentence for a paper's Methods.
  • Check the Hill slope's test by bootstrap repeats that test with a parametric bootstrap of 199 runs, after the fit is shown. Stop ends it and keeps the fit.
  • When another choice of what varies has an AIC lower by 4 or more (considerably more support; Burnham & Anderson 2002), the tab names it.
  • With fewer than about 10 sources, maximum likelihood tends to underestimate the SD between them. When the data show no variation between sources, that SD is 0 and the fit is the one with every value independent.

What is reported

  • The EC50's interval in the tab is profile-likelihood where the fit gives one, else Wald. The Data Log has both, with every parameter's SE and CI, R², and an F test that a dose–response exists.
  • Plateau rule: when a fitted plateau lies beyond the range of the doses' mean responses by more than its own SE, the doses never reached it, so it and the EC50 rest on the curve's assumed shape. The tab says so once and suggests a vehicle group or lower doses, or higher doses, or fixing that plateau.

Relative and absolute EC50

  • Under EC50, Relative (between plateaus), the default, is the dose halfway between the fitted Bottom and Top.
  • Absolute (response = value) is the dose at which the fitted curve reaches the response you type under Response, in the data's units. Left blank, the response is the plateaus' midpoint, (Bottom + Top)/2, averaged over the curves and rounded to two significant digits. The tab says which response it used.
  • The absolute EC50's confidence interval is the delta method's on log10(dose), from the fit's covariance, with t on the fit's residual degrees of freedom. It counts the uncertainty in Bottom and Top too, so even at the halfway response it differs from the relative EC50's interval.
  • When the response typed lies outside the data's responses (50 typed for fractions, say), or a curve never reaches it, the tab says so. A dose beyond the doses fitted is marked as extrapolated in the Data Log.
  • The Data Log has both EC50s. Competition binding reports Kᵢ from the relative IC50 only.

Compare curves

With two or more curves fitted per data set or per group, choose a question under Compare curves: One curve for all data sets?, or whether LogEC50, Bottom, Top or the Hill slope differs. The test is the extra-sum-of-squares F test; check "Add AICc to the F test" for AICc as well. The tab shows each curve's EC50 ratio to the first curve with its CI, then the test. For competition binding the ratios are of IC50 and Kᵢ, and the Hill slope isn't compared.

Show lines at a percentage of the response

After a fit, check Show lines at and choose a percentage (50% by default; 10, 20, 25, 75, 80 and 90% too). Dashed lines are drawn at that percentage of each curve's response, from the Y axis to the curve and from the crossing down to the X axis, each labeled with its value and listed in a table below the control.

  • The percentage runs from the curve's low-dose plateau toward its high-dose one: 50% is (Bottom + Top)/2, and its crossing is the EC50 (or IC50). On a rising curve, 10% gives the EC10. On a falling curve it is measured down from Top, the low-dose plateau: 80% is 80% of the way down (80% inhibition), and its crossing is labeled EC80. Curves that share their plateaus share one horizontal line.
  • With the absolute EC50 chosen, the lines are at its response instead.
  • With the endogenous-agonist model, the lines mark the applied EC50. A level the dose-0 group already passes has only its horizontal line, and the tab says why.
  • The lines follow each new fit and are saved with the graph. A label or a line's end that you drag stays where you drop it.
  • Schild Analysis, Kinetics & Binding and the thermal shift have the same control.

Open the Statistics window

Open Full Statistics Window opens Statistics › Regression on a copy of the curves' data, with Dose-Response (4PL) or Competition Binding (Kᵢ) chosen and the tab's settings carried over, for the full output, assumption checks, reports and exports (see Other Analyses › Dose-Response Curves). Statistics fits log doses with every value independent, so the button is grayed out, with the reason in its tooltip, while doses of 0 are fitted or Values from the same is on; the Data Log has that fit's full output. The 5PL is fitted in this tab only. The window holds a copy: later changes to the graph don't reach it.

Open a means figure

The fits always use every replicate. For presenting, the Figure section at the bottom of the tab opens a new graph with each dose's mean, its error bars and the fitted curves, each curve in the color of its means.

  1. Under Figure, choose Error bars: SD (the default), SEM or CI (at the confidence level in Settings).
  2. Choose Curve and, after an endogenous-agonist fit, X axis (see the table below).
  3. Click Open Means ± SD Graph (the button names the error bars chosen). The curves are fitted first if they aren't yet.
SettingWhat the figure draws
Error barsSD, the replicates' scatter; SEM, the precision of each mean; or the CI of the mean at the confidence level in Settings (95% by default; t on n − 1 df). The legend names which, with n, as a figure's legend should (Cumming, Fidler & Vaux 2007). A dose measured once has no error bar; a note names those curves.
CurveOver the X values measured (the default), or Beyond them (extrapolated): a decade further each side on a log axis, a tenth of the X range on a linear one. A note asks the legend to call that part extrapolated.
EC50 linesOn by default: the dashed level lines, at the percentage Show lines at uses (50% when none is shown) or at the absolute EC50's response.
X axisTotal (applied + endogenous), the default, adds the fitted ce to every dose, so the curve is a plain Hill curve in total agonist, rising from the baseline. The vehicle sits at ce, as an open circle with ce's confidence interval as a horizontal error bar with caps. Its X comes from the fit, not from a dose that was set, which the legend should say. The EC50 lines mark the total EC50. Applied dose keeps the doses as given, with the vehicle as a dashed line; the curve then levels off at the vehicle's response, not at the baseline.
ce's CI on every pointWith the Total axis, on by default: ce's interval through every mean, as the same capped horizontal bar, since each mean's X is its dose plus ce. The bars share one ce, so they move together and aren't independent errors; they are left out of the legend.
  • On a log X axis, which has no place for dose 0, the vehicle group's mean is a dashed line across the figure, and the curve runs a decade below the lowest dose so it can be seen to level off. A note gives the mean. This holds under Fix Bottom at their mean too; under Leave them out, the vehicle is left out of the figure as it is of the fit.
  • Data sets that are replicate columns (one value each at shared doses), fitted one by one, are shown as one series: each dose's mean across them, with one curve fitted to all their values.
  • Under Values from the same, the curve is the typical data set's, which needn't pass through the means when the data sets weren't all measured at the same doses.
  • The figure's curves are fits, not data, so tools used on that window leave them out.

With only a few replicates, show the individual points: they tell the reader more than any error bar.

Schild Analysis

Schild Analysis measures an antagonist's potency (pA₂ or pK_B) from agonist dose–response curves at several antagonist concentrations, one of them 0. Each curve needs at least 5 points at 4 or more agonist doses.

  1. Open the curves as an X-Y graph and choose Pharmacology & Biochemistry › Schild Analysis.
  2. Choose Curves: One per sweep (the default) or One per group (replicates).
  3. Check "X is already log10(agonist dose)" when it is.
  4. Choose the Antagonist unit (nM by default): pA₂ is −log10 of a molar concentration.
  5. Under Antagonist concentration of each curve, type each curve's concentration, 0 for the control. A number in a curve's own name, such as "10 nM", fills the field; sweep numbers don't.
  6. Click Fit Schild Model. The tab shows pA₂, the Schild slope and pK_B.
  7. Click Open Schild Plot, shown when the global fit converged, for the classic plot with the global fit's line.
ResultHow it is found
pA₂ and Schild slope SThe global Gaddum/Schild fit (Lew & Angus 1995) fits every curve at once, sharing Bottom, Top and the Hill slope, with each curve's LogEC50 shifted by log10(1 + ([B]·10^pA₂)^S), [B] being its antagonist concentration. Both have CIs.
pK_B and KBThe same fit with S fixed at 1, with pK_B's CI. A slope of 1 is expected for a competitive antagonist at equilibrium; then pA₂ = pK_B.
Test of the slopeFor unweighted fits, an F test of whether S differs from 1.
Schild plotlog(dose ratio − 1) against log[antagonist], from each curve's own 4PL, with its regression. Prefer the global fit: the plot's regression treats each estimated EC50 as exact.

Show lines at marks each curve's EC50 on the graph, so the shift between curves, the dose ratio, can be seen. The Figure section opens a means figure as in Dose–Response.

Kinetics & Binding

Kinetics & Binding fits enzyme kinetics, enzyme inhibition, saturation binding and binding time courses, with concentration or time in X. Every fit is nonlinear least squares on the untransformed data.

  1. Open the data as an X-Y graph and choose Pharmacology & Biochemistry › Kinetics & Binding.
  2. Choose Curves: One per sweep (the default) or One per group (replicates).
  3. Choose the Model (Michaelis–Menten by default) and fill in the fields it shows (see the table below).
  4. Choose Weighting: None (equal weights), the default; 1/Y² (relative); or 1/Y.
  5. Click Fit. Each curve's main constant (Km, Kᵢ, Kd or a rate constant) with its CI, its Vmax, Bmax or plateau, and R² show in the tab.
ModelEquationFields and results
Michaelis–MentenV = Vmax·S/(Km + S)For this and the next two models, type the enzyme's total concentration under [E]t for kcat (optional) to add kcat = Vmax/[E]t and kcat/Km, with kcat/Km's CI by the delta method.
Substrate inhibitionV = Vmax·S/(Km + S·(1 + S/Ki))Adds the optimal substrate concentration, √(Km·Ki).
Allosteric sigmoidal (Hill)V = Vmax·S^h/(Khalf^h + S^h)h above 1 means positive cooperativity. Khalf is not a Km, so with [E]t only kcat is added.
Enzyme inhibition (several [I])Competitive, uncompetitive, noncompetitive and mixed inhibition, each fitted to all the curves togetherUnder Inhibitor concentration of each curve, type each curve's concentration (0 without inhibitor); at least two must differ. The four models are compared by AICc, and the one chosen under Report in full (Mixed by default) is reported in full.
Saturation binding (specific)B = Bmax·L/(Kd + L)Reports Kd and Bmax.
Saturation binding (total + nonspecific)Total and nonspecific binding fitted together, sharing the nonspecific slopeChoose which curve is which under Total binding and Nonspecific binding.
Dissociation kineticsY = (Y0 − NS)·e^(−koff·t) + NSAdds the half-life.
Association kineticsY = Ymax·(1 − e^(−kob·t))With Ligand [L] (optional) and koff (optional), from a dissociation experiment: kon = (kob − koff)/[L] and Kd = koff/kon.
  • Show lines at marks Km, Khalf, Kd, each inhibitor concentration's apparent Km, or a time course's half-time, measured from 0 (or the start) toward the fitted plateau. Substrate inhibition and total binding have no such lines.
  • Open Lineweaver–Burk Plot (enzyme models) and Open Scatchard Plot (specific binding) show the transformed points with the fitted curve transformed the same way, for display only: fitting a transformed plot distorts the scatter.
  • Open Full Statistics Window opens Statistics › Regression for Michaelis–Menten, enzyme inhibition and saturation binding, carrying the weighting, the inhibition model reported in full, each curve's inhibitor concentration (in its column's title) and the total and nonspecific curves chosen (see Other Analyses › Enzyme Kinetics, Binding and Assays).
  • The Figure section opens a means figure as in Dose–Response, with its Curve choice and, where the model has a halfway point, its level lines.

Initial Rates

Initial Rates measures the initial rate v₀ of each progress curve (absorbance, fluorescence or product against time): the slope of a straight line through its first part. Each visible sweep is one trace.

  1. Open the traces as an X-Y graph and choose Pharmacology & Biochemistry › Initial Rates.
  2. Choose Range: First part of each trace, with First % of the time span (10 by default), or Between the cursors.
  3. To subtract a blank, choose its trace under Subtract a blank's slope.
  4. To convert absorbance rates to concentration per unit of time, check Absorbance to concentration (Beer–Lambert) and type ε (M⁻¹ cm⁻¹) and Path length (cm).
  5. Under Substrate concentration of each trace, type each trace's concentration. A number in the trace's own name fills the field.
  6. Click Measure Initial Rates. Each rate with its CI and R² shows in the tab.
  7. Click Open v₀ vs [S] Graph to open the rates against substrate as a new graph, at the Kinetics & Binding tab.
ResultHow it is found
v₀The least-squares slope over the range, with its SE, confidence interval and R². Traces with fewer than 3 points in the range are named in the tab.
Curvature checkWhen a quadratic term fits significantly (p < 0.05), the rate is already falling within the range, and the trace is marked ⚠︎: shorten the range.
BlankThe blank's slope is subtracted. Each rate's SE then combines its own and the blank's, and its CI uses Welch–Satterthwaite df.
Beer–LambertRate/(ε·path length).

Pharmacokinetics (NCA)

Pharmacokinetics (NCA) runs a noncompartmental analysis of each visible concentration–time profile, following the default rules of the PKNCA R package (Denney et al. 2015).

  1. Open the profiles as an X-Y graph, with time in X, and choose Pharmacology & Biochemistry › Pharmacokinetics (NCA).
  2. Choose Route: Extravascular (oral, s.c., i.m.), the default; IV bolus; or IV infusion, with its Infusion duration, which is required.
  3. Choose AUC: Linear-up/log-down (the default) or Linear trapezoidal.
  4. For clearance and volumes, type the Dose (optional) and its unit.
  5. Choose λz from: Automatic (best adjusted R²), the default, or The points between the cursors.
  6. Click Analyze. The tab shows each profile's AUC0–∞, Cmax and half-life, and the λz line is drawn on each profile.
  7. Click Log Y Axis to show concentrations on a log scale, where the terminal phase is straight.
ResultHow it is found
Cmax, TmaxObserved.
Clast, TlastThe last concentration above 0.
Concentrations at or below 0Below the limit: kept as 0 before the first measurable concentration and left out between measurable ones (the table counts them).
C(0)0 after an extravascular dose or an infusion. After an IV bolus, the concentration measured at time 0 when there is one; otherwise back-extrapolated log-linearly from the first two concentrations when they fall, or else taken as the first.
AUC and AUMC to TlastThe linear-up/log-down trapezoidal rule, or linear trapezoids. AUMC on a rising segment is the trapezoid of t·C.
λz, the terminal slopeFitted to log concentration over the last 3 or more points after Tmax, choosing the best adjusted R² (within 0.0001, the most points); or over the points after Tmax between the cursors, at least 3.
From λzThe half-life; AUC and AUMC to infinity, with the percentage extrapolated (above 20% is unreliable); the mean residence time (minus half the infusion); and, with the dose, clearance and volume (CL/F and Vz/F after an extravascular dose; CL, Vz and Vss after IV dosing).
Summary across profilesWith two or more profiles: geometric means with their CIs and geometric CVs, each with its n, and Tmax's median and range.

qPCR & Melt Curves

qPCR & Melt Curves has three analyses. Each visible sweep is one well: fluorescence against cycle for amplification, against temperature for melt and thermal-shift curves.

  1. Open the wells as an X-Y graph and choose Pharmacology & Biochemistry › qPCR & Melt Curves.
  2. Choose Analysis: Amplification (Cq, efficiency), Melt curve (−dF/dT, Tm) or Thermal shift (DSF Tm).
  3. Set its options (below) and click Analyze.

Amplification

Setting or resultWhat it is
Baseline cycles3 to 15 by default. A straight line through these cycles is subtracted. A well already rising within them is flagged.
Threshold (blank: automatic)The automatic threshold is 10 times the median of the wells' baseline SDs, so one well rising early can't lift it.
Cq (threshold)Where the corrected fluorescence crosses the threshold, interpolated in log fluorescence.
Cq (2nd derivative max)The second-derivative maximum of a logistic fitted to the curve.
Amplification factor10^slope of log10 fluorescence over a window of linearity in the exponential phase, after Ramakers et al. (2003) and Ruijter et al. (2009): the cycles running back without a break from the last at or before the second-derivative maximum while the fluorescence stays at or above the threshold, at least 3. A factor of 2 is 100% efficient.

One well's factor, from a few noisy cycles, is rough, and windows of only 3 cycles are named. Use the mean over an amplicon's wells for relative quantification (Ruijter et al. 2009), for example in Statistics › Regression › qPCR Relative Expression (ΔΔCt).

Melt curve

  • −dF/dT is found by local quadratic (Savitzky–Golay) derivatives over the Derivative window (7 points by default), and each peak's Tm is refined by a parabola through it. Peaks above (% of tallest), 5 by default, sets the smallest peak reported.
  • Open −dF/dT Graph shows the curves in a new window. A second, lower peak often means primer dimers or a second product.

Thermal shift (DSF)

  • Tm from: Boltzmann fit (the default), a fit of the unfolding transition that gives Tm with its SE and CI; or Derivative maximum, the steepest point, whether the signal rises or falls on unfolding.
  • Place the cursors around the transition to leave out any drop from aggregation.
  • ΔTm is against the first well, its CI combining both wells' SEs. When the first well has no Tm, no ΔTm is given.
  • With the Boltzmann fit, Show lines at marks each well's Tm on the graph.

Back to Contents

Gels and Blots
