Part of the Pharmacology & Biochemistry toolkit.

Gel / Blot Lanes, in the image inspector's Toolkits tab, measures the bands of a western blot, a stained gel or a TLC plate (densitometry). It finds the lanes and their bands, measures each band's volume above its background, sizes the bands from a ladder, normalizes them to total protein or a loading control, checks a dilution series' linear range, and gives a table with one row per band, ready for statistics. Gels and blots open in an image window; see Imaging for the window itself.

The lanes, bands and settings are saved with the image (see Imaging › Saving and Reopening Image Sessions), and every edit undoes with ⌘Z. A new image starts with the settings used last, the ladder included.

Measure a Western Blot

  1. Open the imager's or scanner's raw image (such as a 16-bit TIFF or OME-TIFF), not one adjusted for display: the measurement needs the values as captured.
  2. Open the image inspector's Toolkits tab and choose Pharmacology & Biochemistry › Gel / Blot Lanes from the menu at the top of the tab.
  3. Under Lanes, set Lanes run (Top to bottom or Left to right, as the image is shown) and Bands: Dark on light, the default, for blots on film and stained gels; or Light on dark, for fluorescence and chemiluminescence, which is how an imager stores a raw capture. For an image with several channels, choose the Channel.
  4. Click Find Lanes. It finds the lanes across the image and the bands in each, and numbers the lanes from the left (or the top). If the number of lanes is wrong, type it in Lanes to find (0, the default, finds the number too) and click Find Lanes Again.
  5. Click a lane on the image to select it. Under Lanes, type its Name and choose its Role: Sample or Ladder (size marker). For a sample lane, set Group, Known load and Control as needed (see the table below).
  6. Under Bands, check the selected lane's profile: its background is dashed and its bands are shaded and numbered (red when saturated). Add, move or delete bands as needed (see Find and edit bands, below).
  7. Under Background, choose the Method (Rolling disk on the lane (Image Lab) by default). The dashed background on the profile should run under the bands, not through them.
  8. Read the Results section at the bottom of the panel, which updates as you edit. Click Open Results Table for every lane, column and digit.
  9. Click Measure to log the full table to the Data Log at full precision, with how it was measured.
  10. To take the numbers to statistics, click Copy Table, Open as Spreadsheet or Open as Chart.

When Find Lanes finds no lanes, check Lanes run and Bands.

Lanes

ControlWhat it does
ChannelThe channel whose bands are measured. Bands belong to the channel they were found on: changing the Channel finds that channel's own bands on each lane that had bands. An orange note says so while the measured channel is hidden on the image.
Show Only This ChannelHides the other channels on the image. A hidden channel is still measured where the tool uses it, such as for total protein.
Name, RoleEach lane is a Sample or the Ladder (size marker), one per image.
GroupWhich lanes are replicates in Open as Chart. Empty: the name less a trailing number, so Control 1 and Control 2 are Control; an unnamed lane is a group of its own.
Known loadThe amount loaded in a dilution series, or a standard's amount (see Check the Linear Range).
ControlMarks the lanes that Rel. Quant. is relative to.
X, Y, W, HThe selected lane's rectangle in image pixels. You can also drag a lane to move it, and drag its sides to resize it.
Every Lane This WideGives every lane the selected lane's width.
Add Lane, Delete LaneAdd Lane adds a lane the size of the last one, beside it. Delete Lane deletes the selected lane.
Show lanes in exportsOn by default: File › Export… and copies of the image draw the lanes, their bands and numbers, and TLC's lines, as the image shows them. Turn it off for a clean image.
  • Right-click a lane on the image for Sample, Ladder, Control Lane, Find Bands in Lane and Delete Lane.
  • The frame and Z slice (or projection) shown are measured, drift-corrected when drift correction is on. A turned image is measured as shown.

Find and edit bands

ControlWhat it does
SensitivityHow faint a band Find Bands takes (50 by default). At 50 a band must stand above the lane profile's noise; each 50 higher divides the smallest band height it takes by ten, and each 50 lower multiplies it by ten.
Bands at least … px apartHow close two bands may be (3 px by default).
Find BandsFinds the bands in every lane again, replacing those there, bands placed by hand included.
Find Bands in LaneDoes the same for the selected lane. It is also on the lane's right-click menu.
Add bandsWhile on, a click in a lane, on the image or the profile, adds a band at the highest point nearby. Esc turns it off.
SaturatedOn by default: outlines saturated pixels in red on the image, with a light red tint.
  • Drag a band's end, on the image or on the profile, to move it. The band's top moves to the highest point between its ends.
  • Select a band to type its From and to (pixels along the lane) or to click Delete Band. On the image, right-click a band to delete it.
  • Bands found on another channel than the one measured are neither measured nor drawn. An orange note at the top of the panel says so, and its Find Bands button finds the measured channel's bands.

Results

  • The Results section shows a line with the channel measured and the number of lanes, bands and flagged bands, then the selected lane's bands. Each band has its size (or its band row) and the value chosen under Show: Rel. Quant., Normalized, Adj. Volume or Amount, whichever the measurement has. Values are shortened to fit (such as 4.75 M). Click a line to select its band, and hover over a flag for why it is there.
  • Open Results Table opens every lane and column in a window that follows the measurement as you edit. Its numbers are rounded for reading: hover over one for its full value. Click a column's title to sort, and a row to select its band. Flagged rows are orange, or red when saturated.
  • Copy Table copies the whole table as tab-separated text, and Open as Spreadsheet opens it in a new spreadsheet, both at full precision.
  • Open as Chart charts one band row of the value chosen under Show: choose the row from its menu. The chart has a bar for each group with each lane as a point, and its Statistics compare the groups.
  • Open Profiles as Graph opens each lane's profile less its background (the raw profile under Border, whose background is one value per band), one sweep per lane against position along the lane.
ColumnWhat it is
Lane, Lane Name, GroupThe lane's number on screen, its name and its group.
Band No., Band RowThe band's number in its lane, and its row: bands at the same place across the lanes, numbered from the lanes' start.
RfThe band's relative mobility (see Size Bands with a Ladder).
Mol. Wt.The band's size from the ladder, in kDa or bp.
VolumeThe sum of the band's pixels, in pixel value × pixels.
Bkgd.The background under the band: Volume − Adj. Volume.
Adj. VolumeThe band's pixels above its background: Σ (profile − background) × lane width over the band's points. It is signed, so a point below the background counts against the band.
Peak HeightThe band's top above its background.
Saturated PxThe number of saturated pixels in the band.
Lane Signal, Norm. Factor, Normalized, Rel. Quant.With normalization or control lanes (see Normalize to Total Protein or a Loading Control).
Amount, Amount Lower, Amount UpperWith a standard curve (see Check the Linear Range).
FlagsWhat to check about the band (below).
FlagWhat it means
saturatedThe band has pixels at the image's full scale, so its volume is too low. Image again with a shorter exposure.
above ladder, below ladderThe band lies beyond the ladder's largest or smallest marker, so it has no Mol. Wt. unless sizes are extrapolated.
size extrapolatedMol. Wt. is extrapolated beyond the ladder.
lane signal saturatedThe lane's loading-control band or total protein is saturated, so the lane's Normalized values are too high.
no lane signalThe lane has no band in the loading-control row.
no control bandNo control lane has a usable band in this row.
outside linear rangeThe band's signal is outside the standard curve's linear range.
below standards, above standardsAmount is read beyond the standards' loads.
interval unboundedAmount's 95% interval is open.

Bent lanes

On a smiling or bowed gel, where a straight lane would cut off part of its lower bands, bend the lanes to follow the gel.

  1. Under Lanes, check Bend lanes to follow the gel before you click Find Lanes, or click Bend Lanes to bend the lanes already there.
  2. Select a bent lane to see its control points in yellow on the image, and drag a point to adjust the curve.
  3. Right-click a lane for Bend Lane to Follow the Gel (or Bend Lane Again), Add Lane Point Here, Delete Lane Point (on a point) and Straighten Lane. Straighten Lanes, under Lanes, straightens them all.

Moving a bent lane moves its curve with it; dragging its ends changes its length, and its width is typed as W.

Rectangle ROIs as lanes

While the tool has no lanes of its own, each visible rectangle ROI (not a background ROI) is measured as a lane: the Results list each lane's density (the whole lane above its background, points below it counting 0) and its percentage of the first lane. Click Use ROIs as Lanes to make them the tool's lanes, with roles and bands, or Find Lanes to place lanes of the tool's own. The ROIs stay either way.

To try the tool, choose More Samples › Western Blot (Image) in the Welcome window, under Pharmacology & Biochemistry. It opens a blot imaged in two channels (immunoblot and total protein stain), already measured: a ladder, a 2-fold dilution series with its loads, and control and treated lanes. A note in the Data Log describes how the blot was made.

Size Bands with a Ladder

  1. Make the ladder's lane the ladder: choose Ladder (size marker) as its Role, choose Ladder on its right-click menu, or choose it as Ladder lane under Molecular weight and Rf.
  2. Give the ladder's sizes. Choose a marker from the Ladder menu (it reads Choose… until you do), or type the sizes under Sizes from the top of the gel down, largest first, and choose kDa or bp.
  3. Read the ladder check below the settings. In orange, it names a size that seems to have no band, a band that looks extra, or a band out of line with its neighbors; otherwise a note says the bands fit the sizes. Add or delete bands, or edit the sizes, as it suggests.
  4. Choose the Fit and the Rf scale (below). The section says how many ladder bands were fitted, and Open Ladder Fit as Graph shows the ladder's sizes against Rf on a log axis, the fitted curve, and every sample band.
  5. Read each band's Mol. Wt. in the results. A band beyond the ladder's largest or smallest marker has none and is flagged; check Extrapolate beyond the ladder to extrapolate its size by the chosen fit, flagged size extrapolated.
  • The Ladder menu holds Precision Plus Protein Dual Color, All Blue, Kaleidoscope and Unstained (Bio-Rad 1610374, 1610373, 1610375 and 1610363), PageRuler Prestained and PageRuler Plus Prestained (Thermo Scientific 26616 and 26619) and GeneRuler 1 kb (Thermo Scientific SM0311), with the sizes their makers state. Prestained protein markers are sized for Tris-glycine SDS-PAGE and run differently in other buffers.
  • Ladder bands are paired with the sizes from the top of the gel: the band that ran least far gets the largest size.

Rf

Rf, a band's relative mobility, is (position − origin) ÷ (front − origin), at the band's top (a TLC spot's at its center; see Measure a TLC Plate). It is one scale for the whole gel: positions are in pixels along the lanes from the image's top as shown (its left, for lanes running left to right), and the origin and front are lines across every lane. Moving or resizing a lane never changes an Rf or a size.

RfOrigin and front
Gel top to bottom (Image Lab)The default: 0 at the gel's top and 1 at its bottom. These are the image's ends unless you type Top at and Bottom at (in pixels), such as for an image with a margin above the wells.
Wells to dye frontThe classical Rf: type Wells at and Front at. Until both are typed, the gel's top and bottom are used.
TLC: origin to solvent frontThe lines are drawn on the image (see Measure a TLC Plate).

Fits

FitHow size is found from Rf
Point to point (semi-log)The default. Straight lines in log₁₀(size) between neighboring ladder bands. It passes through every marker, assumes nothing about the gel and needs only 2 bands.
Linear (semi-log)One least-squares line, log₁₀(size) = a + b·Rf, with its R², for a gel where log size falls in a straight line with Rf (Bio-Rad suggests it for gradient gels). Needs 2 bands.
Logistic (4PL)size = a + (d − a) ÷ (1 + (Rf ÷ c)^b), fitted to size itself, with its R², for a ladder whose sizes follow an S-shaped curve down the lane. Needs 5 bands.
Cubic spline (semi-log)A natural cubic spline through every ladder band in log₁₀(size). Needs 5 bands.

How the ladder check works

  • A ladder's log₁₀(size) falls smoothly as Rf rises, so the check asks that its bands lie on a smooth curve. When the lane has up to 3 bands more or fewer than the sizes, the check names the way of leaving out the extra sizes or bands that puts the bands closest to a smooth curve (least squares of Rf on a cubic in log₁₀(size)), and any other choice nearly as close.
  • The semi-log line, log₁₀(size) = a + b·Rf, gives R² and each band's residual. R² below 0.95 is flagged.
  • Each band's size is also predicted at its Rf from its four nearest other bands (a least-squares quadratic). A band is out of line when its size is more than 1.2 times off that prediction (1.41 times for the first and last band).
  • A ladder shifted by a whole marker can still look smooth: check the reference bands by eye. Measure logs the check to the Data Log, with every ladder band's residual.

Measure a TLC Plate

A thin-layer chromatography plate is measured as a gel is, each track a lane and each spot a band, with an Rf for every spot from an origin line and a solvent front drawn on the image.

  1. Open the plate's image, choose Gel / Blot Lanes, and find the lanes, one per track, as for a gel. Lanes run follows the plate's tracks as shown, whichever way the solvent ran.
  2. Under Molecular weight and Rf, set Rf to TLC: origin to solvent front. A green Origin line and a pink Solvent front line appear across the image.
  3. Drag each line to where the spots were applied and where the solvent stopped. Drag a line's ends to tilt it, as a front often runs unevenly. Place the Lines Again puts both lines back where they started.
  4. Read each spot's Rf in the results, with its volume above the background. Find Bands finds the spots, and the band tools edit them as on a gel.

Rf = (spot − origin) ÷ (solvent front − origin), distances along the lane. The spot is taken at its center: the intensity-weighted mean place of its pixels above the background. The origin and the front are where the lane's center crosses each line, so a tilted line gives each lane its own. A spot that ran past the front has an Rf above 1, and one below the origin a negative one. Until both lines are drawn, the spots have no Rf, and the section says so.

Normalize to Total Protein or a Loading Control

Normalization corrects each band for how much protein its lane holds. Current guidance prefers total protein (Pillai-Kastoori et al. 2020): a housekeeping protein such as β-actin, GAPDH or tubulin can change with the treatment, and its band often saturates at loads where the target is still in its linear range, while a total protein stain sums the whole lane.

  1. Mark the control lanes: check Control under Lanes, or choose Control Lane on a lane's right-click menu.
  2. Under Normalization, choose Normalize to: Total protein, Loading-control band, or None (the default).
  3. For total protein, choose Total protein in: another channel of this image, or another open image of the same size (a stain-free, Ponceau or total-protein-stain image of the same membrane), whose lanes are measured over these lane rectangles. For an image with several channels, choose Its channel. When two open images have the same name, each is listed with its folder; the image you choose is remembered by its file.
  4. Still for total protein, set Its bands (Light on dark by default) and Its background (Running median beside the lane by default).
  5. For a loading control, choose its band row under Loading control. Rows are listed by number with their size (or Rf) and how many lanes have a band there.
  6. Choose the Reference lane: The highest signal (LI-COR), the default; The mean of the lanes; or one lane (as Image Lab does).
  7. Read Normalized and Rel. Quant. in the results.
ValueHow it is computed
Lane SignalFor a loading control, the Adj. Volume of the lane's band in the loading-control row. For total protein, the whole stain lane's sum above its background (signed).
Norm. FactorLane Signal ÷ the reference lane's Lane Signal (÷ the mean of the lanes' signals for The mean of the lanes). This is LI-COR's lane normalization factor; Image Lab's is its reciprocal.
NormalizedAdj. Volume ÷ Norm. Factor: the band as if its lane held as much protein as the reference lane.
Rel. Quant.The fold change against the controls: Normalized ÷ the mean Normalized of the same band row in the control lanes, so the controls' mean is 1. Without normalization, Adj. Volume ÷ the controls' mean Adj. Volume.
  • The Reference lane scales every Normalized value alike and leaves Rel. Quant. unchanged.
  • For total protein the whole lane is the signal. A background from beside the lanes, or a rolling ball wider than a lane, keeps the lane's smear; a rolling disk on the lane removes some of it.
  • Check that a loading control is in its linear range too. A saturated loading-control band, or saturated pixels in a stain lane, flag the lane's bands lane signal saturated.
  • When the loading control or the stain can't be used (a reference lane with no loading-control band, say), the section says why in orange and the bands are left unnormalized.

Check the Linear Range

A band's volume is proportional to the protein in it only over a range of loads: above it the band saturates, and below it the band fades into the membrane's background (Taylor et al. 2013). Run a 2-fold dilution series of a pooled sample on the blot to find the range for each antibody and exposure, or standards of known amount to read amounts from.

  1. Under Lanes, type each dilution lane's Known load, in any unit, the same in every lane. A unit after the number, such as 10 µg, is ignored.
  2. Under Standard curve and linear range, choose the Band row to fit, such as the target's or the loading control's. Check Through the origin to fit a line through 0.
  3. Read the note below: how many lanes have a known load, the line Adj. Volume = intercept + slope × load with its R², the linear range, and the saturated lanes left out. Open Standard Curve as Graph shows the loads' Adj. Volumes and the line over the linear range.
  4. Check the samples. A band of that row whose Adj. Volume lies outside the signals of the linear range is flagged outside linear range: load less (or more) of that sample, or image again with a shorter (or longer) exposure.
  5. Read each band's Amount, in the loads' unit, with Amount Lower and Amount Upper, its 95% interval. With a dilution series of a pooled lysate, it is the band's amount as µg of the pool's worth.

How the linear range and amounts are found

  • The linear range: the guidance defines it as the loads over which signal stays proportional to load, without a numeric test. Gel / Blot Lanes takes the calibration acceptance of ICH M10 (2022) plus R² ≥ 0.98. Saturated loads are left out first. Of the runs of 3 or more neighboring load levels whose least-squares line has a positive slope and R² ≥ 0.98, and in which every level's mean back-calculated load is within ±15% of its known load (±20% at the lowest level), the linear range is the run with the most levels, then the most lanes, then the higher R².
  • The standard curve is the line over the linear range. When no run meets the rule, it is the line over every unsaturated load, and no band is flagged outside it.
  • Amount is found by inverse prediction, (signal − intercept) ÷ slope, from Adj. Volume (not from Normalized), and only for the row of the standard curve.
  • Its interval is the classical calibration (Fieller) interval (Eisenhart 1939; Draper & Smith 1998): every load whose predicted signal lies within t·s·√(1 + 1/n + (x − x̄)²/Sxx) of the band's signal, with s the line's residual SD, n its lanes, x̄ their mean load, Sxx the sum of squares of the loads about it, and t at 95% on n − 2 degrees of freedom. Through the origin, 1/n is left out, x̄ is 0 and there are n − 1.
  • When the slope isn't clearly nonzero at 95%, the interval has no ends and the band is flagged interval unbounded.

Automate Gel / Blot Lanes

Measure a folder of images

  1. Set up one image: its settings, ladder lane, control lanes, known loads, names, groups and reference lane.
  2. Under Results, click Measure Folder… and choose a folder. Every image file in it (not its subfolders) is measured with this image's settings.
  3. A progress bar shows the file being measured. Click Stop to finish that image and keep what was measured.
  4. Read the table, which opens as a spreadsheet with one row per band: File first, then the tool's usual columns. The Data Log gets the same table, how the images were measured, and a line for each file.
  • For each image, the lanes and bands are found as Find Lanes finds them, and the lanes take this image's roles by their number on screen.
  • The loading-control and standard-curve rows are found by size when a size is given (an image whose ladder gives no sizes then has no such row, and the results say so), else by row number.
  • The settings' channel is measured in each file, at its first frame and first Z slice.
  • Top at and Bottom at, Wells at and Front at, and the TLC lines apply only to images the same size in pixels as this one. An image of another size has Rf from its own top to its bottom and no TLC Rf, and its line in the Data Log says so.
  • A file that wasn't measured is listed in the Data Log with the reason: it couldn't be read, it lacks the channel, or no lanes or bands were found. Images left unnormalized are named.
  • Total protein from another image window doesn't apply to a folder, so those images aren't normalized.

Protocols

In the Protocols window, Add Step › Pharm › Gel / Blot Lanes… adds a step that measures an image and logs the full table to the Data Log. It is a protocol's only step, since its result is a table rather than a window. Its changes undo with ⌘Z in the image window.

SettingWhat it does
ImagesThe image window chosen under Run, or Every image in a folder (Choose… picks the folder, which the step remembers). A folder is measured as Measure Folder… measures it, and its table also opens as a spreadsheet.
Lanes and bandsFind lanes and bands (the default), Keep the lanes, find bands, or Keep the image's lanes and bands.
Use the settings saved with the imageOn by default: the background, ladder, normalization and the rest are as the tool's panel last set them on that image. Off: the step's own settings.
Ladder lane, Control lanes, Known loadsLane roles by lane number, such as control lanes 8 9, or loads 40 20 10 5 2.5 1.25 from lane 2. Empty fields and 0 keep the image's.
Loading control at, Standard curve atThe band row by size, in kDa or bp: the row within ±10% of it, which needs the ladder. An image with no row that near isn't normalized, and the Data Log says so. Or give the row by number.

AI Assistant

Ask the AI Assistant to find an image's lanes and bands; to set lane names, roles, groups, controls and loads; to set the ladder, the fit, the background, the normalization, the loading control's and standard curve's rows, bent lanes and the Rf scale; and to measure. It works through the tool's own settings and gives the panel's table. Its changes undo with ⌘Z in the image window.

How Gel / Blot Lanes Measures

  • Profiles: a lane's profile is, at each pixel along it, the mean of the lane's pixels across it. Pixels with no value are left out. Dark bands are measured inverted from the image's full scale (its bit depth's maximum: 255 for 8 bits, 4,095 for 12; or 65,535 when any frame of the channel holds a brighter value), so darker bands count more. A Sum projection is measured as its true sum.
  • Lanes: Find Lanes takes the image's profile across the lanes, lightly smoothed. The gaps between lanes are its valleys, and the lane spacing is the median distance between neighboring gaps, refined by a straight line through the gaps' positions, so a missing gap is skipped. Each lane lies midway between two gaps and is at least 80% of the lane spacing wide, so the bands' edges stay inside. The lanes run the image's whole length. With a number typed in Lanes to find, they are that many neighboring lanes whose bands are the most prominent, or that many equal lanes across the image.
  • Bent lanes: a bent lane keeps its length and width, and its center follows a natural cubic spline through its control points. Its profile is read along that curve, across the lane's width on the perpendicular, scaled so that the profile times the lane's width still sums the lane's pixels. The backgrounds and the saturated pixels follow the curve too. Bend Lanes traces each lane's center down the gel through its bands, with a control point at each band; a lane with no clear band stays as it was.
  • Bands: found on the lane's profile less a rolling disk of half the lane's width, so broad stains and smears aren't taken for bands. A band is a peak whose prominence (its height above the higher of the lowest points on either side before higher ground, as in SciPy's find_peaks; Virtanen et al. 2020) is at least the noise floor × 10^((50 − Sensitivity)/50). The noise floor is 2σ√(2 ln n) for the profile's n points, with σ estimated from the median absolute deviation of the profile's second differences. A peak closer than Bands at least … px apart to a higher one is left out. Each band ends at the lowest point between it and the next band or, on a side with no band near, at the lowest point within 3 half widths at half prominence.
  • Rows: bands at the same distance along the lanes are matched into rows, within 2.5% of the lanes' median length (at least 3 px). The ladder's bands are left out of the rows.
  • Total protein: the stain's lanes are measured over the same lane rectangles, each lane's whole profile above its background times the lane's width. A rolling ball or disk there has a radius of half the widest lane plus 1 pixel, so the lane's smear stays signal.
  • Saturation: a pixel at the image's full scale (for dark bands, 0 before inversion) is saturated. A band with any is flagged saturated and left out of the linear range and the standard curve. A Sum projection is checked slice by slice.

Backgrounds

MethodHow the background is taken
Rolling disk on the lane (Image Lab)The default. A disk rolled under the lane's profile: the background at each point is the highest disk surface below the profile there. Its radius is in pixels and its height in pixel values. A smaller disk follows the profile more closely and removes more. To match an Image Lab disk size given in mm, divide it by the pixel size in mm.
Rolling ball on the image (ImageJ)ImageJ's Process › Subtract Background (Sternberg 1983) on the whole image, with Light background for dark bands. Sliding paraboloid slides a paraboloid instead of rolling a ball. Each lane is measured on what it leaves.
Border median around each band (Image Studio)LI-COR Image Studio's background: the median of the pixels in a border (Border, 1 to 5 px; 3 px by default) around each band's box, one value under the whole band. Top/Bottom, the default, takes the rows above and below the box; Left/Right, the pixels beside it; All, the whole frame. The sides are as the image is shown.
Running median beside the lane (21 px)At each point along the lane, the mean of two medians of the pixels in a border (Border, 1 to 5 px) on either side of the lane, each over 21 pixels along it. It follows the membrane's background along the lane. It is the default background for total protein.
Line between lane endsA straight line between the profile's two ends, each the mean of its first or last 3 points, as a baseline drawn by hand.
Lowest pointThe profile's lowest value, as a constant.
NoneAdj. Volume is the band's whole volume.

The disk's and the ball's radius follow the suggestion shown below the field while the field is empty: half the largest band's extent along the lane for the disk, and half the largest band's larger side for the ball (ImageJ's advice is a radius at least that of the largest object that isn't background). Type a radius to fix it; Use goes back to the suggestion.

Plate Maps

Part of the Pharmacology & Biochemistry toolkit.

A Plate Map window holds one microplate of 6 to 1536 wells: its layout (which wells hold blanks, standards, samples and controls), the plate reader's values, and the analysis. It subtracts a reference read and the blanks, summarizes the replicates, fits a standard curve, reads the samples off it and checks the plate's quality. A plate map is saved as its own .@graph file, which @Graph Reader opens too, and every edit undoes with ⌘Z.

Analyze a Plate

  1. Choose Toolkits › Pharmacology & Biochemistry › Plate Map…, or find it with Find a Tool. A 96-well plate opens.
  2. Under Plate, choose the plate's Size (6, 12, 24, 48, 96, 384 or 1536 wells) and type the standards' Concentration unit, such as pg/mL.
  3. Select wells and, under Layout, give them a Role, a name and a standard's Concentration or a sample's Dilution factor (see Lay Out the Wells, below).
  4. Under Values, click Read Values from File… and choose the reader's export (CSV, TXT or Excel), or drop the file on the window. Paste Values takes a block copied from a sheet or the reader's software.
  5. In the sheet that opens, check the reads to add and click Read (see Reading Plate Values, below).
  6. Under Analysis, choose the Read to analyze, the reference to subtract, the Blanks and the Standard curve (see Analysis Settings, below). The plate is analyzed again after every change.
  7. Above the plate, choose what the wells show (see What the Wells Show, below).
  8. Under Results, read the summary, then click Open Results Sheet for a table with one row per well, or one of the other buttons there (see Results, below).

Choosing another Size for a plate that already has a layout or values keeps the layout of the wells both sizes have and removes the values.

Try it: in the Welcome window, More Samples › ELISA Plate opens a generated ELISA read at 450 nm with a 570 nm reference, with standards, blanks, controls and samples at two dilutions. More Samples › Compound Screen Plate opens a 384-well screen with an edge effect: above the plate, compare Corrected, B-score and % activity.

Lay Out the Wells

Select wells

  • Click a well, or drag over a rectangle of wells. Click a row's letter or a column's number for the whole row or column, or the corner for the whole plate. ⌘-click adds wells or takes them out; ⇧-click selects the rectangle from the last well clicked.
  • Or type the wells under Layout › Select wells and press Return: A1, A1:B7, row H, column 12, separated by commas, or all.
  • From the keyboard, click the plate or Tab to it. The arrow keys move from well to well, ⇧ with an arrow stretches the selection, and Space adds or removes a well.
  • The line under the plate describes the well under the pointer: its layout, its values and, once the plate is analyzed, its results.

Assign roles

  • Choose a Role: Blank, Standard, Sample, Positive control, Negative control or Empty. Type its name (a sample's name, "Std 1"), and a standard's Concentration or a sample's Dilution factor (10 for a 1:10 dilution; 1 when left empty). Then click Assign to Selected.
  • Exclude leaves the selected wells out of every calculation (a bubble, a spill) and draws them crossed out; Exclude again brings them back. Clear empties them. The right-click menu on the plate has the same commands.
  • Replicates are the wells with the same role and name and, for standards, the same concentration, or, for samples, the same dilution. One sample read at 1:2 and at 1:10 is two groups, each summarized on its own.

Fill a dilution series

  1. Select the wells of the series, with its replicates.
  2. Under Series and replicates, choose Runs: Down columns (the default) or Across rows.
  3. Type the Top concentration (1000 by default) and the Dilution step (×) (2 by default, a 2-fold series).
  4. Click Fill Standards.
  • Each position along the series gets its name (Std 1, Std 2, …) and its concentration: the last divided by the step, or multiplied by it with Decreasing (a dilution series) off.
  • The selection's other columns (or rows) repeat the series as replicates: A1:B7 filled down columns gives seven standards in duplicate. To put replicates next to each other along the series instead (A1 and A2 = Std 1, A3 and A4 = Std 2 across a row), raise Replicates side by side.
  • Fill Sample Dilutions gives one sample, named as typed under Layout, its dilution factors: the first, then each the last multiplied by the step. With Role set to Sample, the first field reads First dilution.
  • Number Samples names the selected wells Sample 1, 2, 3, … in the same direction; replicates side by side share a name.

Templates and plater files

  • Apply Template lays a saved layout over the plate. The built-in ELISA template for 96 wells has standards 1–7 in duplicate down columns 1–2 with blanks in row H, and samples 1–40 in duplicate. Save as Template… keeps the plate's layout for every plate map.
  • Export Layout (plater CSV)… writes the layout and the values in plater's format (Hughes 2016), which R's plater::read_plate reads: one block per variable (Role, Group, Concentration, Dilution, Excluded, then each read). Import Layout… reads such a file back.

Reading Plate Values

Read Values from File… and Paste Values find every plate-shaped block, wherever it is in the file, and list the blocks so that you can choose which to add. Each read takes the name the export gives it; the pencil beside it under Values renames it.

What is read

  • A plate-shaped block: a row of the column numbers 1, 2, … (3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24 or 48 of them) with the row letters A, B, … down the column to its left (AA to AF after Z on 1536-well plates, or the lowercase a to f some readers write). Two blocks side by side under one header row, such as two wavelengths, are two reads.
  • The same row of column numbers with exactly the plate's rows of values under it and no letters, as SoftMax Pro writes it; and a block of numbers alone, the size of a plate (8 rows of 12 for 96 wells).
  • A long table with one row per well: a Well column (A1 or A01; also Well ID, Wells, Well Position) or Row and Column columns, with each column of numbers a read. A Plate column with several plates gives each plate its reads. A well on more than one row keeps its last row's value, and the window says so.
  • The exports of Gen5 (BioTek/Agilent), MARS (BMG LABTECH), SoftMax Pro (Molecular Devices), and Magellan, i-control and SparkControl (Tecan), each recognized by what the file says. A layout in the file (Gen5's Well IDs with Conc/Dil, SoftMax Pro's Group tables, a plater file's blocks) is offered as Use the file's layout.
  • Text files may be tab-, comma- or semicolon-separated; every sheet of an Excel workbook is searched. A kinetic export gives one read per time point (see Kinetic Plate Reads, below).

What you may see

  • Replace the plate's reads, in the sheet, takes out the reads the plate already has; turn it off to add to them.
  • Text a reader writes in place of a number (OVRFLW, *****) is kept and shown, and the well has no value.
  • The decimal mark is judged once for the whole file or paste: commas are decimal commas in numbers written like 0,125 and thousands separators in numbers written like 1,234,567. When every comma in the file could be either, as in 12,345, your Mac's number format decides. Numbers in an Excel workbook are read as Excel stores them.
  • Reading a file of another plate size changes the plate to that size, keeping the layout of the wells both have.
  • File › Open File… (or the Finder, or dropping the file on @Graph) opens an export that one of the named readers recognizes as a new Plate Map window named after the file, with the Read Values sheet showing. Click Open as Table Instead to open it as a table. Other files, including plater CSV files, open as tables: read them into a plate map with Read Values from File….

Analysis Settings

SettingDefaultWhat it does
ReadThe first read addedThe read analyzed.
Subtract referenceNoneA reference wavelength's read, subtracted well by well before anything else (450 − 570 nm for a TMB ELISA). When the reads added are named for 450 nm and for 540, 570, 620, 630, 650, 655 or 690 nm, the 450 nm read is analyzed and the other subtracted.
BlanksMean of the blanksWhat is subtracted from every well: Mean of the blanks, Median of the blanks or None.
Standard curve4PLStraight line, 4PL or 5PL. A straight line can be fitted On log10 concentration.
WeightingNoneNone, 1/Y or 1/Y².
Flag replicate CV above (%)20A replicate group with a higher CV is flagged.
Accept standards within ± (%)20How far from its nominal concentration a standard may back-calculate.
… at the lowest and highest (%)25The same limit for the lowest and the highest standard.

What the Wells Show

The control above the plate chooses what colors the wells. The value is written in each well, and the color scale is below the plate.

ShowThe wells are colored by
LayoutEach well's role.
ValuesThe reader's values. With several reads, choose the Read beside it.
CorrectedThe values after the reference read and the blanks are subtracted.
RateEach well's rate, on a kinetic plate.
ConcentrationThe concentration read off the standard curve, × the dilution. A well out of range shows the limit it is beyond, × its dilution, such as <15.6 or >1000.
% activityEach well's percent activity between the controls.
B-scoreEach well's B-score, which takes out row and column effects such as edge effects.
As it looksThe color the wells have in the plate, from their absorbance, for the Assay chosen beside it: TMB, stopped (yellow, 450 nm), BCA (purple, 562 nm) or Bradford (blue, 595 nm).
  • Log color scale (for Values, Corrected and Concentration; on for Concentration at first) colors by log10, for values spanning decades.
  • In every view, each well's outline shows its role, excluded wells are crossed out, and an orange dot marks the wells of a replicate group whose CV is above the limit.
  • When a view can't be shown (no standard curve, controls that don't separate), an orange line under the plate says why.

Results

The Results section lists the blank subtracted, the curve's R² and range (LLOQ–ULOQ), how many standards are accepted, how many samples are in range, the groups with a high CV, and the controls' Z′, S/B, SSMD and CV%.

ButtonWhat it gives
Open Results SheetA sheet with one row per well, ready for Statistics and charts: the layout, the read, the corrected value, the replicate's mean, SD and CV% (of signals and, with a curve, of concentrations), the reading off the curve and × dilution, recovery, range, percent activity, z-score, robust z and B-score.
Open Summary Sheet, Log SummaryThe corrections, the curve's parameters, the standards' back-calculation, the samples, the controls and the plate's quality, as a sheet or in the Data Log.
Open Standard Curve GraphThe standards, the fitted curve and the means of the samples in range.
Open Profiles GraphThe scored wells' median by row and by column, which shows edge effects.
Open Heatmap ChartThe values the plate shows, as a heatmap chart.
Plate PictureCopies or saves (PDF or PNG) the plate as shown, with its legend, for a figure.

Kinetic Plate Reads

A kinetic run reads the plate again and again over time: an enzyme's product appearing, cells growing. Each well's reads form a curve over time, and its rate, the slope of that curve, stands in for a read in the rest of the analysis: the blanks' rates are subtracted, replicates are summarized, standards are fitted to rates, and percent activity and Z′ use the rates.

  1. Read a kinetic export (Gen5's kinetic table, SoftMax Pro's kinetic plate, SparkControl's cycles) as any other file. Each time point becomes a read with its time, Analyze is set to Rate (kinetic), and the plate shows Rate.
  2. With several runs in one file (OD600 and GFP, or two wavelengths), choose the Kinetic run under Analysis.
  3. Choose Rate: Slope over the window, or Vmax: steepest of n points with its Points per slope.
  4. To limit the reads used, type Window (min) from and to, or leave both empty and set First % of the run.
  5. Select wells on the plate. Kinetic Curves draws their reads over time, each with the line its rate was measured on. Open Curves as Graph opens them (or every well with a role, up to 96) as a graph.
SettingDefaultWhat it does
RateSlope over the windowSlope over the window fits one line through every read in the window (SoftMax Pro's Slope, Gen5's Mean V). Vmax: steepest of n points fits a line through each run of n consecutive reads in the window and reports the steepest, rising or falling (SoftMax Pro's Vmax, Gen5's Max V).
Points per slope5The n of Vmax. 5 is SoftMax Pro's FlexStation default; Gen5's is 2.
Window (min) from, toEmptyOnly the reads between these times are used.
First % of the run100With no window, the first part of each curve's time span, as Initial Rates takes it.
× 1000OffRates are per minute in the read's unit (OD/min, RFU/min). On, they are in thousandths (mOD/min).
  • Each line is an ordinary least-squares fit on time in minutes: slope = Sxy/Sxx, its SE = √(s²/Sxx) with s² the residuals' sum of squares over n − 2 (none from 2 reads), and R² = 1 − SSres/SStot. Missing reads (flagged or empty) are left out.
  • Vmax's time is the middle of its run's first and last times; of equally steep runs, the first is reported. Lag time, as Gen5 defines it for growth curves, is where the line of the steepest slope meets the window's first signal: (first signal − intercept)/slope, from the run's start.
  • A well with fewer than 2 reads in the window has no rate, and the summary says how many.
  • The results sheet adds each well's rate with its SE, R², the points fitted and in the window, the fitted reads' first and last times, the time of the rate and the lag time.
  • No reference read is subtracted from rates. To analyze a single read instead, a kinetic time point among them, choose Analyze › One read (endpoint).

How Plate Map Analyzes

  • Order: the reference read is subtracted first, well by well; then the blanks' mean (or median) is subtracted from every well. Excluded wells and wells with no value are left out of everything.
  • Replicates: n, the mean, the SD (n − 1) and CV% = 100 × SD/|mean| of each group's corrected values. With a standard curve, standards and samples also get the CV% of their wells' concentrations read off the curve, and that CV is the one flagged above the limit (ICH M10). Without a curve, the CV% of the signals is flagged.
  • Standard curve: fitted as in Statistics › Regression › Standard Curve (Interpolate). Every standard well is a point; replicates are not averaged first. The 4PL is Y = Bottom + (Top − Bottom)/(1 + 10^((LogEC50 − log10 X) × Hill slope)) and the 5PL is Y = Bottom + (Top − Bottom)/(1 + 10^((LogXb − log10 X) × Hill slope))^S, the asymmetric curve ELISAs often follow (Gottschalk & Dunn 2005). Both are fitted on log10 concentration, so a zero standard is left out of the fit, and the summary says so. With 1/Y or 1/Y², the weights come from the fitted curve, refitted until they settle.
  • Back-calculation: each standard level's mean signal is read off the curve, and its recovery is 100 × back-calculated ÷ nominal. A level is accepted when its recovery is within ±20% (±25% at the lowest and the highest standard), and a curve with at least 6 levels passes when at least 75% of them are accepted (FDA 2018; ICH M10, 2022). With fewer than 6 levels the curve isn't judged. The LLOQ and ULOQ are the lowest and the highest accepted standard, or the range of all the standards when none is accepted.
  • Samples: each group's mean corrected signal is read off the curve, with a confidence interval from the curve's uncertainty (the delta method), and multiplied by its dilution factor. A reading below the LLOQ or above the ULOQ, or a signal beyond one of the curve's plateaus, is flagged (< LLOQ, > ULOQ) and given as the limit it is beyond, × the dilution (<15.6, >2000). A sample read at several dilutions is also summarized over its dilutions in range: the mean of concentration × dilution, and its CV, which shows whether the dilutions agree.
  • Plate quality, from the positive and negative controls: Z′ = 1 − 3(SDp + SDn)/|mean p − mean n| (Zhang, Chung & Oldenburg 1999); signal to background, mean p ÷ mean n; SSMD = (mean p − mean n)/√(SDp² + SDn²) (Zhang 2007); and each control's CV%. Judge a plate on its controls' CV, the signal window and the heatmap as well as Z′ (NCBI Assay Guidance Manual).
  • Percent activity, per well: normalized percent = 100 × (value − mean N)/(mean P − mean N), 0 at the negative and 100 at the positive controls (Malo et al. 2006). With positive controls alone it is % of positive control = 100 × value ÷ mean P. No percent is given, and a note says why, when the controls don't separate (|mean P − mean N| within 3 × (SD P + SD N)) or, with positive controls alone, when their mean is within 3 SD of 0.
  • Scores: the z-score is (value − mean)/SD and the robust z-score (value − median)/MAD, over the scored wells: the samples or, on a plate with none, every well with a value except the blanks. MADs are scaled by 1.4826, so robust z- and B-scores read on the scale of z-scores.
  • B-score (Brideau et al. 2003): Tukey's two-way median polish of the scored wells (a row's and a column's median taken out in turn until the residuals' sum changes by less than 1%, at most 10 times), each residual divided by the residuals' MAD.
  • As it looks: white light transmitted through the well (Beer–Lambert), the assay's colored product absorbing as a Gaussian band at its maximum (TMB stopped with acid, 450 nm, 80 nm wide at half height; BCA, 562 nm, 130 nm; Bradford, 595 nm, 110 nm), scaled so that its absorbance at the read's wavelength is the well's: the read less the reference read, not less the blanks. The color is computed for the CIE 1931 2° observer (Wyman, Sloan & Shirley 2013) and shown in sRGB. Fluorescence and luminescence have no such color.

Automate Plate Maps

  • Protocols: in the Protocols window, Add Step › Pharm › Plate Map… adds a step that runs on the Plate Map window chosen under Run. It can lay a template over the plate; it analyzes the plate with the window's settings or its own (the read analyzed and the reference by name, the blanks, the curve and its weighting), logs the summary to the Data Log and, if asked, opens the results sheet. It is a protocol's only step: read each plate's values in its window, then run the protocol on it.
  • AI Assistant: ask it to lay out a plate (blanks, standards with their concentrations or a dilution series, samples with their dilutions, controls, wells to exclude) and to analyze it with the reads, blanks, curve, weighting and limits you name, or a kinetic plate by its rates. It gives the summary.
  • Changes made by a protocol or the AI Assistant undo with ⌘Z in the Plate Map window.

Plate Photos and Colonies

Part of the Pharmacology & Biochemistry toolkit.

Two tools in the image inspector's Toolkits tab measure photos: Plate Photo reads a microplate's wells from a photo of the plate, and Colony Count counts the colonies on a photo of a Petri dish. Both work in an image window; see Imaging for the window itself.

Read a Plate from a Photo

Plate Photo needs a photo or a scan of a microplate of 6 to 1536 wells. It lays a grid on the plate by its four corner wells, measures each well's color, and opens the wells' values as reads in a new Plate Map, where the layout, blanks, standard curve and plate quality are analyzed as for a plate reader's export (see Plate Maps). The grid and settings are saved with the image (see Imaging › Saving and Reopening Image Sessions), and every edit undoes with ⌘Z.

  1. Photograph the plate from above, flat on an even light source (a light box, or a white sheet in daylight), so that every well is seen through its bottom. Take the lid off, to avoid reflections.
  2. Open the picture. In the image inspector's Toolkits tab, choose Pharmacology & Biochemistry › Plate Photo from the menu at the top of the tab.
  3. Choose the plate's size under Plate and click Place Grid. A grid is laid over most of the picture.
  4. Drag the four yellow corner wells onto the centers of those wells in the photo: the first row's first and last wells and the last row's first and last (A1, A12, H1 and H12 on a 96-well plate). The grid follows the plate's tilt and perspective. For a plate photographed turned, drag A1 to where A1 is. Or type each corner well's center, X and Y in pixels from the photo's top left, in the fields under the grid's steps.
  5. Set Well circle so that the circle read in each well stays inside the well's bottom, clear of its walls and their reflections.
  6. Under Analyze, choose Absorbance (for colorimetric assays such as ELISA, BCA or MTT), Mean or Median, and the Channel: the color the assay's product absorbs most.
  7. For absorbance, choose I₀ from, the reference light, and type the blank wells as the Plate Map's wells are typed (such as H11, H12, H1:H12 or row H).
  8. Click Open in Plate Map, and lay out the wells there.
SettingDefaultWhat it does
Plate96 wellsThe plate's size: 6, 12, 24, 48, 96, 384 or 1536 wells. Choosing another size lays a new grid, as Place Grid Again does.
Well circle60% of the spacingThe diameter of the circle read in each well, as a share of the distance between neighboring wells.
AnalyzeAbsorbanceThe read the Plate Map analyzes first. Every channel's values are sent as reads whichever you choose.
ChannelBlue, in a color pictureA yellow product (TMB stopped with acid, p-nitrophenol) absorbs blue; a purple one (BCA, MTT formazan, crystal violet) absorbs green.
I₀ fromBlank wellsBlank wells: the wells you type, drawn in blue-green on the image. ROIs on white: rectangle or ellipse ROIs drawn on a white or empty part of the plate or the light box. The image's white: the top of the image's scale.
Decode sRGB before averagingOnConverts each pixel to linear light first, as a camera's or phone's picture needs. Turn it off for a raw or linear image.
Show the grid in exportsOnDraws the grid in exported and copied images.

What Plate Photo reports

  • The wells are read as the grid moves. The panel shows each well's color as read and, for absorbance, the range of A.
  • Open in Plate Map opens a new Plate Map of the plate's size with each channel's mean and median as reads and, when there is an I₀, its absorbance (A). With Absorbance chosen and no I₀, the chosen channel's mean is analyzed, and the Plate Map's note says so.
  • Open as Spreadsheet opens a table with one row per well: each channel's mean, median, SD and A. Log Table puts it in the Data Log with how it was read.

How Plate Photo Reads

  • The grid: the four corner wells' centers define the projective transform (homography) from the plate's flat grid of wells to the photo (Hartley & Zisserman 2004). It carries straight lines to straight lines, so it holds for a flat plate seen at any angle.
  • Each well's pixels: those whose centers, carried back to the grid, lie within the Well circle of the well's center. The circle is laid in the plate's plane, so in the photo it is foreshortened as the well is.
  • Each well's mean, median and standard deviation (n − 1) on every channel, on the image's values in the plane shown (the Z slice or projection, and the frame).
  • Absorbance: A = −log10(I ÷ I₀), with I the well's mean light and I₀ the reference: the mean of the blank wells' means, the mean of the ROIs' pixels, or the image's white (1 in linear light, or the top of the image's scale).
  • Decode sRGB before averaging: each pixel's value v, as a fraction of full scale, is first converted to linear light by the sRGB transfer function (IEC 61966-2-1): v/12.92 up to 0.04045, else ((v + 0.055)/1.055)^2.4. A camera's picture stores light through that curve, not in proportion to it.
  • A is absorbance-like, not a spectrophotometer's absorbance: a camera's channel spans a band of wavelengths, so A is lower than at the product's peak and bends away from Beer–Lambert's straight line at high concentrations. The standard curve in the Plate Map calibrates it.

Count Colonies

Colony Count needs a photo of a Petri dish. It finds the dish, separates the colonies from the agar, splits colonies that touch, and gives each one's size, circularity and intensity. You can take colonies out or add them by clicking. The dish, settings, colonies and edits are saved with the image, and every edit undoes with ⌘Z.

  1. Photograph the dish from above, lid off, evenly lit against a plain background.
  2. Open the picture. In the image inspector's Toolkits tab, choose Pharmacology & Biochemistry › Colony Count.
  3. Click Find Dish. The dish's circle is drawn dashed in cyan, and a dotted circle inside it shows the rim margin left out. Drag the circle's center to move it, or its edge to resize it, or type the dish's center (X and Y in pixels from the photo's top left) and radius in the Dish fields.
  4. Under Settings, choose what to Measure, whether the Colonies are lighter or darker than the agar, the Threshold, and the limits on size, contrast and circularity (see the table below).
  5. Click Count. Each colony found is outlined in yellow and numbered, and the count is shown in the panel.
  6. Check the count on the image. Turn on Edit by clicking, then click a colony to take it out of the count (dust, a bubble, a reflection), or click the agar where one was missed to add it (drawn in orange). Escape turns editing off.
  7. Under Results, click Open as Spreadsheet or Log Table.
SettingDefaultWhat it does
MeasureLuminanceThe plane counted: a color picture's luminance, or the one channel where the colonies stand out best from the agar.
ColoniesLighter than the agarLighter than the agar or Darker than the agar.
Rim margin3% of the radiusThe band inside the dish's edge that is left out, where the wall's reflections lie.
Flatten the agar's lightOnSubtracts a smooth background, to even out light falling off across the dish. Box is the side of the boxes it is estimated in (0: an eighth of the dish's radius); make it several colonies wide.
ThresholdOtsuOtsu: the level that best separates the dish's pixels into two classes. Above the Agar's Noise: the agar's level + k × its noise (k = 3 by default), for a few small colonies on a large dish. Typed: a level above the background.
Fill holes in coloniesOnFills holes inside colonies (a glint, a pale center) up to the size of a circle 10% of the dish's radius across.
Split touching coloniesOn, Depth 2 pxSplits colonies that touch at their narrowest part. Depth is how much narrower than both colonies the neck must be.
Diameterauto to noneThe equivalent diameters kept, in pixels. Left empty: from 0.5% of the agar's diameter, with no upper limit. Nothing under 3 pixels across is counted.
Contrast ≥5The least contrast against the agar, in units of the agar's noise. 0 turns the test off.
Circularity ≥0.3The least circularity (1 for a circle). Scratches and bubbles' edges score low.
Show colonies in exportsOnDraws the dish and the colonies in exported and copied images.

What Colony Count reports

  • Open as Spreadsheet opens a table with one row per colony: its position, area, equivalent diameter, circularity and mean intensity, and whether it was added by hand. Log Table puts it in the Data Log with the settings used and how many objects each limit left out.
  • Count Again keeps the colonies taken out or added by hand. Clear Hand Edits puts the count back as found.

When the count looks wrong

  • Single colonies split in two: raise Depth. Touching colonies counted as one: lower it.
  • Specks of agar counted: raise Contrast, the smallest Diameter or Circularity. With a few small colonies on a large dish, choose Threshold › Above the Agar's Noise.
  • The panel says, in orange, when the Threshold doesn't suit the dish and which to choose instead: when Otsu's threshold falls within the agar's noise, and when, with Above the Agar's Noise, colonies cover more than about an eighth of the dish.
  • The panel says the photo is small when the agar is under 600 pixels across: colonies under 3 pixels across can't be told from the agar's texture, and a larger photo resolves smaller ones.

How Colony Count Counts

  • The dish: Find Dish takes the strongest circle in the picture (a gradient Hough transform), with a radius between a quarter and 0.62 of the picture's shorter side. Only the agar inside the rim margin is counted.
  • The plane: a color picture's luminance, 0.2125 R + 0.7154 G + 0.0721 B (ITU-R BT.709), or the channel chosen; negated for colonies darker than the agar.
  • Flatten the agar's light: the background is the median of each box of pixels in the dish, smoothed by a 3 × 3 median of the boxes and interpolated between box centers, as SExtractor estimates a sky (Bertin & Arnouts 1996).
  • Otsu's threshold (Otsu 1979): the level that maximizes the variance between two classes of the dish's flattened pixels, on a histogram of 256 equal bins. It needs enough colonies to make a second peak in the histogram.
  • Above the Agar's Noise: the agar's level + k × its noise, the mean and standard deviation of the dish's flattened pixels after clipping those beyond 3 standard deviations of the median, repeated up to 10 times, as SExtractor sets its detection threshold (Bertin & Arnouts 1996). The clipping leaves the colonies out only while they cover less than (3 − √5)/6, about an eighth, of the dish.
  • Touching colonies: a watershed on the distance transform, as in OpenCFU (Geissmann 2013). The distance from each colony pixel to the nearest agar pixel is computed, each peak of that distance at least Depth deep becomes a marker (the h-maxima transform; Soille 2003), and the colony is divided between its markers. A colony too small to hold a marker stays one colony.
  • Each colony: its area in pixels, centroid, perimeter, equivalent diameter √(4 × area/π), circularity 4π × area/perimeter² and mean intensity on the plane counted. A colony is kept when its equivalent diameter is within the Diameter limits (never under 3 pixels) and its contrast and circularity reach theirs; the Data Log counts the objects each limit left out.
  • Contrast: the sum over the object's pixels of the flattened value less the agar's level, divided by the agar's noise × √area. The agar is the dish's pixels outside the colonies; its level is their median and its noise their robust SD (1.4826 × the median absolute deviation). 5 is Rose's criterion (Rose 1948). The test treats the agar's pixels as independent, so it rejects specks more surely than broad patches.
  • Hand edits: a click on a colony records the place, and a later count leaves out the colony there. A colony added by hand is a circle of the found colonies' median diameter.

Automate Plate Photos and Colony Counts

  • AI Assistant: with Pharmacology & Biochemistry › Plate Photos & Colonies on, it can lay a plate photo's grid by its corner wells and read it into a Plate Map (then lay out and analyze the plate with the Plate Map tools), and count the colonies on a dish's photo with the settings you name. Its changes undo with ⌘Z in the image window.
