Biosignals: ECG, Breathing, EEG and EMG

Part of the Biosignals toolkit.

Four tabs in the inspector's Toolkits category › Biosignals measure physiological recordings such as those from EDF, WFDB, BIOPAC or LabChart files: ECG / HRV, Respiration, EEG Band Power and EMG Envelope. Each works on the visible sweeps of the channel you choose (hidden groups and sweeps outside Review sweeps are left out), shows a summary in the panel and writes the full table to the Data Log. Batch Processing and Protocols run all four, and ECG / HRV's intervals as ECG Intervals, on every sweep of a channel named in the step (see Batch Processing and Protocols).

ECG / HRV

ECG / HRV finds each heartbeat's R peak in an ECG and measures heart-rate variability (HRV) from the intervals between beats.

  1. Open the recording and, in the inspector's Toolkits category, choose Biosignals › ECG / HRV.
  2. Choose the ECG's Channel, and set R waves and Fastest heart rate (see the table).
  3. Click Detect Beats and Measure HRV. The panel shows each sweep's beats, heart rate, SDNN, RMSSD and LF/HF, and the full table goes to the Data Log.
  4. Click Open Tachogram to see the NN intervals against time, one series per sweep, in a new graph window.
SettingDefaultWhat it does
R wavesDetectDetect inverts an ECG whose QRS clearly points down. Upright and Inverted set the direction yourself.
Fastest heart rate200/min (people)The rate the heart can reach, not its usual rate: 200/min (people), 400/min (rabbit, guinea pig), 600/min (rat), 900/min (mouse) or 1200/min (hummingbird). It sets the shortest time between beats (60 / the rate), HRV's frequency bands and pNN threshold, and the species rules of ECG Intervals. Each graph window keeps its own setting, shared by ECG / HRV and Respiration and saved with the graph; a new window starts with the Default heart in Settings › Toolkits.
Leave out ectopic and missed beats (20% rule)OnLeaves flagged intervals, and the successive differences that include them, out of the HRV measures.

How R peaks and intervals are found

  • R peaks are found after NeuroKit2's default method (Makowski et al. 2021). The ECG is high-passed at 0.5 Hz to remove baseline wander. QRS complexes are where the absolute slope, smoothed over 0.1 s, rises above 1.5 times its 0.75 s average. Each complex's most prominent peak is its R peak, kept when it comes more than 0.3 s after the last. These times are for people; a faster Fastest heart rate shortens all three in proportion.
  • Mains hum at 50 or 60 Hz, when present, is smoothed out (a moving average over one hum period) before the R peaks are found. This is done at the 200/min setting only, since it would blunt the narrow QRS of a faster heart.
  • The intervals between beats (RR) are checked: one more than 20% away from the median of the intervals around it is flagged as an ectopic or missed beat. With the flagged intervals left out, the rest are NN intervals.

What is reported

MeasureHow it is computed
Mean NN, Mean HRThe mean NN interval in ms, and the mean of the intervals' rates (60,000 / NN) in beats a minute.
SDNN, RMSSD, SDSD, pNN50Time domain (Task Force 1996): the SD of the NN intervals; the root mean square and the SD of the successive differences; and the percentage of successive differences above 50 ms, out of the NN intervals.
VLF, LF, HF, LF/HF, LF (nu), HF (nu)Frequency domain: the Lomb–Scargle periodogram of the NN series against beat time, which needs no resampling of the uneven intervals, as a density in ms²/Hz, integrated over each band. LF and HF in normalized units (nu) are percentages of LF + HF.
SD1, SD2, SD1/SD2Poincaré plot (Brennan et al. 2001): the spread across (SD1) and along (SD2) the line of identity when each interval is plotted against the next, using only intervals that were next to each other.
DFA α1, DFA α2Detrended fluctuation analysis (Peng et al. 1995): α1 over windows of 4 to 11 beats, α2 over 12 beats to a tenth of the series. α2 needs at least 129 intervals.
SampEnSample entropy (Richman & Moorman 2000): patterns of 2 intervals, matching within 0.2 SD.
HTI, TINNThe HRV triangular index (the number of NN intervals over the tallest bin of their histogram) and TINN (the base of the triangle fitted to it), on bins of 1/128 s.
  • Read LF and VLF only from recordings of at least 5 minutes, as the Task Force recommends; HF needs about 1 minute.
  • The nonlinear and geometric measures are computed on the NN intervals as NeuroKit2 computes them. The 1/128 s bins suit people: at a faster setting, compare the triangular index and TINN only within a species.

Frequency bands and pNN threshold by species

People keep the Task Force's (1996) bands and pNN50. No standard exists for the other species, so each other Fastest heart rate setting takes the values recommended by published studies, and the results name them as recommendations with their source: "No standard exists for this species: these are recommendations from the studies named".

Fastest heart rateLF and HF (Hz)pNN thresholdSource
200/min (people)LF 0.04–0.15, HF 0.15–0.4pNN50Task Force 1996
400/min (rabbit, guinea pig)LF 0.088–0.341, HF 0.341–1.155pNN17Behar et al. 2018
600/min (rat)LF 0.2–0.75, HF 0.75–2.5None publishedCarnevali et al. 2023
900/min (mouse)LF 0.152–1.24, HF 1.24–5pNN6Bands: Behar et al. 2018. pNN6: Thireau et al. 2008
1200/min (hummingbird)None publishedNone publishedFor birds, the frequency domain and pNN are left blank

VLF is 0.0033–0.04 Hz in people; at the other settings it runs from 0.0033 Hz (0.0056 Hz for the mouse) up to LF. The Data Log names the bands used with each run.

What you may see

  • When no sweep gives at least 3 beats at a rate a heart could keep (from 20 a minute up to the Fastest heart rate), the panel says the channel doesn't look like an ECG: choose the ECG channel. For a breathing trace, Go to Respiration switches to that tab.
  • When many tall complexes come too soon after a beat to count, the panel suggests a faster Fastest heart rate. At 1200/min it says when the recording is sampled below 2 kHz.

ECG Intervals

The Intervals section of the ECG / HRV tab measures the ECG's waves on a median beat, as clinical ECG programs do. It uses the Channel, R waves and Fastest heart rate settings at the top of the tab; Fastest heart rate chooses the rules (see Rules by species, below).

  1. When the file has several channels, choose Leads: This channel, or All leads (global). With All leads, check the channels to measure as ECG leads.
  2. Click Measure Intervals. The panel shows each sweep's PR, QRS, QT and QTc in ms, and the full table goes to the Data Log.
  3. Click Open Median Beat to see each median beat with its points marked, or Open QT Over Time to see each beat's QT against time.
MeasureHow it is measured
P, PR (ms)P onset to P end, and P onset to QRS onset.
QRS, QT (ms)QRS onset to QRS end (the J point), and QRS onset to T end.
RR, QTc (ms)The median RR interval of the beats used, and QT corrected for it by the species' formulas (below).
ST level; P, R, S and T amplitudesMeasured from the isoelectric level at QRS onset. The ST level is taken a set time after the J point (below).

A wave whose onset or end isn't found leaves its intervals blank (—). A sweep with fewer than 3 regular beats has no median beat.

How the median beat is built and measured

  • R peaks are found as Detect Beats finds them. The waves are measured on the ECG high-passed at 0.05 Hz, which leaves the ST segment's level as it is, with any mains hum subtracted.
  • Beats next to an ectopic or missed beat are left out. Each other beat is cut from 0.45 RR before its R peak to 0.8 RR after it, aligned on its R peak and then by correlation over the QRS; a beat whose shape differs (a correlation below 0.9) is left out. The median beat is the median of these beats, sample by sample.
  • The median beat is delineated by the wavelet method of Martínez et al. (2004): onsets and ends are where the wave's slope, at the scale suited to it, falls to a set fraction of its steepest, or stops falling. The T wave is the tallest wave after the QRS (the earliest of those nearly as tall), so a U wave isn't taken for it.
  • All leads (global) measures each checked lead's median beat, cut at the same beats, and adds the global intervals: the earliest onset and the latest end of each wave over the leads. Channels named or measured as another signal (breathing, blood pressure, EMG, EEG; units such as mmHg, % or °C) start unchecked; Batch, Protocols and the AI Assistant take that default set. A lead with no QRS at the chosen channel's R peaks is left out, and the Data Log names it.
  • Each beat's QT is measured the same way on the beat itself, and kept when its QRS onset and T end lie close to the median beat's. The Data Log gives its mean, SD and range.
  • Record at 500 Hz or more for people (AHA/ACC/HRS 2007), and proportionally faster for faster hearts; the panel says when a recording is sampled more slowly.

Rules by species

The Fastest heart rate setting chooses the rules, so each species' ECG is measured by its own:

  • People (200/min): T end by the wavelet threshold; QTc by Bazett (QT/√RR), Fridericia (QT/∛RR), Framingham (QT + 154 × (1 − RR)) and Hodges (QT + 1.75 × (heart rate − 60)), RR in seconds, as in Lab Tools › QTc; ST level at J + 60 ms.
  • Rabbit or guinea pig (400/min): waves as in people, since these hearts have a plateau and an ST segment; ST level at J + 30 ms. QTc by Bazett and Fridericia only: the corrections published for rabbits and for guinea pigs differ and disagree across heart rates, and this setting covers both, so no species formula is applied. Report QT with RR.
  • Rat (600/min) and mouse (900/min): there is no isoelectric ST segment, since the J wave follows the QRS straight away (Boukens et al. 2014). The QRS ends where the S wave meets the isoelectric level; the QT ends where the last wave after the QRS returns to the isoelectric level (Mitchell et al. 1998; Speerschneider & Thomsen 2013). The J wave's height is reported in place of an ST level. QTc for rats by Kmecova & Klimas (2010), QT / √(RR / 150 ms); for mice by Mitchell et al. (1998), QT / √(RR / 100 ms). No correction is agreed for rodents, so QT and RR are always given beside QTc.
  • Birds (1200/min): no QT correction or ST rule has been published for birds, so QT and RR are reported uncorrected, the QT ending where the last wave returns to the isoelectric level, as in rodents, with no ST level.

Respiration

Respiration finds the breaths in a breathing trace (a belt, thermistor, flow or impedance signal) and measures their rate, timing and depth. With an ECG recorded alongside, it also measures respiratory sinus arrhythmia (RSA).

  1. In the inspector's Toolkits category, choose Biosignals › Respiration. A channel named for breathing is chosen for you, and a channel named ECG or EKG as the ECG for RSA.
  2. Set "Breathing in moves the trace" (Up by default), the Low-pass (3 Hz by default, which suits people; raise it for species that breathe faster) and the Smallest breath (30% of the typical swing by default).
  3. For RSA, choose the ECG for RSA, and its R waves and Fastest heart rate, which are shared with ECG / HRV. The ECG can be in another window of the same file: an EDF, WFDB or BIOPAC file opens each sample rate in its own window, so a sleep study's ECG and chest belt open apart. Keep both windows open; the list names the other window's channels with their part.
  4. Click Detect Breaths. The panel shows each sweep's breaths, rate, Ti/Te and, with an ECG, heart rate and RSA. The full table goes to the Data Log.
  5. Click Open Breaths to check the detection, or Open Breathing Rate to see each breath's rate against time.
MeasureHow it is computed
Breaths, RateThe whole breaths found, and 60 / the mean breath length.
Breath length, SD, CVThe mean, SD and CV of the breath lengths.
Ti, Te, Ti/Te, Ti/TtotThe mean inspiratory time (trough to peak) and expiratory time (peak to next trough), their ratio, and the duty cycle Ti/Ttot.
Depth, Depth SDPeak minus trough of the band-passed trace.
Mean HR, Mean RRThe paired ECG's mean heart rate and RR interval, from the NN intervals as in ECG / HRV.
RSA, RSA SD, RSA breaths, Scored 0The mean and SD of the breaths' RSA in ms, the number of breaths judged, and how many of them scored 0.
RSA / mean RRRSA normalized for heart rate (Hayano et al. 1990).

How breaths are found

  • The whole recording is measured, whatever part of it the graph shows.
  • The trace is band-passed from 0.05 Hz to the Low-pass, the cleaning of Khodadad et al. (2018) as NeuroKit2 applies it: a zero-phase Butterworth band-pass, of order 4 as the Filter panel counts it, each edge −3 dB after both passes. The ends are first extended by a mirrored copy, so that the first and last breaths aren't distorted.
  • A peak (the end of breathing in) or a trough (the end of breathing out) counts once the trace has turned back by the Smallest breath percentage of its typical swing, the range from the 5th to the 95th percentile, so small wiggles within a breath are passed over. A breath runs from a trough, through the next peak, to the next trough.
  • Open Breaths marks each breath's start (green) and peak (red) on the band-passed trace. A recording longer than a minute opens on its first 30 s, or on the stretch the graph is zoomed to.

How RSA is measured

  • RSA is measured by the peak–valley method as Grossman, van Beek & Wientjes (1990) specify it. The R peaks are found as in ECG / HRV, and each RR interval is timed at the R peak that ends it.
  • In each breath, breathing in is the window for the shortest interval and breathing out the window for the longest. Both windows end 750 ms later, because heart period follows breathing with a lag; for a faster heart (Fastest heart rate above 200/min) the lag is scaled by heart period, 750 ms × 200 / that rate (250 ms for a rat, about 167 ms for a mouse), an approximation the results point out, since no lag has been measured on an animal's heart. A breath's RSA is the longest minus the shortest, in ms.
  • The 750 ms lag is the one measured in people. With an animal's heart chosen in Fastest heart rate, RSA is measured with the same lag, and the panel and the Data Log say so: a small animal's breath is shorter than the lag, so RSA can read high. Compare it only within a species.
  • The shortest counts only when the interval before it is longer, and the longest only when the interval before it is shorter. Otherwise the breath scores 0 (no respiratory modulation seen), and that 0 is averaged in. A breath whose overlapping windows make the difference negative also scores 0.
  • Two steps are added to the published method: intervals flagged as ectopic or missed beats (as in ECG / HRV) are left out, and so is a breath that can't be judged (a window with no interval, or a flagged interval just before the shortest or longest).
  • The first visible breathing sweep is paired with the first visible ECG sweep, and so on.
  • RSA changes with breathing rate and depth as well as with vagal tone, and it means little without heart rate (Grossman & Taylor 2007). Report heart rate with RSA, and compare RSA across conditions only alongside the breathing rate and depth.

EEG Band Power

EEG Band Power measures the power in each of the classic EEG bands.

  1. In the inspector's Toolkits category, choose Biosignals › EEG Band Power, and the Channel.
  2. Choose Window: 1, 2 (the default), 4 or 8 s. Longer windows resolve frequency more finely but average fewer segments.
  3. Click Measure Band Powers. The panel shows each band's share of the total from 0.5 to 45 Hz; the Data Log also gives the absolute powers, in the channel's unit squared.
  • The bands are delta (0.5–4 Hz), theta (4–8), alpha (8–13), beta (13–30) and gamma (30–45).
  • Each sweep's power spectral density is computed by Welch's method (Hann windows of the length chosen, rounded to a power of 2 samples, 50% overlap, each segment's mean removed), as Spectrum does. It is integrated over each band from edge to edge, the density interpolated at the edges.
  • A window longer than a sweep is shortened to fit it, and the Data Log gives the window used.
  • Remove artifacts (with Review sweeps, or by cutting the recording into episodes) before measuring.

EMG Envelope

EMG Envelope makes the envelope of an EMG recording and finds the bursts of activity that rise above a quiet baseline.

  1. In the inspector's Toolkits category, choose Biosignals › EMG Envelope, and the Channel.
  2. Leave "Band-pass 20–450 Hz first" checked, or uncheck it to skip the band-pass.
  3. Choose Envelope: Moving RMS with its RMS window (50 ms by default), or Linear envelope (low-pass) with its Low-pass cutoff (6 Hz by default).
  4. Under Bursts, set the Baseline (the first 0.5 s by default), the Threshold (baseline mean + SD × 3 by default) and the Shortest burst and gap (50 ms by default).
  5. Click Make Envelope and Find Bursts. The Data Log lists each burst's onset, offset, duration, peak and mean.
  6. Click Open Envelopes to see the envelopes in a new graph window on the sweeps' own time axis, where Measure and Peaks work on them.
  • Each sweep is band-passed (zero-phase, kept below the Nyquist frequency), rectified, and smoothed by a moving RMS over the window or by a zero-phase low-pass at the cutoff.
  • A burst is where the envelope stays above the mean + k SD of the quiet baseline at the start of the sweep for at least the shortest duration; gaps shorter than that are joined.
  • A cutoff at or above the Nyquist frequency is refused, with a note in the panel.

Back to Contents

Spectroscopy

Spectra on a Graph

Part of the Spectroscopy toolkit.

Four tabs in the inspector's Toolkits category, under Spectroscopy, work on spectra opened as X-Y graphs (Raman, infrared, UV–visible, fluorescence and others): Spectral Baseline, Peak Fitting, Spectral Axis and Wavelength Calibration. They use the visible sweeps (hidden groups and sweeps outside Review sweeps are left out) and open their results in new windows. The toolkit's other two tabs are on the Mass Spectrometry page; reading a spectrum from a picture is on Spectrum from Image.

Spectral Baseline

Spectral Baseline removes a slowly varying background (fluorescence, scattering, drift) from under the peaks of each visible spectrum.

  1. In the inspector's Toolkits category, choose Spectroscopy › Spectral Baseline.
  2. Choose the Method: arPLS (automatic), the default, or Asymmetric least squares (AsLS).
  3. Set Peaks point to Up (the default), or to Down (dips) for spectra whose bands are dips, such as transmittance.
  4. Set Smoothness λ (10^5 by default). For AsLS, also type Asymmetry p (0.01 by default).
  5. Click Open Corrected Spectra. The corrected spectra open in a new window, each with its baseline beside it while "Show the baselines too" is checked (the default).
  • The baseline is a Whittaker smoother, a smooth curve that follows the background but not the peaks. The points are taken as evenly spaced.
  • arPLS (Baek et al. 2015) sets its weights from the noise below the baseline, so it needs only λ. AsLS (Eilers & Boelens 2005) weights points above the baseline by p (between 0 and 1; typically 0.001–0.05) and those below by 1 − p.
  • A larger λ gives a stiffer baseline that stays under broad peaks; 10^4 to 10^7 suits most spectra of a few hundred to a few thousand points. If the baseline rises under the peaks, raise λ.

Peak Fitting

Peak Fitting finds the peaks in the first visible sweep and fits them together, so overlapping peaks each get a center, a width and an area.

  1. In the inspector's Toolkits category, choose Spectroscopy › Peak Fitting. To fit part of the spectrum, show the cursors and place them around it.
  2. Choose the Peak shape: Gaussian, Lorentzian or Pseudo-Voigt (the default).
  3. Leave "Fit a straight baseline under the peaks" checked (the default) unless the baseline is already removed.
  4. Set "Find peaks above (% of range)" (5 by default) and the most peaks to fit (6 by default; 1 to 12).
  5. Click Find and Fit Peaks. The tab lists each peak's center, FWHM and area with confidence intervals, and R². Every parameter with its SE and CI goes to the Data Log.
  6. Click Open Fit as Graph to see the data, the total fit, the baseline and each peak in a new window.
ReportedHow it is computed
Height, Center, FWHMEach peak's height A, position c and full width at half maximum w. Gaussian: A·exp(−4 ln 2 (x − c)²/w²). Lorentzian: A/(1 + 4(x − c)²/w²). Pseudo-Voigt: A·(η·Lorentzian + (1 − η)·Gaussian), the two with the same width.
η (Lorentzian fraction)Pseudo-Voigt only: fitted for each peak and kept within 0–1. A peak whose η reaches 0 or 1 is refitted as a pure Gaussian or Lorentzian, and the tab says so.
AreaGaussian: height × FWHM × √(π/(4 ln 2)). Lorentzian: height × FWHM × π/2. Pseudo-Voigt: the two weighted by η and 1 − η. Its SE is by the delta method.
SE and CIFrom the fit's residual variance, at the confidence level in Settings › Statistics. They show "—" when the fit did not converge.
  • A peak is found by its prominence, how far it stands above the lowest point between it and higher ground (as SciPy's find_peaks measures it). It must stand out by the percentage of the range you set and by more than the noise alone is likely to reach.
  • That noise floor is 2σ√(2 ln n), twice Donoho and Johnstone's universal threshold for n points, with the noise SD σ estimated from the spectrum's second differences (1.4826 × their median absolute deviation, ÷ √6). It applies from 22 points.
  • Each peak's height, position and width at half its prominence start the fit, which is by Levenberg–Marquardt on all peaks and the baseline together.
  • If the fit doesn't converge, narrow the range, change the number of peaks, or try another shape.
  • Batch Processing and Protocols run Peak Fitting on every sweep (see Batch Processing and Protocols).

Spectral Axis

Spectral Axis converts the X axis of the visible spectra between wavelength, wavenumber, photon energy, frequency and Raman shift, in a new window.

  1. In the inspector's Toolkits category, choose Spectroscopy › Spectral Axis.
  2. Check "X is in", which the tab guesses from the X axis, and choose Convert to: Wavelength (nm), Wavelength (Å), Wavelength (µm), the same in air, Wavenumber (cm⁻¹), Energy (eV), Frequency (THz) or Raman shift (cm⁻¹).
  3. For a Raman shift, in either direction, type the Laser wavelength (nm) (785 by default). When either axis is a wavelength in air, type the laser's wavelength in air too.
  4. For spectra measured per unit of X (emission, fluorescence, photoluminescence), check "Scale intensities as a density (Jacobian)".
  5. Click Open Converted Spectra.
  • The guess is a Raman shift when the axis is named for Raman and its unit is cm⁻¹: a Raman shift is measured from the laser line and is not an absolute wavenumber.
  • The guess is a wavelength in air when the axis is named "Wavelength (air)", as Wavelength Calibration, Spectrum from Image and spectral cubes name it. Air wavelengths are taken to vacuum before they become wavenumbers, energies, frequencies or Raman shifts, with the IAU standard air index (Morton 2000). A wavelength in air converted to another wavelength unit stays in air unless you choose a vacuum wavelength.
  • When the X axis's unit is none of nm, Å, µm, cm⁻¹, eV or THz (pixels, for example), the tab says so and waits for you to choose what X is in.
  • Intensities are kept as measured unless the Jacobian is checked. Then each intensity is multiplied by |d(old X)/d(new X)|, so a band keeps its area and its peak moves as the new axis says (Mooney & Kambhampati 2013).
  • Points with no converted value (at 0 or below, or past the laser line) are left out.

Wavelength Calibration

A spectrograph records a spectrum along its detector's pixels. An arc lamp's spectrum taken with the same setup gives each pixel its wavelength. Wavelength Calibration finds the arc's lines, matches them to the lamp's known lines, fits the wavelength scale and applies it to the other spectra.

  1. Open the arc and the spectra to calibrate in one graph window, with X their pixel positions (0, 1, 2 …), and choose Spectroscopy › Wavelength Calibration in the inspector's Toolkits category.
  2. Choose the Arc (the sweep that holds it) and the Lamp: helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon, mercury, cadmium, zinc, or a mixture (HgAr, NeAr, HeNeAr, HgCd, ThAr).
  3. Choose Wavelengths: In air (the default; most optical spectrographs above 200 nm) or In vacuum (SDSS, PypeIt and space spectra).
  4. Choose Identify and click Find & Identify Lines. Automatic (the default) suits lamps with few lines (mercury, neon, HgAr) over a moderate range. With a Hint takes the Central wavelength (nm) at the middle of the arc and the Dispersion (nm/pixel; negative when the wavelength falls along X), and is needed for dense lamps such as ThAr. From a Saved Solution moves an earlier arc's solution (Load Solution…) onto this arc, for a series of arcs on one setup: Load Solution… sets the Lamp and Wavelengths to the solution's, and with the other medium chosen its wavelengths are converted.
  5. Check the lines in the table: each line's pixel, wavelength, residual and ion. Untick a line to leave it out.
  6. Choose the Fit (Chebyshev by default, Polynomial or Legendre), its Order (3 by default; 1 to 7) and the Rejection (3 rounds at 3 × RMS by default; 0 to 5 rounds). The tab gives the lines used, the RMS (in nm and in pixels), the dispersion and the range, and plots the residuals against pixel, with rejected lines hollow.
  7. Choose the Unit (nm, Å or µm) and click Apply to Spectra. The spectra open in a new window with wavelength as X. Check "Include the arc" to open the arc too.
  8. To use the solution again, click Save Solution…, which writes it with the arc its lines were found on as a .json file: for From a Saved Solution, Batch Processing › Spectra › Apply Wavelength Solution and a Protocol's Calibrate Wavelengths… step. Choosing another Arc or Lamp clears the lines found.
  • Switching In air / In vacuum after identifying converts the lines' wavelengths. Choosing another lamp clears them.
  • "Resample onto an even grid" (off by default) puts each calibrated spectrum on evenly spaced wavelengths, the arc's dispersion at its middle pixel apart. Each new bin's flux is divided among the old bins it overlaps (Carnall 2017, SpectRes), so the flux over any stretch is unchanged.
  • The Data Log records the lines, their residuals and the fit.

How wavelength calibration works

  • The lamps' lines are from the NIST Atomic Spectra Database (Kramida, Ralchenko, Reader & NIST ASD Team): each element's lines from 300 to 1100 nm with at least 1% of the strongest line's intensity. Except in thorium's lists, components within 0.1 nm of each other, which no arc spectrograph resolves, are one line at their intensity-weighted wavelength. Air wavelengths come from vacuum ones by the refractive index NIST uses (Peck & Reeder 1972).
  • The arc's lines are found by their prominence above the noise and centered by a Gaussian on a straight baseline, as Peak Fitting fits peaks.
  • Automatic and With a Hint each try two starts and keep the one that explains the arc's lines better: pairs of the arc's most prominent lines against pairs of the lamp's strongest, each giving a trial scale; and groups of four neighboring lines matched to the list by the ratios of their spacings. From a Saved Solution shifts the earlier scale by cross-correlating the two arcs.
  • The start is then grown to the whole arc: the matched lines are fitted, the stretch they cover is widened by 5% each side, and lines there are matched to the list within 3 × the fit's RMS (at least a pixel), until the matches stop changing.
  • The fit is least squares in the pixel position scaled to −1…1 over the arc, with the functions and rejection of IRAF's identify: lines farther than the limit × the RMS from the fit are left out and the fit is repeated. An order above 1 needs at least order + 2 lines. The residual is the line's wavelength minus the fitted one, and the RMS is √(Σr²/n) of the lines used.

Spectrum from Image

Part of the Spectroscopy toolkit.

Spectrum from Image reads a spectrum from a picture of one: a spectrometer camera's frame, a photo from a phone or DIY spectroscope, or a long-slit spectrum (FITS). It reads the intensity along a trace laid on the spectrum, gives it a wavelength scale from known lines, and opens it as an X-Y graph for the tabs of Spectra on a Graph. With a multichannel image whose channels are wavelength bands, it can instead read each channel's mean in an ROI (see Channels in an ROI, below).

Read a Spectrum Along a Trace

  1. Open the picture. Use the camera's raw or least processed image when you can (a 16-bit TIFF or FITS frame). Keep the spectrum unsaturated: clipped lines can't be centered or measured.
  2. In the image inspector's Toolkits tab, choose Spectroscopy › Spectrum from Image from the menu at the top of the tab.
  3. Click Find Trace (check Curved first for a band that bends). Or draw a line along the spectrum with the Line tool (ROIs tab) and choose it under Use Line ROI; its width becomes the trace's.
  4. Check the trace drawn on the image: its center and edges, the background strips beside it (shaded) and a dot at its start. Type Start, End or Width to adjust it, and click Reverse to run it the other way.
  5. Check the profile in the panel: the spectrum along the trace from its start (left), with its background dashed. Open Reading to change how the channels, the width and the background are read.
  6. Under Wavelength scale, choose the lamp or source under Known lines and click Identify Lines. Or click each line on the profile to mark it, and choose its wavelength from the line's menu (or Type…).
  7. Check each line's residual in the table, then choose the Fit.
  8. Click Open Spectrum Graph. The spectrum opens as an X-Y graph against wavelength in air (nm), or against position along the trace (px) when there is no scale, at Peak Fitting. The Data Log gets how it was read, the wavelength scale and each line's residual.
  • Edits undo with ⌘Z. The trace, settings and lines are saved with the image (.@graph).
  • Typing a trace end keeps the marked lines at their places on the image. A trace turned by more than 2° clears them, and the panel says so.

The trace

  • The spectrum is read at 1-pixel steps along the trace, from its start. At each step, the pixels across the trace's width, 1 pixel apart, are averaged or summed, each read by bilinear interpolation between the four pixels around it.
  • Find Trace takes the direction in which the image (its channels summed), projected across it, shows the brightest line; it tries every degree, then every tenth of a degree near the best. The trace ends where the band stands 5 noise SDs and 0.5% of its peak above the background beside it, with a margin. Its width is twice the band's full width at half maximum (at least 3 pixels). Its center follows the band's intensity-weighted centroids: a straight line or, with Curved, a quadratic.
  • Straighten makes a curved trace straight again, as does typing an end.

Reading

SettingWhat it does
ChannelsFor a color picture: Luminance (Rec. 709), the default, combines red, green and blue as 0.2126 R + 0.7152 G + 0.0722 B (ITU-R BT.709); Sum of channels adds them; Each channel gives a spectrum per channel; or choose one channel. With Each channel, lines are found on the luminance (or the sum).
Undo sRGB gammaOn by default for an 8-bit color picture, off otherwise. A photo's values are encoded with sRGB's gamma (IEC 61966-2-1) and aren't proportional to the light. Each pixel is decoded first (V/12.92 up to 0.04045 of full scale, ((V + 0.055)/1.055)^2.4 above). Turn it off for a camera's raw frames.
AcrossMean (the default), which the trace's width doesn't change, or Sum, the light in the trace, as long-slit spectroscopy extracts it.
BackgroundBoth sides (the default), one side only, or None. Strips parallel to the trace, Gap pixels beyond its edges (2 by default) and Strips pixels wide (5 by default), are read the same way, and their Median (the default) or Mean at each step is subtracted: dark current, sky or stray light. Strips on both sides remove a background that changes linearly across the trace exactly. A star, a cosmic ray or a hot pixel in a strip barely moves the median.

The plane shown is the one read: the Z slice, or the Z projection while it is shown, at the time point shown.

Wavelength scale

  • Each marked line is centered by least squares: a Gaussian on a straight baseline over 1.5 half-widths either side of the peak, as Peak Fitting fits. Check Dark lines when the lines are dips (absorption). Find Lines shows the profile's lines as ticks above it; click near one to mark it.
  • Fit: the scale is the least-squares polynomial of wavelength in the position along the trace (pixels from its start). A Straight line (the default) needs 2 lines, a Quadratic 4 and a Cubic 5, so a fit beyond a straight line always has residuals that show how well it fits.
  • The table gives each line's residual (its wavelength minus the fitted one). Below it are the polynomial, the RMS residual √(Σr²/n) and the dispersion (nm per pixel) at the trace's middle. A scale that turns back along the trace, giving one wavelength twice, is refused.
  • Identify Lines matches the list's strongest lines to the profile's 15 most prominent lines. Every pair of the profile's lines against every pair of the list's gives a straight scale. A listed line landing within 0.6% of the trace's length (at least 2.5 pixels) of a profile line is a match, and each match counts 1 − (miss / tolerance)², weighted by the square root of its line's prominence (MSAC scoring; Torr & Zisserman 2000). The best scale is refitted to its matches, as a quadratic once four match. It needs 3 matches. Check them: a faint line may be missing, and the residuals show a wrong match.
Known linesLines (air wavelengths, nm)
Fluorescent lamp (Hg, Tb, Eu)The default. Mercury's 404.66, 435.83, 546.07, 576.96 and 579.07, and the phosphors' band peaks (approximate): terbium's 487.7 and 542.4, europium's 587.6, 611.6 and 631.1. At a spectroscope's resolution mercury's 546.07 nm line may merge with terbium's 542.4 nm band, which pulls its center a little toward shorter wavelengths.
Mercury (Hg), Neon (Ne), Argon (Ar)The lamps' strong lines.
Hydrogen (Balmer)Hα 656.28 to Hε 397.01.
Sun (Fraunhofer, dark)Dark lines: A and B of oxygen, C (Hα), the sodium D lines, E, b₁, F (Hβ), G, H and K.
Lamps marked NISTThe arc lamps of Wavelength Calibration (helium to ThAr), from 350 to 1000 nm. For their fuller fits, open the spectrum as a graph and use Wavelength Calibration (see Spectra on a Graph).
Typed onlyNo list: type each line's wavelength in air, as the lists give them.

Atomic lines are from the NIST Atomic Spectra Database.

Response correction

A spectrometer or camera is more sensitive at some wavelengths than others. To correct for it, use a picture of a source whose spectrum is known, taken with the same setup and of the same size.

  1. Open the reference picture. In the spectrum's image, under Response correction, choose it under Divide by.
  2. Choose Its spectrum: Flat (the default), or Blackbody with its color temperature (2856 K by default, CIE illuminant A) for a tungsten-halogen lamp.

The reference's spectrum along the same trace, read the same way and divided by its known spectrum (Planck's law for a blackbody), is the response, scaled to 1 at its largest. The spectrum is divided by it, and left out where the response is below 1% of its largest. A blackbody needs the wavelength scale first.

Channels in an ROI

For an image whose channels are wavelength bands: under Trace, set Read to Channels in an ROI, draw an ROI (a small rectangle for one place) and click Open Spectrum Graph. Each channel's mean in the ROI is one point. X is each channel's wavelength when every channel's name gives it ("532 nm", "Band 12 (532.1 nm)"); otherwise it is the channel's number.

Mass Spectrometry

Part of the Spectroscopy toolkit.

Two tabs in the inspector's Toolkits category, under Spectroscopy, work on mass spectra. Ion Chromatograms makes chromatograms from an LC-MS run. Isotope Pattern calculates a molecule's masses and isotope pattern, compares it with a spectrum, and centroids profile spectra; it works on any spectrum with m/z on X, from mzML, CSV or another file.

To open a run, choose File › Open File… and its .mzML file (convert vendor files and mzXML with ProteoWizard's msconvert first). Its chromatograms open in one Graph window and its spectra in a window for each MS level, each spectrum a sweep of intensity against m/z.

Ion Chromatograms

  1. In any window of the run, choose Spectroscopy › Ion Chromatograms in the inspector's Toolkits category.
  2. Choose Spectra: MS1 (the default), MS2, MS3 or Every level.
  3. Check Total ion current (TIC) (on by default) and Base peak as you need them.
  4. For extracted-ion chromatograms, type the XIC m/z values, separated by spaces, commas or semicolons, and the Tolerance ± in ppm (10 by default) or Da.
  5. Choose Within the window: Sum the intensities (the default) or Largest intensity.
  6. Click Open Chromatograms. The chromatograms open in a new window against retention time, and a table goes to the Data Log.
ReportedHow it is computed
TICEach spectrum's intensities summed.
Base peakEach spectrum's largest intensity.
XIC (also called EIC)For each m/z typed: the intensities of the points within ± the tolerance of it, summed or their largest; 0 where there are none.
XEach spectrum's scan start time, in minutes. When some spectra have no time, the spectrum's number.
Data Log tableFor each trace: its m/z window, the time and intensity of its apex, and the FWHM, the width of the apex's peak at half its height. For the TIC and the base peak, also the base peak's m/z at the apex.
  • The chromatograms are computed from the spectra's data, in the order of the file, not taken from the chromatograms the instrument wrote.
  • A tolerance of 5–10 ppm suits high-resolution instruments (Orbitrap, TOF). Use Da for low-resolution ones (0.5 Da for a unit-resolution ion trap or quadrupole).
  • To measure a peak's area, use the Measure tab on the new window.
  • A spectrum with no points counts as 0 on every trace, in its place in the run.
  • A run larger than the memory budget is read up to the first spectra that fit. The tab and the Data Log say how many.

Isotope Pattern

  1. In the inspector's Toolkits category, choose Spectroscopy › Isotope Pattern.
  2. Under Molecule, choose Formula and type it (C6H12O6), or Peptide and type its sequence in one-letter codes.
  3. To add a modification or label, type its formula under Plus (formula), such as C2H3NO for each carbamidomethylated cysteine or O for an oxidation. A negative count takes atoms away (H-2).
  4. Choose the Ion and, where a stepper shows below it, its charge.
  5. Set the Total probability (0.999 by default) and the Resolving power (m/Δm) (60000 by default; at most 10⁸).
  6. Click Calculate Pattern. The tab shows the formula, the masses and the unit-mass pattern, and every form of the pattern goes to the Data Log.
  7. Click Open as Graph to open the pattern at the resolving power as a profile, with the fine structure and the unit-mass pattern as sticks, each in % of its largest peak.
  • Formula, written as pyteomics writes it (Goloborodko et al. 2013): each element's symbol and count, in any order. A mass number in brackets labels an isotope (C[13]6H12O6 for glucose with every carbon ¹³C, H[2] for deuterium). Parentheses with a count are expanded (Ca(OH)2).
  • Peptide: the 20 amino acids, U for selenocysteine and O for pyrrolysine. The molecule is the residues plus H₂O.
  • Ion: the neutral molecule M; [M+H]⁺ or [M−H]⁻; an adduct ([M+Na]⁺, [M+K]⁺, [M+NH₄]⁺, [M+Cl]⁻, [M+HCOO]⁻); or a radical ion that has lost or gained an electron (M⁺•, M⁻•). The stepper multiplies the protons or adducts, as in [M+2H]²⁺.
ReportedHow it is computed
Monoisotopic massThe mass with each element's most abundant isotope (¹²C, ¹H, ¹⁴N, ¹⁶O, ³²S…).
Average massThe mass with each element's isotopes weighted by their natural abundances.
m/zProtonated ions: (M + z × the proton's mass, 1.00727646677 u)/z; deprotonated ions: M less z protons, over z. Other ions: the mass of M plus its adducts, less z electrons (0.00054857990943 u each; plus them for a negative charge), divided by |z|.
Fine structureEvery isotopologue (each way the molecule's atoms can be spread over their isotopes, such as ¹³C₁ or ¹⁵N₁ at M+1), with its exact mass and its probability (multinomial, from the natural abundances). The most probable are taken, in order, until their probabilities add up to the Total probability: the smallest set that reaches it (IsoSpec's method; Łącki et al. 2017).
Unit massThe isotopologues summed by nucleon number (M, M+1, M+2…), each at their probability-weighted mean m/z, as a low-resolution instrument sees the pattern.
At the resolving powerEach isotopologue drawn as a Gaussian peak of width m/R at half its height (R the resolving power, taken as the same across the pattern), the peaks summed and the profile centroided (see Centroid Spectra, below).
  • Masses and abundances are those of pyteomics' table: NIST's Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions (relative atomic masses from the 2003 Atomic Mass Evaluation, IUPAC's representative isotopic compositions).
  • At low resolving powers the fine structure merges into one peak per nominal mass. It separates where its peaks lie more than about m/R apart.

Compare with This Spectrum

This part of the tab compares the pattern with the first visible sweep, whose X is m/z.

  1. Choose the Pattern to compare: At the resolving power (the default; set the resolving power to the instrument's), Fine structure (for very high resolving powers) or Unit mass (for low-resolution spectra, with a tolerance in Da).
  2. Leave "The spectrum is" on Automatic, which takes mzML centroid spectra (drawn as sticks) as they are and centroids anything else; or choose Profile (centroid it) or Centroided (peak list).
  3. Type the Tolerance ± in ppm (10 by default) or Da, and "Theoretical peaks from (% of largest)" (1 by default).
  4. Click Compare with Spectrum. The tab and the Data Log list each peak, and Open Comparison as Graph shows the spectrum above and the pattern mirrored below (a head-to-tail plot).
ReportedHow it is computed
Theoretical and observed m/zEach theoretical peak of at least the percentage you set of the most intense is matched to the most intense observed peak within ± the tolerance of its m/z.
Observed %The observed intensity as a % of the peak matched to the pattern's most intense one (of the largest matched peak when that one has no match).
Error (ppm) and Error (mDa)The mass accuracy: (observed − theoretical m/z) / theoretical × 10⁶ in ppm, and observed − theoretical in mDa.
Normalized dot productThe cosine similarity of the theoretical and observed relative intensities over the pattern's peaks (Stein & Scott 1994), an unmatched peak counting as 0: 1 for a pattern matched exactly, lower as the intensities differ or peaks are missing. Observed peaks away from the pattern don't count.
Spectral contrast anglearccos of the normalized dot product, in degrees.
Mean m/z errorThe matched peaks' errors in ppm, weighted by the theoretical intensities.

Graph windows keep m/z to about 0.06 ppm, well within any tolerance.

Centroid Spectra

To turn each visible profile spectrum into its peaks, type "Ignore peaks below (% of each spectrum's largest)" (0 by default) to leave out noise, and click Open Centroided Spectra. The peaks open as sticks in a new window. Each peak is a local maximum (no lower than the point before it and higher than the point after), placed at the intensity-weighted mean m/z of the points around it down to half its height (stopping where the intensity rises again), with the maximum's intensity. Spectra already centroided (drawn as sticks) are left out.

Flow Cytometry

The Cytometry Window

Part of the Flow Cytometry toolkit.

FCS files (2.0 to 3.2, and Beckman Coulter's .lmd) open in a Cytometry window: every event of every file, compensated, on cytometry's axes, gated through a hierarchy, with each population's statistics. With the toolkit hidden (Settings › Toolkits), or with Open as Table, FCS files open as spreadsheets of events instead (see Flow on X-Y Graphs). Lab Tools has the toolkit's calculators. @Graph is a research tool: it is not validated for diagnostic or clinical use.

Open Samples and Gate Them

  1. Open an FCS file with File › Open File…. Or choose Toolkits › Flow Cytometry › Cytometry Analysis… for an empty window and drop FCS files on it.
  2. To add more samples, click + by Samples and choose Add FCS Files… or Add a Folder of FCS Files….
  3. Click a sample in the Samples list to show its plots. The gates and statistics cover every sample.
  4. Under the Samples list, check the Compensation (From each file by default) and click Axes… to check each channel's scale.
  5. On each plot, choose its population, its plot type and its X and Y channels. Add Plot copies the selected plot.
  6. Choose a gate tool above the plots and draw on a plot. The new gate is a child of the plot's population.
  7. With the Select tool, double-click inside a gate to show its population in a new plot, on the next channels, and gate again.
  8. Read each population's count and percent of parent in the Gates list, and its statistics in the table under the plots.
  • Each data set of a file is a sample, read in full. A Beckman Coulter .lmd file, which holds the same events as FCS 2.0 and as FCS 3.0, gives one sample, its FCS 3.0 data set.
  • The files are referred to, never copied or changed. Locate… reconnects a file that moved.
  • Sample columns: the button by Samples opens your own columns for the samples (Group, Condition, Donor…), typed or taken From a Keyword (TUBE NAME, $DATE…). They head the statistics table and say which group each sample is in.
  • The analyses below are in the panel on the right: click the Analyses button at the right of the toolbar, and choose one from the Analysis menu at the panel's top. Each runs in the background, one at a time, with a Stop button; stopping changes nothing.

FlowJo Workspaces

  1. Open a FlowJo 10 workspace (.wsp) with File › Open File…, or choose Toolkits › Flow Cytometry › Open FlowJo Workspace….
  2. Allow access to the workspace's folder when asked (once), so its FCS files can be found.
  3. Check the Data Log, which compares each population's count with the count FlowJo saved.
From the workspaceHow it is read
SamplesEach sample's FCS file is looked for where the workspace says, in the workspace's folder and in the folders inside it.
Renamed FCS filesA renamed file (as archives such as FlowRepository rename them) is still found when exactly one FCS file there agrees with what the workspace recorded of the sample: its original name ($FIL) and event count ($TOT), and its date and start time ($DATE, $BTIM) where the workspace has them. The sample's note says so. When two files agree, neither is used and the import's warning names them; reconnect the sample with Locate….
Compensation and transformsEach sample's matrix, and each channel's transform, FlowJo's biex and log included.
Gating treeFlowJo stores gates in data values; they are placed on each sample's own transforms. Ellipses become 128-point polygons. Populations of events outside a gate are kept as such. Gates that differ for one sample become that sample's adjustments.

The workspace is read as FlowKit reads it. FlowJo's biex is a lookup table, so events on a gate's edge can differ slightly from FlowJo's counts. Workspaces from FlowJo 9 or earlier aren't read.

Compensation

CompensationWhat the plots, new gates and statistics use
None (as recorded)The values as recorded.
From each fileThe default. Each file's own $SPILLOVER, SPILL or $DFCnTOm matrix S, applied as compensated = raw · S⁻¹.
A matrix of the analysisOne you edited, computed from controls, or read from a workspace or a Gating-ML file.

The raw values are never changed. Each gate keeps the compensation it was drawn with, and a plot draws a gate only while it shows that compensation's values for the gate's channels (scatter gates always); it names the gates it leaves out.

Edit and check a matrix

  1. In the analyses panel, choose Compensation. It lists the analysis's spillover matrices.
  2. Click Edit a Copy to copy the shown file's own matrix into the analysis, or Edit beside a matrix. The coefficients show as percentages.
  3. From the matrix's menu, choose Add N × N Check Plots to plot every pair of its detectors: well-compensated single-stained events lie flat. The menu also has Use for Plots and New Gates, and Delete Matrix (not while a gate was drawn with it).

Compute a matrix from single-stain controls

  1. Add the controls' FCS files as samples.
  2. In the analyses panel, choose Compensation and, under From single-stain controls, choose the Method.
  3. Under Events, choose the population whose events to use (usually a scatter gate on the cells).
  4. Choose the Unstained control (AutoSpill needs none) and, for each detector, its control. Guess from Names matches them by name.
  5. Click Compute. The plots then use the new matrix; check it on its N × N plots.
MethodHow it is computed
Classical (medians)Each control's median above the unstained control's in each detector, over its own detector's (as flowStats computes it).
AutoSpillFits each detector against the control's own by robust regression and refines the matrix until the compensated controls lie flat (Roca et al. 2021). It uses the events you chose, not its own automatic scatter gate.
Spectral, least squaresBuilds reference spectra: each control's median above the unstained one's, scaled to its brightest detector, and, with "Autofluorescence as an endmember" (on by default), the unstained control's spectrum. Least squares unmixes through that matrix, whose rows (each dye, and Autofluorescence) become channels of their own.
Spectral, weighted least squaresThe same spectra, each detector weighted by 1 over its signal plus its background variance (Novo et al. 2013). It unmixes every event into new channels named "… (WLS)".

Axes and Plots

Axes… sets each channel's scale on every plot and for new gates: Linear, Log, Logicle, Arcsinh or Hyperlog. Suggested puts a channel's default back.

  • Defaults: scatter and Time are linear; fluorescence is on Logicle with T the top of the channel's values, W 0.5, M 4.5 and A 0; mass cytometry is on arcsinh with cofactor 5. Flow on X-Y Graphs › Logicle / Arcsinh Axes explains the parameters.
  • The top of a channel's values is $PnR made linear as the values are: 10⁴ for a channel log-amplified over 4 decades (FCS 2.0), $PnR / $PnG with a gain, and $PnR × $TIMESTEP for Time, in seconds.
  • Logicle, arcsinh (with a cofactor, or Gating-ML's T, M and A), hyperlog (Bagwell 2005), log and linear are Gating-ML 2.0's transforms, computed as it defines them.
  • Gates already drawn keep the scale they were drawn on. Transformed axes are numbered in data values: 0 and ±10^k, with minor ticks at 2–9 × 10^k.

Each plot shows one population (All Events or a gate's) on two channels, or one channel as a histogram. It is drawn from every event of its population, never a subsample; events beyond an axis are piled on its edge.

Plot typeWhat it draws
PseudocolorThe events per bin, colored from blue (few) to red (many) on a log scale.
Dot, DensityEvery event as a dot, or the events smoothed.
Contour, ZebraEqual-probability contours on a 256 × 256 grid. Each encloses a further 5% of the events (or 2, 10 or 20%, from the menu beside the plot type), with the events outside the outermost as dots. Zebra shades the bands between contours.
HistogramOne channel's events counted in 256 bins across its axis, so its counts are the same on any screen and in an exported figure. Check Smooth to smooth it.

Gates

The gate tools above the plots are Select, Rectangle, Polygon, Ellipse, Quadrant and Interval. The hint beside them says how the chosen tool draws.

  • Quadrant makes four gates where you click, Q1 (upper left) to Q4 (lower left), named for the channels' stains. Interval, on a two-channel plot, makes a band across the x axis, open above and below.
  • With Select, click a gate to select it, drag inside it to move it, and drag its handles to reshape it. A gate can be moved only on a plot with the scales it was drawn on.
  • A gate's events are those inside it that are also in its parent.
  • A gate's context menu in the Gates list has Rename…, Show in a New Plot, Backgate on All Plots and Delete Gate, which deletes everything below it too.
  • Boolean gates: the button by Gates makes Not (the selected gate), or the selected gate And or Or another. Each operand is a whole population (with its parents), as Gating-ML defines them.
  • One template for every sample: gates apply to all samples. Hold ⌥ while moving or reshaping a gate to change it for the shown sample only. The gate is marked as adjusted, and Use the Template's Gate for This Sample, in its context menu, puts the template's gate back.
  • To apply the same gating to new files, choose Add Gates from Another Analysis… from the button by Gates: it adds the gates, matrices and axes of another saved analysis. Add Gates from Gating-ML… adds a Gating-ML file's gates.
  • Backgating: Backgate on All Plots colors a population's events on every plot, to see where it lies on its ancestors' plots. Stop Backgating takes it off.

Which events a gate holds

Membership is as Gating-ML 2.0 defines it. A rectangle or interval holds min ≤ x < max (either end may be open). A polygon holds the points its edges wind around an odd number of times. An ellipse holds (x − μ)ᵀ C⁻¹ (x − μ) ≤ D². A quadrant holds the events between its dividers. Events with no value on a scale (0 or below on a log scale) are in no gate on it.

Population Statistics

The table under the plots has a row for every sample and population, with your sample columns first. Choose the channels to report from the Channels menu.

ColumnHow it is computed
CountThe events in the population.
% of Parent, % of Total100 × count / the parent population's count, and 100 × count / the sample's events.
Median, MeanOf the channel's compensated values, on the data's own scale, not the axis's. Percentiles are interpolated linearly.
Geo. MeanThe geometric mean. It needs every value above 0.
rCVThe robust CV, 100 × robust SD / median, where the robust SD is half the distance between the 15.87th and 84.13th percentiles. For normal data they equal the CV and SD, and outliers barely move them.

These are the statistics FlowJo reports. Open in Sheet opens the table as a spreadsheet for @Graph's statistics; Export › Statistics as CSV… saves it.

Quality Control (PeacoQC)

PeacoQC finds the stretches of an acquisition whose signal or flow rate departs from the rest (Emmaneel et al. 2022).

  1. In the analyses panel, choose Quality.
  2. Leave "Remove margin events first" checked (the default), and check the Channels to test.
  3. Click Run PeacoQC on Every Sample. A PeacoQC channel marks each event kept (1) or removed (0), and the gate PeacoQC Kept holds those kept.
  4. Click Put Gates Under PeacoQC Kept to make your other top gates its children, so the analysis leaves out the removed events.
  • Method: the events are split into bins in acquisition order, and each chosen channel's density peaks are found per bin. Unstable bins are flagged by an isolation tree and by the median absolute deviation (beyond 6 MADs), then short runs of kept bins are removed: the PeacoQC R package's steps and defaults, on the channels' compensated values on their axes.
  • The Data Log has each sample's percentages and PeacoQC's own warnings.

Clusters and Embedding

FlowSOM and PhenoGraph group the events into clusters; UMAP and t-SNE lay them out in two dimensions. All four use the markers you check, as compensated values on their axes, over a population's events from every sample.

  1. In the analyses panel, choose Clusters. Choose the Events (a population) and check at least two Markers.
  2. Set an analysis's settings (see the table below) and click Run FlowSOM or Run PhenoGraph. For an embedding, choose the Method and click Run UMAP or Run t-SNE; its two channels and a pseudocolor plot of them are added.
  3. Under Clusters, choose a set of clusters. Make Cluster Gates turns each cluster into a gate, whose counts go into the statistics. Open Heatmap shows each cluster's median of each marker as a clustered heatmap.
  4. To color a gate's or a cluster's events on the embedding, backgate it.
  5. To try other settings, run the analysis again. Gates made on the earlier run keep its events: its channels stay, named “(earlier run)”, with the plots that showed those gates, and the gate list marks them. Make Cluster Gates then makes the new run's gates.
AnalysisSettings and method
FlowSOMA self-organizing map (Grid 10 × 10 by default; 2 to 30 each way) and consensus metaclusters (10 by default; 2 to 100, and at most 90% of the nodes), trained and clustered by the FlowSOM R package's steps from the Seed (Van Gassen et al. 2015). The channels FlowSOM Node and FlowSOM Metacluster number each event.
PhenoGraphEach event's nearest neighbors (30 by default; 2 to 200), a graph weighted by how many neighbors two events share (Jaccard), and communities found by the Leiden algorithm with the seed (Levine et al. 2015; Traag et al. 2019). Clusters of 10 events or fewer are left unassigned. A PhenoGraph Cluster channel numbers the clusters, the largest first.
UMAPNeighbors (15 by default; 2 to 200) and Minimum distance (0.1 by default; 0 to 1). It follows umap-learn's published method: a fuzzy neighbor graph from exact nearest neighbors, a spectral start and its layout optimization (McInnes, Healy & Melville 2018). Distances between clusters on a UMAP plot aren't meaningful.
t-SNEPerplexity (30 by default; 1 to 100, and at most (events − 1) ÷ 3). t-SNE (van der Maaten & Hinton 2008) with opt-SNE's settings (Belkina et al. 2019): affinities of each event's 3 × perplexity nearest neighbors, a PCA start, Barnes–Hut gradients (θ 0.5), a learning rate of n/12, and early exaggeration (12) ended as soon as the divergence's relative change passes its peak; 750 steps in all.
Events per sampleFor UMAP and t-SNE: 10,000 by default; 1 to 100,000. They are picked at random with the seed, and the others get no place.
  • Markers are fluorescence channels, as recorded or unmixed; never scatter, Time or an analysis's own channels.
  • An event with no value on a chosen marker's axis (at or below 0 on a Log axis, for instance) gets no cluster and no place. The message and the Data Log say how many each sample lost.
  • The seed makes each run repeatable.

Compare Groups of Samples

  1. Give the samples a group column (the button by Samples), and run FlowSOM or PhenoGraph.
  2. In the analyses panel, choose Compare. Choose the Clusters, the Groups column, the group to Test and the group to test it Against.
  3. For samples paired across the groups, choose under Paired by the column that names each sample's donor (or block).
  4. Click Test. Each cluster's log₂ fold change and adjusted p-value are listed; Open in Sheet opens the results for @Graph's charts.
  • Compare tests whether clusters' share of the cells differs between the groups, by diffcyt's edgeR method (Weber et al. 2019): each sample's count of cells in each cluster, a negative binomial model with the sample as the unit (never the cells), empirical-Bayes dispersions, a likelihood-ratio test of the test group against the other, and Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted p-values.
  • Clusters with fewer than 3 cells in half the samples are left out. The test needs more samples than the model's coefficients (each group, and each pair, more than once).

Cell Cycle

The Cell Cycle analysis finds the share of a population in G0/G1, S and G2/M from its DNA content: a histogram of a DNA stain's linear values (PI, DAPI, DRAQ5, Hoechst, FxCycle…), area rather than height, on every sample.

  1. In the analyses panel, choose Cell Cycle. Choose the Events (a population) and the DNA channel.
  2. Gate the singlets first: two G0/G1 nuclei through the beam together have the DNA of one G2/M cell. Choose the DNA channel's Height (or width) and click Suggest Singlets Gate. Check on the plot that the gate keeps the whole G2/M peak (choose 99.9% to widen it), then choose the new Singlets gate under Events.
  3. Choose the Model (Dean–Jett–Fox by default) and its options.
  4. Choose the Bins: 256 (the default) suits most data; 512 or 1024 are for very narrow peaks. To leave out debris below G0/G1 or a high tail, check Range and type From and To in the channel's units; a To of 0 leaves the top open.
  5. Click Fit All Samples. The shown sample's fit is listed and drawn over its histogram, each phase shaded. Open as Sheet opens every sample's fit as a table.
ModelWhat it fits
Watson pragmaticG0/G1 and G2/M are Gaussians, each fitted only to the side of its peak away from S phase (G0/G1 from 3 SDs below its mean to 1 above; G2/M from 1 SD below to 3 above). S is what remains between them (Watson, Chambers & Smith 1987). Its S runs low when many S-phase cells lie under the peaks.
Dean–Jett–FoxG0/G1 and G2/M Gaussians and S phase as a second-order polynomial between their means, each part of it broadened like the peaks, all fitted at once (Dean & Jett 1974; Fox 1980). Synchronous S adds Fox's Gaussian for a cohort of cells moving through S together (synchronized cultures); it is often poorly determined otherwise.
Rectangle, debris and aggregatesG0/G1 a Gaussian, G2/M one at the linearity times its mean with twice its SD, and S a rectangle between them (Bagwell 1993), as flowPloidy fits it. Debris: Single-cut (Bagwell et al. 1991), for fixed or frozen nuclei, Multiple-cut, for fresh material, or None. Aggregates (on by default) models the doublets, triplets and quadruplets the singlets gate let through. "Linearity fixed at 2 (flowPloidy)" holds G2/M's peak at twice G0/G1's. It reports the debris and aggregates as percentages of the events fitted.

Watson and Dean–Jett–Fox model no debris or aggregates. In their place they report Below the fit % and Above the fit %: the events below and above the cycle window (G0/G1 less 3 SDs to G2/M plus 3 SDs), as percentages of the events in the range. When no G2/M peak is found, Above the fit holds the S and G2/M cells the fit left out, so it is not a count of aggregates.

  • Suggest Singlets Gate makes a polygon gate on the DNA channel's height against its area: a robust (Huber) line of height on area and its 99% prediction band, as flowStats' singletGate makes it.
  • Constraints (Watson and Dean–Jett–Fox): CVs equal (on by default) holds G2/M's CV at G0/G1's. When a fit is still unstable, check G2/G1 ratio (about 1.95 to 2; it can be held from 1.5 to 2.5). G0/G1 CV % and G2/M CV % hold a peak's CV at a value (at most 50%); a fixed G2/M CV takes the place of CVs equal.
  • Reported: each phase's fraction of the cycle (debris and aggregates left out) ± its standard error from the fit, the peaks' CVs and the G2/G1 ratio. RMSD is the typical distance between the fit and the histogram. The reduced χ² (Dean–Jett–Fox and the Rectangle) is near 1 for a fit as good as counting noise allows.
  • The DNA channel is fitted on its linear values whatever its axis. A fit needs at least 200 events with DNA content above 0.
  • Where models disagree on the same data, S is uncertain. Fits of a few hundred events, of broad peaks (CVs above about 8%) or with much debris are unreliable whatever the model. The fit is for research use, not for clinical ploidy or S-phase reports.

Counting Beads

The Counts analysis gives absolute counts, cells per µL, from beads of a known number added to each tube (BD Trucount, Invitrogen CountBright and similar).

  1. Draw a gate on the beads. They sit apart on scatter and in every fluorescence channel.
  2. In the analyses panel, choose Counts, and choose the Bead gate.
  3. Under Beads, choose Beads per tube and type the number (Trucount: the pouch's lot-specific number). Or choose Beads per µL and type the lot's concentration and the µL of beads added (CountBright).
  4. Type the µL of sample and the Dilution before staining (2 for 1:2; 1 for none). To give each tube its own value, choose a sample column (From …) beside a field.
  5. Click Show Cells per µL. Every population of every sample gets Cells per µL and its 95% interval in the statistics table.
  • Cells per µL = (the population's events ÷ the bead events) × (beads in the tube ÷ µL of sample) × dilution.
  • The 95% interval is exact: the cell and bead events are independent counts, so it comes from the binomial split of the two (Clopper–Pearson). The relative error is √(1/cells + 1/beads).
  • The panel lists each sample's bead events and warns below 1,000, the manufacturers' minimum.
  • The Lab Tools calculator (Absolute Count) does the same arithmetic for one tube typed in.

Thresholds from FMO Controls

A fluorescence-minus-one (FMO) control is stained with every antibody of the panel but one. Its events in that marker's channel show how far the other dyes' spread reaches there, which is where positive staining has to begin (Roederer 2001; Maecker & Trotter 2006). The FMO analysis makes that boundary a gate.

  1. In the analyses panel, choose FMO, and choose the FMO tube. A tube named for its missing marker picks the Channel; check it.
  2. Choose the Parent population, gated the same way in every tube.
  3. Choose the Percentile (99.5 by default; 99 or 99.9, or type one).
  4. To gate each group of samples at its own group's FMO, choose a sample column (Day, Batch…) under Pair by. One FMO for all is the default.
  5. Click Make Gate from FMO. An interval gate "marker+", from the FMO's percentile up, is added under the parent for every sample.
  • The threshold is the percentile of the FMO's events in the parent, interpolated as R's quantile computes it (openCyto's gate_quantile).
  • With Pair by, a group uses its tube with the same name, or its only FMO tube for that marker; a group with neither uses the chosen FMO. The other groups' samples carry their thresholds as adjustments to the gate.
  • After the compensation or the parent gate changes, click Update to make the gate again from its FMO; it never changes on its own.
  • Isotype controls are not recommended for setting gates: their dye-to-protein ratio, concentration and nonspecific binding differ from the panel's antibody, so they misplace the threshold (Keeney et al. 1998; Hulspas et al. 2009; Cossarizza et al. 2021).

Export and Files

CommandWhat it writes
Export › Selected Population as FCS…The selected gate's events (or all events) of the shown sample as an FCS 3.1 file, compensated or as recorded. It keeps the source file's keywords and adds @GRAPHSOURCE and @GRAPHPOPULATION. A compensated file leaves out $SPILLOVER, so other software doesn't compensate it again, and keeps the matrix used in @GRAPHAPPLIEDSPILLOVER. With an unmixing matrix (Spectral, least squares), the file keeps the detectors as recorded and their $SPILLOVER, and adds each unmixed row as a channel (@GRAPHUNMIXEDBY names the matrix).
Export › Gates as Gating-ML 2.0…The gating hierarchy with its transforms and matrices, for FlowJo, FlowKit, flowCore and other software that reads Gating-ML. Gating-ML has no FlowJo biex, so an ellipse on FlowJo's biex axes is written as a 256-sided polygon. A polygon or ellipse on a FlowJo log axis can't hold events at or below the axis's offset in Gating-ML; the message names any such gate.
Export › Open MIFlowCyt ReportA report of the minimum information about a flow cytometry experiment (Lee et al. 2008), in a text window. Its four sections (experiment overview, samples, instrument, data analysis) are filled from the FCS files' keywords and from the analysis, with what the files can't say marked [to fill in].
Export › Plots as PNG…, Plots as PDF…, Copy PlotsThe shown sample's plots as a figure.
File › SaveThe analysis as an @Graph file (.@graph): the samples (with their FCS files' locations), compensation, axes, gates and plots, and a picture of the results. @Graph Reader shows that picture and the statistics without the FCS files.

Flow on X-Y Graphs

Part of the Flow Cytometry toolkit.

FCS files opened as spreadsheets (with the toolkit hidden, or with Open as Table) plot as X-Y graphs: two parameters against each other (a dot plot), or one against time. Two tabs in the inspector's Toolkits category, under Flow Cytometry, work on such graphs.

Logicle / Arcsinh Axes

This tab shows the visible events on the scales cytometry uses. The values are unchanged.

  1. In the inspector's Toolkits category, choose Flow Cytometry › Logicle / Arcsinh Axes.
  2. Choose a scale for X and for Y: Linear (unchanged), Logicle (the default), Arcsinh or Log10 (values > 0), and set its parameters (see the table below).
  3. Click Open on Cytometry Scales. The plot opens in a new window, with the events as dots.
ScaleWhat it is and its settings
LogicleLinear near zero and logarithmic above it, so compensated values below zero stay visible instead of piling up on an axis (Parks, Roederer & Moore 2006). Computed by Moore & Parks's (2012) reference algorithm, as Gating-ML 2.0 defines it. Top of scale T (262144 by default, the top of most 18-bit instruments); Linear width W in decades (0.5 by default; widen it when negative values spread); Decades M (4.5 by default); Extra negative decades A (0 by default).
Arcsinhasinh(x / cofactor), also linear near zero. Cofactor: 150 by default, which suits fluorescence; 5 suits mass cytometry.
Log10 (values > 0)Leaves out values at or below 0. The tab says how many.
  • Each transformed axis is numbered in data values: 0 and ±10^k where those values fall (10³, 10⁴, 10⁵, and −10³ on the negative side), with minor ticks at 2–9 × 10^k, in the window and in exported figures. To number an axis on its own scale instead, click Use Plain Ticks in the Axes & Labels tab.
  • The tab and the Data Log list where 0 and each decade of the data fall on the axes, to read values and place gates.
  • When T is far from the data's maximum (the data above twice T, or below an eighth of it), the tab offers Set T to the power of 2 at or above the maximum.

Population Statistics (X-Y Graphs)

This tab measures the Y values of each visible sweep, with the statistics FlowJo reports.

  1. In the inspector's Toolkits category, choose Flow Cytometry › Population Statistics.
  2. To gate the events, show the cursors and place them. Only the events whose X lies between the cursors count: an interval gate on X (for example on a parameter plotted against event number or time).
  3. Click Measure. The tab names the gate and lists each sweep's count, percentage, median and robust CV. Every statistic goes to the Data Log.
StatisticHow it is computed
Count and %The events in the gate, and their percentage of the sweep's events.
Mean, median, SD, CV (%)Of the Y values in the gate; CV is 100 × SD / mean. Percentiles are interpolated linearly.
Geometric meanNeeds every value above 0.
Robust SD and robust CV (%)Robust SD is half the distance between the 15.87th and 84.13th percentiles; robust CV is 100 × robust SD / median.
  • For normal data the robust SD and CV equal the SD and CV, and outliers barely move them.
  • A sweep with fewer than 2 events in the gate gets its count and percentage only. Moving the cursors clears the results.
  • Batch Processing and Protocols run Population Statistics on every sweep (see Batch Processing and Protocols).

Astronomy

Sky Coordinates and Regions

Part of the Astronomy toolkit.

FITS images open in Image windows (a folder of frames as one time series), and FITS tables and light curves, such as Kepler or TESS light curves, open as spreadsheets and graphs. This page covers what a sky image shows: sky coordinates under the pointer, the pixel scale, the coordinate grid and DS9 regions.

The toolkit's other tools have their own pages: Plate Solving, Calibrate Frames, Stack Frames, Aperture Photometry and Transit Fit, and Transit Search and Phase Fold. Toolkits: Overview lists where each is found. Batch Processing and Protocols run Transit Search and Transit Fit on every light curve, and Protocols also run Plate Solve, Calibrate Frames, Stack Frames and Aperture Photometry (see Batch Processing and Protocols).

Sky Coordinates Under the Pointer

When a FITS image's header gives a World Coordinate System (WCS: the header cards that map each pixel to a place on the sky), the readout under the pointer shows the sky coordinates beside the pixel and its value. An image without a WCS gets one from Plate Solve (see Plate Solving).

  • Equatorial systems show right ascension (RA, in hours, minutes and seconds) and declination (Dec, in degrees, arcminutes and arcseconds); Galactic systems show l and b, and ecliptic systems λ and β.
  • Coordinates are shown as the header gives them, without conversion between frames. The readout ends with the frame when the header names one, such as ICRS or FK5 J2000.
  • On a series whose frames each have a header, the readout and the coordinate grid on a frame use that frame's own WCS. Otherwise they use the image's, moved with the frames by drift correction.
  • The coordinates are saved with the image.

Pixel Scale

The scale bar and ROI sizes of a sky image are in arcseconds. The scale comes from the first of these the header has:

SourceScale, in arcseconds a pixel
The WCSThe WCS's own scale
PIXSCALEIts value
SECPIX1 and SECPIX2, or SECPIXTheir values
FOCALLEN (mm) and XPIXSZ (µm)206.265 × XPIXSZ ÷ FOCALLEN, with YPIXSZ for the height of pixels that aren't square

The ROIs tab's Microscopy Setup and the Metadata window name the source, such as 1.1138 ″/px (FOCALLEN and XPIXSZ). With none of them, type a pixel size in Microscopy Setup to get a scale bar.

How a Sky Image Is Shown

A two-dimensional FITS image or a series of frames opens with Auto Stretch of its first frame, unless a .@graph file saved another range. In the Channels tab, Auto and ZScale then set Min and Max by zscale of the frame shown, with a Linear stretch (see Imaging › Channels Panel and Imaging › Show Native Image).

Show a Coordinate Grid

  1. Open an image that has a WCS, or plate solve it.
  2. In the image inspector's Channels tab, check Coordinate grid.

The grid draws lines of constant right ascension and declination (or l and b, or λ and β) at round values, about 3 to 6 of each across the field, each traced through the WCS and labeled where it enters the image. The grid is drawn in exports too.

Load and Save DS9 Regions

@Graph loads SAOImage DS9 region files (.reg) as ROIs and saves ROIs as a region file.

  1. Open the image and go to the image inspector's ROIs tab.
  2. To load, choose DS9 › Load DS9 Regions… and pick the file. The regions are added to the image's ROIs, each named by its region's text, and the Data Log says which were left out.
  3. To save the image's ROIs, choose DS9 › Save as DS9 Regions… and name the file.
  • Shapes loaded: circles, ellipses, boxes, polygons, points, lines and annuli. A rotated ellipse or box becomes a polygon, and an annulus becomes a circle for each radius. Excluded regions and regions outside the image are left out.
  • Coordinates loaded: image, physical (through the FITS header's LTM and LTV, for a binned or cropped frame) or sky (fk5, icrs, fk4, galactic, ecliptic). Sky regions need the image's WCS.
  • Regions in another frame (ICRS, FK5, FK4 B1950, galactic or the ecliptic of J2000) are converted to the image's first. An image whose own frame isn't one of these takes only regions in its own frame (wcs).
  • Sizes and angles on the sky are placed with the local pixel scale and north at each region. A size in ″, ′ or degrees on a region in image coordinates uses the WCS's scale there.
  • A saved file is in DS9 4.1 format, which DS9 and astropy-regions read: on the sky in the image's frame (ICRS, FK5, FK4 or galactic) when the image has a WCS, otherwise in image coordinates.
  • On a series, regions are loaded and saved on the frame shown, through the sky coordinates that frame's readout and grid use: its own WCS when each frame has a header, else the image's, with drift correction taken into account.
  • DS9 counts pixels from 1 at the bottom left, as FITS does; @Graph converts.

Which Coordinate Systems Are Read

  • Projections: TAN (gnomonic), SIN (orthographic), ARC, ZEA, STG, CAR, SFL and AIT, with the CD matrix, PC with CDELT, or CDELT with CROTA2, following the FITS WCS papers (Greisen & Calabretta 2002; Calabretta & Greisen 2002).
  • Distortion: SIP polynomials, which describe how the optics bend the field (Shupe et al. 2005).
  • Axis units: degrees, arcseconds, arcminutes, milliarcseconds or radians.
  • An image with another projection, or with distortion terms or units @Graph doesn't read (such as PV terms on TAN or lookup-table distortions), says so when it opens and shows pixels only, rather than wrong coordinates.
