Plate Solving

Part of the Astronomy toolkit.

Find an Image's Sky Coordinates

Plate solving finds where on the sky an image points: its World Coordinate System (WCS), which gives every pixel's right ascension (RA) and declination (Dec). With it, the pointer shows sky coordinates, the coordinate grid and DS9 regions line up, Aperture Photometry records each star's RA and Dec, and Stack Frames can align frames by the sky. Plate Solve matches the image's own stars to a star catalog, so it works on any image of the sky: a FITS frame, a stack, or a photo.

  1. Open the image and, in the image inspector's Toolkits tab, choose Astronomy › Plate Solve from the menu at the top of the tab (or Find a Tool: "plate solve", "astrometry").
  2. Check Where to look. Plate Solve reads the image's approximate position from its header (RA and DEC, which telescopes and capture programs write; else OBJCTRA and OBJCTDEC; or the WCS the image already has, on a series the frame's own, a galactic or B1950 one converted to ICRS) and its pixel scale (the WCS, PIXSCALE, SECPIX, or FOCALLEN with XPIXSZ). A typed position is used in place of the header's, its WCS included. Type either when the header lacks it: RA as 09:16:03.3 (hours) or 139.014 (degrees), Dec as +52:50:39 or 52.844, and Scale in arcseconds a pixel (206.265 × the pixel size in µm ÷ the focal length in mm).
  3. Click Solve with Gaia (a near solve: Gaia DR3 stars around that position) or Solve Blind… (astrometry.net, for an image with no position or scale; it needs your own free API key). The first time, @Graph asks whether it may send what it needs, and to where (see Privacy and Credits below).
  4. Read the solution: the stars matched, how closely they fit (RMS, in arcseconds and pixels), the center, the pixel scale, the orientation (the position angle of the image's top, east of north, and whether it is mirrored), and the distortion fitted. The pointer now shows sky coordinates, and Coordinate grid draws them.
  • The solution is written into the image: its WCS and, in its FITS header, the WCS cards and a HISTORY record naming the services and the catalog. The original file is never changed.
  • To take it back, choose Edit › Undo or click Restore Header WCS, which puts back the sky coordinates the header had (or none). On a series, every frame solved gets its own header's back.
  • To keep it, save the image as a .@graph file, or click Save Solved Copy… to write the solved frame as a new FITS file with the solution in its header. On a series, that is the frame that was solved, whichever frame is shown. A color picture is written as the mean of its red, green and blue.

A series of frames is solved one frame at a time: the frame shown. When each frame has its own header, the solution goes into that frame's header, and the pointer and grid on each frame use that frame's own sky coordinates; Aperture Photometry follows the stars from frame to frame as before.

Near and Blind Solving

  • Solve with Gaia: the Gaia DR3 stars around the hint are fetched from the service chosen under Catalog: the ESA Gaia archive (the default), VizieR at CDS in Strasbourg, or ESA's partner data center at ARI Heidelberg. All three hold the same catalog; if one is down or slow, choose another. An image that already has a WCS in ICRS or FK5 is refined from it, over the search Radius.
  • Radius (1 field diagonal by default, 0.1 to 5) sets how far from the hint the center may be; a diagonal counts as at most 1°. Scale within ± (10% by default, 1% to 50%) sets how far the true pixel scale may be from the hint's; a focal reducer or binning changes it.
  • Solve Blind…: astrometry.net's public service finds the field anywhere on the sky from the positions of the image's brightest stars. Set your key once with Set API Key… (sign in at nova.astrometry.net and copy the key from your account's API page); it is kept in your Keychain. The service may queue a request for a few minutes; Stop ends the wait.
  • After a blind solve, refine it with Gaia (on by default) matches the blind solution to Gaia DR3 stars as a near solve does, which gives the matched-star table and a fit of the distortion you chose.
  • Distortion: Automatic (the default) fits SIP polynomials of order 2, which follow most optics' distortion across the field, when at least 30 stars match, and otherwise a plain TAN projection. Or choose None (TAN) or SIP order 2 to 5.
  • Show matched stars circles the stars matched to Gaia on the image, each with its residual (where the image star is relative to the catalog star, drawn 50 times longer), so a poor fit in one corner shows at a glance.
  • Open Matched Stars opens them as a spreadsheet: each star's image position, RA and Dec, its Gaia DR3 source_id and other names (see Which Star Is That?), its G, BP and RP magnitudes (useful for choosing comparison stars), parallax and proper motion, and the fit's residual. The matched stars are saved with the image, so the table and the circles are there when it is opened again.

Which Star Is That?

On a solved image, point near a star: the readout under the pointer gains a second line naming it, and a ring marks the star it means. Any Gaia star in the frame counts, matched or not, down to the faintest the catalog query reached. The pointer has to be within about 8 screen points of it at the current zoom.

  • The line gives, as far as they are known: the star's proper name, its Gaia DR3 source_id, its Hipparcos (HIP), Tycho-2 (TYC) and 2MASS names, its G magnitude and BP−RP color, its distance or parallax, its proper motion (μα* = μα cos δ and μδ, in milliarcseconds a year) and, for a matched star, how far the fit is from it (in pixels). Names are written as SIMBAD writes them, so they can be searched there.
  • The HIP, Tycho-2 and 2MASS names come from Gaia DR3's own cross-matches with those catalogs (Marrese et al. 2019): after the match, the stars' Gaia source IDs are sent to the same catalog service, which returns the names. The ESA Gaia archive and ARI Heidelberg have the cross-matches; VizieR's copy of Gaia DR3 doesn't, so a solve from VizieR names stars by their Gaia DR3 source_id only. Uncheck Ask for the stars' HIP, Tycho-2 and 2MASS names (under Search) to send no IDs. A close double can have two Tycho-2 entries for one Gaia star: both are given.
  • Proper names are the IAU's (the Working Group on Star Names' Catalog of Star Names, which @Graph carries; about 640 names). A star is named by its Hipparcos number or, for names without one, by its position within 2″ (at J2000).
  • Distance is 1000 ÷ parallax (in milliarcseconds), in parsecs, and is given only when the parallax is at least 5 times its error. Otherwise the parallax alone is shown, since inverting a poor parallax gives a badly biased distance (Bailer-Jones 2015).
  • A blind solve keeps the frame's stars only when it is refined with Gaia. An image that shows no names was solved before @Graph kept them: solve it again.
  • @Graph Reader shows the same line: on a Mac when pointing, on iPhone and iPad when tapping near a star.

Privacy and Credits

Plate Solve is the only part of @Graph's Astronomy toolkit that uses the internet, and nothing is sent until you agree. Each service asks first, saying what it will receive. Check Don't ask again in that dialog to allow the service for later solves. To be asked again, click Forget beside the service in Settings › Toolkits, under Astronomy: Plate Solve.

  • A near solve sends an approximate sky position (right ascension and declination) and a search radius to the catalog service you choose, which returns the Gaia stars in that area. Then, to name them, it sends the Gaia source IDs of the stars in the image to the same service (unless that is turned off).
  • A blind solve sends the pixel positions of the image's brightest stars (up to 200), its size in pixels and, when known, its approximate position and pixel scale to astrometry.net, under your API key. astrometry.net keeps submissions on its servers; @Graph marks them not public, not for commercial use and not to be modified. With refinement on, the position it finds then goes to the catalog service, as in a near solve.
  • Images, pixel values and file names are never sent.
  • Credit: the solution, the Data Log and the FITS HISTORY carry the acknowledgments the data's providers ask for: Gaia (ESA/Gaia/DPAC; the data under CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO), VizieR (CDS, Strasbourg) or ARI Heidelberg when used, the Two Micron All Sky Survey when its names are given, and astrometry.net (Lang et al. 2010) for a blind solve. Quote them when you publish the result.

Automate Plate Solving

  • Protocols: in the Protocols window, Add Step › Astro › Plate Solve… solves the frame shown on the image window chosen under Run, near or blind, using the header's position and pixel scale. The step saves its own catalog, distortion, search radius, scale tolerance, refinement with Gaia and star names; a new step starts from the panel's settings. A protocol never asks while it runs, so allow the services once in the panel with Don't ask again. Plate Solve is a protocol's first step; Aperture Photometry (Series) may follow it on the solved image.
  • AI Assistant: ask it to plate solve an image window (Astronomy › Plate Solving). @Graph still asks you before anything is sent; the assistant can't answer that for you. On a solved image it can also name the star at a position, find a star by name ("where is HIP 10245?"), or list the frame's named stars, from what the solve saved; that sends nothing.

How Plate Solving Works

  • The image's stars: the sky background is mapped and subtracted first, as SExtractor does (Bertin & Arnouts 1996), so a gradient or an uncalibrated frame's glow isn't taken for stars. Up to 300 stars, brightest first, are found and centered by a 2-D Gaussian fit, as Stack Frames finds them. A one-shot color frame is read on its green pixels.
  • The catalog: the brightest Gaia DR3 stars in a cone around the hint (half the field's diagonal plus the search radius). Each star is moved from Gaia's epoch (2016.0) to the image's date (DATE-OBS) by its proper motion (Butkevich & Lindegren 2014), so fast-moving stars are where the image saw them.
  • Matching: at trial centers around the hint, nearest first, the catalog stars are projected onto the image's pixels at the hint's scale. Triangles of the brightest stars, each star with its 4 nearest neighbors, are matched by their side ratios, as Stack Frames aligns frames (Beroiz, Cabral & Sanchez 2020). A mirror image is tried too.
  • Accepting a match: each candidate is tested as astrometry.net tests one (Lang et al. 2010). The odds that the match is real rather than chance must reach a billion to one.
  • The fit: a gnomonic (TAN) projection about the image's center (Calabretta & Greisen 2002) and, when chosen, SIP distortion polynomials (Shupe et al. 2005), fitted by least squares to the matched stars. Pairs further than 3 × the RMS are left out and the fit is repeated until the pairs stop changing. The SIP inverse (AP, BP) is fitted too, so other programs read the WCS as @Graph does.
  • The blind solve is astrometry.net's own: its service matches the star positions against its index of the sky and returns its WCS, which @Graph reads as it reads any FITS header.

Calibrate Frames

Part of the Astronomy toolkit.

Calibrate Frames takes the camera's own signature out of raw CCD or CMOS frames before you measure or stack them. Every pixel starts from an offset the electronics add (the bias), collects a thermal signal that grows with the exposure (dark current), and responds a little differently from its neighbors, with less light reaching the corners (vignetting) and faint rings from dust (dust donuts). The calibrated light is (raw − bias − dark) ÷ flat. Bias, dark and flat are each measured from a set of calibration frames, combined into a master.

Calibrate Your Frames

  1. Open Calibrate Frames: choose Toolkits › Astronomy › Calibrate Frames…, use Find a Tool (type "calibrate", "bias" or "flat"), or click Open Calibrate Frames… at the top of an image's Aperture Photometry tool.
  2. Add the frames: click Add Files… or Add Folder… (its subfolders too), or drop files and folders on the window. The frames are sorted into Bias, Darks by exposure, Flats by filter and Lights by filter. Click a group to see its frames.
  3. Fix any type the headers get wrong. A frame whose IMAGETYP isn't known goes under Unknown type and isn't used: give it a type with the menu beside it, or the whole group's with Change All. The × beside a frame takes it out of the list (the file isn't touched).
  4. Read the orange warnings: frames of another size or binning, a light without a flat in its filter, darks whose exposure doesn't match the lights' when darks aren't scaled, and darks taken at another temperature. Each says what it means.
  5. Check the settings below the frames (see Settings). They are remembered from one use to the next; Restore Default Settings brings back the defaults.
  6. Click Build Masters. The table lists the master bias, a master dark for each exposure, a master flat for each filter and the bad pixels, with each master's Frames (the number combined), Median, MAD std (its spread) and Rejected (the share of values left out by clipping). Open opens one as an image. Calibrate Lights… builds the masters itself if you skip this step.
  7. Under Preview, choose a light and click Show Preview. The raw and the calibrated frame show side by side, each with its own Auto Stretch. Pixels with no value show in red.
  8. Click Calibrate Lights… and choose a folder (New Folder makes one). The masters and the calibrated lights are written there, the summary goes to the Data Log, and the calibrated lights open, one series per filter, at the image inspector's Toolkits tab on Aperture Photometry (see Aperture Photometry and Transit Fit).
  9. To stack the calibrated lights, click Open Stack Frames…, which brings them with it (see Stack Frames).

To try it, choose More Samples › CCD Calibration Frames (under Astronomy) in the Welcome window. It makes a small set of raw frames from a made-up camera and opens Calibrate Frames with them.

Frames to take

FramesHow to take themHow many
BiasThe shortest exposure the camera allows (0 s), with the shutter closed or the telescope covered.10 to 20
DarkShutter closed, at the same sensor temperature as the lights, and either the same exposure as the lights or, with bias frames, any exposure (the dark is scaled).10 or more
FlatAn evenly lit field (the twilight sky, a dome screen or a light panel) through each filter you use, with the focus and the camera's rotation as for the lights, exposed to about a third to a half of full scale. Take their own darks, or bias frames.5 to 10 per filter
LightThe frames of your target.—

The camera's FITS headers say which is which (IMAGETYP), with the exposure (EXPTIME), the filter (FILTER) and the temperature (CCD-TEMP).

Settings

SettingDefaultWhat it does
Combine byAverageHow frames are combined into masters: Average or Median.
Clip outliers beyond … σ below, … σ aboveOn, 5 and 5Leaves out values this far from the pixel's median across the frames, so cosmic rays and satellites don't enter the master. Use the Guide's Recipe brings back the default (the CCD Data Reduction Guide's).
Overscan: RegionBIASSECThe overscan strip: from the header's BIASSEC, Typed in FITS notation such as [2049:2080,1:4128], or None. It must span every row. When a header's doesn't, the window says so, and choosing Typed starts from a corrected one.
Fit a polynomial of degreeOffSubtracts a smooth fit to the rows' overscan values instead of each row's own.
Trim: KeepTRIMSECThe part of the frame kept: from the header's TRIMSEC (else DATASEC), Typed, or None (the whole frame).
GainFrom the headerElectrons per ADU, from GAIN or EGAIN, or Typed. A typed gain is written into the calibrated frames. Some cameras write a nominal value whatever their setting, so type the measured gain if you know it.
Convert the lights to electronsOffMultiplies the calibrated lights by the gain; their GAIN becomes 1.
Scale darks by exposureOnSubtracts the master dark scaled to each frame's exposure. It needs bias frames or an overscan, because a raw dark holds the bias level too, which doesn't grow with exposure. Without either, each frame uses the dark nearest its exposure, unscaled.
Replace flat values belowOff (0.1)Raises tiny flat values, such as in dark corners, to the minimum before dividing by them. The window suggests it when the master flat has values that would give huge or infinite results.
Equalize a color camera's flat (CFA)OnFor a one-shot color camera (its header names a Bayer pattern): scales the master flat's red and blue pixels so their means match green's, as Siril's Equalize CFA does, so the flat doesn't tint the frames.
Hot pixels: dark current aboveOn, 4 e⁻/sSee Bad Pixels.
Dead and cold pixels, from the flatOnSee Bad Pixels.
Remove cosmic rays (L.A.Cosmic)OffSee Remove Cosmic Rays.

What is written

  • The masters go into a Masters folder inside the folder you chose: Master Bias.fits, a master dark for each exposure (such as Master Dark 60s.fits), a master flat for each filter (such as Master Flat V.fits) and Bad Pixels.fits.
  • Each light is written as "name calibrated.fits": a 32-bit floating-point FITS file with the raw header, plus HISTORY records naming each step and the master it used.
  • Each calibrated light also carries the keywords ccdproc writes for its steps (SUBOSCAN, TRIMIM, GAINCOR, SUBBIAS, SUBDARK, FLATCOR), BUNIT (adu or electron), and SATURATE and DARKCUR for the calibrated values (see How Calibration Works). Its GAIN is 1 in electrons, or the gain typed.
  • The raw frames are never changed, and a calibrated frame is never written over one.

Remove Cosmic Rays

Cosmic rays leave sharp spots and short streaks in single frames. Combining already leaves them out of the masters. To take them out of the lights:

  1. Under Cosmic rays (lights), check Remove cosmic rays (L.A.Cosmic).
  2. Set Detection limit (4.5σ by default): how far above the noise a pixel's sharpness must be to be a candidate. Lower finds more, and more false ones.
  3. Set object limit (5 by default): how much sharper than a star a candidate must be. Raise it if star centers are flagged.
  4. Choose Read noise: From the header (RDNOISE; 6.5 e⁻ is taken when the header has none) or Typed. The noise also uses the gain set under Gain.
  5. Click Show Preview to check one light before calibrating them all.
  • Each flagged pixel is replaced by the mean of its unflagged neighbors, and the count goes into the frame's HISTORY and the Data Log.
  • A color camera's lights are searched, and cleaned, one color at a time.
  • Stars within about 4 pixels of the frame's edge can be flagged as cosmic rays, so keep targets and comparison stars away from the edge. Saturated stars are never flagged.

Bad Pixels

  • Hot pixels: pixels whose dark current (master dark × gain ÷ exposure) is above the threshold (4 e⁻/s by default). They are found only from bias-subtracted darks, so they need bias frames or an overscan.
  • Dead and cold pixels: pixels far below (or above) their neighbors in the master flat, such as a dead column.
  • Bad pixels, and pixels with no value in every frame of a master, are written as NaN (not a number) in the calibrated lights rather than filled in, and the HISTORY says so. Aperture Photometry leaves NaN pixels out of apertures and sky annuli and flags a star whose aperture holds any.
  • The mask is saved as Bad Pixels.fits in the Masters folder (1 = bad, 0 = good). Open beside Bad pixels in the masters table shows it.

Automate Calibration

A Protocol calibrates the raw FITS frames behind an image window with masters built earlier and the Calibrate Frames window's settings:

  1. Open the raw frames in an image window.
  2. In the Protocols window, choose Add Step › Astro › Calibrate Frames…. It must be the first step.
  3. In the step, click Choose… and pick the Masters folder of an earlier Calibrate Lights. The calibrated frames go into a folder inside the raw frames' folder (Calibrated, unless you name another).
  4. Choose the window under Run and click Run Protocol.
  • The calibrated series opens with the raw window's apertures (moved by the trim), so an Aperture Photometry (Series) step after it measures the calibrated frames, and the steps after that run on its light curve.
  • When the frames were opened one by one rather than as a folder, @Graph asks once where to write.
  • AI Assistant: ask it to sort a folder of raw frames by type, with the warnings, or to calibrate them, with the window's settings unless you ask for others. It asks you to choose the folders unless you have opened them this session.

How Calibration Works

The steps and their order are those of ccdproc, the Astropy package for CCD reduction, as the CCD Data Reduction Guide (Craig et al.) uses them.

  • Order: the overscan is subtracted, the frame trimmed, the master bias subtracted, the master dark subtracted (multiplied by the frame's exposure ÷ the dark's when darks are scaled), the frame divided by the normalized master flat and, when asked, multiplied by the gain.
  • Combining: each pixel is combined across the frames. With clipping on, values more than 5σ (or the limits typed) from the pixel's median are left out in one pass, σ being 1.4826 × the median absolute deviation, and the rest are averaged. The median is the alternative. Pixels with no value are left out.
  • Master bias: the bias frames, overscan-subtracted and trimmed, combined. Master dark: each dark with the master bias subtracted, combined, one per exposure. Master flat: each flat calibrated by the bias and the dark (scaled to the flat's exposure), scaled by 1 ÷ its median so that flats of different brightness combine evenly, then combined, one per filter.
  • Flat normalization: the master flat is divided by its mean when it is applied, so the calibrated frame keeps the level the light had at the flat's average response. With a flat minimum, flat values below it are raised to it first.
  • Overscan: the median of each row's overscan pixels is subtracted from that row or, with Fit a polynomial, a least-squares polynomial of the chosen degree through those medians.
  • Dead and cold pixels: ccdproc's ccdmask with its defaults. A pixel is bad when it differs from the 7 × 7 running median by more than 9 times the local spread, which is half the distance between the 30.9th and 69.1st percentiles in a 15 × 15 window. A color camera's flat is searched one color at a time.
  • Cosmic rays: L.A.Cosmic (van Dokkum 2001), as astroscrappy implements it. The frame's Laplacian, on a grid twice as fine, picks out edges sharper than any star. Candidates above the detection limit, in units of the noise (from the gain, the read noise and the frame's own level), are kept when they are sharper than the fine structure around them by the object limit; their neighbors are added above a lower limit; and the search is repeated four times.
  • Saturation: the raw frame's saturation level (SATURATE or SATLEVEL, else the integer data's full scale, 65535 for 16-bit frames) is kept as SATRAW. SATURATE becomes the lowest value a pixel at that level can take after this calibration, over the pixels that aren't masked; pixels more than 10 times the pixel-to-pixel spread below the 5 × 5 median around them are set aside as hot pixels. Aperture Photometry flags a star whose peak reaches SATURATE.
  • Dark current: when a master dark is subtracted and the gain is known, each calibrated light records DARKCUR, in e⁻ per pixel per second: the median of the master dark, with bias taken out of it (the master bias or the overscan), over its unmasked pixels, times the gain, divided by the dark's exposure. Aperture Photometry adds this dark term to each star's errors (Howell 2006). Without a gain, or with neither bias frames nor an overscan, no DARKCUR is written, and the Data Log's summary says why.

Stack Frames

Part of the Astronomy toolkit.

One exposure of the night sky is noisy; many, averaged, are clean (the noise falls as the square root of the number of frames). Stack Frames aligns calibrated light frames to one reference frame, sets aside the poor ones, and averages the rest pixel by pixel, leaving out values far from the others (satellite and aircraft trails, cosmic rays, hot pixels). It makes one stack per filter, and a color picture from three of them.

Stack Your Frames

  1. Open Stack Frames: choose Toolkits › Astronomy › Stack Frames…, use Find a Tool (type "stack" or "align"), or click Open Stack Frames… in Calibrate Frames once the lights are calibrated, which brings them with it.
  2. Add the frames: click Add Files… or Add Folder… (its subfolders too), or drop them on the window. Frames are listed in the order they were taken. Bias, dark and flat frames, masters and stacks aren't added.
  3. Click Measure and Align. Every frame is measured: its stars, their sharpness (FWHM, in pixels) and roundness, the sky's background level and its noise. The reference frame, marked with a star, is the one with the smallest weighted FWHM (sharp, with many stars). Every other frame is aligned to it.
  4. Read the table. A frame set aside is unticked and says why in orange: its stars didn't match, they are blurred, there are few of them (cloud), or its background is bright (the Moon, haze, dawn). Each frame is compared with the other frames of its filter; a color camera's frames are compared by their green. Tick or untick any frame yourself; the reference stays in.
  5. Check the settings at the right (see Settings). They are remembered between uses.
  6. Click Stack… and choose a folder (New Folder makes one). If the frames haven't been measured and aligned yet, or the alignment settings changed, Stack… does that first. Each filter's frames are stacked, the summary goes to the Data Log, and the stacks open.

To align to another frame, choose it under Reference and click Measure and Align (Stack… does it first).

To try it, choose More Samples › Stacking Frames (R, G, B) (under Astronomy) in the Welcome window. It makes 24 frames of one field in three filters and opens Stack Frames with them.

Settings

SettingDefaultWhat it does
Align byStarsStars; Sky Coordinates (WCS), through each frame's WCS (its sky coordinates) when every frame is plate-solved; or Already Aligned, which stacks the frames as they are.
MovementShift, Rotation and ScaleCovers drift, field rotation and a meridian flip, with up to a 2% change of scale. Or Shift Only.
InterpolationLanczos-3Lanczos-3 keeps stars sharpest, with their flux. Lanczos-3, Clamped (pictures) avoids dark rings around bright stars but adds a little to their flux. Also Bicubic, Bilinear and Nearest Pixel.
Conserve fluxOnKeeps a star's total light when frames differ in scale (values × the change of pixel area).
Combine byMean, with RejectionOr Median, or Sum.
Rejection, with Low (σ) and High (σ)Winsorized Sigma Clipping, 3 and 3How outlying values at a pixel are left out of the mean (see Rejection methods).
NormalizationAdditive with ScalingAdditive with Scaling makes each frame's background and spread the reference's; Additive matches the background only; the Multiplicative ones divide instead. Or None.
StatisticsIKSSHow background and spread are measured. Or Median and MAD (faster).
WeightsNoiseHow much each frame counts in the mean (see How Stacking Works). Also Star Count, Weighted FWHM and Equal.
FWHM above1.5 × the medianSets aside blurred frames.
Stars below50% of the medianSets aside frames through cloud.
Background above the median by5 spreadsSets aside frames with a bright sky. A spread is 1.4826 × the median absolute deviation.
Crop to the area all frames coverOnCuts every filter's stack alike to the rectangle all the stacked frames cover. Edges that fewer frames cover are noisier, and off-color in a picture.
Keep the aligned framesOffWrites each aligned frame into an Aligned folder beside the stacks.
Write uncertainty and count mapsOffWrites, beside each stack, each pixel's standard error and how many frames it came from.

What a stack holds

  • Each filter's stack is a 32-bit floating-point FITS file named for the frames in it, such as "Stack R 8 frames.fits". The frames themselves are never changed.
  • A stack keeps the reference frame's header and its sky coordinates (WCS) when it has one. A super-pixel or drizzled stack's XPIXSZ, YPIXSZ, PIXSCALE and SECPIX (and a super-pixel stack's XBINNING and YBINNING) are for its own pixels, so its pixel scale is right without a WCS. A stack records NCOMBINE (the frames stacked), LIVETIME (the total exposure), EXPTIME (one frame's, since a mean stack's values are per frame), and HISTORY of every step. With cropping, the sky coordinates move with the pixels, and LTV1 and LTV2 record the cut.
  • Photometry on a stack: a mean of N frames holds N frames' worth of electrons, so the stack's GAIN is N times a frame's, its RDNOISE (read noise in electrons) √N times and its DARKCUR N times. For a weighted mean, N is the effective number of frames, (Σw)² ÷ Σw². A median counts as a mean of 2N/3 frames (Massey and Davis's approximation, noted in a COMMENT card). A sum keeps GAIN and DARKCUR (its EXPTIME is the total) and has √N times the read noise. A super-pixel green stack's pixels are each the mean of two green pixels, so its GAIN and DARKCUR are a further 2 times and its RDNOISE √2 times. GAINRAW, RDNRAW and DARKRAW keep one frame's values.
  • For photometry, choose Lanczos-3 (not clamped) and, when the frames' noise differs, Additive normalization, which keeps star fluxes in the reference frame's scale.

Drizzle

When a camera's pixels are large for the telescope's star images (stars narrower than about 2 pixels), they lose detail that frames moved by fractions of a pixel between exposures (dithered) still hold. Drizzle (Fruchter & Hook 2002) recovers it: each frame's pixels, shrunk to drops, are laid onto a finer grid and averaged where they land, with no interpolation smoothing the noise.

  1. In the Drizzle section, check Drizzle onto a finer grid.
  2. Choose the Scale (2× by default): 2× makes each camera pixel 2 × 2 output pixels, and 1× keeps the grid.
  3. Set the Drop size (0.8 by default): the drop's side as a fraction of a pixel, 0.1 to 1.
  4. Choose the Kernel: Square (the default and the standard) uses each drop's exact outline, Turbo is an upright square and faster, and Point drops each pixel into one output pixel and needs many frames.
  5. Read the line below, which says how well the frames' offsets cover the sub-pixel positions (dithering), then click Stack….
  • Rejection is decided first, on an ordinary stack of every frame. Each frame is then drizzled from its own pixels, normalized and weighted as for the stack, leaving out the rejected pixels (those whose centers land on a rejected aligned pixel).
  • The stack is named "Stack R 24 frames drizzle 2x.fits", with "… weights.fits" beside it: each pixel's drizzle weight (the share of each drop that landed on it, summed over the frames). Its sky coordinates are those of the finer grid; LTM1_1, LTM2_2 and LTV1, LTV2 relate its pixels to the reference frame's.
  • Values are per output pixel (an input pixel's value ÷ scale²), so a star's total, and Aperture Photometry on the stack, are unchanged. RDNOISE and DARKCUR are per output pixel too.
  • The stack's HISTORY gives the weight map's spread (RMS ÷ median; below about 0.2 is smooth, and a larger drop size or more frames lower it), any pixels no drop reached, and R: neighboring drizzled pixels share drops, so the noise measured in one pixel is √R times smaller than its own.
  • Bayer drizzle (no debayering), for one-shot color frames, drops each raw pixel into its own color's stack. It needs well-dithered frames, usually 15 or more. At Scale 1× and Drop size 1 it replaces debayering.

Make a Color Picture

Three stacks taken through red, green and blue filters (or any three filters given those colors) make a color picture, written once as a new 16-bit RGB TIFF beside the red stack. The stacks stay as they are. Stacks from one Stack Frames run already lie on the same pixels.

  1. After stacking, check Red, Green and Blue in the Color Picture section. They are filled in from the stacks' filter names (R, G, B, or the SDSS and Johnson filters); Choose… picks any stack for a color.
  2. Choose the Stretch. Lupton Asinh Color (the default) stretches the total brightness once and keeps each pixel's color ratios, so bright stars keep their color instead of turning white (Lupton et al. 2004): Q (8 by default) brings out faint light, Stretch (20 × noise) sets where the stretch turns from linear to logarithmic, and Black point (1 × noise below the sky) sets where black lies. Linked Auto Stretch uses the image window's Auto Stretch, the same for all three colors.
  3. Leave Neutralize the background on to subtract each stack's sky, so the sky is neutral gray.
  4. Choose White balance: From the Stars (the default) scales red and blue so the average star is white; Typed takes your own factors.
  5. Leave Align the stacks to the red one on for stacks made separately: it aligns green and blue to red by their stars.
  6. Click Make Color Picture. The picture opens in an image window, and the Data Log records how it was made.

The picture is finished: its stretch is already in its values, so the Channels tab offers nothing to stretch or color again. To change its look, make it again.

One-Shot Color Cameras

A color camera puts a red, green or blue filter over each pixel in a 2 × 2 pattern (the Bayer pattern, named in the frame's BAYERPAT keyword). Calibrate its raw frames as they are, then stack the calibrated lights: Stack Frames debayers each one and stacks red, green and blue as three filters, aligned once by the green. The three stacks then make a color picture. Choose the method under Debayer, shown when a frame is a mosaic:

DebayerWhat it does
Malvar–He–Cutler (the default)Keeps detail (Malvar, He & Cutler 2004).
Menon (directional)Estimates green along rows and along columns and keeps, at each pixel, the direction whose color differences vary less, with its refining step (Menon, Andriani & Calvagno 2007). Edges are sharper, with fewer colored fringes.
BilinearThe softest.
Super-Pixel (half size)Makes each 2 × 2 cell one pixel, with no interpolation, at half the size. A plate-solved frame's WCS is carried onto the half-size grid.
  • The pattern is read from the top row, as Siril reads it; ROWORDER, XBAYROFF and YBAYROFF are honored.
  • A trim by an odd number of rows or columns moves the pattern; the calibrated frames' BAYERPAT is written for the trimmed frame.
  • With well-dithered frames, Bayer drizzle stacks the raw pixels without debayering (see Drizzle).

Automate Stacking

  • Protocols: in the Protocols window, Add Step › Astro › Stack Frames… stacks the FITS frames behind the image window chosen under Run with the Stack Frames window's settings, into a folder inside the frames' folder (Stacks, unless you name another), and opens the stacks. Check Make a color picture from three stacks in the step to make one too.
  • AI Assistant: ask it to stack a folder of calibrated lights, with any of the window's settings (drizzle and Bayer drizzle included), and to make a color picture from the stacks. It asks you to choose the folders unless you have opened them this session.

How Stacking Works

The alignment is astroalign's (Beroiz, Cabral & Sanchez 2020), and the normalization, rejection and weights are Siril's (version 1.4.5).

  • Stars for aligning: the brightest 50 peaks more than 5σ above the sky whose 3 × 3 median is also above it (so not a hot pixel or a cosmic ray), round ones first, each centered by a 2-D Gaussian fit.
  • Matching: triangles of each star and its 4 nearest neighbors are matched by their side ratios, which stay the same however a frame is shifted, turned or scaled. The movement that brings the most stars within 2 pixels wins and is refitted by least squares on every matched star, leaving out any more than 3 robust spreads off.
  • Sky Coordinates: each pixel of the reference frame goes to the sky through its WCS and back to the frame's pixels through the frame's own.
  • Interpolation: Lanczos-3 is sinc(x)·sinc(x/3) over 6 × 6 pixels, its weights corrected to sum to 1. Clamped, it damps its negative lobes when they pass 30% of the sum (PixInsight's clamping). Bicubic is the cubic B-spline. Pixels that move in from outside a frame are missing there and are left out of the stack.
  • Frame quality: FWHM and roundness are the medians, over the brightest round stars, of their Gaussian fits (roundness = narrow width ÷ wide width). The background is the frame's median. The noise is the standard deviation of differences between neighboring pixels, clipped, over √2. The weighted FWHM is FWHM × (1 + 2 (Nmax − N) / Nmax), with N the frame's stars.
  • Normalization: each frame's background level and spread are measured on the frame as recorded, before it is moved, since interpolation smooths a moved frame's noise. IKSS leaves out values beyond the median ± 6 MAD, then takes their median and the square root of the biweight midvariance.
  • Combining: the mean of the values kept, weighted by Noise (1 ÷ the variance of the frame's normalized background noise), Star Count or Weighted FWHM; or the median of all the values; or their sum.

Rejection methods

RejectionAt each pixel
Winsorized Sigma ClippingEstimates the spread robustly (values pulled in to the median ± 1.5σ until σ settles), then leaves out values more than Low σ below or High σ above the median, and repeats.
Sigma ClippingThe same, with the plain standard deviation.
MAD ClippingThe same, with the median absolute deviation.
Median Sigma ClippingAs Sigma Clipping, but replaces the values instead of leaving them out.
Linear Fit ClippingFits a straight line to the sorted values. For 15 or more frames under a changing sky.
Generalized ESDRosner's (1983) test. For 50 or more frames.
Percentile ClippingLeaves out values beyond a fraction of the median. For 6 or fewer frames.

At least 4 values are always kept.

Drizzle and color

  • Drizzle follows STScI's drizzle package: each output pixel keeps the mean of the drops on it, weighted by the overlapped share of each drop times the frame's weight.
  • The noise-correlation ratio is Fruchter & Hook's: with r = drop size × scale, R = r ÷ (1 − 1/(3r)) for r ≥ 1, else 1 ÷ (1 − r/3).
  • Lupton's stretch divides each color by the total brightness I = (R + G + B) / 3 and multiplies it by asinh(I·Q / stretch) × 0.1 / asinh(0.1 Q), then scales down a pixel whose brightest color passes the top, as astropy's make_lupton_rgb does.
  • White balance from the stars takes the median of the same stars' green ÷ red and green ÷ blue in the three stacks, leaving out the brightest tenth, which may saturate.
  • Where a bright star passes SATURATE in a stack, its clipped core takes the color of the light in the 3 pixels around it, keeping its brightness.

Back to Contents

Aperture Photometry and Transit Fit

Part of the Astronomy toolkit.

Aperture Photometry measures the stars in a FITS image: it sums the counts in a circle around each star, subtracts the sky measured in a ring around it, and gives each star's net counts, error, signal-to-noise ratio and magnitude. On a series of frames it measures a target star against comparison stars in every frame and plots the target's relative flux against time: a differential light curve. Transit Fit then fits a transit to one night's light curve and gives its mid-transit time.

Aperture Photometry is in the image inspector's Toolkits tab; Transit Fit is a tab in a graph's inspector. Aperture Photometry measures the frames as they are, so calibrate raw frames first (bias, dark and flat field): click Open Calibrate Frames… at the top of the tab (see Calibrate Frames), or put a Calibrate Frames step before Aperture Photometry in a Protocol.

Make a Light Curve from FITS Frames

  1. Open the frames: drag the folder of FITS frames onto the Dock icon, the Data Log or the Welcome window, or choose several FITS files together in File › Open File…. They open in one Image window as a time series, in the order they were taken (see Imaging › Supported File Formats).
  2. Read the Data Log's line for the series: how many frames opened, which header keywords their times come from, and which files were left out and why.
  3. Open the image inspector's Toolkits tab. A FITS image opens it on Aperture Photometry; otherwise choose Astronomy › Aperture Photometry from the menu at the top of the tab.
  4. Click Place apertures, then click the target star. Its aperture snaps to the star's center and is named T1.
  5. Click the comparison stars (C2, C3…): several, about as bright as the target and of a similar color, not saturated, and clear of other stars and of the image's edges. Click Place apertures again, or press Esc, when you are done.
  6. Open Seeing profile, select the target, click Measure Profile and then Use Suggested Radii.
  7. Open Detector and type the camera's Gain if the header has none. Open Site and target and type whichever of the site and the target's coordinates is missing: BJD_TDB and airmass need both.
  8. Click Measure Frame to check the apertures on the frame shown. An orange row in the table is flagged, and hovering over it says why. Check a frame with poor seeing or the most drift too. An aperture placed on another frame is measured there at its placed position; Measure Series carries it to the start frame by matching the two frames' stars, whatever Measure Frame found, and the Data Log says so.
  9. Click Measure Series (the button gives the number of frames). It runs in the background, with its progress and Cancel. The light curve opens in a graph window, and the full table, one row per frame, goes to the Data Log.
  10. Under Add to the light curve, check Comparison stars and click Open Light Curve. A comparison star whose curve isn't flat is variable: make it a check star or delete it, and measure the series again.
  11. To time the transit, go on to Time a Transit from One Night, below. To find a period from two transits or more, see Transit Search and Phase Fold.

Measure Series needs a target and at least one comparison star. Changing an aperture or a setting clears the result, so measure the series again. The apertures and settings are saved with the image in its .@graph file, and a new image starts with the settings used last.

Try it: in the Welcome window, More Samples › Transit Observation (FITS Frames), under Astronomy, makes a night's 160 frames of a made-up star field and opens them at Aperture Photometry with the target and four comparison stars already placed. Click Measure Series.

Apertures

  • While Place apertures is on, clicks place apertures instead of selecting or drawing ROIs. When no star is found under a click, the aperture stays where you clicked and the tab says so.
  • Roles: the menu beside an aperture's name in the list, or a right-click on its circle, makes it the Target, a Comparison star or a Check star. A check star is measured against the comparison stars as the target is; its curve should be flat.
  • Names follow each aperture's role and place in the list (T1, C2, C3…); a check star is K, or K1, K2… when there are several. To rename one, double-click its name in the list, or choose Rename… from the menu beside it. On the image the target is green, comparison stars red and check stars cyan, each with its sky annulus dashed.
  • To move an aperture, drag it. To delete one, click × in the list, or right-click it and choose Delete Aperture. ⌘Z undoes every change to an aperture.
  • For an exact position, select the aperture and type X and Y below the list, in FITS pixels (X from 1 at the left, Y from 1 at the bottom, on the frame it was placed on) or, when the image has a WCS, RA and Dec; then press Return or Tab. RA is in hours (14 14 12.35 or 14:14:12.35) or degrees (213.551), Dec as +27 53 41.2, +27:53:41.2 or degrees.
  • Add at Coordinates places a new aperture without a click: choose FITS pixels or RA, Dec, type both, choose its role under As (Automatic makes the first aperture the target and the rest comparison stars) and click Add.
  • A typed position isn't snapped to a star, but measuring recenters it while Recenter on each star in every frame is on.
  • Show apertures in exports (on by default) draws the apertures, their annuli and names into the image's exported and copied pictures and movies.

Radii from the seeing profile

  1. Open Seeing profile and select the target (click it in the list or on the image).
  2. Click Measure Profile. The chart shows the star's radial profile with a Gaussian (blue) and a Moffat (orange) fit and the radii now set, with the curve of growth below it. The note gives the FWHM (the star's full width at half maximum), the suggested radii and how much of the star's flux that aperture holds.
  3. Click Use Suggested Radii: the aperture 1.7 × FWHM and the sky annulus 1.9 to 2.55 × FWHM (Collins et al. 2017), which give the aperture and the annulus the same number of pixels.
  4. If the seeing changes through the night, set the unit beside Aperture radius and Sky annulus to × FWHM. Each frame then uses these multiples of its own mean FWHM.
  • For a faint target a smaller aperture (about 1 × FWHM) gives a better signal-to-noise ratio; for bright stars a larger one is safer against changing seeing.
  • With the aperture and the annulus in different units (× FWHM and px), frames whose seeing puts the aperture over the annulus are flagged. An orange note gives the FWHM at which that happens.
  • Open Profile as Graph opens the profile, its fits and the curve of growth in a graph window.

Settings

SettingDefaultWhat it does
Aperture radius8 px (1.7 in × FWHM)The radius of the circle whose counts are summed.
Sky annulus12 to 18 px (1.9 to 2.55 in × FWHM)The ring the sky is estimated from. It must start outside the aperture.
SkySigma-clipped median (photutils)How the sky per pixel is found from the annulus. Also Sigma-clipped mean; Mode, SExtractor (2.5 median − 1.5 mean); and AstroImageJ (2σ-rejected mean).
Recenter on each star in every frameOnOff: apertures stay where they were placed, moved only by the drift correction (Correct tab).
ChannelThe firstThe channel measured, in an image with several.
Detector › GainThe header's GAIN or EGAIN; else 1 e⁻/ADUElectrons per count. With 1 e⁻/ADU the errors are understated for most cameras.
Detector › Read noiseRDNOISE, READNOIS or RDNOIS; else 0In electrons per pixel.
Detector › Dark currentDARKCUR; else 0Electrons per pixel per second. It adds noise even when the dark was subtracted.
Detector › SaturationSATURATE or SATLEVELA star whose peak reaches it is flagged. With none, integer frames take the 2ⁿ − 1 ceiling their values reach (4095 for 12-bit data), and the Data Log says so.
Detector › Linearity limitNoneA star whose peak reaches it is flagged.
Site and target › Latitude, E longitude, Height mThe header's siteThe observatory, in degrees (31.9583 or 31:57:30), east positive, and meters.
Site and target › RA, DecT1's position on the WCS; else the header'sThe target's ICRS (J2000) coordinates.
Site and target › Track by each frame's WCSOnShown when the frames have a WCS. With every frame plate-solved, each star is looked for at its sky position in each frame.
Magnitude zero pointEmpty (0)Added to every magnitude. Empty or 0 gives instrumental magnitudes.
Normalize to the medianOnDivides each light curve by its median.
  • Each Detector field shows the header's value and keyword in gray, or "none in header". Type a value to use it instead; an orange line says so, and Use Header's clears it.
  • What you type for one image (site, target, detector values, zero point) is saved with that image. Where the header lacks a value, a Use Last button (Use Last Site, for example) fills in what you last typed on another image. Check that it is right for these frames.

The light curve

  • Y is the target's relative flux (rel_flux_T1) with its error bars, divided by its median while Normalize to the median is on.
  • X is BJD_TDB in days from the whole Julian day before the first frame, which the axis title gives: "BJD_TDB − 2461203 (d)", for example. Add the day back to read a time as BJD_TDB; the Data Log table has full BJD_TDB to 8 decimals.
  • When a frame has no BJD_TDB (the site or the target is missing), X is JD_UTC. When the frames give no observation times, X is the image's own frame time in seconds, else the frame number.
  • A frame where the target or a comparison star is flagged is left out. The tab says how many frames were left out and why, and the Data Log lists every one.
  • Under Add to the light curve, Comparison stars adds each comparison star's relative flux and Check stars each check star's. Open Light Curve opens the light curve again with what is checked.
  • Under Detrending graph, check Airmass, Sky, FWHM or X, Y (the field's move from the start frame; when the series is drift-corrected or plate-solved, the target's move from the first frame) and click Open Detrending Graph. It has one panel for each against the light curve's X, to show whether a trend in the light curve follows one of them. Transit Fit can remove such a trend (Detrend against).

Measure Stars in One Image

  1. Open the FITS image and the image inspector's Toolkits tab.
  2. Click Place apertures and click each star, or type each star's position under Add at Coordinates.
  3. Choose the radii from a star's Seeing profile (Measure Profile, then Use Suggested Radii), and check the Detector values.
  4. Click Measure Frame. The table shows each star's X, Y, FWHM, SNR, Mag and Rel on the frame shown. The full table goes to the Data Log, with the radii, the detector values used and where each came from, and the frame's mid-exposure JD_UTC, BJD_TDB and airmass.
  5. Click Copy Table to copy the table, with its column names, for a spreadsheet.
  • Mag is instrumental. The difference between two stars' Mag in one image is their magnitude difference in that filter.
  • To put the stars on a catalog's scale, type a zero point in Magnitude zero point: a star's catalog magnitude minus its Mag. Click Measure Frame again: every magnitude adds it, and the column reads Mag+ZP. Color terms are left aside. Measure Series's Mag columns use it too.
  • Roles matter only for the relative flux (Rel).

Measure Other Nights of the Same Field

  1. Place and check the apertures on one night's frames. The frames need a WCS (see Plate Solving), so that every aperture has a right ascension and declination; Measure Other Nights… is dimmed until then.
  2. Click Measure Other Nights… and choose one or more folders of FITS frames of the same field, one folder per night.
  3. Wait while each night is measured in the background, with its progress and Cancel. The apertures are placed by their RA and Dec on that night's frames, recentered, and measured with these settings.
  4. Read the graph that opens: the target's light curve for every night, one curve per night, against BJD_TDB (JD_UTC when a night has no BJD_TDB) in days from the first night's whole Julian day. Each night's table goes to the Data Log.

A folder that can't be measured is named in the tab with the reason: no FITS frames, no WCS in its first frame, or an aperture that falls outside its frames.

Export the Results

The light curve and detrending graphs are ordinary graph windows: save, export or analyze them as any graph. The Data Log keeps each Measure Frame and Measure Series table at full precision. For files to send on, measure the series, then use the Export menu under the series' result in the tab. Each file is written from the measurements, not from the graph, and the Data Log notes what was written.

Export menuWhat it saves
AAVSO Report…A file in the AAVSO Extended File Format (version 1.2), ready to upload to WebObs.
ExoClock Light Curve…A text file for ExoClock: "#" header lines (the target, the comparison stars, the time scale and the filter), then the time, the relative flux divided by its median, and its error.
ETD Light Curve…A text file for the ETD (now VarAstro), with no header lines: the time, the differential magnitude (0 at the median) and its error.
Measurements Table…The whole Measure Series table, one row per frame, tab-separated (.tsv).
  • The ExoClock and ETD files hold the light curve's frames, not detrended. Choose their time first in the Time menu beside Export: BJD_TDB (the default), JD_UTC or HJD_UTC, each at mid-exposure. On the upload form, choose the same time scale and the middle of the exposure, and flux for the ExoClock file or magnitudes for the ETD file.
  • AAVSO Report… opens a sheet for what the frames don't say: your Observer code, the Star, the Chart, the Filter, Magnitudes, Date and Camera, and each comparison and check star's AUID or chart label with its catalog magnitude in the filter reported. Click Export…. A field missing or typed wrong is named in the sheet before anything is saved.
  • Date is JD (mid-exposure, UTC) or HJD: AAVSO doesn't accept BJD.
  • Magnitudes STD gives the target's magnitude from the comparison stars' catalog magnitudes (not transformed, TRANS=NO); DIF gives the instrumental difference from one comparison star. Several comparison stars are reported as an ensemble (CNAME=ENSEMBLE), which needs a check star: its label goes in KNAME and its computed magnitude in KMAG.
  • MERR is the measured error of the flux ratio. The catalog magnitudes' errors are not added to it; they go in NOTES.

Time a Transit from One Night

Transit Fit fits a limb-darkened transit to one night's light curve and gives the mid-transit time T0, with its uncertainty, in the light curve's time scale (BJD_TDB for a light curve from Measure Series with a site and target): the number transit-timing programs such as ExoClock ask for.

  1. Open the light curve (from Measure Series, or any graph of relative flux against time in days) and, in its inspector's Toolkits category, choose Astronomy › Transit Fit. If the graph has several curves, choose one under Light curve.
  2. Type the planet's period in P (d), and a/R★ and the impact parameter b (or choose i (°) for the inclination), from its published values, for example in the NASA Exoplanet Archive. Leave their Fit boxes unchecked: one night can't measure the period and constrains the other two poorly.
  3. Leave T0 and Rp/R★ blank with Fit checked.
  4. Choose the Limb darkening: Fixed u1, u2, typed from tables for your filter and the star, or Fit (Kipping q1, q2).
  5. Choose the detrending: Detrend in time for a slow drift, and under Detrend against any of Airmass, Sky (T1), FWHM, X shift, Y shift or Rotation.
  6. Click Fit. The best fit is drawn on the graph.
  7. Click Run MCMC for the uncertainties to report. It runs in the background, with its progress and Cancel.
  8. Read the results in the tab; the table also goes to the Data Log. Copy Results copies it, and Open Residuals as Graph shows the data minus the model.
  9. For O − C, open Exposure, noise and ephemeris and type the reference T0 (a full BJD_TDB) and P, with their errors.

Transit Fit settings

SettingDefaultWhat it does
T0Fit; blank starts at the dipThe mid-transit time, in X's days, or the full date when the X axis's title names its origin.
Rp/R★Fit; blank starts from the depthThe planet-to-star radius ratio.
a/R★FixedThe orbit's semi-major axis in stellar radii. Left blank, it is fitted, with a warning.
b or i (°)b, fixedThe impact parameter, or the inclination in degrees. Left blank, it is fitted, with a warning.
P (d)Fixed; requiredThe orbital period in days.
Limb darkeningFixed u1, u2The quadratic law's coefficients. Fit (Kipping q1, q2) fits them within physical limits (Kipping 2013), as does leaving u1 or u2 blank.
Detrend in timeNoneLinear or Quadratic adds a drift in time to the baseline.
Detrend againstNone checkedAdds a baseline term for each quantity checked: the light curve's own detrending values, and other open graphs' curves, listed as "Title › sweep".
Exposure (s)BlankThe exposure the model is averaged over. Blank: the frames' median EXPTIME, which a light curve from Measure Series carries; else the spacing of the points.
e, ω (°)0, 90The orbit's eccentricity and argument of periastron, fixed.
Inflate errors by the red-noise β (Winn et al. 2008)On; bins from 10 to 30 minSee How the fit works.
Ephemeris for O − CEmptyA reference T0 and P, each with its error.

Keep a term under Detrend against only when it lowers the BIC by more than 2: the results give ΔBIC for each. In a Protocol or Batch step, type the terms' names, such as Airmass.

What Transit Fit reports

ResultWhat it is
T0The mid-transit time as a full date (the X axis's day added back), with its uncertainty, also in minutes.
Rp/R★, a/R★, b or i, P, u1, u2Each parameter, with its uncertainty or marked fixed.
Depth (Rp/R★)² (ppt)The squared radius ratio, in parts per thousand.
T14, T23 (h)The time from first to fourth contact, and from second to third (Winn 2010).
ρ★ (g/cm³)The star's mean density that a/R★ and P imply, when a/R★ is fitted.
Residual RMS (ppt)The scatter of the data about the model.
Reduced χ², Error scale, Red-noise βSee How the fit works.
BIC, ΔBICχ² + the number of free parameters × ln(the number of points), and its change from adding each baseline term.
Epoch, Predicted mid-transit, O − CWith an ephemeris: the transit's number from the reference time, its predicted time, and observed minus predicted, in minutes with its error.
  • After Fit the ± are 1σ from the fit's curvature. After Run MCMC each value is the median with its 16th–84th percentile interval.
  • With an ephemeris typed, the light curve must be in BJD_TDB with its full dates (its X axis title names the origin, such as BJD_TDB − 2461203), and the reference T0 within 10,000 periods of the night: otherwise Transit Fit stops and says why. Clear the ephemeris to fit without O − C.
  • Transit Fit models relative flux, so convert a light curve in magnitudes first (10^(−0.4 Δm), with Data Transform).
  • When the tab says there is no transit-like dip, the best transit fits little better than a flat line: check that the light curve covers the transit and that P, a/R★ and b are right.

How the fit works

  • Model: Mandel & Agol's (2002) transit with quadratic limb darkening, averaged over each exposure (Kipping 2010), times the baseline c0 × (1 + Σ cₖ dₖ), where each dₖ is a detrending term: time about the starting T0, or a quantity about its mean.
  • Best fit: bounded Levenberg–Marquardt from several starts.
  • Errors: the light curve's error bars (1 for each point when it has none) are multiplied by the Error scale, which makes the reduced χ² 1. While Inflate errors by the red-noise β is on, they are then multiplied by β: the ratio of the residuals' scatter in bins of 10 to 30 minutes to what white noise would give, never less than 1 (Winn et al. 2008).
  • Uncertainties: an affine-invariant ensemble MCMC (Goodman & Weare 2010, as emcee), with uniform priors within each parameter's bounds, run until the chains are 50 autocorrelation times long. When it reaches its step limit first, the tab says the intervals are rough.

Protocols, Batch Processing and the AI Assistant

  • Protocols: in the Protocols window, Add Step › Astro › Aperture Photometry (Series)… measures the series on the image window chosen under Run, with the apertures and settings saved with that image, opens its light curve and logs the full table. It is the protocol's first step, or follows a Calibrate Frames or Plate Solve step; the steps after it run on the light curve, for example Transit Fit or Transit Search. Place the apertures in the tool first.
  • Batch Processing has no Aperture Photometry operation. Its Astro group, like a Protocol's, runs Transit Fit and Transit Search on light curves.
  • AI Assistant: ask it to list an image's apertures, to place one on a star (at a FITS pixel position, or at a right ascension and declination through the image's WCS) or delete one, to run Measure Frame or Measure Series and open the light curve, and to run Transit Fit. It uses the apertures and settings saved with the image, and the apertures it places or deletes undo with ⌘Z. It can't change the radii, sky, detector, site, target or zero point, export the reports, or run Measure Other Nights: do those in the tab.

How Aperture Photometry Measures

The methods follow AstroImageJ (Collins et al. 2017) and photutils, the Astropy photometry package, and the Data Log tables use AstroImageJ's column names.

ColumnHow it is computed
X(FITS), Y(FITS)The star's center where it was measured, in FITS pixels (from 1, Y from the bottom).
Sky/PixelThe Sky statistic of the pixels whose centers lie in the annulus.
Source-SkyThe star's net counts F, in ADU: the aperture's sum less Sky/Pixel × the aperture's area. Each pixel counts by the exact fraction of it inside the circle.
Source_Error, Source_SNRThe error is σ ÷ g, from the CCD equation: σ² = g F + n (1 + n ÷ nsky) (g S + D + R²), in electrons. SNR is F ÷ the error.
Mag, Mag_err−2.5 log₁₀(F ÷ EXPTIME) plus the Magnitude zero point, and 1.0857 ÷ SNR (2.5 ÷ ln 10).
PeakThe highest pixel in the aperture, before the sky is subtracted.
FWHM, FWHM_MeanThe star's FWHM, from a Gaussian fit to its sky-subtracted radial profile, and the frame's mean over its stars that aren't saturated or lost.
rel_flux, rel_flux_errFor the target or a check star, F over the comparison stars' summed F. For a comparison star, F over the sum of the other comparison stars (with two or more). The error is rel_flux × √((σT ÷ FT)² + (σE ÷ FE)²), where FE is that sum and σE² the sum of its stars' σ².
JD_UTC, BJD_TDB, HJD_UTCThe frame's mid-exposure time on each scale.
AIRMASS, AIRMASS_headerThe airmass computed from the target's altitude, and the header's AIRMASS.
  • CCD equation (Merline & Howell 1995; Howell 2006): g is the gain (e⁻/ADU), n the aperture's area in pixels, nsky the number of sky pixels the sky estimate kept, S the sky per pixel (ADU), D the dark electrons per pixel in the exposure (dark current × EXPTIME) and R the read noise (e⁻). It has no scintillation term.
  • Sky: Sigma-clipped median is the median after clipping at 3σ about the median, up to 10 times, so stars in the annulus don't raise it; Sigma-clipped mean is the mean after the same clipping. SExtractor's mode is 2.5 median − 1.5 mean, or the median in a crowded annulus, where |mean − median| ÷ SD ≥ 0.3. AstroImageJ's is the mean after rejecting pixels beyond 2σ of the mean, repeated until it settles.
  • Recentering, as AstroImageJ does it: the sky from the annulus is subtracted, the aperture moves to the center of mass of the pixels within its radius (at least 3 px), and this repeats until a step moves it less than 0.01 px (at most 100 times). A single pixel far above its neighbors (a hot pixel or a cosmic ray) counts as its neighbors' median while recentering; the counts use every pixel's true value.
  • Seeing: a star's FWHM counts toward the frame's mean only between 0.7 px and the annulus's outer radius and within 2.5 times the neighboring frame's.
  • Tracking: frames are measured outward from the one the target was placed on. Each star is looked for where it was in the neighboring frame, moved by the drift correction or, without one, by the field's move: each frame's brightest stars are matched to the previous frame's, by their common shift or by star triangles as astroalign does (Beroiz et al. 2020), which follows jumps of tens of pixels and a turning field. With Track by each frame's WCS on and every frame plate-solved, it is looked for at its sky position instead. It is then recentered. An aperture placed on another frame is carried to the target's frame first: by the drift correction or the frames' WCS when there is one, else, with Recenter on, by matching the two frames' stars. With Recenter off and neither, place every aperture on the target's frame; the Data Log says when one wasn't.
  • Lost stars: a star that moves more than 2 px or half the aperture radius, whichever is larger, away from the other stars' median move, or that can't be recentered, is tried once more from where that move puts it. Failing again, it is measured there without recentering and flagged lost in that frame.
  • Flags: a star is flagged in a frame when its peak reaches the saturation level or the Linearity limit, when its aperture runs off the image or holds pixels with no value (NaN or BLANK, which are left out of the sums), when it is lost, when a hot pixel or cosmic ray in its aperture adds more than 3 times its error, when its annulus has no usable sky or starts inside its aperture, or when no star is found (SNR below 3). The frame stays in the Data Log table with the reasons. A flagged check star leaves that frame out of its own curve only.

Times, airmass, site and target

  • Mid-exposure: each frame's mid-exposure UTC comes from DATE-AVG or MJD-AVG; else the mean of DATE-BEG and DATE-END (or MJD-BEG and MJD-END); else the start (DATE-BEG, MJD-BEG, DATE-OBS with TIME-OBS, UT or UTSTART when it holds only the date, MJD-OBS, JD-OBS or JD) plus half of EXPTIME (or EXPOSURE). TIMESYS names the scale (UTC, TAI, GPS or TT; UTC when absent). Without an exposure time the start stands in for the middle, and the Data Log says so.
  • BJD_TDB: UTC goes to TAI through the leap-second table (checked through 30 June 2027, by IERS Bulletin C 72; frames dated later get a Data Log note, since a leap second announced after that would put their times 1 s off), to TT (TAI + 32.184 s), and to TDB by Fairhead & Bretagnon's (1990) series. BJD_TDB is TDB plus the light travel time from the observatory to the solar-system barycenter along the target's direction (Eastman, Siverd & Gaudi 2010), as astropy computes it, without the Shapiro delay (at most 0.1 ms). HJD_UTC is the same to the Sun's center, labeled in UTC.
  • Airmass: from the target's altitude at mid-exposure, without refraction, by Kasten & Young (1989). The Detrending graph shows the header's AIRMASS only in frames where the airmass can't be computed (no site or target coordinates), and the Data Log says which it shows.
  • Site: typed, else the header's OBSGEO-X/Y/Z, or SITELAT and SITELONG (or LAT-OBS and LONG-OBS, OBSGEO-B and OBSGEO-L, or LATITUDE and LONGITUD, west-positive) with SITEELEV, ALT-OBS or OBSGEO-H (0 m when absent).
  • Target: typed, else T1's position on the WCS where it was placed, else the header's OBJCTRA and OBJCTDEC (or RA_OBJ and DEC_OBJ, OBJRA and OBJDEC, RA and DEC), precessed to J2000 from another EQUINOX. FK4 (B1950) coordinates aren't converted, so type ICRS ones. RA and DEC may be the telescope's pointing, and the Data Log says when they were used: type the target's coordinates if they could differ.

Back to Contents

Transit Search and Phase Fold

Part of the Astronomy toolkit.

Two tabs in the inspector's Toolkits category, under Astronomy, work on a light curve (a graph of flux or magnitude against time). Transit Search (BLS) finds the period of repeating box-shaped dips, such as exoplanet transits or eclipses. Phase Fold lays every cycle on the others at a period, so the dip's shape shows. Both need a light curve that covers two cycles or more; to time one night's transit, use Transit Fit (see Aperture Photometry and Transit Fit › Time a Transit from One Night).

Transit Search

  1. Open the light curve and, in the inspector's Toolkits category, choose Astronomy › Transit Search (BLS). The search uses the first visible curve with 10 or more points.
  2. In Durations, type the transit durations to try, separated by spaces (0.05 0.1 0.2 by default). Durations and periods are in the X axis's unit, days for most light curves.
  3. Leave Shortest period and Longest period blank to search from 3 × the longest duration to half the time span, or type a range.
  4. Check Dips are: Decreases in Y (flux) or Increases in Y (magnitudes). It is set for you from the Y axis's name or unit.
  5. Choose the Objective, the statistic that ranks the periods: Log likelihood (the default) or Depth signal-to-noise.
  6. Click Search. The search runs in the background, with its progress and Cancel.
  7. Read the best period, transit time, duration and depth in the tab. The full table goes to the Data Log.
  8. Click Open Periodogram to see the objective against period in a new window.
  9. Check the best period's harmonics (half and twice it), and fold the curve in Phase Fold to see the transit.

Try it: in the Welcome window, More Samples › Transit Light Curve, under Astronomy, opens 20 days of a made-up star's brightness, with a planet's transits, at Transit Search.

What is reported

ValueHow it is found
Best periodThe period whose best box scores highest on the Objective.
Transit time (mid-transit)The middle of that box, in the X axis's own time: the first transit at or after the first point.
DurationThe one of the durations you typed that gave that box.
DepthThe weighted mean out of transit minus the weighted mean in transit, each point weighted by 1/error² (equally when the curve has no error bars). For magnitudes it is the rise, in magnitudes.
Depth uncertainty (1σ)√(1/Σw_in + 1/Σw_out), where w is each point's weight in and out of transit.
Depth CIDepth ± z × its uncertainty, at the confidence level in Settings › Statistics.
Depth SNRDepth ÷ its uncertainty.
Log likelihoodHow much better the box fits the points in transit than the out-of-transit level does: ½ Σ w [(y − mean out)² − (y − mean in)²] over those points.
NoiseThe light curve's error bars, when every point has one. Otherwise the SD of the flux about the best box (each side about its own mean, n − 2 degrees of freedom), which slow stellar variation and flares inflate.

How the search works

  • The method is Box Least Squares (Kovács, Zucker & Mazeh 2002), computed as astropy's BoxLeastSquares computes it. The flux is taken relative to its median. At each period and for each duration, boxes are tried on a grid of transit times spaced by a tenth of the duration, and the box with the highest Objective and a positive depth is kept.
  • Periods are spaced evenly in frequency, with a step of the shortest duration ÷ the time span², fine enough not to miss a transit (astropy's autoperiod spacing). A range that needs more than 300,000 periods is not searched: the tab gives the longest period that fits.
  • The shortest duration must be at least the points' median spacing, and the shortest period must be longer than the longest duration.
  • A light curve in magnitudes is searched as its mirror image about the median, so a dip is still a decrease.
  • Graphs keep X to about seven digits, so full Julian dates are stored too coarsely to find a transit's edges. When the tab says so, subtract a start time from X (for example BJD − 2457000) and search again.

Batch Processing and Protocols run the same search (Astro › Transit Search) on every light curve of a file or graph that has 10 or more points, with Dips are set to From the Y axis unless you choose, and the AI Assistant can run it too. The table is the one the tab writes.

Phase Fold

  1. Open the light curve and, in the inspector's Toolkits category, choose Astronomy › Phase Fold.
  2. Type the Period, in the X axis's unit. After a Transit Search on this graph, the tab starts with its best period and transit time; Use This Graph's Transit Search fills them in again.
  3. Type the Epoch, the time that becomes phase 0 (a transit's or a minimum's time). Left blank, it is the first time in the data.
  4. Set Bins, the number of phase bins that are averaged (50 by default, 10–500).
  5. Click Open Folded Curve. The folded curve opens in a new window, and the Data Log notes the period, epoch and bins.
  • Every visible light curve is folded. Each point's phase is (time − epoch) ÷ period, wrapped into −0.5 to 0.5.
  • The larger red points are the means of the points in each of the equal phase bins; a bin with no points is left out.
  • The period must be shorter than the data's time span, so that two cycles or more overlap.
