Resources
Statistics

Statistics: Overview

Statistics run in two places that share the same tests, settings and wording: the Statistics window, described here, and the Statistics tab of a chart's inspector, which draws its results on the chart as effect size brackets (see Statistics on a Chart).

Open the Statistics Window

FromDo this
The Data Log or a text windowSelect a table (one group per column, tabs or commas between the columns, an optional header row) and choose Text Tools › Statistics… (⌘T).
A Spreadsheet windowClick Data Statistics. Select cells first to analyze only those.
A chartOn the inspector's Statistics tab, click Open Full Statistics Window. The window is linked to the chart (see Statistics on a Chart › Linked to a Chart), and each chart has one: clicking again brings it forward.
A Graph windowOn a Pharmacology tab that fits curves, click Open Full Statistics Window, which opens on a copy of the curves' data. For other measurements, select their table in the Data Log and press ⌘T.

From text or a spreadsheet, @Graph works out whether the groups are in rows or columns, and asks when it isn't sure.

Run an Analysis

  1. Open the Statistics window. It shows the Descriptive table of the data and has run no test.
  2. In the Analysis box, choose Compare, Categorical, Correlation or Regression.
  3. In DATA, check the columns to analyze.
  4. Set the analysis up: the zones for Compare (see The Zones, below), or the test or model and its columns under Options for the others.
  5. Click Determine Effect, or press Return. The result appears on the right.
  6. Click Send to Data Log to keep the result, or Export Report… (⌘S) to save it as a text or PDF file. File › Print… (⌘P) prints it.

Each analysis reports its own effect sizes and confidence intervals:

AnalysisWhat it runsSee
CompareGroups or conditions, and the one-sample, two-way, split-plot, mixed-model and whole-distribution designsCompare and Effect Sizes; Tests
CategoricalFisher's exact (2×2 and r×c), McNemar's, Cochran's Q, chi-square goodness-of-fit and independence, one-sample binomialOther Analyses › Categorical Tests
CorrelationPearson r, Spearman ρ and Kendall's τ-bOther Analyses › Correlation and Regression
RegressionSimple linear, multiple regression, ANCOVA, a 4-parameter dose-response fit, and enzyme kinetics, binding and assay modelsOther Analyses
  • Once a result is showing, changing a setting re-runs it. Choosing another Analysis or Design clears the result until you click Determine Effect.
  • Descriptive table and Normality tests, in the DATA zone of every analysis, show those tables at any time without changing the analysis that Determine Effect runs (see Data Checks and Suggestions › Descriptive Statistics). The window returns to the Descriptive table when the data change.
  • Nothing is logged until you click Send to Data Log. The report is headed with the settings and columns that produced it.
  • μ₀ can be typed with a decimal point or a comma. Text that isn't a number stops the run with a message.

The Zones

For Compare, the settings are laid out in zones, in the same order and with the same wording in the Statistics window and on a chart's Statistics tab.

ZoneWhat it sets
Paired / RepeatedOn when each row is one subject measured in every group: the paired form of each comparison then runs, matching values by row. In the window it reads Paired / Repeated measures data.
DATAThe Groups checklist: uncheck a group to leave it out. The window adds Descriptive table, Normality tests and what the design needs (μ₀, the levels of the two factors, the group column). A chart with 2 or more series adds Within category (compare series, not categories).
DATA CHARACTERISTICSChecks of normality, variance, outliers and shape, and the Compare choice they suggest. Advisory only (see Data Checks and Suggestions › Data Checks Are Advisory).
EFFECT SIZECompare (Means, Ratio, Trimmed, H-L shift or Ranks); for Means, Spreads or Question; then the effect size (see Compare and Effect Sizes). On a chart the zone ends with Show Estimation Plot.
TESTIn the window, Design comes first (see Tests › Design). With 3 or more groups, Comparisons: All pairwise (the default) or vs. Control. Then the "Will run: …" line, which names the test, and for Means, Multiple comparisons (3 or more groups) and Tails (see Tests). In the window, "About this test" (ⓘ) explains the test that will run.
DISPLAYIn the window: Show the comparison on other scales, on by default (see Tests › Sensitivity: The Same Comparison on Other Scales).
BRACKETSOn a chart: Compute Brackets, then Display and Position (see Statistics on a Chart).
  • The control starts as the first group. A group named like a control (control, vehicle, baseline, sham, placebo, WT, pre, 0h, t0 and similar) is only suggested, with a Use button: a name never changes the comparisons by itself.
  • In the window, the columns that hold numbers start checked. A text column, such as subject IDs or group labels, starts unchecked and is marked "text"; the designs that read one find it without its being checked.
  • One value column beside a column of group labels (Subject | Treatment | Value) is offered with a Use button, which opens a linked chart of the table read as One Row per Value, so that the window compares those groups.
  • On a chart, or in a window linked to a chart with one series, an unchecked group leaves the chart and every statistic; its data are kept.
  • On a chart, Values from the same sits below Paired / Repeated, for values that aren't independent (see Statistics on a Chart › Values from the Same (Clustered Data)).

Effect Size First: How @Graph Approaches Statistics

@Graph follows the estimation ("new statistics") approach of Cumming & Calin-Jageman (2024): the estimate and its confidence interval are the main result, and the p-value is supporting context. You choose what to compare and the test follows, so the p-value and the CI always answer the same question (see Compare and Effect Sizes); to run a different test, choose a different Compare option. Results show p-values and effect sizes side by side, with no significance stars: you decide what threshold suits your field.

Back to Contents

Compare and Effect Sizes

Compare sets what the groups are compared on: means, a ratio, trimmed means, a Hodges-Lehmann shift or ranks. That one choice fixes the estimate, its effect size and the test, so the p-value and the confidence interval always answer the same question. The choices are the same in the Statistics window and on a chart's Statistics tab, and the ⓘ beside Compare explains each.

Compare Groups

  1. Open the Statistics window, or the Statistics tab of a chart's inspector (see Statistics: Overview).
  2. Turn on Paired / Repeated when each row is one subject measured in every group.
  3. Read DATA CHARACTERISTICS. When the shape of the data suggests another Compare choice, it says so, and Use applies the suggestion (see Data Checks and Suggestions).
  4. Under EFFECT SIZE, choose Compare: Means, Ratio, Trimmed, H-L shift or Ranks. A line below it states the estimate it reports.
  5. For Means, set Spreads (independent groups) or Question (paired data), and choose the effect size (see Effect Sizes for Means, below).
  6. With 3 or more groups, under TEST choose All pairwise or vs. Control. The "Will run: …" line names the test.
  7. Click Determine Effect in the Statistics window, or Compute Brackets on a chart.

The Five Compare Choices

CompareUse it forEstimateEffect size
MeansRoughly symmetric data without far-out valuesDifference in meansHedges' g family
RatioPositive values where a change is proportional, such as concentrations, expression levels and titersRatio of geometric meansThe ratio itself
TrimmedData with outliers or long tails, which pull means and SDs aroundDifference in 20% trimmed meansAKP robust d
H-L shiftSkewed data, where the mean is not a typical valueHodges-Lehmann estimate, in the data's own unitsThe estimate itself
RanksOrdinal scores, and any data whose units don't carry meaningDominance δ, from −1 to 1δ itself

Each choice runs these tests:

Compare2 groups: independent / paired3 or more groups: independent / paired
MeansWelch's t (Student's t with Spreads Assumed equal) / paired tWelch's ANOVA (the classical F with Spreads Assumed equal), then the chosen post-hoc / repeated-measures ANOVA (Greenhouse-Geisser), then paired t-tests
RatioWelch's t on logs / paired t on logsWelch's ANOVA on logs, then Holm-adjusted pairs / Holm-adjusted pairs only
TrimmedYuen's trimmed t / Yuen's paired ttrimmed-means ANOVA, then Holm-adjusted pairs / Holm-adjusted pairs only
H-L shiftMann-Whitney U / Wilcoxon signed-rankKruskal-Wallis, then Holm-adjusted pairs / Friedman, then Holm-adjusted pairs
RanksBrunner-Munzel / exact sign testKruskal-Wallis, then Holm-adjusted pairs / Friedman, then Holm-adjusted pairs
  • Means: the mean difference is reported with its CI, on the test's own standard error and degrees of freedom. Welch's tests are the default because they lose very little power when the variances are equal (Delacre, Lakens & Leys 2017). With paired data, rows missing a value in either column are left out, and the result says how many. Only Means offers one-tailed tests.
  • Ratio: the t-test runs on the natural logs of the values and the result is transformed back, so a ratio of 1 means no difference. It is offered only when every value is above zero, and is not for values already on a log scale. An estimation plot shows it on a log axis marked in ratios.
  • Trimmed: the highest and lowest 20% of each group are set aside. Yuen's trimmed t (Yuen 1974) does not assume equal variances; its paired form uses the Winsorized covariance between conditions. With 3 or more independent groups the omnibus test is Wilcox's trimmed-means ANOVA. With 3 or more repeated conditions no established omnibus test matches this estimate, so the Holm-adjusted pairwise tests stand on their own.
  • H-L shift: for independent groups, the median of all differences between a value in one group and a value in the other. For paired data, the median of the Walsh averages (all pairwise averages) of the paired differences. It is a shift only when the groups have the same shape, or the paired differences are symmetric, and is not in general a difference in medians.
  • Ranks: for independent groups, Cliff's δ = P(A > B) − P(A < B), how much more often one group's values exceed the other's (Cliff 1993). The Brunner-Munzel test allows unequal spreads (Brunner & Munzel 2000; Karch 2021). For paired data, δ is the share of subjects higher in the first condition minus the share higher in the second, leaving out subjects with equal values, with the exact sign test.

Small samples

  • Mann-Whitney and Wilcoxon p-values are exact with fewer than 50 values in each group (or fewer than 50 non-zero paired differences), ties included. Beyond that the table marks the p-value as an approximation.
  • Brunner-Munzel: with 10 or fewer values in a group, p and the CI come from the studentized permutation distribution (Neubert & Brunner 2007; Pauly, Asendorf & Konietschke 2016). It is exact when there are at most 200,000 possible splits of the data, and otherwise uses 10,000 random splits.
  • When every value in one group exceeds every value in the other (δ = ±1), no CI exists and "—" is shown.
  • At very small n a rank-based CI may be unable to reach the requested level. The table then states the level it reaches.
  • H-L shift on independent groups whose spreads differ (Levene's test): a note warns that Mann-Whitney then rejects too often for a difference in medians, and points to Ranks or Trimmed.

Effect Sizes for Means

Means reports a standardized effect size: the mean difference divided by an SD. Two settings in the EFFECT SIZE zone decide which SD, and the test follows the same setting, so an effect size never assumes something its test doesn't.

  • Spreads, for independent groups. May differ (the default) gives Hedges' g* with Welch's tests. Assumed equal gives Hedges' g with Student's t and the classical ANOVA; choose it only when the spreads are known to match, from the design or earlier data. Levene's test is shown beside Spreads for information and never switches it: a Levene p above 0.05 doesn't show that the spreads are equal, and choosing a test from a variance pretest distorts its error rates (Zimmerman 2004).
  • Question, for paired data. Magnitude (the default) gives Hedges' gav: how big was the typical change? Consistency gives Hedges' gz: how consistently did subjects change? The two can differ widely on the same data, and neither is more correct.
  • g or d. Each g is the matching Cohen's d with Hedges' small-sample correction, and is the default. The correction matters most at small n and fades as n grows. Choose d only to match a journal's or a field's convention.
  • Glass's Δ, for a control group. It is offered with Spreads May differ, for two groups (the Control picker beside it chooses which is the control) or for each group vs. a control.

Which effect size, when

DesignSettingEffect size (alternative)Test it goes with
2 independent groupsSpreads: May differHedges' g* (Cohen's d*)Welch's t
2 independent groups, one a controlSpreads: May differ; effect size: Glass's ΔGlass's ΔWelch's t
2 independent groupsSpreads: Assumed equalHedges' g (Cohen's d)Student's t
3+ independent groups, each pairSpreads: May differHedges' g* (Cohen's d*)Welch's ANOVA, then Games-Howell or Dunnett's T3
3+ independent groups, each vs. a controlSpreads: May differ; effect size: Glass's ΔGlass's ΔWelch's ANOVA, then Dunnett's T3 or Games-Howell
3+ independent groups, each pairSpreads: Assumed equalHedges' g (Cohen's d)classical ANOVA, then Tukey, Dunnett or adjusted t-tests
2 paired conditions (or each pair of 3+)Question: MagnitudeHedges' gav (Cohen's dav)paired t (repeated-measures ANOVA, then paired t-tests)
2 paired conditions (or each pair of 3+)Question: ConsistencyHedges' gz (Cohen's dz)paired t (repeated-measures ANOVA, then paired t-tests)
1 column vs. a value (μ₀)AnyHedges' g (Cohen's d)one-sample t

What each one divides by

Effect sizeThe mean difference is divided by
d, gThe pooled SD of the two groups, which assumes equal variances. For one column against a value, the column's own SD.
d*, g* ("d star", "g star")√((s₁² + s₂²)/2), the square root of the average of the two groups' variances (Delacre et al. 2021). A pooled SD weights each variance by its group's size; this weights the two equally.
Glass's ΔThe control group's SD alone (Glass 1976), with the small-sample correction on the control's n − 1 degrees of freedom (Hedges 1981). For a treatment expected to change the spread as well as the mean.
dz, gzThe SD of the paired differences. It shrinks as subjects agree, so a small but consistent change can give a large value.
dav, gavThe average of the two conditions' SDs, (SD₁ + SD₂)/2 (Lakens 2013). It can be compared directly with an independent-groups d or g.
AKP robust d (Trimmed)The 20% Winsorized SD; the result is multiplied by 0.64194 (the 20% Winsorized SD of a normal distribution) so that it matches Cohen's d for normal data (Algina, Keselman & Penfield 2005). For paired data, the two conditions' pooled Winsorized SD.

As a rough guide for d and g, 0.2 is small, 0.5 medium and 0.8 large. A standardized effect size is only as good as its SD: when the data are skewed, or one or two extreme points set the SD, Trimmed or H-L shift answers the same question without being dominated by those points.

Effect Sizes of Other Analyses

The other designs and analyses report these effect sizes (alternatives in parentheses). Overall effect sizes (η², Kendall's W and the like) describe the whole test; the others describe each comparison.

AnalysisDesignEffect size
One-sample t, trimmed t, Wilcoxon or sign test (by Compare)1 column vs. μ₀g (d); AKP robust d; Hodges-Lehmann difference from μ₀; δ = P(X > μ₀) − P(X < μ₀)
Welch's or classical one-way ANOVA3+ independent groups, Meansη², ω², Cohen's f
Repeated-measures ANOVA3+ repeated conditions, Meanspartial and generalized η², Cohen's f
Two-way ANOVAtwo crossed factorspartial η² and Cohen's f for each effect; each post-hoc pair: d
Split-plot (mixed) ANOVAone between-, one within-subjects factorpartial and generalized η², Cohen's f
Linear mixed modelgroups × repeated conditions, missing values allowedmodel-based means and differences; marginal and conditional R²
Kolmogorov-Smirnov2 independent groups, whole distributionsD (0 to 1)
Fisher's exact2×2, independentln(odds ratio) (odds ratio, relative risk)
McNemar's2×2, pairedΔp, the difference in proportions (paired odds ratio, ln(odds ratio), Cohen's g)
Cochran's Q; χ² independence; χ² goodness-of-fitbinary or categoricalKendall's W; Cramér's V and its bias-corrected form (Bergsma 2013); Cohen's w
One-sample binomial1 binary column vs. p₀observed proportion − p₀
Correlationone X, one YPearson r (Spearman ρ, Kendall's τ-b)
Multiple Regressionone Y, 2+ predictorsR² and Cohen's f
ANCOVAgroups adjusted for covariatespartial η² and Cohen's f; each adjusted pair: d
  • η² describes the sample and runs high at small n. ω² is the less biased estimate of the population's share of variance.
  • Generalized η² (Olejnik & Algina 2003; Bakeman 2005) keeps between-subject variability in the denominator, so it can be compared with η² from a between-subjects study of the same effect. Partial η² from a within-subjects design is larger and cannot be compared that way. It is shown without a CI.
  • D (Kolmogorov-Smirnov) is the largest gap between the two cumulative distributions, from 0 (identical) to 1 (no overlap).
  • For Cohen's w, 0.1 is small, 0.3 medium and 0.5 large.

Direction of an Effect

Effect sizes are signed: negative when the first-named group or condition is lower. On a profile with a control group (one you chose, or one named like a control, such as Control, Vehicle or WT), a bracket with the control reads as the other group minus the control, so each treatment's effect has its own sign.

Settings › Statistics › Always show effect sizes as positive restates a negative comparison the other way round: the group names are swapped, and the estimate, its CI, the test statistic and the effect size are given for that order.

  • A one-tailed table of all pairs keeps its tested order, since the row order is the hypothesis, and says so.
  • A chart bracket names no direction, so its effect size and CI are shown as positive.
  • An Estimation Plot stays signed as plotted: the later group minus the earlier.
  • η², ω², Cramér's V and Kendall's W have no sign and are never changed.

Confidence Intervals

Settings › Statistics › Default confidence level (90%, 95% or 99%; 95% unless changed) applies to every CI. Its α (1 − the level) is also the threshold of the verdicts the tables state: Mauchly's test, the interaction verdicts of the two-way and split-plot ANOVA, and Levene's test. Changing it re-runs a result already shown.

Estimate or effect sizeHow its CI is found
Mean differenceFrom the test's own standard error and degrees of freedom.
d, g, d*, g*, dz, gzBy inverting the noncentral t distribution of the test that goes with it (Steiger & Fouladi 1997; Cumming & Finch 2001). It is usually asymmetric, so it is shown as a range, never ± a margin.
Glass's ΔA noncentral t on the control's degrees of freedom (Hedges & Olkin 1985).
dav, gavBootstrap (Fitts 2025): no validated formula exists for this divisor in a paired design.
AKP robust dBootstrap. The trimmed-mean difference itself gets Yuen's CI.
Hodges-Lehmann estimateBy inverting the Mann-Whitney or signed-rank test (Hollander, Wolfe & Chicken 2014). Exact for small samples; otherwise from the tie-corrected normal approximation.
Dominance δFrom the Brunner-Munzel test or, for paired data, the sign test's exact Clopper-Pearson interval.
η², partial η², ω², Cohen's fBy inverting the noncentral F distribution (Steiger 2004; Smithson 2001), at 1 − 2α.
R² (multiple regression)By inverting Fisher's (1928) exact distribution of R², which treats the predictors as measured rather than set by design; at 1 − 2α. R's MBESS package approximates the same interval (Lee 1971).
Pearson rFisher's z-transform.
Spearman ρ, Kendall's τ-bBootstrap up to n = 1,000. Above that, Fisher's z with Bonett & Wright's (2000) variances.
Kendall's W, Cramér's V, Cohen's wBootstrap, keeping each test's paired or independent structure.
Odds ratiosExact intervals (see Other Analyses › Categorical Tests).

Each interval comes from the same test as its p-value where one exists, so the two normally agree: a CI that excludes zero goes with a significant p. With 3 or more groups, pairwise CIs are simultaneous (see Tests › Multiple Comparisons).

Variance-explained effect sizes

  • 1 − 2α is 90% when the confidence level is 95%. At that level the CI excludes zero exactly when the F test is significant at α (Steiger 2004).
  • For a repeated-measures or split-plot within-subjects effect, the interval uses the Greenhouse-Geisser df of the p reported.
  • The interval is for the population's share of variance, the quantity a power analysis plans with (Cohen 1988): the noncentral-F interval for the noncentrality λ, converted by λ/(λ + N). N is the number of observations the effect is estimated from: all values for a between-subjects effect, subjects × conditions for a within-subjects effect, and the subjects for a split-plot's between-subjects effect.
  • R's MBESS package computes the same interval (Kelley 2007). R's effectsize package and JASP convert by λ/(λ + df_error) instead, so their intervals come out higher and wider. The two are not interchangeable.
  • With Welch's ANOVA, η², ω², their CI and Cohen's f still come from the classical ANOVA table, so with very unequal spreads the CI need not agree with Welch's p-value.
  • The sample η² overestimates the population's share at small n, so it can sit near or above the upper end of its interval.

Bootstrap intervals

A bootstrap is used only where no formula fits. Each uses 10,000 resamples and is seeded from the data, so unchanged data give the identical interval. Settings › Statistics › Bootstrap CI method chooses BCa (bias-corrected and accelerated; the default) or Percentile. A plain percentile interval is too narrow at small n, and BCa corrects it for bias and skew (Efron & Tibshirani 1993); choose Percentile only to reproduce a number computed with it.

  • A result row names the method, such as "(BCa bootstrap)", and a chart bracket draws a bootstrap CI in curly braces.
  • Warn on small-sample bootstrap CIs (Settings › Statistics; on, below n = 5, by default) adds a note when a bootstrap CI rests on fewer values per group or pair than that.
  • The Estimation Plot's medians and trimmed means always use the smoothed bootstrap's percentile interval.

Back to Contents

Tests

The TEST zone of the Statistics window sets how a comparison is tested: the design, which comparisons are made with 3 or more groups, the post-hoc and the tails. The test itself follows from the Compare choice (see Compare and Effect Sizes). The "Will run: …" line names it, and the ⓘ beside "About this test" describes it.

Design

The Design picker, at the top of the TEST zone, sets which family of tests the comparison uses. What a design needs from the data (μ₀, the levels of the two factors, the group column) is set in DATA. Choosing another Design clears the result until you click Determine Effect.

DesignDataWhat runs
Groups or conditions (the default)2 or more columns: one per group, or one per condition with Paired / Repeated measures data on.The analysis the Compare choice sets (see Compare and Effect Sizes).
One sample vs. a valueOne column, and the hypothesized value μ₀ typed in DATA.By Compare: the one-sample t-test (Means); the one-sample t-test on logs, for the geometric mean over μ₀ (Ratio); the one-sample trimmed t (Trimmed); the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, with the Hodges-Lehmann pseudo-median minus μ₀ (H-L shift); or the exact sign test, with δ = P(X > μ₀) − P(X < μ₀) (Ranks).
Two-way (factorial)One column for each cell of two crossed between-subjects factors, ordered A1B1, A1B2, …, A2B1, … (B changes fastest), with Factor A levels and Factor B levels set in DATA.Two-way ANOVA on means, then its own post-hoc.
Split-plot (mixed)One row per subject: one column per repeated condition, and the groups, as codes (0, 1, 2…) or labels (WT, KO), in the column chosen under Group column (between-subjects factor).Split-plot ANOVA on means. Rows missing a value are left out, and a note gives the count.
Mixed model (repeated measures)The split-plot layout, or one value per row with a column naming each row's source.A linear mixed model, which keeps subjects with missing conditions (see Linear Mixed Model, below).
Whole distributions (KS)Exactly 2 columns, taken as independent groups.The two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, which responds to any difference in location, spread or shape.
  • Two-way: columns named for both levels, such as WT Veh, WT Drug, KO Veh, KO Drug, give the levels their names in the result. See Two-Way ANOVA, below.
  • Split-plot and Mixed model: the data checks look at each group × condition cell, and the Variance line tests the groups' spreads at each condition (Levene's test). For split-plot ANOVA, see ANOVA Tables, below.
  • Whole distributions (KS): D, the largest gap between the two groups' cumulative distributions (0 to 1), is both the statistic and the effect size. The p-value is exact unless the two group sizes multiply to more than 10 million. A significant D says that the distributions differ, not how; for a difference in location with its CI, use Groups or conditions.
  • The Compare choice applies only to Groups or conditions and One sample vs. a value; for the other designs, the EFFECT SIZE zone says what they report. Two-way and Whole distributions take every value as a different subject, and warn when the data are marked paired.

Multiple Comparisons (3 or More Groups)

  1. In TEST, set Comparisons to All pairwise (the default) or vs. Control, which compares each group only with the group chosen under Control: a smaller family, and so more power. A group named like a control (Control, Vehicle, WT) is suggested with a Use button.
  2. For Means, choose the post-hoc under Multiple comparisons. The ⓘ beside the picker describes the one selected.

For Means, the Multiple comparisons picker lists only the post-hocs that fit the design, the recommended one first:

  • Independent groups, Spreads May differ: Games-Howell (recommended) or Dunnett's T3 (Dunnett 1980) for all pairs; Dunnett's T3 (recommended) or Games-Howell for vs. Control. Both compare each pair on its own two variances, beside Welch's ANOVA. With small groups (fewer than about 50 each) prefer T3 for all pairs too: Games-Howell can then reject slightly too often.
  • Independent groups, Spreads Assumed equal: Tukey HSD for all pairs or Dunnett for vs. Control, or Holm-Bonferroni, Šidák or Bonferroni, all on the pooled variance, beside the classical F.
  • Paired / Repeated: paired t-tests adjusted by Holm-Bonferroni (recommended), Šidák or Bonferroni. Tukey, Games-Howell and Dunnett assume independent groups and are not offered.
  • Ratio, Trimmed, H-L shift and Ranks: the pairwise p-values are Holm-adjusted over the comparisons tested.
Post-hocIts p-values and CIs come from
Tukey HSDThe exact studentized-range distribution (Tukey-Kramer for unequal group sizes).
Games-HowellThe studentized-range distribution, with each pair's own variances and Welch's degrees of freedom.
Dunnett's T3The studentized maximum modulus distribution for the whole family, with each pair's Welch t-test at its own degrees of freedom.
Dunnett (vs control)The exact joint distribution of the comparisons with the control.

Pairwise CIs are simultaneous, so all the rows can be read together. A mean-difference CI is adjusted as its p-value is. With Holm, and for every effect-size CI, the interval is the Bonferroni one at level 1 − α/m for m comparisons (98.3% for three comparisons at 95%). The exception is Cohen's d in a two-way ANOVA's post-hoc: its CI is per comparison, at the confidence level itself. Holm's procedure has no exactly matching interval, so a Holm p just under the threshold can sit beside a CI that still includes zero.

  • A pair that can't be tested (too few values) is left out, with a note saying so.
  • With paired data and 3 or more conditions, each pairwise comparison uses every subject observed in both of its conditions, and the omnibus test uses the subjects observed in all of them.

One- and Two-Tailed Tests

Tests are two-tailed by default. The Tails picker (Means only) offers one-tailed t-tests and one-tailed Dunnett, Dunnett's T3, Holm, Šidák and Bonferroni comparisons. Tukey HSD and Games-Howell have no one-tailed form, so the picker is hidden for them. A one-tailed choice shows an orange reminder that an effect in the other direction cannot be significant. The CIs become one-sided too (the bound in the tested direction), so each excludes zero exactly when its one-tailed p is significant.

  • The choices are One-tailed (first > second) and One-tailed (first < second). Against a control they read as each group vs. the control; for one sample, as above or below μ₀.
  • Where the picker is hidden the test runs two-tailed, whatever was chosen before.

ANOVA Tables

AnalysisWhen it runsWhat the table reports
One-way ANOVAMeans, 3 or more independent groupsWelch's F, or the classical F with Spreads Assumed equal, and its p; η², ω² and Cohen's f, with 90% CIs for ω² and f; then the post-hoc table.
Repeated-measures ANOVAMeans, 3 or more repeated conditionsF; partial η² and Cohen's f with 90% CIs; generalized η²; Mauchly's test with the Greenhouse-Geisser and Huynh-Feldt corrections (see below); then the post-hoc rows, each with the mean difference and a CI adjusted like its p-value.
Split-plot (mixed) ANOVADesign: Split-plot (mixed)F, p, partial η² and Cohen's f with 90% CIs, and generalized η², for the between-subjects effect, the within-subjects effect and their interaction, with the same sphericity handling.
  • For what each effect size means and how its CI is found, see Compare and Effect Sizes.
  • ω² can be slightly negative when F is below 1.
  • Split-plot: with unequal group sizes the within-subjects effect uses Type III sums of squares (the groups weighted equally), as SPSS and R's afex report. The group column is never used as a within-subjects condition, even if it is checked.

Repeated-Measures ANOVA and Sphericity

Sphericity means that the differences between every pair of conditions have the same variance. When it fails, the uncorrected F test gives p-values that are too small.

Repeated-measures ANOVA and split-plot ANOVA show Mauchly's test and the uncorrected, Greenhouse-Geisser and Huynh-Feldt p-values side by side. The Greenhouse-Geisser p is the result reported, whatever Mauchly's test says: that test has too little power at typical sample sizes to show that sphericity holds, and the correction costs almost nothing when it does (Maxwell & Delaney 2004). In split-plot ANOVA the covariance is pooled within the between-subjects groups. With 2 conditions, or too few complete subjects, the table says that sphericity doesn't apply or can't be tested.

In the tableMeaning
Mauchly's WFrom 0 (severe violation) to 1 (perfect sphericity). Sphericity is not rejected when its p is at or above α, which is 1 − the confidence level in Settings › Statistics (0.05 at 95%).
Greenhouse-Geisser εMultiplies both degrees of freedom of the F test. 1 means no correction; 1/(k − 1), for k conditions, is the strongest correction possible.
Huynh-Feldt εA less conservative correction, which some prefer when the Greenhouse-Geisser ε is above 0.75. Split-plot ANOVA applies Lecoutre's correction to it (Lecoutre 1991).

Two-Way ANOVA

Design: Two-way (factorial). It tests two crossed between-subjects factors, such as genotype × treatment, and their interaction on means, and reports each effect's F, p, partial η² and Cohen's f with 90% CIs.

  1. Give each combination of levels its own column, ordered A1B1, A1B2, …, A2B1, … (B changes fastest), and check those columns.
  2. In TEST, set Design to Two-way (factorial). In DATA, set Factor A levels and Factor B levels.
  3. In TEST, choose the post-hoc under Multiple comparisons: Tukey HSD (the default), Dunnett (vs control), Holm-Bonferroni, Šidák or Bonferroni.
  4. Click Determine Effect.
  • Sums of squares: with the same number of values in every cell, the classical ones (Types I, II and III agree). With unequal numbers, Type III with sum-to-zero contrasts, as SPSS and R's afex report: each effect is adjusted for every other term, and the main effects are about the equal-weight marginal means, the means the post-hoc compares. The table's note says which was used. Every cell needs at least one value.
  • The post-hoc compares the levels of each factor and, when the interaction is significant (p < α, from the confidence level), the simple effects: one factor's levels within each level of the other. All use the ANOVA's pooled error term (the within-groups mean square, MSW). Dunnett compares every level with the first level of its factor, so order the columns with the control first.
  • With unequal cell sizes, the main-effect comparisons use estimated marginal means (each level's cell means averaged with equal weight), each with its own SE.
  • Each post-hoc row gives the difference with a CI adjusted like its p-value (simultaneous within each family; for Holm, the Bonferroni simultaneous CI), and Cohen's d, the difference ÷ √MSW, with a per-comparison CI.
  • Levene's test and the normality check of each cell are shown for information and don't change the test. A failed check is a reason to weigh the result on ranks too (see Sensitivity, below).
  • When one factor is the same subjects measured repeatedly, use Split-plot (mixed) or Mixed model (repeated measures) instead.

Linear Mixed Model

Design: Mixed model (repeated measures). For subjects in 2 or more groups, each measured at several conditions: neurons of different subtypes recorded at 10 stimulus intensities, say. A subject missing some conditions is kept, and every value it has counts; repeated-measures and split-plot ANOVA leave out the whole subject. Whether the groups' profiles differ in shape is the Group × Condition interaction.

Fit the model

  1. Lay the table out with one row per subject: a group column, as codes (0, 1, 2…) or labels that repeat (WT, KO), and one column per condition.
  2. In TEST, set Design to Mixed model (repeated measures). When the checked columns look like this layout, DATA offers the design with a Use button.
  3. In DATA, check the condition columns and choose the group under Group column (between-subjects factor). For one group measured repeatedly, choose None (one group): the result then compares the conditions.
  4. If several subjects come from one source, choose its column under Values from the same (see Nested data, below).
  5. In TEST, set Trend, Covariance and Spreads, then click Determine Effect.

Settings

SettingWhat it does
TrendNone (any shape), the default: each group has its own mean at every condition. Linear trend, Quadratic trend or Cubic trend fits that curve to each group instead (orthogonal polynomials over the condition values), with fewer parameters and so more power when the profiles are smooth. The interaction then compares the groups' curve coefficients beyond the level.
CovarianceUnstructured (MMRM), the default: every condition has its own variance and every pair its own correlation, so the tests hold whatever the true pattern. Random intercept: each subject has its own level. Random intercept + slope: its own linear trend too. Random intercept + AR(1): residuals correlated as ρ^(lag), fading with distance. The result shows the AIC of each structure that can be fitted (none when values past a limit are fitted), and names another structure when it fits clearly better.
SpreadsAssumed equal, the default: one covariance for every group. May differ, the repeated-measures counterpart of Welch's test: each group has its own residual SD or, with Unstructured, its own covariance. Choose it from the design, such as a treatment expected to change the variability.
Fit on a log scaleOff by default. Fits the natural logs of the values, for data where effects multiply and spreads grow with the mean. Means read as geometric means and differences as ratios (1 is no difference). Every value must be above zero, and standardized effect sizes aren't offered.
Fit values past a limitOff by default. See Values past a limit, below.
  • Unstructured needs at least as many subjects as conditions plus one per group (with Spreads May differ, one more subject than conditions in every group), at most 30 conditions, and every pair of conditions measured together in at least 2 subjects. Otherwise the structure with the lowest AIC among the other three is used, and a note says why.
  • Condition values come from the column names when each holds a distinct number and they share one unit ("0", "5 min", "30 min"); otherwise they are 1, 2, 3…. The panel lists them. The trends and the slope and AR(1) structures use them, so the columns can be any ordered measure, such as times, concentrations or stimulus intensities.
  • A condition where every observed value is the same, such as a normalization baseline, is left out of the model, with a note.
  • The ⓘ beside each setting says more.

What the result shows

Part of the resultWhat it gives
TestsType III F tests of the group, condition and group × condition effects, with Satterthwaite's denominator df. With 3 or more groups, each pair's difference in shape is tested too, Holm-adjusted.
Rate of changeEach group's slope across the conditions (the least-squares line through its model-based means) with its CI, and each pair's difference in slope with its CI and p. With 3 or more groups the CIs are simultaneous, the p-values adjusted, and a test asks whether all slopes are equal.
Means and differencesThe model-based mean of each group at each condition with its 95% CI, and the group differences at each condition, with Hedges' g* and Cohen's d* (see Method, below). All conditions and pairs form one family, with simultaneous CIs and adjusted p-values that match them: a difference is significant exactly when its CI excludes 0.
Difference in levelEach pair of groups' difference averaged over the conditions, with its CI: the follow-up when two groups share a shape.
The fitThe covariance estimates; the REML criterion, AIC and BIC; marginal R², plus conditional R² for the random-effect structures (Nakagawa & Schielzeth 2013; Johnson 2014); and a singular-fit note when a variance is estimated at 0.
Each subject's slopeEvery subject's own least-squares slope over the conditions, by row, and each group's mean and SD of them. They are descriptive; the group slopes are the model's estimates.
  • When one group rises or falls faster than another, report the rate of change beside the interaction: it tests a steady divergence more sensitively than any single condition.
  • To plot or export one rate per subject, click Send to Data Log, select the rows of subject slopes, then choose Text Tools › Send to Spreadsheet….

Values past a limit

A cell such as <0.5 or >29 says only that its value lies past that limit. With Fit values past a limit checked, each such value counts as lying somewhere past its limit, not as missing: a censored mixed model (the mixed-model form of Tobit regression), fitted by maximum likelihood.

  1. In TEST, check Fit values past a limit.
  2. To count empty cells too, set Empty cells to Below a limit or Above a limit (Missing by default) and give the limit: One number, or a column chosen under Limit. A column is offered there only while it is unchecked in DATA. An empty cell whose row has no limit there stays missing, and the result says how many.
  3. Click Determine Effect. A large fit can take up to a minute; Cancel stops it.
  • Means are model-based and can lie beyond anything measured.
  • Tests are likelihood-ratio F tests and CIs are Wald intervals on t, with subjects − groups denominator df. No standard small-sample correction exists for this model, so p-values are approximate and read p ≈ (somewhat liberal with fewer than about 12 subjects per group).
  • The model assumes a normal shape past the limit, so fit on the log scale when that is the better shape.
  • If every value of a group at a condition is past a limit, that mean can't be estimated: choose a trend, or leave that condition out.
  • Chart brackets show Δ, not a standardized effect size. The model can't yet be combined with Values from the same.

Nested data (Values from the same)

When several subjects come from the same source (a batch, plot, classroom, site, plate, litter or animal), they are not independent. In DATA, choose the column naming each subject's source under Values from the same (None by default; text or numbers). The model then adds a random intercept for each source above the subjects' own: (1 | source) + (1 | subject) in lme4's notation.

  • A column named like a source (Animal, Mouse, Slice, Litter, Subject, Classroom, Plate or Site) whose labels repeat is offered with a link.
  • Effects that differ between sources (the groups, when each source gives one group) are tested against the spread between sources, with degrees of freedom near the number of sources, not the number of subjects.
  • When each group comes from one source of its own, sources can't be told apart from groups, so the model is refused: comparing the groups needs more than one source per group, or sources that hold several groups.
  • The result adds the between-source SD and the number of sources, and notes when that variance is estimated at 0.

One value per row (clustered data)

For a table where each row is one measurement (a sample, a plant, a student, a cell) and rows come from shared sources (batches, plots, classrooms, animals).

  1. Set Design to Mixed model (repeated measures), check only the value column, and choose the group column or None (one group). A table laid out this way is recognized in the Groups or conditions and One sample vs. a value designs, which offer this design with a Use button.
  2. Under Values from the same, choose the column naming each row's source. A second level inside the first (classrooms within each school, slices within each animal) goes under Within that, values from the same.
  3. In TEST, set Spreads: May differ (the default) gives each group its own residual SD, the counterpart of Welch's test; Assumed equal uses one.
  4. Click Determine Effect.
  • The model is value ~ group + (1 | source) in lme4's notation, fitted by REML, with Satterthwaite CIs.
  • The result gives each group's mean and the differences with CIs, and Hedges' g, Cohen's d and Δ (see Method, below); the between- and within-source SDs; the ICC, the share of the variation that lies between sources; n rows and n sources for each group; and the same comparison with the rows treated as independent (Welch's, when spreads may differ), with the ratio of the interval widths.
  • A second level, repeated measures in a long table, and the brackets a chart draws from this model are described under Statistics on a Chart › Values from the Same (Clustered Data).

The chart

With the Split-plot or Mixed model design, Make Chart opens a repeated-measures chart linked to this window, and the button then reads Show Chart. In a window opened from a chart of the same table, choosing either design turns that chart into the profile instead (Undo in the chart turns it back). The chart's brackets come from this model, its Statistics tab shows a MIXED MODEL zone in place of Compare, and the settings are shared both ways (see Statistics on a Chart › Repeated Measures by Group).

Method

  • Fitting: REML, as R's mmrm (Unstructured), lme4 (Random intercept, + slope) and nlme (+ AR(1)) fit it.
  • Degrees of freedom: Satterthwaite's. When the covariance estimates sit at a boundary (a variance component at 0 with a random slope, for example), a note says how they were found. When the fit may not have converged (its likelihood curves the wrong way in some direction), a warning says so, and Unstructured falls back to another structure. When they can't be computed at all, the tests and intervals use the residual df, and the table, the brackets and the chart caption say so.
  • The adjustment: single-step, from the multivariate t distribution of the comparisons (Genz & Bretz 2009), which accounts for how they correlate and so is less conservative than Bonferroni. A re-run gives the same p. When it can't reach its accuracy, or the family has more than 40 comparisons, the adjustment is Bonferroni instead, and the table and the brackets say so.
  • Standardized differences divide each difference by the two groups' SDs of a single value, every level's variance included, such as √(σₐ² + σₑ²) with one value per row (Hedges 2007; Westfall, Kenny & Judd 2014). The two SDs are combined as their root mean square, √((S₁² + S₂²)/2), for groups of different subjects or sources (g* and d*; Delacre et al. 2021), or, with one value per row, as their average, (S₁ + S₂)/2, for groups measured within the same sources (gav and dav; Lakens 2013). Hedges' g adds the exact small-sample correction at the df of that SD, ν = S²/(2·Var S). The CIs are approximate (delta method) and a little wider than the differences' own, so one can reach 0 when p is just below α.

Sensitivity: The Same Comparison on Other Scales

In the DISPLAY zone, Show the comparison on other scales (on by default) adds a sensitivity section below a Groups or conditions result: the same comparison on the other Compare scales (Ratio only when every value is above zero). With 2 groups each scale gives its estimate, CI, p-value and test; with 3 or more, its omnibus p (for paired trimmed means, which has no omnibus test, its smallest Holm-adjusted pairwise p). For a Two-way design it adds the same analysis on ranks (Scheirer-Ray-Hare), with H and a chi-square p-value for each factor and the interaction. That needs the same number of values in every A×B cell, and gives too many false positives for the interaction in small samples. A conclusion that holds on only one scale is worth a second look.

Data Checks and Suggestions

The DATA CHARACTERISTICS zone, in the Statistics window and on a chart's Statistics tab, checks the data and suggests what to compare. It updates whenever the data, the checked groups, the pairing or the design changes.

Data Checks Are Advisory

Nothing in the zone changes the analysis: choosing a test from normality or variance pretests is unstable and distorts error rates (Rochon, Gondan & Kieser 2012).

  1. Set Paired / Repeated first: the checks depend on it.
  2. Read each line of DATA CHARACTERISTICS. Its ⓘ gives the detail.
  3. If "Suggested: compare …" differs from your Compare choice and suits your study design, click Use.
LineWhat it reportsHow it is judged
NormalityWhether each group departs from a normal distribution. Normality affects how accurate a Means comparison's p-value and CI are at small n; it does not decide what is compared.By sample size (Kim 2013). n ≤ 50: Shapiro-Wilk (below n = 15 a pass is flagged as weak evidence). n = 51–299: the z-scores of skewness and kurtosis against 3.29. n ≥ 300: |skewness| > 2 or |excess kurtosis| > 4.
VarianceFor independent groups: whether the spreads differ, with the largest/smallest variance ratio for scale. For information: the Spreads choice, not this check, sets the test (see Compare and Effect Sizes › Effect Sizes for Means).Levene's test, Brown-Forsythe version (centered on medians). A p-value within 40% of α (0.03 to 0.07 at 95% confidence) is marked borderline.
OutliersPoints outside their group's Tukey fences, each with its modified z-score for context (Iglewicz & Hoaglin 1993). On a chart, Show possible outliers rings them in orange (see Statistics on a Chart).More than 1.5×IQR outside the quartiles; "far out" beyond 3×IQR.
ShapeThe reason for the suggestion, in words.See The Compare Suggestion, below.
  • With Paired / Repeated on, the checks look at what the paired analysis models, not at each condition's raw values: each subject's difference (2 conditions) or the residuals after removing subject and condition means (3 or more).
  • Paired data get no Variance line, and need none: the paired tests work on each subject's difference. With 3 or more repeated conditions the matching assumption is sphericity, which the repeated-measures ANOVA corrects for itself (see Tests › Repeated-Measures ANOVA and Sphericity).
  • In "Within category" mode, each series is pooled across the categories after centering each category's values on their own mean, so the checks describe the comparison that runs in every category.

The Compare Suggestion

The suggestion is based on the data's shape, not on a normality test. Strong skew is |skewness| ≥ 1 (Bulmer 1979); far-out values lie beyond 3×IQR, in a group of 7 or more.

  • Each independent group is read on its own, since groups may differ in shape. A group needs 8 or more values, and its skew must also be beyond chance by D'Agostino's test, Bonferroni-corrected for the number of groups. The test is run on each group, never on groups pooled together.
  • Skew shared by the groups is read from them together, each centered on its own mean and scaled by its own SD (at least 16 values).
  • Paired data and a single column are one set of at least 16 values: the differences, the within-subject residuals or the column.

The first row that fits gives the suggestion:

The data showSuggested
Strong skew, but every skewed group is large enough for its mean to stay reliable (n ≥ 25 × skewness²; Cochran 1977)Means
Strong right skew, gone on a log scale, in positive values spanning at least a tenfold rangeRatio
Strong skew caused by the far-out values aloneTrimmed
Any other strong skewRanks, which assume no particular shape
No strong skew, but far-out values that make the 20% trimmed mean clearly more precise than the mean (Tukey & McLaughlin 1963; Jaeckel 1971)Trimmed
None of theseMeans
  • Ratio is a prompt, not a rule: no standard cutoff exists for a log scale, so whether changes are proportional comes from what the values are.
  • "Suggested: compare …" is shown in green, with a Use button when it differs from your Compare choice. Nothing switches by itself: Compare opens on Means and changes only when you choose or click Use.
  • A chart saves its Compare choice at its first Compute Brackets, or when it becomes an Estimation Plot, so it reopens on the same analysis.

What the Window Suggests

When the window opens, and whenever the checked columns change, @Graph suggests (never forces) an analysis. A choice you have made is left alone.

SettingWhat the window does
AnalysisColumns that hold only 2 distinct values between them, such as 0 and 1, open on Categorical instead of the data checks, with the suggested test marked ✦: One-sample Binomial for one column; Fisher's Exact for two, or McNemar's when paired; Chi-square independence for three or more, or Cochran's Q when paired. A window opened from a Scatter opens on Correlation.
CountsOne-sample Binomial and Fisher's Exact fill their count fields from your data, and follow a change of columns until you type in them. McNemar's picks up the two checked columns. McNemar's and Cochran's Q need 0/1 coding, and the panel says so when the two values are something else.
Paired / RepeatedPairing is always your choice: @Graph never changes the checkbox from the data. With equal sizes an orange note asks you to check whether the observations are matched. With the box checked and different numbers of values per column (a missing value, say), a note says that the paired tests use only the subjects with a value in every compared column.
DesignThe design follows the data until you pick one: a single column opens as One sample vs. a value, a linked chart with several series per category (not paired) as Two-way (factorial), a linked repeated-measures chart as Mixed model (repeated measures), and anything else as Groups or conditions.
ComparisonsAll pairwise. A column named like a control is offered with a Use button, which switches to vs. Control with it as the control.
CompareMeans (Welch's t or Welch's ANOVA) until you choose, or click Use on the suggestion. A chart shows Means until you first open its Statistics tab or a linked Statistics window, or ask the AI Assistant to run its statistics; from then on it follows your Compare choice.

Skewness and Kurtosis

@Graph reports bias-corrected skewness (G1) and excess kurtosis (G2), the convention used by R, SPSS, GraphPad Prism and Excel.

  • G1 = g1 × √(n(n−1)) / (n−2), where g1 is the uncorrected sample skewness.
  • G2 = (n−1)/((n−2)(n−3)) × ((n+1)×g2 + 6), where g2 is the uncorrected sample excess kurtosis. A normal distribution has G2 = 0.
  • The D'Agostino-Pearson K² normality test uses the uncorrected skewness and kurtosis (√b1 and b2), as its formulas require, not G1 and G2.

Descriptive Statistics

  • Descriptive table (in DATA): n, mean, SD, SEM, median, IQR, min, max, skewness (G1), excess kurtosis (G2) and the 95% CI of the mean for every checked column, whichever analysis is chosen.
  • Normality tests (in DATA): Shapiro-Wilk (n = 3–5,000), D'Agostino-Pearson K² (n ≥ 20) and Kolmogorov-Smirnov (Lilliefors) for every checked column. With Paired / Repeated measures data on, the table adds the paired differences, or the subject + condition residuals with 3 or more conditions: what the test assumes normal, and what the data checks judge.
  • For the Split-plot and Mixed model designs, both tables describe each group × condition cell.

Back to Contents

Other Analyses

Beside Compare, the Statistics window's Analysis box offers Categorical, for counts and yes/no outcomes; Correlation, for one X against one Y; and Regression, for linear models and curve fits. Choose the analysis, set it up under Options, and click Determine Effect (see Statistics: Overview › Run an Analysis).

Categorical Tests

When the checked columns hold only 2 distinct values between them (such as 0 and 1), the window opens on Categorical with the suggested test marked ✦ (see Data Checks and Suggestions › What the Window Suggests). Otherwise choose Categorical under Analysis, then the test. Each test's effect size is listed under Compare and Effect Sizes › Effect Sizes of Other Analyses.

TestData
One-sample BinomialSuccesses (k), Trials (n) and Hypothesized p₀ (0.5 by default), typed under Options. One checked column of two-valued data fills in the counts.
Fisher's Exact (2×2)Two independent groups: the cell counts (a b / c d), typed under Options. Two checked columns of two-valued data fill them in.
McNemar's (Paired 2×2)The same subjects measured twice on one 0/1 outcome, such as before and after: two columns, one row per subject, chosen under Condition 1 column and Condition 2 column.
Cochran's Q (Paired k≥2)2 or more repeated 0/1 conditions: the checked columns, one row per subject. For 2 conditions use McNemar's test: Cochran's Q gives McNemar's exact p only when fewer than 12 subjects changed, and from 12 on McNemar's χ² p without continuity correction.
Chi-square goodness-of-fitObserved counts against an expected distribution: one column, one row per category.
Chi-square independence (r×c)2 or more groups against 2 or more categories: one checked column per group, each cell a category code (0, 1, 2…).
Fisher's Exact (r×c)The same table as chi-square independence.
  • Fisher's exact test reports the conditional maximum-likelihood odds ratio with the exact interval matched to its p-value (Fay 2010), the same CI the chart's brackets show, and the relative risk with a Koopman score interval. When a cell is empty the odds ratio is 0 or ∞, and is printed as such. The CI excludes 1 exactly when p is below α. The headline effect size is ln(odds ratio), on which an odds ratio of 0.2 and one of 5 are equally far from 0. Only the odds ratio is valid for a case-control (retrospective) design.
  • McNemar's test reports the difference in proportions, Δp = (b − c)/n, with Tango's score interval (Tango 1998), which uses every subject. From the discordant pairs alone it reports the paired odds ratio (b/c) and Cohen's g, with the exact Clopper-Pearson interval. Its p-value is the exact binomial test. The table gives the discordant counts b and c, and notes when fewer than 10 subjects changed, since the odds ratio and Cohen's g then rest on very few of them. Cohen's g is b/(b + c) − 0.5: how far the discordant pairs depart from an even split. Its CI and the odds ratio's exclude the null exactly when p is below α.
  • The one-sample binomial test reports the observed proportion and its difference from p₀, each with an exact Clopper-Pearson CI, beside the exact two-sided p. For p₀ other than 0.5 the CI and p can disagree just at the threshold; the table then says so, and the p-value decides the test.
  • Cochran's Q reports an exact permutation p-value beside the χ² one. When few subjects changed (n below 4 or n·k below 24, n counting only the subjects whose responses differ across conditions; Tate & Brown 1970), the exact p is the test's p, the one the result and chart brackets report; otherwise the χ² p is. The result says which rule applied. With many subjects the exact p is a Monte Carlo estimate from 100,000 rearrangements, seeded from the data.
  • Cochran's Q post hoc: with 3 or more conditions, pairwise McNemar tests follow, for all pairs or for each condition against a control (Comparisons, under Options), as on a chart's brackets. Each pair uses every subject with values in both of its conditions, p is Holm-adjusted, and the paired odds ratio and Cohen's g have simultaneous (Bonferroni, 1 − α/m) exact CIs.
  • Chi-square tests report the smallest expected count. When one is below 1, or more than 20% are below 5 (Cochran 1954), the χ² p-value is unreliable, and the result and the panel suggest Fisher's Exact (r×c), with a Use button.
  • Fisher's Exact (r×c) gives the same table and effect sizes with the exact p-value of the Freeman-Halton extension: the probability, given the row and column totals, of every table no more likely than the one observed. A table too large to enumerate gets a Monte Carlo p-value from 100,000 random tables with the same totals, with its seed shown.
  • Chi-square goodness-of-fit tests the first checked column, one count per category. Under Options, type the expected counts or proportions, separated by commas (or by semicolons when the values use a decimal comma: 0,3; 0,5; 0,2). Left empty, the expected distribution is uniform.
  • McNemar's test and Cochran's Q need 0/1 coding, and the panel says so when the two values are something else.

Correlation and Regression

Correlation takes two columns of measurements, chosen as X column and Y column under Options. It reports Pearson r, Spearman ρ, Kendall's τ-b and the least-squares line together.

  • Pearson r is the headline effect size, with a 95% CI from Fisher's z-transform. The regression slope and intercept each have a 95% CI too.
  • Spearman ρ and Kendall's τ-b each have a bootstrap 95% CI, which resamples the (x, y) pairs together; above n = 1,000 the CI is asymptotic.
  • Kendall's p-value is exact when there are no ties and n is below 50, and comes from a permutation for n ≤ 10 with ties. Spearman's is exact (permutation) for n ≤ 10; above that, with no ties, it comes from the Edgeworth series of Best & Roberts (1975). Otherwise both use large-sample approximations. Exact p-values are marked "(exact)".

Regression has a picker of models: Simple Linear (one X, one Y), the default, which fits the line Correlation reports; Multiple Regression; ANCOVA; Dose-Response (4PL); and six kinetics, binding and assay models. The sections below describe them.

  • Every fit's result includes its model and its fitted equation: a "Model:" line in symbols and a "Fitted:" line with the estimates filled in, one per curve or group. A fit that doesn't converge shows only its model.
  • A row missing Y, X or any included predictor is left out of that fit.

Multiple Regression and ANCOVA

These two take one row per observation (a cell, a sample, a participant), with the outcome (Y) and each predictor in its own column, not one column per group.

Run a multiple regression

  1. Under Analysis, choose Regression, then Multiple Regression in the picker below it.
  2. Under Options, choose the outcome in Y (outcome) column. In the Columns list, check 2 or more predictor columns.
  3. Check any of the three options (below), then click Determine Effect.
  • The model is Y = b₀ + b₁X₁ + b₂X₂ + …, so each coefficient is that predictor's effect with the others held constant. The result reports R² and Cohen's f, with 90% CIs from the exact distribution of R², which treats the predictors as measured rather than set by design (Fisher 1928); adjusted R²; the overall F test; and each term's B, SE, 95% CI, t and p.
  • VIF (variance inflation factor) is shown for each predictor, for up to 20 predictors. Above 5 it flags moderate multicollinearity: read that coefficient with caution. Above 10 it flags severe multicollinearity: that coefficient is unreliable, so consider removing or combining the correlated predictors.
  • If a predictor is constant, or a combination of the others, the message names it.

Options for Simple Linear and Multiple Regression

Three checkboxes under Options add to the table. All are off by default.

OptionWhat it adds
Standardized coefficients (β)A Std. β column beside each B: the change in Y, in SDs, per SD of that predictor, B × SD(X) / SD(Y) over the rows used. It uses this sample's SDs, so compare it between predictors in one model, not across studies. With one predictor it equals Pearson r.
Robust (heteroscedasticity-consistent) SEsEach coefficient's SE, 95% CI, t and p come from the sandwich estimator chosen under Robust SE: HC3 (the default, recommended at lab sample sizes; Long & Ervin 2000), HC2, HC1 or HC0 (White 1980), with t on the residual degrees of freedom. Use them when the spread of Y changes with a predictor, such as a fan shape in the Residuals vs Fitted plot. R², the model F test and VIF stay the ordinary ones.
Residual diagnostics (plots and influential rows)R's four plot.lm plots under the result (Residuals vs Fitted, Normal Q-Q of the standardized residuals, Scale-Location, and Residuals vs Leverage with Cook's distance contours at 0.5 and 1), each with its lowess smooth and the most extreme rows numbered, and a table of the rows with the largest Cook's D, leverage and studentized residuals.
  • The diagnostics table flags rows by these rules: Cook's D > 4/n (worth a look) or > 1 (highly influential; Cook 1977); leverage h > 2p/n, twice the average hat value, p counting the intercept (Belsley, Kuh & Welsch 1980); and |studentized residual| > 2 or > 3 (externally studentized; about 5% of rows pass 2 by chance). Rows are numbered as in your data. A flag is a reason to check that row, not to delete it.
  • The table goes into exported reports and the Data Log. Export Plots saves the four plots as a PDF or PNG.

Run an ANCOVA

ANCOVA compares group means on Y after adjusting for one or more continuous covariates.

  1. Under Analysis, choose Regression, then ANCOVA in the picker below it.
  2. Under Options, choose the outcome in Y (outcome) column. In the Columns list, check the factor column and the covariate columns.
  3. Choose the Categorical factor column: a checked column of group codes (0, 1, 2…), or a column of text labels (WT, KO), which needn't be checked. Every other checked column is a covariate.
  4. Choose the Post-hoc: Tukey HSD (the default), Holm-Bonferroni, Šidák or Bonferroni. Then click Determine Effect.
  • The table reports each term's partial F test and partial η², each adjusted for every other term; 90% CIs for the factor's partial η² and Cohen's f; the covariate-adjusted group means; and the pairwise comparisons of those means.
  • Each comparison gives the mean difference with a 95% CI adjusted like its p-value (for Holm, the Bonferroni simultaneous CI), and Cohen's d. d divides the adjusted difference by the pooled within-group SD of Y before adjustment, not by the smaller covariate-adjusted residual SD.
  • Homogeneity of slopes is tested automatically. When the factor × covariate interaction is significant (p < α, from the confidence level), a warning says that the covariate's relationship with Y differs between the groups, so the adjusted means can't be compared as reported. With too little data to test it, the table says so.
  • Levene's test (Brown-Forsythe version) on the model's residuals across the groups is shown, with a warning when their spread differs: ANCOVA assumes equal error variance, the spread around each group's line.
  • ANCOVA takes one categorical factor.

Dose-Response Curves

Dose-Response (4PL) fits a 4-parameter logistic (Hill) curve, with Bottom, Top, LogEC50 and Hill slope, to a dose or concentration column and a response column.

  1. Under Analysis, choose Regression, then Dose-Response (4PL) in the picker below it.
  2. Under Options, choose X column (dose) and Y column (response).
  3. Check X is already log10(dose) when it is. Otherwise the doses must be above 0, and are log-transformed before fitting.
  4. Set Constraints, Weighting and Compare as needed (below), then click Determine Effect.
SettingWhat it does
ConstraintsCheck Bottom, Top or Hill slope to hold it at the value you type (for example Bottom = 0 and Top = 100 for data normalized to percent). A fixed parameter is not fitted, so it has no SE or CI and gives its degree of freedom back to the residuals.
WeightingNone (equal weights), the default; 1/Y² (relative), for scatter that grows with the response; or 1/Y, for Poisson-like counts. The weights come from the fitted curve's response, re-estimated until they settle (iteratively reweighted least squares, as in GraphPad Prism 5 and later; Carroll & Ruppert 1988). R², the SEs, the CIs and every test then use the weighted sum of squares.
Replicates test for lack of fitOffered when some dose is repeated. Pure error is the scatter of the replicates around their own dose mean, which no curve can remove; the F test asks whether the curve misses the dose means by more than that. A small p means another model may fit better.
CompareDon't compare (one data set), the default, or a question about 2 or more data sets (see Compare curves, below).
  • The result gives each parameter's SE and 95% CI, R², and EC50 on the raw dose scale with both a Wald and a profile-likelihood CI. An F test says whether there is any dose-response at all.
  • "Converged: yes" means the fit reached a true minimum with every SE computable; otherwise a warning replaces the SEs and CIs.
  • When the doses never reach one plateau, the profile CI can be one-sided (for example 0 – 2.1e-6): the data cannot rule out an EC50 beyond that side.
  • The fit is the same in any unit of dose or response. It is separate from the Boltzmann (sigmoid) fit in a Graph window's Curve Fitting panel and shares no settings with it.

Compare curves

  1. Under Compare, choose the question: One curve for all data sets?, or whether one parameter differs while the others stay separate (Is LogEC50 different?, and the same for Bottom, Top and Hill slope).
  2. Under Data sets, choose One X column, checked Y columns (each checked column other than X is a data set at the X column's doses) or Checked columns as X,Y pairs (X1, Y1, X2, Y2, …, as a Scatter chart lays them out).
  3. For AICc beside the F test, check Also compare by AICc. Then click Determine Effect.
  • The effect comes first: each data set's LogEC50 difference from the first, with its CI, and the matching EC50 ratio.
  • Then come the extra sum-of-squares F test of the shared model against separate curves (F, df, p and both models' SS) and the shared fit's parameters with SEs and CIs. AICc adds the difference and each model's probability of being correct.
  • Constraints and weighting apply to every data set.

Enzyme Kinetics, Binding and Assays

Part of the Pharmacology & Biochemistry toolkit.

Six more Regression models analyze enzyme kinetics, receptor binding and common assays. Hiding this toolkit in Settings › Toolkits leaves them out of the Regression picker. The first four are fitted by nonlinear least squares and report each parameter's SE and 95% CI and R², and, for the unweighted Michaelis–Menten, inhibition and binding fits, AICc. Each can be weighted by 1/Y² or 1/Y and, when a concentration is repeated, run the replicates test, as Dose-Response does.

ModelDataWhat it fits and reports
Enzyme Kinetics (Michaelis–Menten)Substrate concentration (X) and velocity (Y).V = Vmax·S / (Km + S), for Vmax and Km, fitted directly and never through a Lineweaver–Burk plot, whose reciprocals distort the scatter.
Enzyme InhibitionSubstrate concentration (X), and one checked velocity column per inhibitor concentration, each titled with its concentration (0, 5, 10 or "10 µM"), including one without inhibitor.The competitive, uncompetitive, noncompetitive and mixed models, each fitted to all the data at once with Vmax, Km and Ki shared. The model chosen under Report (Mixed by default) is shown in full; a table lists all four with Ki, R², AICc and Akaike weight (the probability that each is the best of the four), lowest AICc first. For the mixed model, α tells which form the inhibitor prefers: above 1 the free enzyme, below 1 the enzyme–substrate complex, and 1 (noncompetitive) neither.
Saturation BindingThe labeled ligand's concentration (X) and specific binding (Y); or total binding as Y, with nonspecific binding chosen under Nonspecific column.Y = Bmax·X / (Kd + X). With a Nonspecific column, total = Bmax·X / (Kd + X) + NS·X and nonspecific = NS·X are fitted together, sharing NS, so every value informs Bmax and Kd.
Competition Binding (Kᵢ)The competitor's concentration (X; raw, or log10 with X is already log10(concentration) checked) and binding (Y). Type the labeled ligand's concentration [L] and Kd, in the competitor's unit.The 4-parameter logistic with its Hill slope fixed at −1, as for one site; Bottom and Top can be held at typed values under Constraints. The result gives IC50 with its Wald and profile-likelihood CIs, and Kᵢ = IC50 / (1 + [L]/Kd) (Cheng & Prusoff 1973) with the same CIs divided by 1 + [L]/Kd.
Standard Curve (Interpolate)Standards of known concentration (X) and their signals (Y), as for an ELISA, Bradford or BCA assay, and the unknowns' signals under Unknowns column (signals); blank rows are skipped.The curve chosen under Curve: Straight line, 4PL (sigmoidal), the default, or 5PL (asymmetric), the last two on log concentration. Each unknown is read off the curve as a concentration, with a 95% CI from the curve's own uncertainty (the delta method; for the 4PL and 5PL on the log scale), not from the unknown's measurement scatter. A signal beyond the curve's plateaus gives no concentration, and one outside the standards is marked as extrapolated. The curve can be weighted by 1/Y² or 1/Y.
qPCR Relative Expression (ΔΔCt)One row per sample: Group column (codes or labels such as Control and Treated), Target gene Ct and Reference gene Ct. Choose the Control group.Each sample's ΔCt = Ct(target) − Ct(reference); each group's ΔΔCt is its mean ΔCt minus the control's, and its fold change is 2^−ΔΔCt (Livak & Schmittgen 2001). Each group is compared with the control by Welch's t on ΔCt, with Holm's adjustment across the groups. The CI is computed on ΔCt and then converted to fold change, so it is asymmetric.
  • The 5PL is Bottom + (Top − Bottom)/(1 + 10^((LogXb − log X)·Hill slope))^S. It needs 7 or more standards at 5 or more concentrations, and also reports LogEC50, the concentration halfway between Bottom and Top.
  • qPCR: Efficiency (%) is 100 for both genes by default, a perfect doubling each cycle. With other efficiencies (from each gene's standard curve), each Ct is weighted by log₂ of its gene's amplification factor, which gives Pfaffl's ratio (Pfaffl 2001).

Back to Contents

Statistics on a Chart

A chart's Statistics tab compares the groups the chart shows and draws the result on the chart, as effect size brackets or as an Estimation Plot. It has the same zones and settings as the Statistics window (see Statistics: Overview). Linear regression on a Scatter (X,Y) chart is described on the Charts page.

Linked to a Chart

A Statistics window opened from a chart is linked to it: a setting changed in one changes in the other, and brackets on the chart are recomputed.

  1. In the chart's Statistics tab, click Open Full Statistics Window. Each chart has one such window; clicking again brings it forward.
  2. Set up the comparison in either place. Paired / Repeated and every Compare setting (Compare, Spreads, Question, effect size, post-hoc and tails) are shared; so are the comparisons and the control, while the window compares exactly the chart's groups.
  3. Click Show Chart, in the window's header, to bring the linked chart to the front.
  • A window opened from a spreadsheet or from selected text shows Make Chart instead. It opens a chart of the data (a repeated-measures chart with the Split-plot or Mixed model design), links the window to it and carries the window's settings over.
  • Edit as Spreadsheet… opens the window's data in a spreadsheet. Edits there update the statistics right away.
  • A repeated-measures chart (a profile) opens its window on the Mixed model design, sharing the group and Values from the same columns, Trend, Covariance and Spreads. Its spreadsheet shows one row per subject: the group column, the conditions and any source column.

Effect Size Brackets

A bracket joins two groups on the chart and shows the effect size of their difference, its confidence interval (CI) and the p-value of the matching test. Brackets are drawn on Bar / Dot, Horizontal Bar and Box Plot charts. A Line chart draws none: change its chart type, or use the Statistics window.

Add Brackets to a Chart

  1. Open the Statistics tab of the chart's inspector.
  2. Turn on Paired / Repeated when each table row is one subject measured in every group.
  3. Read DATA CHARACTERISTICS. When the data's shape suggests another Compare choice, Use applies it (see Data Checks and Suggestions).
  4. Under EFFECT SIZE, choose Compare and, for Means, the effect size (see Compare and Effect Sizes).
  5. With 3 or more groups, under TEST choose All pairwise or vs. Control. The "Will run: …" line names the test.
  6. Click Compute Brackets, at the top of BRACKETS.
  7. Under Display, choose what each bracket shows; under Position, show, hide, nudge or remove brackets.
  • There is no test picker: the test is the one that goes with the Compare choice, so each bracket's p-value and CI answer the same question. Compare stays on Means until you choose another.
  • Brackets stay current: editing the data or changing a setting recomputes those on the chart. If the data can no longer be tested as set up, the brackets are removed and the reason is shown under Compute Brackets.
Settings

The zones above BRACKETS work as in the Statistics window (see Statistics: Overview). On a chart:

  • Within category (compare series, not categories), in DATA on a chart with 2 or more series, compares the series within each category, such as WT vs. KO at each condition. Off (the default), the categories are compared using the first series.
  • Mark possible outliers (off by default), in DATA CHARACTERISTICS, rings each flagged point in orange; the checkbox of that name under Plot Style › Data Points is the same setting. A Box Plot marks its own outliers. With Compare set to Trimmed, a cyan ring marks the points the 20% trim sets aside, and a note in the chart's corner explains the ring.
  • Display: the CI checkbox, labeled with its level; Effect size and p-value, each shown or hidden, Above or Below the line; and Header, drawn once above the top bracket: Test name and, with 3 or more groups, Omnibus test (the overall test's statistic, df and p, plus ω² or partial η² for Means). All are on by default except Omnibus test.
  • Position: the list of brackets. Show or hide, nudge or remove each one; the All row moves them together. Recomputing keeps your positions and choices, and ⌘Z undoes each action.
What a bracket shows
  • The effect size with its CI above the line, and p below it. Compare and Effect Sizes › Direction of an Effect explains the sign.
  • A CI in square brackets [lo, hi] comes from a formula or the test itself; one in curly braces {lo, hi} is a bootstrap (see Compare and Effect Sizes › Confidence Intervals). With 3 or more groups the CIs are simultaneous (Bonferroni), like the adjusted p-values. Each CI keeps the confidence level it was computed at.
  • p is printed to 3 decimals (p < 0.001 and p > 0.999 at the ends), with more when rounding would land on or across 0.05 or 0.01: 0.04996 prints as 0.04996, not 0.050. A p that could not be computed shows as n/a.
Choose which brackets are drawn

Show, above the bracket list, chooses which brackets are drawn. Every comparison is still computed and adjusted as one family, and a line says how many are drawn, with Show All.

ShowDraws
All comparisonsEvery bracket (the default).
Chosen in the listThe brackets checked in the list. Checking or unchecking one switches to this.
Adjusted p < αThe brackets with an adjusted p below α. Offered while p-value is shown.
CI excludes 0The brackets whose CI excludes no difference: 0, or 1 for a ratio or an odds ratio.
|g*| at least…The brackets whose effect size (here g*) is at least the size you type, in either direction.

Choosing the comparisons before looking at the results (vs. Control, or the list) is more defensible than hiding results afterward.

The Chart Legend

The Chart Legend box, below the zones, states what ran: the test and post-hoc, one- or two-sided; the comparisons; how a paired design handled missing values; the effect size with its CI level and method (and the level a rank-based CI reaches, when below the one asked for); and which brackets are drawn. Click Copy Chart Legend to copy it.

Brackets for 0/1 Data

When every compared value is 0 or 1, the brackets compare proportions, whatever Compare is set to (see Other Analyses › Categorical Tests). A chart of two 0/1 series, whatever its chart type, has its series compared once per category.

DesignTestOn the bracket
Independent groupsFisher's exact testΔp, the difference in proportions (first group minus second), without a CI, then the odds ratio with its exact CI: "Δp = 0.40, OR = 5.77 [0.87, 52.2]".
Paired / RepeatedMcNemar's exact test, on the subjects with a value in both groupsΔp with Tango's score interval (the default), the paired odds ratio, ln(Odds Ratio) or Cohen's g, chosen under Question.
3 or more groupsThe same test for each pair, Holm-adjustedSimultaneous CIs (Bonferroni, each at 1 − α/m). Omnibus test adds Fisher's exact test of the whole table, or Cochran's Q when paired.
  • Fisher's odds ratio is the conditional maximum-likelihood estimate, first group over second. Its exact CI is matched to the test (Fay 2010; as R's exact2x2 package gives it), so it excludes 1 exactly when p is below α. No interval for Δp matches Fisher's p, so Δp has none.
