When a group is all 0s or all 1s, the odds ratio and one bound are 0 or ∞.
  • Question, for paired data. Magnitude (the default) shows Δp, which uses every subject. Its menu also offers Odds Ratio (the paired odds ratio, b/c) and ln(Odds Ratio), with exact intervals; they are 0 or ∞ when no subject changed in one direction.
  • Consistency shows Cohen's g: the share of the subjects whose outcome changed that changed toward the first group, minus ½. One changed subject gives its largest size, 0.5. The leftmost such bracket spells out "Cohen's g", since g on other charts is Hedges' g.
  • When Cohen's g or the odds ratio rests on fewer than 10 subjects whose outcome changed (discordant pairs), the bracket adds their number, as in "g = 0.50 [−0.48, 0.50] (n=1)". Always show discordant-pair count (n) adds it to every bracket.
Adjust p across categories

Adjust p across categories (Holm) appears when brackets are computed once per category: with Within category, and on a chart of two 0/1 series.

  • Off (the default): each category is its own family of comparisons. This suits categories that are separate outcomes or conditions.
  • On: the comparisons of all categories are one family, Holm-adjusted once from each unadjusted p-value, so the chance of any false positive in the whole figure stays at α. For Means with 3 or more series, each pair's t-test takes the post-hoc's place. Use it when the categories together answer one question.
  • The CIs then cover the same family, each at the Bonferroni level 1 − α/M for all M comparisons, since Holm has no exactly matching intervals. Where the CI inverts the test (t-tests, Fisher's and McNemar's exact tests), a CI that excludes the null always has a Holm-adjusted p below α, but a Holm-adjusted p below α can still have a CI that reaches the null.

Estimation Plot

An Estimation Plot shows how large each difference is and how precisely it is estimated: the data, each group's center with its CI, and each difference on its own axis with its CI and sampling distribution. It follows Cumming & Calin-Jageman (2024) and the DABEST plots of Ho et al. (2019).

Make an Estimation Plot

  1. Start from a Bar / Dot, Horizontal Bar or Box Plot chart with one series and at least 2 categories.
  2. In the Statistics tab, set Paired / Repeated, and under EFFECT SIZE choose Compare, which decides what the difference axis shows.
  3. Click Show Estimation Plot, at the foot of the EFFECT SIZE zone. The chart becomes an Estimation Plot, and the button stays highlighted.
  4. With 3 or more groups, choose Differences in the Chart tab's Plot Style panel: each group vs. one group, or All pairwise.
  5. Click Show Estimation Plot again to return to the earlier chart type.
  • Estimation Plot under Chart Type, in the Chart tab, does the same, and is the way to switch a Line chart or a profile.
  • An Estimation Plot compares the categories of one series. With 2 or more series the button is grayed out, and its tooltip says why. A profile is the exception (below).
  • Differences starts at the control chosen for the brackets, else a group named like a control (Control, Vehicle, WT), else the first group. Glass's Δ uses the same control.
  • Plot Style also has Hide data points, Hide mean marker & error bars, Hide sampling distributions and Mean offset, which moves each center and its curve sideways.
What the plot shows
CompareEach group's centerDifference axis
MeansMeanMean difference (M diff)
RatioGeometric meanRatio of geometric means, on a log axis marked in ratios
Trimmed20% trimmed meanDifference in trimmed means (Trimmed M diff)
H-L shiftMedianHodges-Lehmann shift or, for paired data, the Hodges-Lehmann median of the paired differences (HL diff)
RanksMedianDominance δ, on an axis of its own from −1 to 1
  • 2 groups make a Gardner-Altman plot: the groups and their difference side by side, with 0 on the difference axis at the first group's center. 3 or more make a Cumming plot: the groups above, with a dashed line at the reference group's center, and the differences below.
  • Each difference is the later group minus the earlier one. The effect size printed beside it has the same sign and is the one set under EFFECT SIZE; for H-L shift, Ranks and Ratio it is the plotted estimate itself.
  • With Paired / Repeated on, lines connect each subject's points, each subject's own difference is plotted too, and each difference uses the subjects with a value in both groups.
  • A difference with fewer than 2 values, or fewer than 2 matched subjects, is left off the plot and shows as n/a in the Statistics tab.
How the intervals are found
  • Every CI on the plot, for each center and each difference, is a bootstrap interval from 10,000 resamples, at the Default confidence level in Settings › Statistics. Each curve is the bootstrap sampling distribution of that estimate, drawn from the resamples themselves. Paired data are resampled as whole subjects.
  • Means, Ratio and dominance δ use the plain bootstrap, with the Bootstrap CI method chosen in Settings › Statistics (BCa by default).
  • H-L shift and Trimmed, and the group medians under Ranks, use the smoothed bootstrap (Silverman & Young 1987), with its percentile interval. Each resampled value gets a little Gaussian noise, scaled to keep the sample's variance, because a plain bootstrap of a median from a small sample lands on only a few values.
  • These CIs are the plot's own. Brackets and the Statistics window report the CIs that go with their tests, so the two can differ slightly.

Estimation Plot of 0/1 Data

When every compared value is 0 or 1, the plot shows proportions instead, after DABEST's proportion plot. In the Statistics tab, a Label choice replaces the data checks and Compare.

  • Upper panel: each group's proportion of 1s as a bar, with its Wilson score CI beside it and the count (successes/n) above it.
  • Lower panel: each difference in proportions (Δp, the risk difference) with Newcombe's hybrid score CI (method 10) or, with Paired / Repeated on, Tango's score CI for paired proportions (Tango 1998), on the subjects with a value in both groups.
  • Label: Δp, or Cohen's h = 2·asin√p₂ − 2·asin√p₁ (Cohen 1988).
  • Score intervals are used because a bootstrap interval is too narrow with few 0/1 values (Brown, Cai & DasGupta 2001; Fagerland et al. 2014, 2015). No sampling distributions are drawn.
  • Brackets on the same data report the odds ratio, a different measure, so their p and CI need not agree with the Δp interval.
  • With paired data, bands between neighboring bars show the fraction of subjects going 1→1, 1→0, 0→1 and 0→0, when every subject has a value in both. Show paired flows, in Plot Style, turns them off.

Estimation Plot with Values from the Same

When Values from the same is set (see Values from the Same, below), the plot draws the same linear mixed model as the brackets. A bootstrap would treat values from one source as independent and give intervals that are too narrow.

  • Each center is the group's model-based mean, and each difference the difference in model-based means. Each has its own t-based CI (Satterthwaite df), not adjusted over the comparisons as the brackets' CIs are, and each curve is the t distribution of that estimate (Cumming 2012).
  • The label beside each difference is the effect size chosen under EFFECT SIZE. Compare must be Means.
  • A checkbox named after your column (Show each batch's mean, for a Batch column; on by default) draws each source's mean as a larger hollow marker (a SuperPlot; Lord et al. 2020).

Estimation Plot of a Profile

For a profile (see Repeated Measures by Group, below), choose Estimation Plot under Chart Type, in the Chart tab. The plot has two panels over the conditions, placed at their values when the column names give them (0, 1, 2, 4, 8 h), and comes from one fit of the mixed model that the brackets use.

  • Upper panel: each group's model-based mean at each condition with its CI, over each subject's line (Show each subject's line, in Plot Style).
  • Lower panel: the differences between the groups at each condition, each with the t distribution of its estimate as a half curve.

The Statistics tab sets what the lower panel shows:

  • At each condition: The difference, or The change since the first condition (the difference minus the difference at the first condition), for groups that start apart.
  • Differences: each group against one group, or All pairwise with 3 or more groups.
  • Scale: Data's units, Hedges' g* or Cohen's d*, as the brackets give them. A change since the first condition is always in the data's units.
  • INTERVALS: At each condition (on by default) is each difference's own CI. All times together is the wider, simultaneous CI over every difference drawn (single-step, from the multivariate t; Bonferroni above 40 comparisons). With both, the thick bar is each condition's and the thin bar the simultaneous one.

The MIXED MODEL zone below them holds the model's settings, shared with the brackets. The legends over the two panels follow Axes & Labels › Appearance and can't be dragged.

Paired / Repeated Measures

Paired / Repeated says that each table row is one subject measured in every group. It stays off until you turn it on, or answer Rows Are Subjects (Repeated Measures) when the app asks how to read a table.

  1. Lay the table out with one row per subject and one column per group or condition. A blank cell is that subject's missing value.
  2. Chart the table, and turn on Paired / Repeated at the top of the Chart tab or the Statistics tab.
  3. Set up and compute the brackets as usual. The "Will run: …" line names the paired test.
  • On the chart, lines connect each subject's points. Brackets and the Statistics window run the paired form of each Compare choice (see Compare and Effect Sizes), and the data checks look at the paired differences or, with 3 or more conditions, the within-subject residuals.
  • Values are matched by table row: row r of every column is the same subject. Each comparison uses the subjects with a value in both of its groups; repeated-measures ANOVA's omnibus test uses the subjects with every value.
  • A chart whose values did not come from a table with one row per subject has no row information. Paired brackets and connecting lines are then not drawn, and the panel says why, rather than pairing values by their position in each list. If every group has the same number of values, and you know they list the same subjects in the same order, click Values are listed in subject order to pair them by position.

Values from the Same (Clustered Data)

Use Values from the same when the values aren't independent: samples from one batch, plants from one plot, students in one classroom, cells from one animal. Brackets then come from a linear mixed model with a random intercept for each source, so their intervals count the sources as well as the values.

  1. Lay the table out with one row per value: a column of values, a column naming each value's group and a column naming its source. Or use a Nested table, with each source as a subcolumn under its category.
  2. Chart the table and, in the Chart tab, set Data Layout to One Row per Value or Nested.
  3. In the Statistics tab, under Paired / Repeated, choose the source column for Values from the same. For a Nested table, choose Subcolumns (from the layout). A likely column (named like Batch, Subject, Classroom or Plate) is offered as a link.
  4. If the picker is grayed out, click Compare Means below it: Values from the same is for differences in means.
  5. Under EFFECT SIZE, choose the effect size and Spreads, then click Compute Brackets.
  • The "Will run: …" line names the model, fitted by REML with Satterthwaite df: in lme4's notation, value ~ category + (1 | source). The numbers equal those of the Statistics window's Mixed model with one value column (see Tests › Linear Mixed Model).
  • Each bracket shows the effect size with its CI, and the p for the difference in model-based means. With 3 or more categories both are simultaneous over the comparisons (single-step, from the multivariate t).
  • The Chart Legend states the model, the ICC (the share of the variance that lies between sources) and the counts of values and sources. With 3 or more categories, Header › Omnibus test adds the ICC and the counts above the brackets.
  • Values from the same needs a table read as One Row per Value or Nested, and Compare set to Means. It compares the categories of one series, and can't be combined with Within category or 0/1 data; the Statistics tab says why.
Effect size and Spreads
  • Effect size: Hedges' g (bias-corrected), the default, Cohen's d, or Δ, the difference in the data's units. g and d divide the difference by the two categories' total SDs, each the SD of a single value with every level's variance included (Hedges 2007). For categories measured within the same sources the two SDs are averaged, giving gav and dav, as for paired data (Lakens 2013); for categories from different sources their root mean square is used, giving g* and d*, as for independent groups (Delacre et al. 2021). The bracket's label says which.
  • The CIs of g and d are approximate and a little wider than Δ's, so one can reach 0 when p is just below α (Tests › Linear Mixed Model gives the formulas).
  • Spreads: May differ (the default) gives each category its own residual SD, the mixed model's counterpart of Welch's test. Assumed equal uses one residual SD for every category.
Second levels and paired data
  • Within that chooses a second level inside the first: classrooms within each school, plants within each plot, slices within each animal. Each unit gets its own random intercept within its source (in lme4's notation, (1 | source/unit)); the same label in two sources is two units. The Chart Legend then gives an ICC for each level, with the counts.
  • Repeated measures in a long table (Participant | Condition | Score, with Values from the same set to Participant): a random intercept per participant. With two conditions and complete data this gives exactly the paired t when the participants' values are positively correlated (otherwise the participant variance is 0 and the fit is singular). Unlike the paired t, it keeps participants with a missing condition.
  • With Paired / Repeated on in a One Row per Value table, say which rows go together under Within that: the column numbering each pair or subject, or In order within each source.
  • In a table of one column per category, with a column saying where each row came from (Data Layout), turning on Paired / Repeated makes each row the second level within its source: the values in one row count as one pair or subject.
  • Nested tables work the same way: with Paired / Repeated on, row 1 of a subcolumn under each category is one pair within that subcolumn, and so on down the rows.

Repeated Measures by Group

A Repeated Measures by Group chart is a profile: groups of subjects, with each subject measured across several conditions. Its brackets come from one linear mixed model of every subject's profile, not from a test at each condition: the Statistics window's Mixed model, with the same numbers (see Tests › Linear Mixed Model).

Make the Chart and Add Brackets

  1. Lay the table out with one row per subject: a column of groups (codes 0, 1, 2… or labels such as WT, KO), one column per condition and, optionally, a column naming each subject's source.
  2. Chart the table and find the Repeated Measures by Group box: in the Chart tab's Plot Style panel or, when the table is recognized as this layout, under Data Layout and in the Statistics tab.
  3. Choose the Group column and, if several subjects come from one source, the Values from the same column.
  4. Click Make Repeated Measures Chart.
  5. In the Statistics tab, under MIXED MODEL, choose what the brackets compare and set the model.
  6. Click Compute Brackets.
  • A Statistics window set to the Split-plot or Mixed model design makes the same chart with Make Chart. A window linked to a chart of a different table opens a separate repeated-measures chart, which follows the window.
  • Paired / Repeated shows checked and can't be changed: the model accounts for each subject's repeated values.
The MIXED MODEL zone
  • Brackets: Each condition (the default) draws a bracket for each pair of groups at each condition. Rate of change draws one per pair, for their difference in slope (below).
  • Trend, Covariance, Values from the same, Fit on a log scale, Fit values past a limit and Spreads set the model, as in the Statistics window (see Tests › Linear Mixed Model).
  • Effect size, for Each condition: Hedges' g* (bias-corrected), the default, Cohen's d*, or Δ, the difference in the data's units. On a log scale the brackets show the ratio of the groups' geometric means; with values past a limit they show Δ, and p reads p ≈.
What each bracket shows
  • A bracket joins two groups at one condition. It shows the effect size of the difference in their model-based means, with a simultaneous CI and a p adjusted over all conditions and pairs (single-step, from the multivariate t; Bonferroni above 40 comparisons).
  • The difference is the first group minus the second; a pair with a control group reads as the other group minus the control (see Compare and Effect Sizes › Direction of an Effect).
  • Δ's CI excludes 0 exactly when p is below α. g* and d* divide the difference by the root mean square of the two groups' SDs of a single value at that condition; their CIs are approximate and a little wider.
  • The bracket list names each comparison in full ("Hit 8: Subtype 0 vs. Subtype 2") and gives its df beside p: Satterthwaite's, the residual df where those can't be computed (the test name then says so), or subjects − groups with values past a limit. With several subjects per source, they lie nearer the number of sources than of subjects.
  • A condition where every observed value is the same, such as a normalization baseline, is left out of the model and gets no bracket.
  • A bracket's ends are spread across its condition, and brackets at neighboring conditions alternate in height, so their labels stay apart. They are drawn in the SVG, PDF and PNG exports.

Header (BRACKETS › Display) has two more checkboxes on a profile:

  • Counts (on by default) adds the subjects (rows) the model used and, with Values from the same, their sources, in all and per group, as in "n = 60 subjects from 17 batches". It names the groups that share sources, whose comparison is then partly within sources.
  • Rate of change (difference in slope), off by default and offered with Each condition, adds each pair's difference in slope, with its simultaneous CI and adjusted p.

Compare Rates of Change

Rate of change asks whether one group rises or falls faster than another, which no single condition tests well.

  1. In the MIXED MODEL zone, set Brackets to Rate of change.
  2. Beside Slope over, choose the first and last condition of the part to compare, such as the response after a treatment begins. It starts as every condition.
  3. Choose the Effect size (below).
  4. Check Show each group's fitted line (off by default) to draw each group's straight line over those conditions, dashed in its color.
  5. Click Compute Brackets.
  • Each group's rate is the least-squares slope through its model-based means over those conditions, in the data's units per unit of the condition. The model is still fitted to every condition.
  • Each pair of groups gets one bracket, spanning those conditions. It shows the difference between the groups (first minus second), with a simultaneous CI and a p adjusted over the pairs.
Effect sizeWhat the bracket reports
Δ change over the window (the default)How much more one group changed than the other over those conditions, in the data's units: the difference in slope times the window's length.
Δ slope per unitThe difference in slope, to 3 significant figures.
dGMA (standardized change)The change over the window in SDs of a single value (Feingold 2009), with the model's SD over the window's conditions in place of the baseline SD, so it works for data normalized to a baseline. Its CI is approximate. Not offered on a log scale or with values past a limit.

Back to Contents

Omics Visualization

The omics plots draw tables of results or expression values. Each opens in an ordinary Chart window, with the same inspector and exports as any chart (see Charts). The plots use your table's own row and column names; this page says "feature" for a gene, protein, metabolite or other row.

PlotWhat it shows
Volcano Plot and MA PlotEach feature of a two-group comparison: its log₂ fold change against −log₁₀ of its p-value, or against its mean expression.
HeatmapA matrix as colored cells, with optional clustering and dendrograms.
PCA PlotA Heatmap's samples at their scores on two principal components.
Dot PlotOne dot per group and feature: its area shows one value and its color another.
Cluster ScatterPoints colored by cluster, such as UMAP or t-SNE coordinates.
GSEA BarOne bar per gene set, left or right of zero by its enrichment score, from results you paste or compute here.
Grouped Diverging Bar and Stacked Composition BarSeveral series per category, as signed bars or as one stacked bar.
Venn Diagram and UpSet PlotThe overlaps of 2 or 3 sets as circles, or of any number of sets as bars.
Manhattan Plot and QQ PlotEach variant's −log₁₀(p) along the genome, and the same p-values against their expected values.

Make an Omics Plot

  1. Put the table in a Spreadsheet window, or select it in the Data Log or a Text Editor window. A table may be separated by tabs, commas or semicolons, with its names in a header row.
  2. Choose the plot from an Omics Plot menu. In a Spreadsheet window, click Omics Plot in the toolbar and choose, say, Dot Plot. For selected text, choose Dot Plot from Selected Text… from File › Omics Plot or from the Text Tools menu's Omics Plot submenu.
  3. A Volcano Plot opens its setup window first. The other plots open at once.
  4. Style the plot in the Chart tab's Plot Style panel, in the box named after the plot. Axes & Labels holds the titles, fonts, grid and Show legend.
  5. For sentences that state how the plot was made (its transforms, thresholds, counting rules and what was left out), open the Statistics tab and click Copy Chart Legend.
  • Quoted cells and decimal commas are read. Blank cells and NA are missing values.
  • MA Plot, PCA Plot and Stacked Composition Bar have no command of their own: make a Volcano Plot, a Heatmap or a Grouped Diverging Bar and switch to them (see each plot).
  • Under Chart Type, the omics types are listed under Omics Visualization. A type is grayed out unless the chart holds that plot's kind of data, so an ordinary chart can't become a Volcano Plot.
  • Text Tools › Smart Visualization… (⇧⌘V) opens a selected table as the plot its headers and shape suggest, and asks when it can't tell.
  • The spreadsheet icon in the plot's toolbar opens its data as a table (see Charts › Edit the Data in the Chart Data Window), and the Export button saves the data as CSV or TSV (see Exporting Results › Export a Table).

Volcano and MA Plots

A Volcano Plot shows each feature's log₂ fold change (X) against −log₁₀ of its p-value (Y), the usual view of a differential-expression or other two-group comparison. It needs a table with a header row and the feature names in its first column, holding either replicate values for two groups, from which @Graph computes the statistics, or fold changes and p-values you already have, such as a DESeq2, edgeR or limma results table.

Make a Volcano Plot

  1. Select the table and choose File › Omics Plot › Volcano Plot from Selected Text… (⌥⌘L), or Omics Plot › Volcano Plot in a Spreadsheet window. The Set Up Volcano Plot window opens.
  2. At the top, choose Compute from Replicates or Already Have Fold Change / p-values. The window starts on the second when the headers name a fold change and a p-value (such as log2FC, padj, FDR or limma's P.Value).
  3. For replicates, set each column to Group A, Group B or Exclude, with at least 2 columns in each group (fold change is Group B relative to Group A). Then choose the Input Scale and the Significance Test.
  4. For results you already have, check the columns chosen for Fold change, p-value, Adjusted p and Mean expression, and how the fold change is read (Read as).
  5. To color, size or shape the points by a spare column from the start, choose it under Aesthetic Mapping (optional).
  6. Click Generate Volcano Plot. The plot opens in a new Chart window.
  • The window explains each setting under it, and counts what it will leave out. A table exported from R, whose header has one name fewer than its rows, is read with the names over the right columns.
  • When a plot computed from replicates has no significant feature, a message says why.
Compute from replicates
SettingWhat it does
Input ScaleAlready log₂ (used as they are), Linear intensities (the default: log₂-transformed before the test) or Raw counts (read counts, such as RNA-seq). A warning appears when the values don't look like the scale chosen.
ZerosFor Linear intensities: Treat as missing (the default) leaves out values of zero or below, which have no logarithm. Add pseudocount adds half the smallest positive value in the table to every value before log₂.
Minimum valid values per groupFeatures with fewer valid values than this in either group are left out before testing, so they enter neither the variance prior nor the p-value adjustment (2 by default; 0 turns the filter off). A zero treated as missing is not a valid value. Not shown for Raw counts.
Significance TestModerated t-test (eBayes), the default, or Welch's t-test. Raw counts always use the moderated t.
Intensity-dependent prior (limma-trend)With the moderated t-test, lets the prior variance follow average intensity, since low-abundance features are noisier (off by default; always on for Raw counts). Recommended for proteomics and other intensity data.
Fold changes and p-values you already have

The values are plotted as they are, without recalculation.

SettingWhat it does
Read asHow the Fold change column is read: Log₂ fold change (as it is), Signed linear (4 is 4-fold up, −4 is 4-fold down) or Ratio (4 is 4-fold up, 0.25 is 4-fold down). The window guesses and says why; change it if the guess is wrong. Values the reading can't hold (a signed value between −1 and 1, a ratio of 0 or below) are left out.
p-valueThe unadjusted p-values. A value outside 0 to 1 is not a probability, and is left out of the plot and of the adjustment.
Adjusted pThe adjusted p-values, used as given. With None (compute BH-FDR from p-value), @Graph applies the Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment to the p-values in the table.
Tests in the original analysisShown when Adjusted p is None. If the table holds only part of the analysis (its significant features, say), adjusting over those rows alone gives adjusted p-values that are too small, and the window warns when the p-values look like such a list. Enter the number of tests the analysis ran, and the adjustment counts them all (R's p.adjust with n).
Mean expressionOptional, for the MA Plot: a column such as DESeq2's baseMean, limma's AveExpr or edgeR's logCPM.

Set the Thresholds and Colors

The Volcano Plot box in Plot Style opens with a note on how the statistics were obtained. The Chart Legend repeats it, and adds the thresholds and how many features are Up and Down.

ControlWhat it does
Use adjusted p-value for y-axis and thresholdsOn by default. Turn it off to plot and threshold the unadjusted p-values. The Y axis title follows the choice ("-Log10(Adjusted P-value)" or "-Log10(P-value)") unless you typed your own.
Fold changeA feature is Up or Down only when its |log₂ fold change| is at or above this value (1 by default, a 2-fold change; 0 to 5)…
Significance…and its p-value is below this one (0.05 by default; 0.001 to 0.2).
Up, Down, N.S., Size, OpacityThe three categories' colors, and the points' size and opacity.
  • The thresholds are drawn as dashed lines. A feature whose log₂ fold change is exactly 0 is never Up or Down.
  • A p-value of exactly 0 (too small for the program that computed it to store) is plotted just above both the smallest p-value above 0 and the significance line, so it is never drawn below a line it passes. The Chart Legend says so when it applies.
  • When @Graph computed the adjusted p-values, a note says so in the Volcano Plot box and in each point's popup.
  • The plot's table and its exports hold one row per feature: Gene, log2FoldChange, its confidence limits, SE, t and df (when computed here), pValue, adjustedPValue and, when there is one, log2MeanExpression.

Show an MA Plot

An MA plot shows the same features as average expression (A, on X, log₂) against log₂ fold change (M, on Y), with a solid line at M = 0 and the fold-change thresholds as dashed lines.

  1. Make a Volcano Plot. With Already Have Fold Change / p-values, choose a Mean expression column in the setup window.
  2. In Plot Style › Volcano Plot, set Display to MA Plot. Set it to Volcano to go back.
  • Computed from replicates, A is the mean of all the feature's log₂ values over both groups, as limma's AveExpr (mean log-CPM for raw counts).
  • An imported column's header decides its scale. One that says log or AveExpr is used as it is. baseMean, or any other mean without "log", is converted to log₂; a mean of 0 has no log₂, so that feature is left off the MA plot. For any other header, negative values mean the column is already on a log scale.
  • Without mean expression, Display is grayed out and a note under it says why.
  • Switching Display changes the chart's title and axis titles to suit, except those you typed yourself. Mappings, labels and search work in both displays.

Map a Column to Color, Size, Shape or Opacity

Any spare column of the table can drive the points' color, size, shape or opacity: a column set to Exclude under Compute from Replicates, or one not chosen for a role under Already Have Fold Change / p-values. Choose a column for each in Plot Style › Aesthetic Mapping, or in the setup window, where a column can drive only one of the four.

MappingWhat it does
ColorA gradient between the Low and High colors you choose, in place of the Up and Down colors.
SizeA point size between Min and Max.
ShapeA symbol for each distinct value: circle, square, triangle, diamond, cross. Past five values, the rest share the fifth symbol, labeled "Other". Best for a column of a few categories.
OpacityAn opacity between Min and Max.

The four are independent, and color, size and shape each get a key above the plot. Color, Size and Opacity need numbers that differ, read with the table's own decimal separator, so decimal commas (12,5) work. A Size or Opacity column without them changes nothing, and a note says so.

Label and Find Features

  1. Click a point. A popup shows its name, log₂ fold change, p-value and adjusted p-value, its value in each mapped column and, when @Graph computed the statistics, the fold change's confidence interval, SE, t and df.
  2. Check Show name on plot to label the point on the chart.
  • To label many at once, use Label Genes Matching Criteria in Plot Style. Set Min |Log₂ FC| and the p-value a feature must be below (1 and 0.05 at first; the adjusted p-value, when those are in use), choose a Category (Any, Significant (Up or Down), Up only or Down only), then click Label Matching Genes (n), where n is the number that match.
  • Labeled Genes (n) lists the labels. Click the × beside one to remove it, or Clear All; ⌘Z undoes either. Labels are saved with the chart.
  • Type in Search / highlight gene… to ring and name every point whose name contains the text, in any capitalization. Exports, prints and copies show the matches until you clear the search.

How the Statistics Are Computed

  • Fold change is the difference of the two groups' means on the log₂ scale, mean(B) − mean(A), never the logarithm of a ratio of raw means.
  • Moderated t-test (eBayes): limma's empirical Bayes method (Smyth 2004), as its lmFit followed by eBayes (with trend = TRUE for the intensity-dependent prior). Each feature's variance is drawn toward a prior estimated from all the features, which gives steadier and more powerful tests with the few replicates usual in omics work.
  • Welch's t-test: an unpaired t-test with unequal variances, on each feature by itself. It needs at least 2 values in each group, whatever Minimum valid values per group is set to.
  • Raw counts follow the edgeR and limma workflow (Law et al. 2014): features with too few counts are removed (edgeR's filterByExpr, with its defaults), the libraries are normalized for sequencing depth and composition by TMM (Robinson & Oshlack 2010), counts become log₂ counts per million (log-CPM, prior count 2), and the moderated t-test runs with the intensity-dependent prior. A feature with a blank or negative count is left out, and the setup window says how many.
  • p-values are adjusted by the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (BH-FDR) over the features tested.
  • Each feature tested gets its log₂ fold change with a confidence interval at the level in Settings › Statistics, its standard error, t and degrees of freedom. For the moderated t-test the interval is that of limma's topTable(confint = TRUE); for Welch's t-test it is the Welch interval.
  • The note in the Volcano Plot box gives the prior (d₀ and s₀²) and the number of features it rests on, and calls it weak with fewer than 10. With fewer than 3 usable features there is no prior: each feature gets an ordinary pooled t-test, and the note says so. With a minimum of 0 or 1, the note also says that a feature with one value in each group is tested on the prior variance alone, as in limma.

Heatmap and PCA Plot

A Heatmap draws a matrix as a grid of colored cells: an expression matrix, a correlation matrix or any table of numbers. It needs row names in the first column and column names in the first row. Opening an expression-matrix file builds one directly (see Supported File Formats › Genomics and Cytometry, which also gives the size limits).

Make a Heatmap

  1. Select the matrix and choose File › Omics Plot › Heatmap from Selected Text… (⌥⌘M), or Omics Plot › Heatmap in a Spreadsheet window. The heatmap opens at once.
  2. In Plot Style › Heatmap, check Log2 transform for raw counts or intensities, and choose how to Normalize.
  3. To order rows or columns by similarity, check Cluster rows, Cluster columns or both (see Cluster Rows and Columns).
  4. Choose the colors with Color Preset…, or set Low, Mid and High yourself.
  • If the samples came in as rows, click Swap Rows and Columns.
  • Click a cell to see its row and column names and its raw value, with its log₂ value and z-score when those are in use.
  • Drag a rectangle to zoom in, and again to zoom further; double-click to return to the whole matrix. Dendrograms are hidden while zoomed.
  • Type in Search rows/columns… to find the names containing the text, in any capitalization. Matches are shown in bold orange, with an orange band across the row or column.
  • In the plot's table, which holds matrices of tens of thousands of rows, double-click a cell to edit it (⌘Z undoes the edit), or drag across cells and press ⌘C to copy them.

Heatmap Settings

ControlWhat it does
Log2 transformTakes log₂ of the values first (off by default). With Add 1 first: log2(x + 1), zeros are kept. Leave it off for data already on a log scale. A value with no logarithm is drawn gray, as missing, and a note counts them.
NormalizeNone (raw values), Z-score per row (the default) or Z-score per column: each value minus its row's or column's mean, divided by the sample SD (n − 1). A row or column whose values are all the same gets 0 (the Mid color), and a note says how many there are.
Hide all-zero rows, Hide all-zero columnsHide the rows or columns with no value other than zero, as in a sparse single-cell matrix (off by default). Clustering is unavailable while either is on.
Show axisThe border around the cells (on by default).
Color Preset…Classic (Blue–Black–Red), Red–Blue (colorblind-safe) or Purple–Green (colorblind-safe). A preset sets the Low, Mid and High colors (blue, white and red at first), which you can then change.
Auto color-scale rangeOn by default. Turn it off to type Min and Max, for example to put several heatmaps on one scale; the Mid color then sits at 0 when the range spans 0, and halfway otherwise.
Show legend, Show cell gridIn Axes & Labels: the color scale, and the lines between cells. The grid starts off when the table has 30 or more rows or columns.

The automatic color range follows ComplexHeatmap's default. Data of both signs in similar amounts (25–75% of the non-zero values positive, as with z-scores or fold changes) get a scale centered on 0 that reaches the 99th percentile of |value|. Other data, such as raw or log₂ expression, run from the 1st to the 99th percentile, with the Mid color halfway. With fewer than 100 distinct values, the full range is used. Cells beyond the range take the end color, and the legend marks that end with ≥ or ≤.

Cluster Rows and Columns

  1. In Plot Style › Heatmap, check Cluster rows, Cluster columns or both. Each is reordered so that similar rows or columns sit together, with a dendrogram (the tree of merges) drawn beside it.
  2. Choose the Linkage: Complete (the default), Average (UPGMA), Single or Ward.
  3. Choose the Distance: Euclidean (the default), Correlation (Pearson) or Correlation (Spearman).
  4. To put the most similar neighbors side by side, check Optimal leaf ordering (off by default).
  • Clustering works on the values as plotted, after Log2 and normalization, and changes only the order shown: unchecking it restores the table's order. It is limited to 2,000 rows or columns.
  • Distance: Euclidean compares levels. Correlation (Pearson) is 1 − r, so rows that rise and fall together sit together whatever their level. Correlation (Spearman) is 1 − ρ, on ranks, so one extreme value matters less.
  • Linkage sets how far apart two clusters count as being; point at the menu for each choice. The tree and its leaf order are those of R's hclust (Murtagh 1985), the order pheatmap draws (Kolde 2019).
  • Ward is R's "ward.D2". It needs Euclidean distances, so with a correlation distance it uses √(2(1 − r)), the Euclidean distance between the standardized profiles (Murtagh & Legendre 2014). pheatmap applies Ward to 1 − r itself, so its tree can differ.
  • Missing values: with Euclidean distance, two rows are compared over the cells both have, scaled up to the full length. With a correlation distance they are correlated over the cells both have, and a pair with a constant row counts as uncorrelated (r = 0).
  • Optimal leaf ordering flips the tree's branches so that neighbors are as similar as the tree allows (Bar-Joseph et al. 2001). The tree and its clusters stay the same. On a large heatmap it can take a few seconds: the unclustered order is shown until it finishes.

Make a PCA Plot

A PCA Plot is a principal component analysis of a Heatmap's matrix: each sample at its scores on two components, each axis title giving that component's share of the variance, and the features' loadings drawn as arrows from the origin.

  1. Make a Heatmap of the matrix, with its row and column names.
  2. Under Chart Type, click PCA Plot (in Omics Visualization).
  3. In Plot Style › PCA Plot, set Samples are to Columns (the default, for features in rows) or Rows.
  4. Check Log2 transform for raw counts or intensities, and Scale variables (unit variance) for features measured in different units.
  5. Choose the two components to plot with X and Y (PC1 and PC2 at first).
ControlWhat it does
Log2 transformRuns the PCA on log₂ of the values. It is the Heatmap's own setting, so both plots analyze the same numbers. A value with no logarithm counts as missing; Add 1 first: log2(x + 1) keeps zeros.
Scale variables (unit variance)Scales each feature to unit variance after centering it on its mean (off by default).
Top N most variable featuresRuns the PCA on the N features with the highest variance across the samples, after the log transform (N is 500 by default, as in DESeq2's plotPCA; Love et al. 2014). It starts on for a new chart with more than 500 complete features and at least 10 times as many features as samples. A note says how many features are in use.
Variance explainedBars showing the first 10 components' share of the variance. Copy Variance Table and Save as CSV… give every component's standard deviation, variance, % of variance and cumulative %.
Show loading vectors, Show sample labelsArrows for the features with the largest loadings on the two plotted components (12 features at first, 1 to 50), on one scale, the longest reaching 40% of the shorter axis (less when an arrow would otherwise end outside the plot); and each sample's name beside its point. Both are on by default.
Ellipse per color groupAn ellipse around each group of samples that share a point color (off by default; see Group ellipses).
Sample color overridesSamples are not grouped for you: to mark a group, give its samples one color here (↺ resets a sample).
Group ellipses
  • Give each group's samples the same color, check Ellipse per color group, and choose the Type and the Level (95% by default). A group needs at least 4 samples; Plot Style and the Chart Legend name the groups that got no ellipse.
  • Normal (the default) is the data ellipse from the group's mean and covariance, ggplot2's stat_ellipse with type = "norm" (Wickham 2016). t (ggplot2 default) fits a multivariate t distribution instead (MASS's cov.trob; Venables & Ripley 2002), so an outlying sample stretches it less. Both are expected to hold about Level of the group: their radius is √(2·F(Level; 2, n − 1)).
  • Confidence (group mean) is the confidence region for the group's center, Hotelling's T² (Hotelling 1931): the covariance divided by n, with radius √(2(n − 1)/(n − 2)·F(Level; 2, n − 2)). It covers the true mean at the stated level for any group size, and shrinks as the group grows.
How the PCA is computed
  • Each feature is centered on its mean and, with Scale variables (unit variance), scaled, as R's prcomp does. Each component's sign is set so that its largest loading is positive.
  • A feature with a missing value in any sample is left out, since PCA needs complete data, and a feature that doesn't vary takes no part. Plot Style counts both.
  • The PCA needs at least 3 samples and 2 complete features. Above 500 samples or 50,000 features, or when no feature varies, the plot shows a message instead.

Dot Plot and Cluster Scatter

Make a Dot Plot

A Dot Plot is a grid of circles, one for each group and feature (such as cell type × gene). A circle's area shows one value, usually the percent expressing, and its color a second, usually the average expression.

  1. Arrange one table with a header row and one row per group and feature, in 4 columns: feature, group, size and color (such as Gene, Cell Type, Percent Expressed, Average Expression).
  2. Select it and choose Dot Plot from the Omics Plot menu (see Make an Omics Plot).
  3. If the headers don't show which of the last two columns is the size (words such as pct or percent, against avg or mean), @Graph asks once.
  4. In Plot Style › Dot Plot, choose how the dots are colored, hidden and ordered.
  • Two tables separated by a blank line also work, each with a header row and a name column: the first gives the sizes and the second the colors. They must name the same rows and columns, in any order; if they differ, a message says which names.
  • Values may carry a percent sign (45%). When a feature and group repeat, the first row is used and the Data Log lists the repeats. Rows that can't be read are counted in the Data Log.
  • Dot area is proportional to the size value, and the size legend's dots are drawn at the plot's own scale. A size of zero, a missing size or a negative one draws no dot. A row with a size but no color value draws a gray dot.
ControlWhat it does
Swap Rows and ColumnsExchanges features and groups.
Order Groups by Similarity, Order Features by SimilarityPuts similar groups or features side by side, by hierarchical clustering (complete linkage, Euclidean distance) of their colors as drawn, as Seurat orders groups (Hao et al. 2024). Each is a one-time reorder, undone with ⌘Z; no tree is drawn.
Hide dots below sizeDraws no dot for a size below this, in the size values' units, such as 5 for 5% (0 by default).
Hide features and groups with no dotsLeaves out every feature and group whose sizes are all zero, missing or below that size (off by default). A note says how many are hidden; the table and exports keep them.
Scale each feature (z-score)On by default: each feature is colored by its z-score across the groups (SD with n − 1), clipped at ±2.5, on the Low, Mid and High colors centered on 0, so it shows where a feature is high or low whatever its level. Off: the values themselves, from light (Low values) to dark (High values). A feature with fewer than 2 values, or the same value in every group, has no z-score and is drawn gray.
log1p before scalingTakes log(1 + x) of the color values first (off by default). Turn it on for averages on a linear scale, as Seurat does, and leave it off for values already on a log scale. A value of −1 or below is drawn gray.
Auto color-scale rangeOn by default: −2.5 to 2.5 for z-scores, and the 1st to the 99th percentile for unscaled values (the full range with fewer than 100 distinct values). Turn it off to type Min and Max. The legend marks a clipped end with ≥ or ≤.
  • Color Preset… and the Low, Mid and High colors work as for a Heatmap. The color legend's title says what it shows: Color (z per feature), Color (z of log1p) or Color (log1p).
  • The plot's table and its exports hold one row per dot as Feature, Group, Size, Color, with the values as entered, so an exported table makes the same chart again.

Make a Cluster Scatter

A Cluster Scatter draws points at their coordinates, such as a UMAP or t-SNE embedding, colored by cluster or cell type.

  1. Arrange a table with a header row and 3 columns in this order: X, Y and cluster name, one row per point.
  2. Select it and choose Cluster Scatter from the Omics Plot menu.
  3. Style it in Plot Style › Cluster Scatter, and set the axis ranges in the Range panel.
ControlWhat it does
Swap X and YExchanges the two coordinates of every point.
Show Cluster OutlinesA straight-edged outline (the convex hull) around each cluster of 3 or more points (on by default).
Label clustersWrites each cluster's name at the median of its points (off by default).
Same scale on both axesKeeps one unit of X as long as one unit of Y, so shapes are not stretched (on by default). A typed axis range is used as entered.
Size, Opacity, Cluster colorsThe points' look. Each cluster's color can be changed; ↺ returns it to the palette. More than eight clusters take their colors from ggplot2's default palette (Wickham 2016).

GSEA and Diverging Bars

Make a GSEA Bar

A GSEA Bar draws one horizontal bar per gene set or pathway, right of zero for a positive enrichment score and left for a negative one, sorted from the highest score to the lowest.

  1. Arrange a table with a header row and 2 or 3 columns: name, score and, optionally, a significance value (a p-value or FDR). Or use a whole results table from fgsea, the GSEA desktop application or clusterProfiler.
  2. Select it and choose GSEA Bar from the Omics Plot menu.
  3. If the headers leave the score column open, @Graph asks which it is.
  4. In Plot Style › GSEA Bar, check Only the top to draw just the sets with the largest |score| (20, until you change the number), and set the Positive (Up) and Negative (Down) colors.
  • With 3 columns, score and significance are told apart by whole words in their headers, such as NES or ES for the score and padj, pval or FDR q-val for the significance.
  • In a results table of 4 or more columns, the columns are found by header, not position: the name from pathway, term, description or name (before an ID); the score from NES (ES only when there is no NES); the significance from an adjusted p (padj, p.adjust, FDR q-val, then qvalue, then FWER) before an unadjusted one. The GSEA Bar box states the columns used.
  • Significance sets each bar's opacity on a log scale: solid at 0.001 or below, about 78% at 0.01, 63% at 0.05 and 35% at 1. The legend shows this key. A bar with no significance value is solid.
  • With Only the top on, the Chart Legend says how many of the sets are drawn; the plot's table keeps them all.

Compute GSEA (Permutation)

Compute GSEA (Permutation)… runs a preranked Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (Subramanian et al. 2005) on a list of genes ranked by a score, such as a log fold change or a t statistic, and plots the result as a GSEA Bar.

  1. Choose Compute GSEA (Permutation)… from any Omics Plot menu. The Compute GSEA window opens; it reads no table.
  2. Paste the ranked gene list in the upper box: 2 columns, Gene and Score, separated by tabs, commas or semicolons. A header row is skipped.
  3. Paste the gene sets in the lower box, one per line, tab-delimited, and choose their layout: ".gmt: name, description, genes" (the MSigDB format, whose second column is always skipped) or "Name, then genes".
  4. Set Gene-set size: a set is tested when this many of its genes are in the ranked list (15 to 500 by default, the GSEA default).
  5. Leave Automatic permutations checked, or uncheck it and type a number (at least 1,000).
  6. Click Compute. A bar shows how far the permutations have got; Cancel, or closing the window, stops the run and opens nothing. The chart opens with the 20 sets of largest |NES| drawn (Only the top).
  • Gene names are matched ignoring capitalization and surrounding spaces. A gene listed more than once keeps its score with the largest absolute value.
  • The plot's table and its exports hold every set tested: Gene Set, NES, FDR (BH), Size, ES, Nominal p, Leading-edge size, Leading-edge genes (separated by "/") and Note. Bars are sorted by NES, and the FDR sets their opacity.
How GSEA is computed
  • Enrichment score (ES): walking down the ranked list, a running sum rises at each gene of the set, by that gene's |score| as a share of the set's total, and falls by an equal step at every other gene. ES is the sum's largest distance from zero, with its sign. When its highest and lowest points are equally far from zero, ES is 0, as in fgsea.
  • Each set is compared with random gene sets of the same size drawn from the ranked list (gene-set permutation, as in the GSEA desktop application's Preranked mode). The same data give the same results every time.
  • NES, the normalized score, is ES divided by the mean |ES| of the random sets of the same sign, so that sets of different sizes can be compared.
  • The p-value compares a positive ES only with the random sets' positive scores, and a negative ES only with the negative ones, because the two tails differ in shape (Korotkevich et al. 2021): p = (1 + the random sets at least as extreme) / (1 + the random sets of that sign).
  • FDR is the Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment of those p-values over the sets tested, as fgsea's padj; it is not the GSEA desktop application's FDR q-value.
  • Leading edge: the set's genes ranked before the running sum's peak for a positive ES, or after its lowest point for a negative one.
  • Automatic permutations: 10 × (sets tested) / 0.05, and at least 10,000. The smallest possible p-value is about 2 / permutations, and the FDR multiplies it by the number of sets, so this lets a strongly enriched set reach an FDR well below 0.05 however many sets are tested. A very large run is limited to a few minutes, and the Chart Legend then says so.
  • When no random set scored as extreme as a gene set, its p-value is at the floor, 1/(n + 1), and the true p may be smaller. The Note column marks each such set, and the Chart Legend counts them.
  • The GSEA Bar box and the Chart Legend record the run: the permutations and how they were chosen, the size range, the sets tested, repeated genes and, when 1% or more of the genes share a score, the ties (the order of tied genes is arbitrary and can shift the scores).

Make a Grouped Diverging Bar

A Grouped Diverging Bar draws signed values either side of zero, with several series in each category, each as its own thin bar: fold changes under several conditions for each feature, for example.

  1. Arrange a table with a header row and 3 columns: category, series and value. A wide table also works: the category, then one number column per series, named in the header.
  2. Select it and choose Grouped Diverging Bar from the Omics Plot menu.
  3. In Plot Style › Grouped Diverging Bar, choose the Orientation: Horizontal (the default, with categories in rows) or Vertical (categories along the X axis).
  • Categories and series appear in the order they first occur. Each series keeps its own lane and color in every category; a category with no value for a series leaves that lane empty, marked NA.
  • When a category and series repeat, the first row's value is used. Plot Style, the Data Log and the Chart Legend say how many rows repeat; combine them in the table first if they should be added.
  • Values may carry a percent sign (45%), and rows that can't be read are counted in the Data Log. The axis titles start as the table's headers.
  • Swap Category and Series exchanges the two name columns and clears the series' color changes. Series colors sets each series' color; ↺ returns it to the palette. More than eight series take their colors from ggplot2's default palette.

Show a Stacked Composition Bar

A Stacked Composition Bar shows a Grouped Diverging Bar's table as one stacked bar per category, for composition, such as cell-type proportions per sample.

  1. Make a Grouped Diverging Bar.
  2. Under Chart Type, click Stacked Composition Bar (in Omics Visualization).
ControlWhat it does
Show as percentageScales every bar to 100% (off by default, so each bar's length is its total). The value axis's title gets "(%)" unless it already says percent.
Show totals (n)Writes each bar's total at its end (on by default): "n = …" in percent mode, where 50% of 4 and 50% of 4,000 look the same.
Label segments with their shareWrites each segment's share of its bar inside it, where it fits (off by default).
Sort bars byData order (the default), or Share of a series: the bars in order of that series' share, largest first.
  • Series stack in the same order in every bar: the order they first appear in the table.
  • Negative values are left out of the stacks, and a category with no positive value draws an empty bar; Plot Style counts both. Repeated rows are handled as in a Grouped Diverging Bar.
  • Orientation, Swap Category and Series and Series colors work as for a Grouped Diverging Bar.

Venn Diagram and UpSet Plot

Both compare named sets of items, such as lists of gene names, protein IDs or samples, from a table with one set per column: the set's name in the header row and one item per line below it. Items match exactly, capitalization included, ignoring only surrounding spaces and quote marks: "TP53" and "Tp53" are different items, so use one naming convention in every set. Missing-value placeholders (NA, N/A, NaN, NULL, None, ".", "-" and "--", in any capitalization) are not items.

Make a Venn Diagram

  1. Arrange 2 or 3 columns, one set in each.
  2. Select them and choose Venn Diagram from the Omics Plot menu.
  3. Click a region to list its items. Copy puts the list on the clipboard, one item per line. A name that matches a point in an open Volcano Plot exactly links to that point.
  4. In Plot Style › Sets, click a set's name to rename it, set its color, or click Edit List… to replace its items, one per line. + Add a 3rd Set adds an empty set, and Remove (with 3 sets) takes one away; ⌘Z undoes it.
  • Each region's count is the number of items in exactly those sets. Show percentages (Plot Style › Labels; off by default) adds each region's share of all the distinct items.
  • With 2 sets, the circles and their overlap are drawn to scale, and a region too small for its count is labeled outside, with a line to it. With 3 sets the layout is a fixed triangle, not to scale. The counts are always exact.
  • The plot's table and its exports give the sets one per column, as pasted. Editing them in the table updates the diagram, as long as 2 or 3 sets remain.
Test whether an overlap is larger than chance
  1. In Plot Style › Overlap Significance, type the Background size: the number of items the sets were drawn from, such as every feature tested. When a set came from a Volcano Plot, the box suggests the number of features that plot tested (those tested in both, for sets from two plots); click Use to take it.
  2. Click an overlap region. Its popup adds the fold enrichment and a p-value for over-representation.
  • Fold enrichment is the number of items the sets share, divided by the number expected if the sets were independent samples from the background: the background size times each set's share of it (Wang et al. 2015). It and the p-value count every item the sets share, including any also in a third set.
  • The p-value is a one-tailed hypergeometric test for two sets, and its exact multi-set extension for the overlap of all three. Below 0.001 it is written in scientific notation, such as 6.5e-12.
  • The background must be at least the number of distinct items across the sets. If it is smaller, a note says so and no p-value is shown. Leave the field blank to skip the test.
Sets from a Volcano Plot
  • From the Venn Diagram: a set's Pull from Volcano Plot… menu lists the open Volcano Plots. Choose one, then Up or Down (all significant), Up only or Down only.
  • From the Volcano Plot: under Send to Venn Diagram in its Plot Style, choose Genes to send, then click New Venn Diagram… (which fills Set 1) or choose a set of an open diagram from Send to….
  • The set holds the features that pass the Volcano Plot's thresholds at that moment. After changing the thresholds, pull or send again.

Make an UpSet Plot

An UpSet Plot suits 4 or more sets, where circles become unreadable. Each set's size is a horizontal bar at the left. Each combination of sets is a vertical bar, largest first, over a column of dots marking the sets it joins.

  1. Arrange 2 or more columns, one set in each (Smart Visualization sends 4 or more here, and 2 or 3 to a Venn Diagram). A 0/1 membership table also works: an optional first column of item names, then one column per set, with 1 for members and 0 otherwise.
  2. Select them and choose UpSet Plot from the Omics Plot menu. With more than 8 sets, @Graph asks before it builds the plot; a plot holds at most 63.
  3. In Plot Style › UpSet Plot, choose Count items: In exactly these sets (the default) or In at least these sets. Set colors, below it, sets each set's color.
  4. Click a bar or its column of dots to list its items, filter the list and copy it.
  • In exactly these sets counts the items in those sets and no others (exclusive intersections, as UpSetR draws them), so the bars add up to the number of distinct items. The axis is titled Exclusive Intersection Size.
  • In at least these sets counts the items in those sets whatever else they are in (inclusive intersections). An item is then counted in several bars, and every combination that shares an item gets a bar. The axis is titled Inclusive Intersection Size.
  • Up to 40 combinations are drawn, the largest first, with equal sizes in set order. A note under the chart says how many were left out and how many of the items the bars drawn cover.
  • Tick Values, under Axes & Labels, sets the set names' font, size and color; the counts and titles follow its size, in the Legend font. Where the bars are too narrow for their counts, the counts get smaller, and then only every second or third bar is labeled.
  • A Venn Diagram and an UpSet Plot hold the same sets, so either can be switched to the other under Chart Type; a Venn Diagram draws only 2 or 3 sets.

Manhattan and QQ Plots

A Manhattan Plot is the usual display of a genome-wide association study (GWAS): one point per variant, placed by chromosome and position along X, with −log₁₀ of its p-value on Y.

Make a Manhattan Plot

  1. Arrange a table with a column each for chromosome, position and p-value and, optionally, a name for labels. A table separated by spaces, as PLINK writes it, is read too.
  2. Select it and choose Manhattan Plot from the Omics Plot menu.
  3. In Plot Style › Manhattan Plot, set the threshold lines, the chromosome layout and the labels.
  4. To check the p-values for inflation, click Open QQ Plot.
  • Columns are found by their headers: chromosome (CHR, CHROM, #CHROM, Chromosome), position (BP, POS, Position, base_pair_location), p-value (P, PVAL, PVALUE, P-value, PBOLT_LMM) and name (SNP, ID, RSID, variant_id, MarkerName). Without those names, the columns are read in the order chromosome, position, p-value, name.
  • "chr1", "Chr1", "01" and "1" are one chromosome, as are "M" and "MT". Chromosomes run in genome order: the numbered ones, then X, Y, XY, Z, W and MT, then any others alphabetically.
  • Rows that can't be read are counted in the Data Log. A row whose p-value is outside 0 to 1 is not plotted, and Plot Style says how many. A plot holds up to 250,000 variants; above that it shows a message instead.
  • A p-value of exactly 0 is plotted just above both the smallest p-value above 0 and the genome-wide line, so its height is a lower bound. Plot Style and the Chart Legend say how many variants this applies to.
ControlWhat it does
Show genome-wide significance lineA dashed line at its Threshold, in the color beside it (5×10⁻⁸ by default, the convention for human GWAS; other species or study designs may need another value).
Show suggestive significance lineA second dashed line (1×10⁻⁵ by default).
Show Bonferroni line (α / m)A line at α divided by m, the number of variants plotted: the p-value each test must beat to keep the chance of any false positive among them at α (off by default; α is 0.05). A note gives the line's p-value and m.
Equal-width chromosomesOn by default: every chromosome gets the same width and each variant sits at its relative position within it, so small chromosomes stay readable. Off: cumulative base-pair position, each chromosome as wide as its largest position in your data. If a chromosome has no positive position, equal widths are used either way.
Read 23–26 as X, Y, XY, MT (PLINK, human)On by default: PLINK's numeric codes are shown as X, Y, XY (pseudo-autosomal) and MT. It applies only when no chromosome is above 26 and none is already named X, Y, XY or MT. Turn it off for a species with more than 22 autosomes.
Chromosome colors, Point size, Point opacityThe two colors that neighboring chromosomes alternate between, and the points' look.
Auto-label top hits, Max labelsNames one lead variant per locus (on by default; up to 10): the smallest p-value at or below the genome-wide threshold, then the next one more than 500 kb from every labeled variant on its chromosome. It needs a name column. A label that would overlap another is moved up, with a line to its point, or left out.
  • Genomic inflation λ, in Plot Style and the Chart Legend, is the median of the χ² statistics (1 degree of freedom) that the p-values imply, divided by 0.4549, its median when no variant has an effect (Devlin & Roeder 1999). Near 1 is what the null gives; well above 1 (say 1.1 or more in a large scan) suggests population structure or other confounding inflating every test.

Open a QQ Plot

Open QQ Plot, in Plot Style › Manhattan Plot, opens the plotted p-values in a new window: each observed −log₁₀(p), sorted, against the value expected if no variant had an effect, with the y = x line and a shaded 95% band.

  • The expected values are R's ppoints, as qqman plots them. The band is each point's 95% interval under the null: for the i-th smallest of m p-values, the interval of a Beta(i, m − i + 1) distribution.
  • Under the null, the points follow the line inside the band. A lift along the whole range points to inflation; a lift only at the top, to real hits.
  • Its own Plot Style sets the point color, size and opacity, and it exports like any chart.

Axes, Legends and Style

  • Axes & Labels holds each plot's titles, fonts, colors, ticks and grid, as for any chart (see Charts › Axes & Labels and Charts › Legend). Volcano and MA plots have no grid. A PCA Plot's axis titles are set by the components plotted, and a Venn Diagram or UpSet Plot has no axis titles to edit.
  • Graph Utilities › Copy Style (⌥⌘C) and Paste Style (⌥⌘V) carry a plot's look to another plot, without its data: colors, fonts, point sizes and mapping. Its thresholds, adjusted-p choice, normalization and clustering stay the target's own (see Charts › Copy and Paste a Chart's Style).
  • The AI Assistant can read a Volcano Plot's results and change its thresholds; run compute_gsea, by the rules above; build a Manhattan Plot and change its thresholds, colors, chromosome widths, points and labels; set a Dot Plot's scaling, size threshold, hiding and ordering; and read a Venn Diagram's or UpSet Plot's item lists and switch an UpSet Plot's counting (see AI Assistant).

Batch Processing and Protocols

The Batch Processing menu repeats work for you in two ways. Batch Process Files… runs one operation on every file you check in a folder and combines the results into one report. Protocols… builds a named list of steps that you save and run on any open window. Both run the calculations of the inspector panels and menu commands, so the same sweeps and settings give the same numbers in a panel, in Batch Processing and in a Protocol.

Batch Processing

Run One Operation on a Folder

  1. Choose Batch Processing › Batch Process Files….
  2. Click Choose Folder… and pick the folder. The files Batch reads are listed.
  3. Uncheck the files to leave out, or use Select All and Deselect All.
  4. Choose a Group: Modify, Signal, Measure, Toolkits or File Handling. For Toolkits, a second row picks the toolkit: E-Phys, Pharm, Bio, Spectra, Flow or Astro.
  5. Choose the Operation and set its options (see Operations, below). To see each file's channel names and units, click Show Channels.
  6. For an operation that saves files, choose the format under Save as. The files go into a folder named Batch output inside the input folder, unless you click Choose Output Folder….
  7. Click Run. It stays disabled, with the reason beside it, until every setting can be read.
  8. Read the report at the bottom of the window. Click Save Report… to save its text, Save Table as CSV… to save its tables, or Show Saved Files to see the new files in the Finder.
  • You can keep working in other windows during a run. Stop (⌘.) ends the run: the file under way stops at its next check (a file stopped partway reports nothing), and the rest are listed as not processed.
  • A file that can't be read or measured is reported as failed, with the reason, and the run goes on.

Choosing Files

  • The list holds every file in the folder that @Graph opens as a graph: recordings, saved .@graph graphs and text tables (.csv, .txt, .tsv, .text, .rtf). Files in subfolders, hidden files and other kinds (images, PDFs, documents) are left out, and the window says how many.
  • Files an earlier run made there (cell1_scaled.abf, cell1_IVplot.@graph, a saved Batch Report or Batch Results) start unchecked, so they aren't processed again as inputs.
  • A text table is read as the Graph Data dialog starts, on Automatic: a first column such as "Time (ms)" with evenly spaced values is the time axis, and otherwise the rows are 1 s apart. The report says how each table was read.
  • A file that holds several parts, each of which opens in its own graph window (streams at different rates, HEKA series, SutterPatch routines), is processed part by part. The report has a section for each part, and outputs are named with the part (cell1 (R2 VI)_scaled.abf).
Pair files for VI / IV Plot
  1. Choose Toolkits, E-Phys and the operation VI / IV Plot. Each file in the list gains a role menu, set to Skip.
  2. Mark each file Voltage or Current. These pair up in list order.
  3. Mark a file Both when it records the voltage and the current itself (Vm and Im channels), or records one of them and its protocol gives the other's steps. It is paired within the file.
  4. Check the line under the list, which counts the pairs. It is orange while the Voltage and Current counts differ.

For a file that records only the response and has no protocol, mark it Both and fill in First step, Increment and Holding (pA for a VI Plot, mV for an IV Plot) and, optionally, Step start and Step end. Files with a step channel or a protocol use their own.

For VI / IV Plot, check every file's role before you run. Pairing goes strictly by list order, so one wrong role pairs the wrong files.

Operations

The table lists the operations of Batch Processing and the steps of a Protocol, by group, with the guide page that explains each analysis. Those marked Protocols only or Batch only are in one of the two.

GroupOperations and stepsExplained on
