SignalAverage Sweeps, Normalize Sweeps, Align PeaksSignal Processing
MeasureLinear Fit, Curve Fit, Exponential / Formula Fit, Peak Measurement, Cursor MeasurementMeasuring & Analysis
E-PhysAP DetectionAP Detection
E-PhysSynapse Detection: Spontaneous or Evoked in Batch; spontaneous only in a Protocol, where the step is Synapse Detection (Detect Events)Synapse Detection
E-PhysVI / IV Plot, Firing Properties, Membrane Test, Sag AnalysisElectrophysiology Commands
E-PhysLFP Power Spectral DensitySignal Processing
MicroscopyProtocols only: Shading Correction, Debayer, Subtract Background, Frame Quality, Registration, Channel Alignment, Average FramesImaging
PharmDose–Response, Initial Rates, Pharmacokinetics (NCA), qPCR AmplificationCurves on a Graph
PharmProtocols only: Gel / Blot Lanes, Plate MapGels and Blots › Automate Gel / Blot Lanes; Plate Maps › Automate Plate Maps
BioECG / HRV, ECG Intervals, EEG Band Power, EMG Envelope & Bursts, RespirationBiosignals: ECG, Breathing, EEG and EMG
SpectraPeak Fitting. Batch only: Apply Wavelength Solution. Protocols only: Calibrate Wavelengths.Spectra on a Graph
FlowPopulation StatisticsFlow on X-Y Graphs
AstroTransit Search, Transit FitTransit Search and Phase Fold; Aperture Photometry and Transit Fit
AstroProtocols only: Calibrate Frames, Stack Frames, Plate Solve, Aperture Photometry (Series)Calibrate Frames › Automate Calibration; Stack Frames › Automate Stacking; Plate Solving › Automate Plate Solving; Aperture Photometry and Transit Fit
File HandlingBatch only: Convert Format, which saves each file again in another format, unchangedExporting Results
  • In Batch, the Modify and Signal operations, LFP Power Spectral Density, Apply Wavelength Solution and Convert Format save a new file for each input. The others add a table for each file to the report; VI / IV Plot and Firing Properties can also save each plot or F–I curve as a .@graph file.
  • Batch measures every sweep of each file, not only the sweeps a window would show. The Bio operations measure every sweep of the channel named. Firing Properties searches every sweep for spikes, including those of a group hidden in a saved graph, as Toolkits › Electrophysiology › Firing Properties does.
  • The Pharm, Bio, Spectra, Flow and Astro measurements run their inspector tab's calculation and give the table the tab writes. All but Bio's read X-Y files.
  • Aperture Photometry and the other Protocols-only tools have no Batch operation. Gel / Blot Lanes can measure a folder of images itself (see Gels and Blots › Automate Gel / Blot Lanes).
  • Competition binding isn't offered by the Dose–Response operation or step, since it needs each file's labeled ligand and its Kd. Fit it in the Dose–Response tab.

Settings

Each operation shows its main settings. Anything not shown is as the operation's panel starts: settings you changed in a panel aren't used. In a toolkit measurement, a field left blank takes the tab's default.

SettingDefaultWhat it does
Channel nameBlankBlank measures every channel for the fits, Peak Measurement, Cursor Measurement and AP Detection, and the first channel for Synapse Detection and the Bio operations. Type a name as Show Channels lists it (the unit can be left off; an unnamed channel is "Channel 2", say) to measure only that channel's sweeps, so a threshold in its unit applies to it alone. A file without the channel fails, with its list of channels.
RangeFull sweepOr Between two times: From (ms) and to. For the fits, Peak Measurement and AP Detection.
Junction potentialAs each graph opensFor the operations that read membrane potential. The default measures each file with the correction its own graph opens with (Settings' default for a recording, a saved graph's own setting), so the numbers match each graph's panel. Or choose Not corrected, or Corrected by and a value for every file.
Correct the voltage axis for RₛAs each saved graph sets itIV Plot only. By default a saved graph whose Rₛ panel corrects its IV Plot uses its own Rₛ, and a recording is not corrected. Measured in each file finds Rₛ from each file's test pulse, as the Rₛ panel's Measure automatically does; a file whose Rₛ can't be measured fails. Or choose One value for every file, or Not corrected.
Baseline-correct each sweep firstOffFor the fits, Peak Measurement, Cursor Measurement and AP Detection. Corrects each sweep before it is measured, by the Method chosen (Mean subtraction or Median subtraction over a region, Linear detrend or Polynomial fit), on one channel or all. The files are not changed. Sweeps that end before the region are left uncorrected, and the report lists them.
Save as@Graph (.@graph)The format of the files an operation saves (see Saving Results).
  • Times are in ms as each file's graph shows them, after a saved graph's Set X = 0 shift. You can type a unit with a number ("2 s", "20 kHz"). A file of X-Y data, whose X isn't time, is refused by an operation that takes a time.
  • Values and thresholds are in the units each file's graph shows. A recording stored in nA shows, and is measured, in pA when that suits its values.
  • Where a toolkit's tab uses the cursors, the measurement takes X from and X to, in the X axis's own unit: Initial Rates' initial part, Pharmacokinetics' terminal phase, Peak Fitting's range and Population Statistics' gate.
  • The window remembers its settings between sessions; which files are checked and their VI / IV roles start fresh each time. Reset to Defaults puts every option back as the window first starts, and the chosen folder and files stay.
  • Settings are read when you click Run, so changing them during a run doesn't affect it.
AP Detection and Firing Properties
  • Both start with the threshold method and the dV/dt threshold set in Settings › Toolkits, as the AP Detection panel does. AP Detection also has the panel's other settings and measurement checkboxes (see AP Detection).
  • Firing Properties takes its step currents from each file's stimulus protocol, or else its current channel. For a file with neither, type First step and Increment (pA). In a file with several voltage/current pairs, each row of its tables starts with the pair.
Synapse Detection
  • Events go sets the direction. By default a current goes down (an inward EPSC) and anything else up.
  • Spontaneous: choose the Method (Threshold, Template or Deconvolution) and its threshold. A channel's sweeps are joined into one recording, as in the panel's Continuous mode (sweep by sweep when their sample rates differ), and the frequency is the events divided by the time searched. The table has the same columns for every file, even one with no events (see Synapse Detection › Synaptic Summary).
  • Evoked: type the Pulse times (ms, as the graph's X axis shows them, separated by commas) and the Onset threshold (in baseline SDs, 4 by default, or in the channel's unit with In baseline SDs unchecked). Choose the Stimulation type, which sets how long after each pulse to search, and set Ignore after pulse (1 ms by default). The report gives the panel's Per-Pulse Summary, a row per pulse.
  • Charge is measured only on a current channel; on any other, the report leaves it out and says why. Evoked charge is integrated over a fixed Window after each pulse (50 ms by default) unless you choose onset to return.
  • Settings not shown are as the Synapse Detection panel starts (see Synapse Detection).
Peak Measurement

Peak Measurement has the Peaks panel's settings (see Measuring & Analysis › Peaks Panel: Peak Detection). For Which set to First or All, set the Threshold, Separate peaks by (50% of the threshold by default) and Min. spacing (0 ms by default: off). Area is a charge in pC on a current channel, and an area in the unit × s on any other.

Dose–Response
  • Check X is already log10(dose) when the doses are logarithms, as in the tab. Doses are also read as log10 when any is negative.
  • Curves fits one curve per sweep, one per group, or one from every sweep's values pooled.
  • Dose 0 treats doses of 0 as the tab's choice does (see Curves on a Graph › Dose–Response). A file with no dose of 0 is fitted with the Weighting and the fixed Bottom and Top given.
  • The report starts with a summary of each curve: its EC50 (relative, or absolute at the response given) with its CI, Hill slope, R² and the weighting used. The curves' full tables follow.
Apply Wavelength Solution

Click Choose Solution… and pick a solution saved from Wavelength Calibration (see Spectra on a Graph › Wavelength Calibration). Each file's spectra, whose X is the pixel position, get the solution's wavelength scale, in its air or vacuum wavelengths and the Unit chosen (nm, Å or µm). Check "Resample onto an even grid (conserving flux)" for evenly spaced wavelengths. The new files are named "…_wavelength".

Running and Results

  • The report starts with the settings used. It appears in the window, is added to the Data Log, and is saved as text with Save Report….
  • Each file's section lists any warnings (a recording read only in part, a paired file whose unit doesn't match its role) and, if the file failed, why. A file whose fits were cut short by Stop is reported as failed, so no partial table is taken for a whole one.
  • Save Table as CSV… saves the report's tables as one CSV file: a row per file and sweep, with the file's name first, then the heading the table had in the report (such as Group 1 · Sweep 3). Cells with nothing measured are empty. A column of values with units, such as resistances, is written in one unit, named in its header.
  • The CSV ends with a File and Status table naming every file it has no rows for: those that failed (with the reason), those with nothing to tabulate, and those not processed because the run was stopped.
  • Each E-Phys table carries what its command's Data Log entry gives, with its notes and the definitions its numbers follow. VI / IV Plot's summary gives the junction potential taken off the resting level in a column of its own (0 when not corrected).

Saving Results

Save as offers @Graph (.@graph), Axon Binary (.abf), AxoGraph (.axgx), MATLAB (.mat), NWB (.nwb) and HDF5 (.h5).

  • @Graph (.@graph), the default, is recommended. The file opens as the panel's result would: one group per channel, a spectrum with its frequency axis, an integral or derivative with its unit. Only this format keeps an average's shaded band.
  • Axon Binary (.abf): Samples picks the sample depth. Match each file (the default) writes 16-bit for a file whose samples are still a 16-bit ABF file's own, which it keeps exactly, and 32-bit for every other. 32-bit saves every sample exactly, as ABF 2. 16-bit is half the size: each channel is rounded to 1/65,534 of its range.
  • NWB (.nwb): NWB Metadata… opens the export's metadata sheet once for the whole batch (see Exporting Results). The subject ID can be the same for every file or come from each file's name: the whole name, or the part before its first space, underscore or hyphen (A150416A 001.axgd gives A150416A). Each file keeps its channels' automatic roles and any electrode details of the NWB file it came from. Without metadata, a file read from NWB keeps its own.
  • Each output is named after its input and the operation (cell1_scaled.abf, cell1_VIplot.@graph). Convert Format keeps the input's name. Decimate with an error type saves the error as a second file (cell1_decimated_SEM.abf).
  • An existing file is never replaced, whether an input, an earlier run's output or a file written earlier in the same run. The new file's name gets a number instead (cell1_scaled 2.abf).

Protocols

A Protocol is a named list of steps that you build once and run on any open window: for example Baseline Correction → Filter → Detect Events for every new cell. A step runs with the settings saved in it, not with whatever its panel shows at the time; the image steps that use an image's or a tool window's own settings say so in the step. To run one operation on every file of a folder instead, use Batch Process Files….

Build a Protocol

  1. Choose Batch Processing › Protocols….
  2. Type a name in the Protocol name field.
  3. Click Add Step and choose a step from its group: Modify, Signal, Measure, E-Phys, Microscopy, Pharm, Bio, Spectra, Flow or Astro. The table under Operations lists them.
  4. Set the step's options and click Save. The step joins the end of the list, with its settings under its name.
  5. Add the other steps in the order they should run. Drag a step to move it, click its pencil to edit it, or right-click it for Edit…, Duplicate, Move Up, Move Down and Delete.
  6. To keep the protocol as a file, click the ⋯ menu beside the name and choose Save Protocol…. It is saved as a .atgproto file.
  • Load Protocol…, in the same menu, opens a saved .atgproto file, and New (Clear Steps) starts an empty protocol. If a loaded file has settings this version of @Graph doesn't know, an alert names them and those steps use their defaults.
  • ⌘Z in the Protocols window undoes changes to the list, including Load Protocol… and New (Clear Steps).
  • The protocol you are building is kept when you close the window.

Run a Protocol

  1. Open the window to run on: a graph window, or an image or Plate Map window for the steps that need one.
  2. In the Protocols window, under Run, choose it beside Window.
  3. Click Run Protocol (⌘R). The steps run in order.
  4. Read each step's result under Results as it finishes. The tables also go to the Data Log, where every table names its window.
  • A step that fails stops the run, and its message says why. Stop (⌘.) ends the run: the step under way stops at its next check and reports nothing, and the steps after it aren't run.
  • Changes a run makes to the chosen window's data are undone with ⌘Z in that window, a few at a time when fits, Detect Events or E-Phys steps come between them.
  • File › Print… prints the steps and the last run's report.

What Each Step Does

  • Baseline Correction, Filter, Smoothing and Scale / Offset change the window's sweeps, as their panels do.
  • Sample Rate, Integrate, Differentiate, Average Sweeps, Normalize Sweeps and Align Peaks open a new window with the result, as their tools do.
  • The Measure steps, AP Detection, Synapse Detection (Detect Events), Membrane Test and Sag Analysis report a table without changing the window.
  • VI / IV Plot, Firing Properties (its F–I curve) and LFP Power Spectral Density report a table and open a window with the plot.
  • The Pharm, Bio, Spectra, Flow and Astro measurements take the same settings as in Batch Processing. Each reports its tab's table without changing the window, and logs it under the step's name.
  • Calibrate Wavelengths applies a wavelength solution saved from Wavelength Calibration to the window's spectra, whose X is the pixel position, and opens them with wavelength as X, where later steps such as Peak Fitting can run.
  • The Microscopy steps run as the buttons of the image window's Correct tab do. Each opens its result and logs to the Data Log; the original image is not changed.

Which Steps Must Come First

Most steps run on a graph window that holds a sampled recording, in any order. A spike-train raster is refused. The steps below run on an image or Plate Map window and have a fixed place:

StepIts place in a protocolWhat may follow
Gel / Blot LanesThe only stepNothing: its result is a table, not a window.
Plate MapThe only stepNothing.
Plate SolveThe first stepAperture Photometry (Series), on the solved image.
Calibrate FramesThe first stepAperture Photometry (Series) or Stack Frames, on the calibrated frames.
Stack FramesThe only step, or the step after Calibrate FramesNothing.
Aperture Photometry (Series)The first step, or the step after Plate Solve or Calibrate FramesSteps that run on its light curve, such as Transit Search, Transit Fit, the fits and Peak Measurement.
Microscopy stepsIn a protocol of Microscopy steps onlyOther Microscopy steps. Each that makes a new image hands it to the next step.
  • Plate Solve sends data to online services, and a protocol never asks for consent while it runs. Allow each service once in the Plate Solve panel, with Don't ask again, before you run the protocol (see Plate Solving › Privacy and Credits). A service that hasn't been allowed stops the run with a message, and nothing is sent.
  • Gel / Blot Lanes measures the image window chosen under Run, or every image in a folder chosen in the step, with that window's settings.
  • Microscopy: Shading Correction takes its dark and flat images from open windows, named by their titles. Registration uses the image's Live Drift channel and reference frame. Channel Alignment applies the alignment last measured on beads. Average Frames can leave out the frames a Frame Quality step flagged.
  • The toolkit steps that read X and Y (all but Bio's) also run on X-Y graphs, a VI / IV plot or a spectrum included.

Step Settings

  • Baseline Correction, Filter, Smoothing and Scale / Offset have a Channel (All channels, or one: then only its sweeps change) and Apply to: All sweeps (the default), Visible sweeps, Selected sweep, Selected group or All groups. Most other steps have the scope options of their on-screen tool.
  • The fits, Peak Measurement, Cursor Measurement and AP Detection also have a Channel (All channels, or one: then only its sweeps within the scope are measured). A window without that channel stops the run, with its list of channels.
  • Baseline Correction turns junction-potential correction off and sets the Y axis back to automatic, as the panel does. Measurements use the window's junction-potential correction, as the panels do.
  • A Filter step starts at order 4, as the Filter panel does. An AP Detection step starts with the threshold method and dV/dt threshold set in Settings › Toolkits.
  • Synapse Detection (Detect Events) detects spontaneous events on one channel, in every group of it the window shows (the panel searches the selected group; the two agree with one group per channel): Threshold, Template or Deconvolution, Continuous or Episodic, optionally within a window of each sweep. Its threshold is in the channel's unit as the window shows it; Template and Deconvolution take theirs in noise SDs. A template is set by its rise and decay times, so a saved protocol works on any recording. For evoked responses, use the panel or Batch Processing.
  • Cursor Measurement measures between the times saved in the step. The window's cursors aren't moved.
  • The E-Phys steps measure the episodes the window shows, as the Toolkits menu commands do; Firing Properties still searches every sweep for spikes. The Pharm, Spectra, Flow and Astro measurements read every sweep's X and Y data, whatever the window shows, and the Bio steps measure the channel picked (the first when none is picked).
  • A VI / IV Plot step corrects the IV axis for Rₛ when its window does. For a window that records only the response and has no protocol, the step can hold the first step, the increment, the holding level and, optionally, the times.
  • Firing Properties opens the F–I curve in a new window; uncheck "Open the F–I curve in a new window" for the table only. Later steps keep running on the step's own window.

Times and New Windows

  • Times saved in a step (a baseline region, a cursor-measurement or search window) are in ms as the X axis of the window the step runs on shows them, after any Set X = 0 shift.
  • A step set to Between cursors A – B uses the cursors of the window it runs on, and needs both placed; otherwise the run stops with a message. Integrate and Differentiate can hold their own times instead ("Use these times instead of cursors A and B").
  • A step that opens a new window (Sample Rate, Integrate, Differentiate, Average Sweeps, Normalize Sweeps, Align Peaks, VI / IV Plot, LFP Power Spectral Density, Calibrate Wavelengths) has a Later steps run on choice, in its editor and beside it in the list. Then: this window, the default, keeps the later steps on the window chosen under Run. Then: new window makes them work on the result instead, for example Decimate → Filter → Detect Events on the decimated data. The list marks those steps "→ new window of step N".
  • A new window from Sample Rate, Integrate, Differentiate, Average Sweeps or Normalize Sweeps shows its source's times and keeps its X shift, cursors and X zoom, so the same times work on either window. After Align Peaks, 0 is the peak.
  • A new window that the run goes on in opens when the run ends, already showing what the later steps did. Those changes have no Undo there (close the window to discard them), and the window chosen under Run keeps its own data.
  • A VI / IV plot or a power spectrum isn't a recording. On one, only Linear Fit, Curve Fit, Exponential / Formula Fit, Peak Measurement and the toolkit steps that read X and Y can run, over the whole plot (it has no cursors). The list marks any other step after it in orange, and the run stops there with a message.

Back to Contents

AI Assistant

The AI Assistant is an optional chat assistant. Ask about your open recordings and results in plain language, and it can run real measurements and analyses for you (detecting action potentials, fitting curves, computing input resistance, running statistics and much more) with the same engines as the inspector panels. The numbers it reports are computed by @Graph, not guessed. It is off until you turn it on, and each AI service asks for your consent the first time you use it (see Opting In to Data Sharing).

Turn On the Assistant and Ask a Question

  1. In Settings › AI Assistant, check Enable AI Assistant.
  2. Choose Window › Open AI Assistant, or press ⌥⌘I from any window. The command is in the View menu too. The assistant opens in its own window, which you can keep beside your data.
  3. At the top of the window, choose who answers in the AI service menu, and a model in the menu beside it (see Choosing Who Answers Your Questions).
  4. For Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini or Grok, click Get an API Key, create a key on that company's page, paste it into the field and click Save Key. Apple Private Cloud Compute needs no key.
  5. Read the consent sheet and click Allow (see Opting In to Data Sharing).
  6. With Apple Private Cloud Compute, click Tools and choose the tool groups to use first.
  7. Type a question, such as "What's the input resistance of this cell?", and press Return or click Send.

Choosing Who Answers Your Questions

@Graph doesn't run a model on your Mac, so the AI service you choose decides whose servers see your questions. The AI Assistant Settings… link beside the menus opens Settings › AI Assistant.

AI serviceCompanyWhat it needs
Apple Private Cloud ComputeAppleNo API key: it runs under your Mac's Apple Intelligence, with a daily limit set by Apple (an iCloud+ plan raises it). It needs macOS 27 or later and a Mac that supports Apple Intelligence (see Using Apple Private Cloud Compute).
ClaudeAnthropicYour own API key, on a pay-as-you-go API account. A Claude.ai subscription doesn't cover it.
ChatGPTOpenAIYour own API key, on a pay-as-you-go API account. A ChatGPT subscription doesn't cover it.
GeminiGoogleYour own API key from Google AI Studio, free or paid. Google uses requests sent with a free key to improve its products (see Opting In to Data Sharing).
GrokxAIYour own API key, on a pay-as-you-go API account. A Grok or X Premium subscription doesn't cover it.
  • The model menu trades capability against speed and cost. It runs from that company's most capable model, which costs the most and can take minutes on a hard question, to the one marked "faster, cheaper", the default, which handles most questions. Choose one above it for harder ones.
  • Changing the model starts a new conversation. Switching to another service sets the conversation aside and brings it back when you switch back.
  • Settings › AI Assistant › Default Backend sets the service (Backend) and Model the window starts with the first time you open it after launching @Graph. Until you choose one, it is Apple Private Cloud Compute, which is free, on a Mac that can use it, and Claude otherwise.

Where the model lists come from

  • Once you have saved a service's API key and allowed it (the consent sheet's Allow, see Opting In to Data Sharing), and while the AI Assistant is on, @Graph asks that company for its current list of models, with your key, and keeps the chat models: those that answer in text, not the image, audio, video, embedding or search models. The request goes only to that company's own API (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google or xAI) and carries only your key; nothing goes through an @Graph server. It is asked again at most every 12 hours, and at once with Update Model Lists in Settings › AI Assistant.
  • The menu then offers the newest model of each family, the most capable first: Claude Fable, Opus, Sonnet and Haiku; ChatGPT's GPT Astra, Sol, Terra and Luna; Gemini Carbon, Argon, Pro and Flash; and for Grok the newest model and the one with the lowest price per token. A family @Graph doesn't know yet is listed just above the default, never as the default.
  • Until the list has been read (no key yet, the service not yet allowed, no internet connection, or the company didn't answer), the menu shows the list built into @Graph. The last list read is kept, so it is used offline too, and clearing a key forgets the list read with it. Settings › AI Assistant says which list the menu shows, when it was read, and why the last update failed if it did. Hold the pointer over the model menu for a model's ID, context window and release date and, for Grok, its price per million tokens.
  • A model you chose stays chosen when the list changes. If it is no longer listed, the newest model of its family takes its place, or the default if its family is gone. A conversation already under way keeps its model.

When a model is refused

A company can refuse a request because of the model: the model isn't available to your account, or, for a model newer than your version of @Graph, it expects a request @Graph doesn't yet send. For example, Anthropic refuses Claude Fable models for an organization with Zero Data Retention, since those models always keep requests for 30 days. The message then gives the company's own explanation, and a Use … Instead button offers the model that last answered for you (or the next one down the list). It starts a new conversation with that model, and your question stays in the box to send again.

Bringing Your Own API Key

Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini and Grok each need your own API key from that company; @Graph does not supply one, and Private Cloud Compute needs none. Keys are stored only in the macOS Keychain, never in an @Graph file, iCloud or an @Graph server. To remove a key, click Clear beside it in Settings › AI Assistant › API Keys.

Opting In to Data Sharing

The first time you use a service, Apple Private Cloud Compute included, a consent sheet appears; nothing is sent until you click Allow. After that, @Graph also asks the service for its list of models; that request carries only your key (see Where the model lists come from). It lists:

  • Provider: the company that receives the data.
  • Data sent: your questions, and what the assistant's tools read to answer them: measurements, statistics and detected events from your open windows and files, and, when a tool reads one, a window's contents (a spreadsheet's cells, a text editor's text, a trace, a spike list). Window titles, and the names and paths of files and folders the tools read; a path can include your macOS user name and the names of your folders. If Attach window screenshots is on (off by default; the checkbox is at the top of the AI Assistant window, and in Settings › AI Assistant as Attach window screenshots automatically), pictures of the windows it works with are sent as well (never to Private Cloud Compute).
  • Purpose: the data are used to generate the analysis on the provider's servers.
  • Your API key: stored in the macOS Keychain and sent directly to the provider, never through an @Graph server (for Private Cloud Compute, that no key is needed).
  • Retention: a summary of that provider's data-retention policy, which differs between providers (for example, Google may use data sent with a free Gemini key to improve its products, but not with a paid key). Some of a provider's models may carry longer retention or other terms than its usual ones (Anthropic's Fable models always keep requests for 30 days); the provider's model pages say which.
  • Allow proceeds. Cancel leaves that service unavailable: click Ask Again to see the request again, or pick another service.
  • "Remember my choice for [Provider]" (on by default) remembers an Allow for that provider only, so you aren't asked again. Unchecked, the Allow lasts until you quit @Graph or turn the assistant off. Allowing Claude doesn't allow ChatGPT, and a Cancel is never remembered.
  • Settings › AI Assistant › Reset Remembered Data-Sharing Consent… makes every service ask again. A request still running is stopped.
  • Every service sends your questions to that company's servers (Apple's, for Private Cloud Compute; the others under your own API key), and that company's retention policy applies.
  • A tool that uses another online service asks you itself. Plate Solve, for one, shows its own consent alert before anything is sent, and the assistant can't answer it for you (see Plate Solving › Privacy and Credits).
  • To read a folder that @Graph hasn't been given access to, the assistant opens a folder panel, and you choose the folder.
  • Voice dictation is transcribed on your Mac; the audio never leaves it (see Voice Input).

Choosing Tool Groups

Every request sends the description of each tool that is on. Turning off the groups you won't need makes each request smaller: it costs less, runs faster, and leaves the assistant fewer similar tools to choose between. All groups are on at first.

  1. Click the Tools button, under the AI service menus. The Tool Groups list opens.
  2. Uncheck the groups you won't need. Click the triangle beside a group to see its subgroups, and check or uncheck each by itself. A group's checkbox shows a dash while only some of its subgroups are on; clicking it turns them all on or off.
  3. To start from nothing, click Deselect All, which leaves only the Basic Tools, and check what you need. Select All turns every group on again.
  4. Click outside the list to close it. Changes apply from your next question, in the current conversation too, and are remembered the next time you open @Graph.
HeadingGroupSubgroupsWhat its tools do
GraphsGraph EditingFilters & Scaling, Display & StyleFilter, smooth, baseline, scale and offset, X = 0, channel gain; sweep grouping, interval bars, plot style.
GraphsGraph TransformsNoneNew windows: average, normalize, align, resample, integrate, combine, histograms.
GraphsMeasurementsNoneWindow statistics, distributions, peaks, fits, power spectra, spectrograms, cross-correlation.
GraphsFolder BatchNoneThe same measurements on every file in a folder, and folder comparisons.
Charts and StatisticsChartsCreate & Brackets, StyleCreate charts (a paired chart included), effect brackets and time-course models; restyle any chart, omics plots included (Charts › Style).
Charts and StatisticsStatisticsTests, ModelsEffect sizes with their tests, by the Statistics window's Compare choices; ANOVA, regression and mixed models.
Charts and StatisticsOmics PlotsGene Sets, Other PlotsDot, GSEA, UpSet and Venn plots; cluster scatter, PCA, Kaplan-Meier and Manhattan plots; read an open Volcano Plot's results and change its thresholds.
Images and TablesImagingDisplay, ROIs, CorrectChannels' display, Z and T, projections and Orthogonal Views; draw, detect, edit and measure ROIs and read their traces; a cube's spectra and band maps; shading, debayer, background, spots, registration, channel alignment, frame quality and frame averaging.
Images and TablesSpreadsheets & TextNoneRead and edit a Spreadsheet's cells or a Text Editor's text, insert or delete rows and columns, open new Spreadsheet and Text Editor windows.
ToolkitsElectrophysiologyCorrections, Cell Properties, APs & Synapses, Spike Trains, LFP, Folder BatchRₛ and junction-potential corrections, cell properties, action potentials and synaptic events, spike trains, LFP, and folders of files.
ToolkitsPharmacology & BiochemistryCurves & Kinetics, Gel / Blot Lanes, Plate Maps, Plate Photos & ColoniesDose–response, initial rates, pharmacokinetics, qPCR, gel and blot lanes, plate maps, plate photos and colony counts.
ToolkitsBiosignalsNoneECG beats and HRV, EEG band power, EMG envelope and bursts, respiration.
ToolkitsSpectroscopyNonePeak finding and fitting, isotope patterns and ion chromatograms, spectra read from images, wavelength calibration.
ToolkitsFlow CytometryCytometry Window, X-Y GraphsA Cytometry window's samples, gates and statistics; population statistics on X-Y graphs.
ToolkitsAstronomyPhotometry, Calibration, Stacking, Plate Solving, TransitsAperture photometry, calibration, stacking, plate solving and star names, transit search and fitting.
  • The Basic Tools at the top of the list are always on: listing open windows, screenshots, the Data Log, saving results to a file, and saving, exporting, duplicating and renaming windows.
  • If you ask for something that needs a group that is off, the assistant tells you which one to turn on.
  • A toolkit hidden in Settings › Toolkits hides its group too: it isn't listed under Tools and its tools aren't sent. The list ends with the hidden toolkits and a link to Settings › Toolkits. Show the toolkit again and its group comes back as you left it.
  • When the window you were working in uses a toolkit's tools whose group is off (a FITS image, a gel, a Plate Map, Calibrate Frames or Stack Frames, or a graph showing a toolkit's tab or Rₛ correction), a line under Tools names them, with Turn On. Nothing is turned on until you click it.
  • Private Cloud Compute uses only a few groups at a time (see Using Apple Private Cloud Compute).

What a request costs

  • An API service bills by the token, a unit of text of a few characters. Each row of the list shows about how many tokens it adds to a request, counted for the service you chose, and the note beside the Tools button shows the total each request starts with.
  • These tokens are sent with every request, but depending on the provider, repeats within a few minutes may cost much less.
  • A question sends one request, plus one more for each round of tool calls, and every request sends the whole conversation. A long conversation gets slower and costs more: click New Conversation to start over.
  • One question runs at most 60 tool calls in 15 rounds. The assistant says so when it reaches the limit; ask again to continue.

Asking Questions and Running Analyses

Type a question and press Return, or click Send. When the answer needs a number from your data, the assistant runs the same measurement and analysis tools as the inspector panels and reports the result. For example:

  • "What's the input resistance of this cell?"
  • "Detect action potentials between 200 and 400 ms and tell me how many fired."
  • "Fit an exponential to the decay after the peak and give me tau."
  • "Run a t-test comparing these two columns." (or "Compare their medians")
  • "Fit a mixed model to this table and show the profile."

The conversation

  • While the assistant works, Send becomes Stop. Changes its tools made before you stop stay, and are listed.
  • New Conversation starts over. Copy Conversation copies the whole chat as plain text.
  • If a request fails, the red message under the conversation says what to do next, such as checking the API key or the billing on the provider's website. Changes made before the failure stay, and are listed.
  • If a tool's result is very long (a whole long trace, say), the assistant sees only the first part, says so, and reads a smaller range instead.
  • With Attach window screenshots on, each tool that uses a graph or image window sends the assistant a picture of it, taken after the tool ran.

Windows, units and options

  • Name the window to work on as its title reads. If a name could mean more than one open window, the assistant asks rather than guessing. With only one window of a kind open, "the graph" or "the image" is enough for a question, but a change made in a window always names it.
  • Times you give and get back are as the graph's X axis shows them, after any Set X = 0. Values and thresholds are in the units the graph shows (pA, mV), also for a file the assistant reads from disk without opening it. A spreadsheet's cells are named as on screen: rows from 1, columns by letter. Sweeps and channels are numbered from 1.
  • You can ask for specific options, such as the fractional derivative threshold method for AP detection (see AP Detection), or a particular channel or time window. If an option doesn't apply to what you asked for (charge on a voltage recording, say), the result says it was ignored and why.
  • Input resistance uses your Settings › Toolkits fit options unless you ask for others. AP detection uses the AP Detection panel's last settings, or Settings before the panel's first run, as Firing Properties does, and the result names them.
  • A tool that reads a file or a folder measures each file as its graph window opens it: a saved graph keeps its own settings (its IV Rₛ correction, Set X = 0 and junction potential correction), as in Batch Processing, and each result says which settings were used.
  • Spontaneous synaptic events are detected as the Synapse Detection panel's Continuous mode, Batch Processing and Protocols detect them, so the assistant's counts, amplitudes and frequency match theirs.
  • To set a graph's or chart's fonts, name a font family as Font Book lists it, such as Helvetica Neue, or say System; a font that isn't installed is refused. A channel's gain (Channel Gain…) is set only to a gain you tell it.

Statistics

  • Answers lead with the effect size and its CI, then p, judged at the α that matches Settings › Statistics › Default confidence level (0.05 at 95%).
  • For repeated measures, give it a table with one row per subject: a group column (codes such as 0 = control, 1 = treated, or labels such as Control, Treated), one column per condition and, optionally, a column naming each subject's source (Values from the same).
  • Its mixed model reports each group's rate of change and how the slopes differ, the difference in level and the difference at each condition (with simultaneous CIs), then the Group × Condition test, and it can open the repeated-measures chart with brackets (see Tests › Linear Mixed Model). On that chart it can change Time, Covariance and Values from the same, and switch the brackets to rate of change over the conditions you name.
  • It also runs split-plot ANOVA and two-way ANOVA (two crossed factors, such as genotype × drug).

Changes and files

  • Every change the assistant makes is listed in the chat in orange, with how to undo it: ⌘Z in that window for a change made in place (including a spreadsheet's cells and a text editor's text), or closing the new window it opened. Each change is its own step, so ⌘Z takes back one at a time.
  • Nothing is written to disk without you. A new file goes through a save panel where you pick it, saving over a file that already exists asks first (Save, Cancel or Save As…), and the export tools open the usual Export panels, where you choose the options and the file.
  • Text the assistant reads from your files, cells and windows is treated as data, never as instructions: only your own messages ask it to act. If a file's text seems to ask for something, the assistant tells you and asks.

What the Assistant Writes to the Data Log

  • A tool writes to the Data Log exactly what its panel or menu command writes when you run it yourself, under the same name, and its answer says so.
  • A tool whose panel writes nothing writes nothing. A chart's significance test, for one, adds its brackets to the chart, as Compute Brackets does.
  • Nothing of the conversation goes there. The assistant adds an entry of its own only when you ask it to log something, and then only a tool's result as the tool gave it.
  • The folder tools, like Batch Processing, don't write an entry for each file.

Using Apple Private Cloud Compute

Private Cloud Compute's context window holds about 32,000 tokens for everything: the instructions, the tools, the whole conversation and each answer. So with it:

  • You choose the tool groups under Tools, up to 12,000 tokens of tools and instructions with the Basic Tools, which leaves the rest of the window for the conversation. Each group and subgroup shows its size, and one that wouldn't fit with those chosen is grayed out until you turn another off. Until you choose one, Send is off. The note beside Tools shows how much of the budget is used.
  • Answers are short: the numbers you asked about. A tool whose panel writes to the Data Log puts its full result there.
  • It never receives window screenshots.
  • When the conversation nears the limit, or you change the groups, @Graph condenses it: the assistant keeps a short summary of the last few questions and answers, and its next reply says so. Everything stays in the chat and the Data Log.
  • Each person gets a daily number of requests, and every round of tool calls counts as one. The window shows when you're near or at the limit, with Apple's options for raising it (Show Options), and the message at the limit says when it resets.

Voice Input

Click the microphone button to dictate a question. The text appears as you speak, and recording stops when you finish or click the button again. Transcription happens entirely on your Mac: in your Mac's language when the Mac can recognize it by itself, and otherwise in US English. A Mac with no microphone connected says so instead of recording. The button is off while a request is running.

Saved Prompts

To save a question you ask often ("Detect APs on the visible sweep and summarize"), type it and click the filled star beside the input field. The star menu on the left lists saved prompts: pick one to put it in the input field, where you can edit or send it, or use Remove… to delete one.

Check a surprising number from the AI Assistant as you would any other measurement.

Statistics

These settings change how statistical results are computed or reported.

SettingDefaultWhat it changes
Default confidence level95%90%, 95% or 99%, for every confidence interval @Graph reports, from a formula or a bootstrap: descriptive statistics, the estimate and effect size of every Compare choice, post-hoc comparisons, regression coefficients, correlation, contingency tables, every interval on an Estimation Plot, Kaplan-Meier hazard ratios, a chart's CI error bars, and the CI error bars of the curve-fitting tabs' means figures. Table headers and notes (such as "95% CI") show the level in use.
Bootstrap CI methodBCaBCa (bias-corrected and accelerated, recommended) or Percentile, for every confidence interval that is bootstrapped because no formula fits. Choose Percentile only to reproduce results made with it. The setting applies the next time an analysis runs, and labels show "(BCa bootstrap)" or "(Percentile bootstrap)".
Warn on small-sample bootstrap CIs, with Warn below n =On, below n = 5 (3–20)Adds a note to a Statistics window result table when a bootstrap CI is built from fewer values per group or pair than this. The note means the interval is imprecise, not that it is wrong.
Always show effect sizes as positiveOffEffect sizes are normally signed: negative when the first group is lower. When on, a result-table row with a negative estimate is restated the other way round: the group names swap, and the estimate, its CI, the test statistic and the effect size are all given for the reversed order. A chart bracket shows its effect size and CI as positive.
  • Confidence level: with 3 or more groups, pairwise CIs are simultaneous at 1 − α/m, except Cohen's d in a two-way post-hoc, whose CI is per comparison. The variance-explained effect sizes (η², partial η², ω², Cohen's f and R²) get a 1 − 2α interval, 90% at the default 95% (Steiger 2004), so each excludes zero exactly when its F test gives p < α. The CI error bars of an averaged AP phase plot follow the level too.
  • Bootstrap CI method applies to AKP robust d (Trimmed means), dav and gav for paired means, the Estimation Plot's intervals for means and dominance δ, Kendall's W for Cochran's Q, Cramér's V, Cohen's w, and Spearman and Kendall correlation. The Estimation Plot's medians and trimmed means always use the smoothed bootstrap's percentile interval. Intervals that come from a test (t, noncentral t and F, Yuen, the rank-inversion Hodges-Lehmann CI, Clopper-Pearson) are never bootstrapped. See Compare and Effect Sizes › Bootstrap intervals.
  • Always show effect sizes as positive: Estimation Plot labels stay signed as plotted (later minus earlier group). The setting also applies to Cohen's g and ln(odds ratio) on proportions charts. η², ω², Cramér's V and Kendall's W are never changed.

Lab Tools & Calculators

The Lab Tools menu lists the calculators: the core ones first, then each toolkit's under its name (a hidden toolkit's calculators are hidden too; see Toolkits: Overview). Choosing one opens the Lab Tools window, which lists them all in its sidebar. Values you enter are kept when you choose another calculator.

  • A result shows a dash (—) until every value it needs is a valid number.
  • In a field that shows a unit, a value can be typed with a unit and is converted to the field's: 50 mg in a g field, 100 mM or 100 mmol/L in an M field, 500 µl in an mL field, 0.8 s in an ms field, 66.5 kDa in a g/mol field. The field's hint shows an example.
  • Where a menu picks the unit, a unit typed with the value wins and is converted to the menu's, which bare numbers and results use.
  • A unit of another kind, or a unit on a plain number such as NA, shows the dash.

Molarity Calculator

Solves concentration (M) = mass (g) ÷ molecular weight (g/mol) ÷ volume (L) for the one chosen under Solve for (Concentration by default), from the other three.

  • Inputs: Mass (g), Mol. Weight (g/mol), Volume (mL) and Concentration (M).
  • Common Molecular Weights lists common compounds (NaCl, KCl, CaCl₂ and MgCl₂ anhydrous and as their usual hydrates, HEPES, EGTA, the disodium salts of ATP and GTP, and others). Use fills in the molecular weight: choose the form you weigh.
  • A result outside 0.1 to 10,000 moves to a better prefix (0.0001 M shows as 100 µM, 0.005 mL as 5 µL).

Dilution Calculator

Solves C₁V₁ = C₂V₂ for the one chosen under Solve for (V₁, the volume of stock, by default). The Serial Dilution box lists the concentration at each step from a starting concentration (1000 µM by default), a dilution factor (10) and a number of steps (6).

  • Type each value with its unit: concentrations as molar (M, mM, µM, nM, pM, fM), mass per volume (g/L, mg/mL, µg/mL, ng/mL…), % (w/v or v/v) or × (a 10× stock to 1×), and volumes in L, mL, µL or nL.
  • The two concentrations must be of one kind; units within a kind convert. Molar and mass per volume are not mixed, since converting needs the molecular weight (use the Molarity Calculator).
  • A number without a unit takes the unit of the other field of its kind.
  • The result is in the unit typed in the other field of its kind (V₁ in V₂'s unit), under a better prefix outside 0.1 to 10,000.
  • A C₂ above C₁ is flagged: a dilution can't raise the concentration, so the values or units are probably swapped.
  • The number of steps must be a whole number; the table shows up to 100 steps and says when it stops there.

Henderson–Hasselbalch

Calculates a buffer's pH from its pKₐ and the concentrations of its base and acid forms, pH = pKₐ + log₁₀([A⁻] / [HA]), or the base-to-acid ratio needed for a Target pH, 10^(pH − pKₐ).

  • Inputs: pKₐ (7.2 to start), [A⁻] and [HA] in molar units (80 mM and 20000 µM give 4:1; a number alone is in mM). Mass per volume is refused, since the base and acid forms differ in molecular weight.
  • Common Buffer pKₐ Values (25 °C) lists HEPES, PIPES, MES, MOPS, Tris, phosphate, bicarbonate and others; Use fills in the pKₐ.
  • The values are for 25 °C. pKₐ falls as the temperature rises (Tris by about 0.028 per °C, so a Tris buffer made to pH 7.4 at 25 °C is near pH 7.1 at 37 °C) and shifts with ionic strength, so check it for your conditions.
  • A very small or large ratio is shown in scientific notation (8.71e-04).

Microscopy Resolution

Calculates an objective's theoretical resolution and the sampling a camera gives it. It opens once per session with the camera and objective chosen in Settings › Imaging, and then keeps what you enter.

InputDefaultNotes
Wavelength550 nm300–1300 nm; for fluorescence, the emission wavelength. Drag the spectrum slider (380–700 nm), step it with the arrows, or type a value, in nm or with a unit such as 0.488 µm.
NA, Refractive index (n)0.90, 1.333The Objective menu (air, water and oil objectives) sets magnification, NA and refractive index; Preset sets the index (Air, Water, Glycerol, Immersion oil). An NA above the refractive index is flagged: it can't be reached in that medium.
Pixel size (µm), Sensor pixels (W × H)6.5 µm, 2048 × 2048The Camera menu fills them in for common sCMOS, CMOS and EMCCD cameras. The Andor Sona comes in two models, the 4.2B-6 (6.5 µm pixels) and the 4.2B-11 (11 µm).
Objective magnification (×), Coupler/relay (×)60, 1.0Total magnification is objective × coupler. The coupler's Preset menu runs from 0.35× to 2.0×.
Binning1 × 1Also 2 × 2, 3 × 3, 4 × 4 or 8 × 8. With n × n binning each image pixel is n camera pixels wide.
ResultFormula
Abbe limitd = λ / 2NA, for incoherent light or a condenser matching the objective's NA.
Rayleigh limitd = 0.61λ / NA.
Nyquist pixelλ / 4NA: the largest pixel at the sample that samples the finest detail a widefield image carries (its cutoff, 2NA/λ) at twice its frequency, as SVI's Nyquist calculator gives it.
Effective pixel sizeThe pixel size at the sample: camera pixel × binning ÷ total magnification.
Sampling status, Min magnification for NyquistWhether the effective pixel size meets Nyquist, with the ratio, and the total magnification that would.
Depth of fieldλ·n / NA² + n / (M·NA) · e, where M is the total magnification and e the image pixel on the sensor (camera pixel × binning).
Field of view, Sensor arrayFrom the image pixels across the sensor after binning and the effective pixel size.
  • Half the Rayleigh limit (0.305λ/NA), a common rule of thumb for the pixel size, is about 22% larger than the Nyquist pixel and undersamples. A confocal image carries finer detail and needs smaller pixels still.
  • The formulas are for one-photon imaging, so they don't give two-photon resolution.

The Objective Recommendations box at the bottom lists the objectives that meet Nyquist sampling with the current camera and wavelength, with each one's pixel size at the sample and field of view, and a Use button. Objectives that undersample are listed below them.

Power Analysis

For a two-sided t-test, finds the sample size needed for a target power, the power of a given sample size, or the smallest effect a given sample size detects. Power comes from the noncentral t distribution, as G*Power and R's pwr compute it, and N is the smallest whole number that reaches the target power.

  1. Choose the Design: Independent (two-sample), Paired or One-sample.
  2. Choose Solve for: Sample Size, Power or Detectable Effect Size.
  3. For a paired design, choose the Question: Magnitude (the default) or Consistency, as on Compare and Effect Sizes. The ⓘ beside it explains both.
  4. Type the effect size (0.5 to start), or turn on Compute from group means (Compute from the mean and μ₀ for one sample) and type the means and the SD. Detectable Effect Size needs neither.
  5. Type α (0.05 to start) and, as the calculation needs, the Target power (0.80) or the sample size (20; a whole number). α and power take 0.05 or 5%, not 5.
DesignEffect sizeN is
Independent (two-sample)Cohen's d: the mean difference ÷ the common SD.N per group; Total N is also shown.
Paired, MagnitudeCohen's dav: the mean difference ÷ the average of the two conditions' SDs, with the expected Correlation r between the conditions (0.5 to start, between −1 and 1).N (pairs)
Paired, ConsistencyCohen's dz: the mean difference ÷ the SD of the differences.N (pairs)
One-sampleCohen's d: (mean − μ₀) ÷ SD.N
  • Magnitude converts dav to dz = dav ÷ √(2(1 − r)), taking the two SDs as about equal, and shows the dz used beside the result. At r = 0.5 the two are equal. Take r from pilot data or earlier studies.
  • Detectable Effect Size gives Cohen's d, or for a paired design dz (Consistency) or dav with the dz it comes from (Magnitude). The target power must be above α.
  • The test has 2N − 2 degrees of freedom for independent groups and N − 1 otherwise, with noncentrality d √(N/2), or d √N for paired and one-sample designs.
  • Power of 99.95% or more shows as > 99.9%, and an N above 1,000,000 as > 1,000,000.

Cohen's conventions (d ≈ 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large) are for d and dav, not dz, which is larger than dav when r is above 0.5 and smaller below it. Enter an effect from independent groups, or one divided by the average SD, under Magnitude with the expected r, and a dz from paired pilot data under Consistency.

Electrophysiology Calculators

Part of the Electrophysiology toolkit.

Nernst Equation

Calculates an ion's reversal potential, E = (RT/zF) · ln([X]ₒ/[X]ᵢ), in mV. R and F are the CODATA 2018 values.

  • Inputs: Valence (z), a nonzero whole number (+1, −1, +2); the extracellular and intracellular concentrations in mM; and the Temperature (22 °C to start).
  • Common Ion Presets fill in the valence and typical mammalian-neuron concentrations for K⁺, Na⁺, Ca²⁺, Cl⁻ and H⁺.

Ohm's Law

Relates voltage, current, resistance and power through V = IR and P = VI. Choose Solve for (Resistance by default) and enter the two values it needs; for Power, any two of V, I and R. Power is always shown too.

  • Units start as mV, pA and MΩ, with power in pW; current goes down to fA. Each unit menu also sets the unit its result is shown in.
  • A value typed with its unit (0.05 V with mV chosen) is converted to the unit chosen beside it.

Pharmacology & Biochemistry Calculators

Part of the Pharmacology & Biochemistry toolkit.

Cheng–Prusoff (Kᵢ from IC₅₀)

Calculates a competitive inhibitor's inhibition constant from its IC₅₀ (Cheng & Prusoff 1973). Choose the Assay: Binding (labeled ligand), Kᵢ = IC₅₀ / (1 + [L] / Kd), or Enzyme (substrate), Kᵢ = IC₅₀ / (1 + [S] / Kₘ).

  • Type each value with its unit (such as 100 nM). [L] and Kd (or [S] and Kₘ) are converted to one unit, a number alone is taken in the others' unit, and Kᵢ is in IC₅₀'s unit.
  • The relation holds for competitive inhibition at equilibrium, with the receptor's (or enzyme's) concentration well below Kd and [L] (or Kₘ and [S]). With more receptor than that, much of the ligand is bound and the relation overestimates Kᵢ. For a noncompetitive inhibitor Kᵢ equals IC₅₀.

Dose Conversion Between Species

Converts a Dose (mg/kg) from one species to another by body surface area: dose₂ = dose₁ × Kₘ₁ / Kₘ₂, with the Kₘ factors (body weight ÷ body surface area) of the FDA's 2005 guidance on starting doses. It starts From Mouse To Human (adult). A mouse dose of 10 mg/kg, for example, is 0.81 mg/kg in an adult human.

  • Species: adult and child humans, mouse, hamster, rat, ferret, guinea pig, rabbit, dog, rhesus monkey, marmoset, squirrel monkey, baboon, micro-pig and mini-pig.
  • It also gives the total dose for a Body weight (left empty, the guidance's reference weight for the target species) and the dose in mg/m².
  • The conversion scales by body size only, not by differences in metabolism or sensitivity.

Half-Life and Clearance

For first-order (exponential) elimination from one compartment. Under Known, choose Half-life or Elimination rate constant and type it to get the other: k = ln 2 / t½.

  • The time unit is chosen beside the field (h to start); a value typed with another unit, such as 30 min or 0.01 /min, is converted to it.
  • With a Volume of distribution (L): clearance, CL = k · Vd.
  • With a Time since dose: the percentage remaining, 2^(−t / t½).
  • For a Fraction of steady state (90% to start): the time to reach it under constant dosing, which is also the time for a dose to fall by that percentage. 90% takes 3.3 half-lives.

Receptor Occupancy

The fraction of receptors bound at equilibrium, [L]ⁿ / ([L]ⁿ + Kdⁿ), and the concentration needed for a Target occupancy θ (90% to start), Kd · (θ / (1 − θ))^(1/n). n is the Hill coefficient (1 to start, for simple one-site binding).

  • Type [L] and Kd with their units (such as 20 nM). They are converted to one unit, a number alone is taken in the other's, and the concentration for the target is in Kd's unit.
  • With n = 1, half the receptors are bound at [L] = Kd and 90% at 9 × Kd.

qPCR Efficiency

Calculates amplification efficiency from the Slope of a standard curve (Ct against log₁₀ of the starting quantity over a dilution series): E = 10^(−1 / slope) − 1, shown as a percentage with the amplification per cycle. The second box gives the slope a chosen Efficiency (%) produces. A perfect doubling (100%) gives a slope of −3.32; 90% to 110% corresponds to slopes from −3.59 to −3.10.

Biosignals Calculators

Part of the Biosignals toolkit.

Heart Rate and RR Interval

Converts between heart rate (beats/min) and the RR interval (ms): HR = 60000 / RR. Type the rate in beats/min, bpm or /min.

QTc

Corrects a QT interval for heart rate, from the QT interval and RR interval in ms, with the corrections the ECG / HRV tab's Intervals give the heart chosen under Heart (People to start).

HeartCorrections
PeopleBazett, QT/√RR; Fridericia, QT/∛RR; Framingham, QT + 154·(1 − RR); Hodges, QT + 1.75·(HR − 60). RR in s.
Rabbit or guinea pigBazett and Fridericia.
RatKmecova–Klimas, QT/√(RR/150), RR in ms (Kmecova & Klimas 2010).
MouseMitchell, QT/√(RR/100), RR in ms (Mitchell et al. 1998).

Bazett's correction overcorrects at fast heart rates and undercorrects at slow ones; the others depend less on heart rate.

Decibels

Converts between decibels and a ratio: 20·log₁₀ of an amplitude ratio (voltage, current) or 10·log₁₀ of a power ratio, chosen under Quantity (Amplitude to start). A filter's −3 dB cutoff is where amplitude falls to 0.708 and power to half.

Spectroscopy Calculators

Part of the Spectroscopy toolkit.

Beer–Lambert

Solves A = ε·l·c for whichever one you leave empty: Absorbance A, Molar absorptivity ε (M⁻¹·cm⁻¹), Path length l (cm; 1 to start) or Concentration c (M). A second box converts between Transmittance (%) and Absorbance, A = −log₁₀(T). The law holds for dilute solutions, up to an absorbance of about 1–1.5.

Photon Units

Converts a value between wavelength (nm), wavenumber (cm⁻¹), photon energy (eV) and frequency (THz): E = hc/λ, ν̃ = 1/λ, f = c/λ, with the exact constants of the 2019 SI (hc/e = 1239.84198… eV·nm). Choose the unit under From (wavelength to start); a value typed with another of these units (2.33 eV with nm chosen) is converted from that unit.

Raman Shift

Converts between a scattered wavelength and its Raman shift, Δν̃ = 10⁷/λ₀ − 10⁷/λ (cm⁻¹, with wavelengths in nm), for the Laser wavelength λ₀ (785 nm to start). Stokes lines give positive shifts.

NMR Shift

Converts between ppm and Hz at the spectrometer frequency of the nucleus observed (400 MHz to start): Hz = ppm × MHz, for chemical shift differences and coupling constants.

Mass Accuracy

The error of a Measured m/z from the Theoretical m/z, in ppm, (measured − theoretical) / theoretical × 10⁶, and in mDa.

Flow Cytometry Calculators

Part of the Flow Cytometry toolkit.

Absolute Count (Counting Beads)

Cells per µL = (cell events / bead events) × (beads in the tube / sample volume in µL) × dilution. It is the Cytometry window's count for one tube typed in.

  • Inputs: the gated Cell events and Bead events, Beads in the tube (from the bead lot), Sample volume (µL) and, for a sample diluted before staining, Dilution (2 for 1:2; blank for none).
  • The 95% CI is exact (Clopper–Pearson, for the cells' share of the cell and bead events), and the Counting CV is √(1/cells + 1/beads).
  • Acquire at least 1,000 bead events.

Stain Index and Titration

The stain index, (median of the positive population − median of the negative) / (2 × robust SD of the negative) (Maecker et al. 2004), for one staining. For a titration, type one line per concentration (concentration, positive median, negative median, negative robust SD); the concentration with the highest index is marked.

Astronomy Calculators

Part of the Astronomy toolkit.

Magnitudes and Flux

Converts between a flux ratio and a magnitude difference, m₁ − m₂ = −2.5 log₁₀(F₁/F₂), and between an AB magnitude and its flux density, 3631 Jy × 10^(−0.4 m).

Distances and Sizes

The distance modulus m − M = 5 log₁₀(d / 10 pc) and back, the distance in light-years, the distance from a Parallax (mas), d = 1/p, and the angle a size subtends at a distance, θ = 2 atan(D/2d), and back. The distance modulus ignores extinction.

Plate Scale and Field of View

Arcseconds per pixel, 206.265 × Pixel size (µm) / Focal length (mm), and the field of view in arcminutes from the sensor's width and height in pixels.

Telescope Resolution

Dawes's limit, 116″ / Aperture D (mm), and the Rayleigh criterion, 1.22 λ/D, at a Wavelength (550 nm to start). These are the optics' limits; from the ground, seeing usually limits long exposures more.

CCD Signal-to-Noise

The CCD equation (Merline & Howell 1995): S/N = N* / √(N* + npix (1 + npix/nB)(NS + ND + NR²)), with every quantity in electrons (ADU × gain) for the whole exposure: the star's signal, the pixels in the aperture and in the sky annulus, and the sky, dark (0 to start) and read noise per pixel. Leave nB blank for a sky known exactly. The magnitude error is 2.5 log₁₀(1 + 1/SNR).

Redshift and Velocity

The relativistic Doppler velocity of a redshift and back, 1 + z = √((1 + v/c) / (1 − v/c)), and the Hubble-law distance cz/H₀ (H₀ 70 km/s/Mpc to start). The distance holds only for small redshifts: beyond z ≈ 0.1 it depends on the cosmological model.

Blackbody (Wien's Law)

From a Temperature (K): the peak of the blackbody spectrum per unit wavelength, λmax = b/T, and per unit frequency, νmax = b′T; the surface flux σT⁴; and, with a Radius in solar radii, the luminosity 4πR²σT⁴ in solar luminosities. From a Peak wavelength (nm): the temperature. The two peaks lie at different places in the spectrum (νmax is not c/λmax). Constants from CODATA 2018, and the IAU 2015 nominal solar radius and luminosity.

Airmass

The airmass at an Altitude above the horizon (0° to 90°) by sec z, Hardie's (1962) polynomial and Kasten & Young's (1989) formula, which holds to the horizon and is the one highlighted. Hardie's shows a dash below 5°, where the polynomial breaks down.
