Exporting Results

A graph, chart, table or statistics report leaves @Graph as an image, a data file, a copy on the clipboard or a printed page. This page gives the steps for each, then the options. Most start at the Export button, the first tool button in a graph or chart window's toolbar.

Export an Image of a Graph or Chart

  1. Click the Export button and choose Image…, or choose File › Export… (⇧⌘E). The Export Graph or Export Chart panel opens.
  2. Choose the Format: PNG, JPEG, TIFF, GIF, PDF or SVG (see Image Formats, below).
  3. Set the size. For a graph, type the Width and Height in points (pt), or click Match window to use the graph's size on screen. For a chart, type the size in pt, in, cm or mm, or choose a journal's column width from Journal width.
  4. For PNG, JPEG, TIFF or GIF, choose the Resolution. The panel shows the output in pixels.
  5. To leave the background out, turn on Transparent background.
  6. Click Export…, then name the file.
  • The panel starts from the format, size, resolution and background set in Settings › Export (PNG, 1200 × 800 pt, 144 dpi and not transparent unless you changed them).
  • The file shows the figure as it was when you clicked Export…, even if you change it meanwhile.
  • If an export takes more than a moment, a progress indicator appears. Click Cancel to stop it; no file is written.
  • An image window has its own Export menu, with Export Image…, Export Movie… and Export Data as TIFF… (see Imaging).

Copy as PDF

  1. Choose Copy as PDF from the Export menu, or right-click the graph or chart and choose Copy as PDF.
  2. Paste into Keynote, Pages, Word or any app that accepts PDF. The copy is a vector PDF, with an image alongside for apps that paste only images.
  • A graph is copied at the size of its graph area on screen, with a PNG at twice that resolution.
  • A chart is copied as PDF, PNG and TIFF, at the size and resolution set in Settings › Export.
  • Drag (the hand beside the Export button) does the same without the clipboard: drag the graph or chart into Keynote, Pages, Word, Mail or the Finder.
  • A Spreadsheet window has Copy as PDF and Send to Keynote… too, which draw the sheet as a table (see Spreadsheets).

Send to Keynote

  1. In Keynote, open the presentation and show the slide the figure should go on.
  2. In @Graph, choose Send to Keynote… from the Export menu, or right-click the graph or chart and choose it.
  3. The first time, macOS asks whether @Graph may control Keynote. Allow it; this is needed only once.
  • The figure is placed as a vector image on the current slide of the frontmost presentation. If no presentation is open, a new one is created.
  • A graph is sent at the size of its graph area on screen.
  • While Keynote takes the figure, the window's subtitle reads Sending to Keynote…, and you can go on working.
  • If Keynote can't take the image, the PDF opens in Preview instead.

Export a Table

  1. In a Spreadsheet window, open the Export menu (next to Data Statistics) and choose Export Data…, or choose File › Export… (⇧⌘E). Select cells first to export only those.
  2. In the Export Spreadsheet panel, choose the Format: CSV, TSV or Excel (.xlsx).
  3. Click Export…, then name the file.
  • Values are exported, not formulas. For what each format keeps, and for Open in Numbers, see Spreadsheets.
  • A sheet whose numbers have decimal commas is written as CSV with semicolons between the cells, as Excel writes CSV in those regions: in R, read it with read.csv2; in pandas, with sep=";" and decimal=",".
  • For a chart's data, click the Export button in the chart window and choose CSV (.csv) or TSV (.tsv) under Data. Every chart type can be saved this way, with the headers of its on-screen table. The Chart Data window's Export… button opens the Export Spreadsheet panel instead.
  • Every CSV @Graph writes opens correctly in Excel, symbols such as µ and ° included.

Save a Statistics Report

  1. Run the analysis in the Statistics window (see Statistics: Overview › Run an Analysis).
  2. Click Export Report….
  3. Choose Text or PDF from Format, then name the file.
  • Send to Data Log adds the same report to the Data Log instead.
  • After a regression, Export Plots saves the four residual plots as a PDF or PNG.

Export a Graph's Data

  1. Click the Export button and choose a format under Data: @Graph (.@graph), ABF (.abf), AxoGraph (.axgx), HDF5 (.h5), MATLAB (.mat), NWB (.nwb) or CSV (.csv).
  2. For ABF, choose 32-bit (exact) or 16-bit (smaller) in the Export ABF sheet. For NWB, fill in the NWB Metadata sheet (see Export to NWB, below).
  3. Name the file. The Data Log records what was written.
FormatWhat is writtenLimits
@Graph (.@graph)The graph as File › Save As… saves it.—
ABF (.abf)32-bit (exact) saves every sample unchanged as ABF 2. 16-bit (smaller) saves ABF 1.8 at half the size; a 16-bit ABF recording stays exact.Up to 16 channels at one sample rate. 16-bit needs sweeps of equal length with no gaps, so sweeps are trimmed to match, and the Data Log reports any trim.
AxoGraph (.axgx)AxoGraph X format: one time column and one column per sweep, in volts and amperes. A table of measurements is written as Y columns against its X column.Every sweep must share one sample rate.
HDF5 (.h5)One dataset per channel, [sweeps × samples], with channel_name, units and sample_rate attributes (and each sweep's length when they differ). A raster writes one dataset of spike times per unit under /units.Every sweep of a channel must share one sample rate. The file is plain HDF5, not NWB.
MATLAB (.mat)Level 5 format: for each channel a [samples × sweeps] matrix with its sample rate, units and (when they differ) sweep lengths. A raster writes one spike-times vector per unit.A variable over 2 GB is refused; use NWB or HDF5.
NWB (.nwb)A Neurodata Without Borders 2 file (see Export to NWB, below).—
CSV (.csv)One column per visible sweep, in group order, holding the data's own values (not junction-potential shifted) in full precision, with the unit in each header.—
  • ABF, AxoGraph, MATLAB, HDF5 and NWB keep channel names, units, sample rates and sweep structure, so the file reopens in @Graph and in tools that read that format.
  • X-Y data (such as an I-V curve) can be exported only as CSV or AxoGraph.
  • A chart's Export menu has @Graph (.@graph) too. Like Save (⌘S) and Save As… (⇧⌘S), it writes a .@graph file that reopens with all series and formatting. A large .@graph file shows a progress indicator while it loads.
  • AxoGraph: a file opened from AxoGraph and exported with the same channels and sweeps keeps AxoGraph's display settings.
  • CSV: sweeps sharing one sample rate share a first Time (s) column: the time within each sweep, starting at the recording's first-sample time (0 for most files, a little later for some, such as AxoGraph's). Otherwise, and for X-Y data, each sweep has its own X column beside it. A gap inside a sweep, or the end of a sweep shorter than the others, is an empty cell. With more than one group visible, each header starts with the group's name. Data to Graph… reads this layout back in.

Export to NWB

@Graph writes NWB 2 files in the layout that pynwb, the NWB Inspector and the DANDI Archive read. With the DANDI fields and each patch-clamp electrode's cell ID filled in (and, for mouse, an Allen Mouse Brain Atlas location), the file passes pynwb's validator, the NWB Inspector with no critical issues or best-practice violations, and dandi validate once dandi organize has named it. @Graph doesn't run these tools itself. Only this export writes NWB: a .@graph file and the HDF5 export are plain HDF5 that NWB software won't open.

  1. Click the Export button and choose NWB (.nwb). The NWB Metadata sheet opens.
  2. Fill in what the data can't say. Everything is optional; a small orange diamond marks what DANDI needs to accept the file.
  3. Read the list at the bottom of the sheet. It checks what you entered and says what DANDI will refuse and what the NWB Inspector's best practices note.
  4. Click Export… to write what you entered, Skip to export without any of it, or Cancel to stop.
  5. Name the file. If you export with blanks, the Data Log says what DANDI will refuse.

The metadata sheet

SectionWhat to enter
SubjectSubject ID; species (pick a common lab species, or type a Latin binomial such as Mus musculus or an NCBI taxonomy link); sex; and the age as a number of days, weeks, months or years (exact, a range, or that age or older, counted from birth or conception) or a date of birth instead. Strain, genotype, description and weight (g, kg or mg) are optional.
SessionExperimenters (Last, First; separate several with semicolons), institution, lab, experiment description, session ID, keywords (separated by commas) and related publications (DOIs, such as doi:10.1523/…).
ChannelsEach channel's Role, and the electrode's details. For a patch-clamp electrode: cell ID, location (for mouse, an Allen Mouse Brain Atlas name or acronym such as CA1 or VISp), slice, electrode description, seal and resistance. For an extracellular channel: location, electrode group, group description, device (the recording system unless you name one), position (x, y, z in µm) and filtering.
Spike Times (a raster)The resolution is filled in when @Graph knows the sampling rate. Otherwise enter the rate the spikes were detected at.
  • Role: a graph doesn't record the amplifier's mode, so the role is guessed from each channel's unit and the recording system (Automatic). Set it to current clamp, voltage clamp, stimulus, extracellular (wideband), extracellular (LFP) or other when the guess is wrong: a file holding only the command current is a stimulus, and LFP channels are never guessed.
  • Extracellular channels with the same electrode group name share one group; the first to give a group description or device sets it. A group named "electrodes", which NWB keeps for the electrodes table, is written as "electrodes group".
  • Intan and Neuralynx files fill in the filtering from their headers, and an NWB file fills in what its electrodes table says.
  • The sheet starts from what you entered for this graph last time (a saved .@graph keeps it) or what an NWB file it came from says, and fills blank experimenters, institution, lab, species and strain from your last export.

What the file holds

DataWritten as
A waveform windowOne series per channel and sweep under /acquisition/, with the data in the graph's own unit, the NWB unit (volts or amperes) and conversion factor, its sample rate and its start time. Each sweep keeps its own rate and length.
Intracellular channelsThe first voltage or current channel sets the mode (voltage: current clamp; current: voltage clamp). Channels of that unit are the responses (CurrentClampSeries or VoltageClampSeries), each with its own electrode on the amplifier device. A channel of the other unit recorded alongside (Im beside Vm) is a response's stimulus, paired in order and kept in the file's stimulus section. Any channel left over is a plain TimeSeries.
Extracellular channelsA voltage in µV, or in mV from an Intan, Open Ephys, Neuralynx, Blackrock, Plexon or TDT file, is an ElectricalSeries: each sweep's channels of one sample rate share a series, one column per channel, each starting at its own time. Every channel is a row of the electrodes table, with its location, electrode group and the group's device. Channels marked LFP go into processing/ecephys/LFP instead. Other units are plain TimeSeries.
A raster windowThe Units table, with each train's spike times in seconds from the session start (its sweep's start added), its name, and the span it was recorded over when known.
  • The session starts at the recording's date and time, with its time zone, when the file has one, and otherwise at the time of export.
  • When no command channel was recorded, an ABF protocol's command waveform is written as the stimulus. The intracellular recordings and simultaneous recordings tables list each sweep's electrode, stimulus and response.
  • @Graph reopens its NWB exports with the same values, sweep names included.

Export Visible Sweeps

  1. Show only the sweeps you want. To export part of each sweep, zoom the X axis to that part.
  2. Click Export Visible…, in the bar above the plot.
  3. With the X axis zoomed, leave "Only the X range on screen" on (the default) to cut each sweep to that range, or turn it off to export whole sweeps.
  4. Choose Open in new window, Save to file (a .@graph file) or Both, then click Export.
  • The panels stay as they are: each group keeps its name, style, Y range and axis title, and the graph keeps its look, labels, overlays and junction-potential setting. Each sweep keeps its own sample rate and length, and X-Y data keep their X values. A raster exports its visible trains.
  • A cut sweep keeps the times it shows now. With sweeps at different sample rates, the cut starts at a time every rate shares, so every sample keeps its exact time.
  • Export Visible… is unavailable while View › Plot Sweeps at Recording Time is on.

To export a single group as its own file, hide all other groups in the Groups panel, then use Export Visible… › Save to file.

Print

  1. Bring the window to print to the front: a graph, chart, image, spreadsheet or data table, a Statistics window, the Protocols window, a Text Editor, the Data Log or this guide.
  2. To set the paper size, orientation and scale, choose File › Page Setup… (⇧⌘P). The window keeps them until it closes.
  3. Choose File › Print… (⌘P). It is dimmed when the front window has nothing to print.
  4. In the print dialog, turn on Print header and footer to add the title, date and page numbers, or Fit to page width to shrink a wide table to fit.
WindowHow it prints
Graph or chartAs vector graphics that fill one page, landscape to start, so lines and labels stay crisp.
Spreadsheet or data tableAcross as many pages as needed, with its header rows and columns on every page.
Data Log, Text Editor, Statistics windowAs text, never splitting a line between pages.
User GuideThe page you're reading, or the whole guide with Print all sections in the print dialog.
  • A graph's Spreadsheet prints every row, with row numbers and the Time column on each page. If that would take more than 2,000 pages, @Graph asks whether to print just the selection or the first 500 pages.
  • Help › Open User Guide in Browser shows the whole guide as one web page in your default browser, with a contents list linking to each section. To keep or share a copy, save it from the browser (in Safari, File › Save As… with Format set to Page Source).

Image Export Options

Image Formats

FormatKindUse it for
PNGImage, losslessPresentations and the web.
JPEGImage, compressedSmaller files. JPEG quality runs from 50% to 100% (92% to start). JPEG can't be transparent.
TIFFImage, losslessThe same uses as PNG, where TIFF is asked for.
GIFImage, 256 colorsSimple figures.
PDFVectorPublications, and editing in Illustrator or Affinity.
SVGVectorEditing in Illustrator, Affinity Designer or Inkscape: elements can be selected one by one, and text stays editable.
  • A PNG, JPEG or TIFF records its resolution, in sRGB color, so it places at its intended size in Word or a journal's submission system.
  • PDF and SVG are sized in points (72 per inch), so a figure opens at the same physical size in Illustrator, Inkscape, Affinity and browsers.

Size and Resolution of a Graph

  • Width and Height are in points (pt, 72 per inch) for every format, from 1 to 20,000. The panel shows the placed size in millimeters and inches.
  • Resolution: 72, 144, 150, 300, 600 or 1,200 dpi. An image is the size in points × dpi ÷ 72 pixels, so 1,200 pt at 300 dpi is 5,000 pixels wide.
  • An image over 30,000 pixels a side or 250 million pixels is too large to make, and the panel says so.
  • Match window sets the size to the graph area on screen and the resolution to 72 dpi. Raise the resolution afterward for a sharper image with the same layout. Copy as PDF and Send to Keynote use the same size.
  • Data resolution (PDF and SVG): how many points each sweep keeps per inch of plot width: 200, 400 (the default), 600, All or a Custom number. The panel shows the points per sweep. Every sweep keeps its highest and lowest values and its first and last points, and gaps stay gaps, so peaks and gaps survive at any setting.

Size and Resolution of a Chart

  • Size: in points, inches, centimeters or millimeters, up to 20,000 pt.
  • Journal width sets a journal's column width (Nature, Cell, Science, PNAS, eLife / PLOS) and keeps the chart's proportions. Text keeps its point size, so check that labels still fit.
  • Resolution (images): 72, 144, 150, 300, 600 or 1,200 dpi. The panel shows the output in pixels.
  • PDF and SVG files are laid out like the chart window, title included, and SVG text stays editable. Heatmaps of more than 250,000 cells (or 2,000 rows or columns) export their cells as an embedded image, with labels, dendrograms and legend still vector.

What a Graph Export Holds

  • The export matches the window in every format: the same axis ranges, ticks and units, junction-potential-corrected Y labels, legend, overlays, scale bars, markers, error bars and cursors A and B.
  • What only matters while you work is left out: the selected sweep's highlight and a panel's highlighted analysis window.
  • In PDF and SVG, each sweep is one editable path, cut off exactly at the plot's edge, with no clipping masks.
  • PDF text: the fonts are embedded as subsets, so text looks the same on every computer and stays searchable and editable. If a font's license doesn't allow embedding, its text is drawn as outlines; characters a PDF can't draw, such as color emoji, are left out. Either way an alert and the Data Log say so.
  • SVG text names each font's family with its weight, italic and width, so it looks the same in browsers, Inkscape and Illustrator as on screen.

Keyboard Shortcuts

The Keyboard Shortcuts menu in the menu bar lists the zoom, inspector, grouping and signal-processing commands below, so you can also click them. Its last item, See All Keyboard Shortcuts, opens this page. A few keys act differently while a Text Editor or the Data Log has the focus: see Text Tools, below.

File

⌘O Open File…

⌘N New Data Importer: a drop zone that lists the files @Graph opens

⇧⌘N New Text Editor

⌥⌘N New Spreadsheet

⇧⌘G Graph Selected Text…: graph the numbers selected in the Data Log or a Text Editor

⇧⌘H Chart Selection…: chart the table selected in the Data Log or a Text Editor

⌥⌘L Volcano Plot from Selected Text… (File › Omics Plot)

⌥⌘M Heatmap from Selected Text… (File › Omics Plot)

⌘S Save: Graph, Chart, Spreadsheet and Image windows as .@graph; Text Editor and Data Log windows as plain text; in a Statistics window, exports the report

⇧⌘S Save As…

⇧⌘K Duplicate: open a copy of the window (Graph, Chart, Spreadsheet, Text Editor and Image windows; the Data Log's copy opens in a Text Editor)

⌃⌘R Rename…: rename the front window, as double-clicking its title bar does

⇧⌘E Export…: a Graph, Chart or Image window as an image; a Spreadsheet as CSV, TSV or Excel

⇧⌘P Page Setup…

⌘P Print…

⌘W Close: the front tab or window

⇧⌘W Close Window: the front window with all its tabs

⌥⌘W Close All: every window

⌘Q Quit. Closing and quitting ask first about unsaved changes

  • Rename… and double-clicking the title bar work in Graph, Chart, Image, Spreadsheet, Text Editor and Statistics windows, including those opened from a chart. Edit the title in place, then press Return to confirm or Escape to cancel. A Text Editor with a file renames the file too.
  • When you rename or move a saved file in the Finder while it is open in @Graph, the window's title and save location follow it.

Edit

⌘Z Undo: filtering, baseline, scale and offset, fits, Set X = 0, Rₛ and junction-potential correction, grouping, titles and units, style changes, ROIs and overlays, an image's display settings, and spreadsheet edits. To step back a zoom, double-click the plot

⇧⌘Z Redo

⌘D / ⌘R Fill Down / Fill Right: copy the selection's first row or column into the rest (spreadsheets)

⌘F Find…: the Data Log and Text Editors show a find bar; in this guide, ⌘F goes to its search field

⌥⌘F Find and Replace…

⌘G Find Next. Find Previous is in Edit › Find, without a shortcut

⌘E Use Selection for Find

View & Navigation

⌘L Show the Data Log, or hide it when it's in front

⌘@ Show the Welcome window, or hide it when it's in front

⇧⌘U Show this User Guide, or hide it when it's in front

⌘, Settings…

⌥⌘I Open AI Assistant (after turning it on in Settings › AI Assistant)

⌘I Show / hide the inspector (Graph windows)

⌘K Show / hide cursors A and B (Graph windows)

Tab / ⇧Tab Step forward / back one sweep

Space / ⇧Space Add the next sweep to those shown / remove the last one added

, / . Jump to the first / last sweep

← → (hold) Pan the X axis when it is zoomed in (not while typing in a text field)

↑ ↓ (hold) Pan the Y axis when it is zoomed in (not while typing in a text field)

Delete Remove the legend entry you double-clicked (the sweep stays on the graph)

Drag on plot Zoom into the rectangle you drag

Drag on Y axis Zoom Y for this group only

Drag on X axis Zoom X for all groups; Y is unchanged

Dbl-click plot Step back one zoom; with none left, fit the data

Dbl-click axis Type exact axis limits, with units if you like (752 ms, -80 mV). A lone comma or period follows your Mac's number format

Dbl-click label Edit an axis label on the plot

⌥⇧-click on plot Log the selected sweep's value at that X position to the Data Log (on X-Y data, the point nearest the click; with no sweep selected, the pointer's position). Needs "Log routine file and window activity" on in Settings › General. Not available on a spike-train raster

Zoom

⌘= or ⌘+ Zoom In X

⌘− Zoom Out X

⌘→ / ⌘← Zoom in / out on the X axis, as ⌘= and ⌘− (not while typing in a text field)

⌘↑ / ⌘↓ Zoom In Y / Zoom Out Y (not while typing in a text field)

⌘0 Reset Zoom: fit X and Y to the data

⌘= / ⌘− / ⌘0 (text) In the Data Log or a Text Editor: larger text, smaller text, the default size

⌘= / ⌘− / ⌘0 (sheet) In a Spreadsheet window: zoom in, zoom out, back to 100%

Inspector Navigation

⇧⌘F Open the inspector to Filter/Smoothing

⇧⌘B Open the inspector to Baseline and focus its Start field

⇧⌘X Open the inspector to Data Transform (Scale/Offset Axes)

⇧⌘M Open the inspector to Measure

⇧⌘D Open the inspector to Peak Detection

⇧⌘J Open the inspector to AP Detection (Electrophysiology toolkit)

⇧⌘I Open the inspector to Rₛ Correction (Electrophysiology toolkit)

⌥⌘R Focus the "Review sweeps:" field; type a range (such as 1-4, 7-10, 11) and press Return

↩ in text field Run the panel's main action (Apply Filter, Measure, Fit, Detect APs and so on)

Grouping

⌥⌘G Single Group: all sweeps in one group

⌥⌘S Separate All Sweeps: each sweep in its own group

Signal Processing

Graph Utilities

⌃⌘H Convert to Histogram…

⌥⌘V Paste Style: apply the copied look to the front window of the same type

Image Windows

⌘S Save the image as a .@graph file with its pixel data, ROIs, LUT, display range and analysis settings; it reopens without the original files

⇧⌘K Duplicate: a second view of the same image, with its ROIs and settings

Space Play / pause a time series; with one time point, step to the next ROI-trace sweep

⌘= / ⌘− / ⌘0 Zoom in or out around the pointer, or back to fit (the ⌘-arrow keys zoom too)

Pinch / two-finger double-tap Zoom around the pointer; go between Fit and 100%

Arrow keys, two-finger scroll Pan the zoomed image

N (hold) Show the other view, Show Native Image's or the image's own, while held

⌥-drag an ROI Drag a copy of the ROI

Spreadsheets

Double-click cell Edit the cell; press Return to commit

Any character Start typing with a cell selected to replace its contents

Cited Works

Cited Works

Every work this guide cites, in one list, most with a note of what it is cited for. The pages cite most of them by author and year, and some by the software that follows them (R's lme4, for example).

Agresti A (2013). Categorical Data Analysis, 3rd edition. Hoboken, NJ: Wiley. The difference of paired (dependent) proportions, Δp, and McNemar's test.

Algina J, Keselman HJ & Penfield RD (2005). An alternative to Cohen's standardized mean difference effect size: a robust parameter and confidence interval in the presence of outliers. Psychological Methods, 10(3):317–328. https://doi.org/10.1037/1082-989X.10.3.317. AKP robust d.

Amarasingham A, Harrison MT, Hatsopoulos NG & Geman S (2012). Conditional modeling and the jitter method of spike resampling. Journal of Neurophysiology, 107(2):517–531. https://doi.org/10.1152/jn.00633.2011. The spike CCG's jitter bands, and pattern jitter for bursting neurons.

Aru J, Aru J, Priesemann V, Wibral M, Lana L, Pipa G, Singer W & Vicente R (2015). Untangling cross-frequency coupling in neuroscience. Current Opinion in Neurobiology, 31:51–61. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.conb.2014.08.002. Pitfalls of phase–amplitude coupling, surrogates, and amplitude bandwidth.

Baek S-J, Park A, Ahn Y-J & Choo J (2015). Baseline correction using asymmetrically reweighted penalized least squares smoothing. Analyst, 140(1):250–257. https://doi.org/10.1039/C4AN01061B. arPLS.

Bagwell CB (1993). Theoretical aspects of flow cytometry data analysis. In Bauer KD, Duque RE & Shankey TV (eds.), Clinical Flow Cytometry: Principles and Application, 41–61. Williams & Wilkins.

Bagwell CB (2005). Hyperlog: a flexible log-like transform for negative, zero, and positive valued data. Cytometry A, 64(1):34–42.

Bagwell CB, Mayo SW, Whetstone SD et al. (1991). DNA histogram debris theory and compensation. Cytometry, 12(2):107–118.

Bailer-Jones CAL (2015). Estimating distances from parallaxes. Publications of the Astronomical Society of the Pacific, 127:994–1009. Why Plate Solving gives a distance only for a parallax at least 5 times its error.

Bakeman R (2005). Recommended effect size statistics for repeated measures designs. Behavior Research Methods, 37(3):379–384. https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03192707. Generalized η² for repeated-measures designs.

Baluev RV (2008). Assessing the statistical significance of periodogram peaks. Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, 385(3):1279–1285. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-2966.2008.12689.x. The Lomb–Scargle periodogram's false-alarm probability.

Bar-Joseph Z, Gifford DK & Jaakkola TS (2001). Fast optimal leaf ordering for hierarchical clustering. Bioinformatics, 17(Suppl 1):S22–S29. The Heatmap's optimal leaf ordering.

Bates D, Mächler M, Bolker B & Walker S (2015). Fitting linear mixed-effects models using lme4. Journal of Statistical Software, 67(1):1–48. The REML fit of the mixed model.

Behar JA, Rosenberg AA, Weiser-Bitoun I, Shemla O, Alexandrovich A, Konyukhov E & Yaniv Y (2018). PhysioZoo: a novel open access platform for heart rate variability analysis of mammalian electrocardiographic data. Frontiers in Physiology, 9:1390. https://doi.org/10.3389/fphys.2018.01390. The rabbit and mouse HRV bands and the rabbit pNN threshold recommended in ECG / HRV.

Belkina AC, Ciccolella CO, Anno R et al. (2019). Automated optimized parameters for T-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding improve visualization and analysis of large datasets. Nature Communications, 10:5415.

Belsley DA, Kuh E & Welsch RE (1980). Regression Diagnostics: Identifying Influential Data and Sources of Collinearity. New York: Wiley. The 2p/n leverage rule in regression diagnostics.

Bendat JS & Piersol AG (2010). Random Data: Analysis and Measurement Procedures, 4th ed. Wiley. https://doi.org/10.1002/9781118032428. Coherence phase and the time lag it implies.

Berens P (2009). CircStat: a MATLAB toolbox for circular statistics. Journal of Statistical Software, 31(10):1–21. https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v031.i10. The Rayleigh test as computed here.

Bergsma W (2013). A bias-correction for Cramér's V and Tschuprow's T. Journal of the Korean Statistical Society, 42(3):323–328. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jkss.2012.10.002. The bias-corrected Cramér's V.

Beroiz M, Cabral JB & Sanchez B (2020). Astroalign: a Python module for astronomical image registration. Astronomy and Computing, 32:100384.

Bertin E & Arnouts S (1996). SExtractor: Software for source extraction. Astronomy and Astrophysics Supplement Series, 117:393–404.

Best DJ & Roberts DE (1975). Algorithm AS 89: the upper tail probabilities of Spearman's rho. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series C (Applied Statistics), 24(3):377–379. The Edgeworth series for Spearman's p above n = 10, as R's cor.test uses.

BioTek Instruments (Agilent). Gen5 Microplate Data Collection & Analysis Software User's Guide, Kinetic Analysis: Well Analysis Calculation Types (Mean V, Max V, Lagtime).

Bonett DG & Wright TA (2000). Sample size requirements for estimating Pearson, Kendall and Spearman correlations. Psychometrika, 65(1):23–28. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02294183. The variances of Fisher's z for Spearman ρ and Kendall's τ-b above n = 1,000.

Boukens BJ, Rivaud MR, Rentschler S & Coronel R (2014). Misinterpretation of the mouse ECG: 'musing the waves of Mus musculus'. The Journal of Physiology, 592(21):4613–4626. The mouse's J wave and QRS end.

Brennan M, Palaniswami M & Kamen P (2001). Do existing measures of Poincaré plot geometry reflect nonlinear features of heart rate variability? IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering, 48(11):1342–1347. SD1 and SD2.

Breslow N (1970). A generalized Kruskal-Wallis test for comparing K samples subject to unequal patterns of censorship. Biometrika, 57(3):579–594. The Gehan-Breslow weighting of the Kaplan-Meier test.

Brideau C, Gunter B, Pikounis B & Liaw A (2003). Improved statistical methods for hit selection in high-throughput screening. Journal of Biomolecular Screening, 8(6):634–647.

Brody CD (1999). Correlations without synchrony. Neural Computation, 11(7):1537–1551. https://doi.org/10.1162/089976699300016133. Why a shared stimulus or slow co-modulation makes a CCG peak, and what the shift predictor and jitter remove.

Brookmeyer R & Crowley J (1982). A confidence interval for the median survival time. Biometrics, 38(1):29–41. The median survival CI on Kaplan-Meier charts.

Brown LD, Cai TT & DasGupta A (2001). Interval estimation for a binomial proportion. Statistical Science, 16(2):101–133. https://doi.org/10.1214/ss/1009213286. Why the Estimation Plot uses the Wilson interval for a proportion.

Brunner E & Munzel U (2000). The nonparametric Behrens-Fisher problem: asymptotic theory and a small-sample approximation. Biometrical Journal, 42(1):17–25. The Brunner-Munzel test.

Buccino AP, Hurwitz CL, Garcia S, Magland J, Siegle JH, Hurwitz R & Hennig MH (2020). SpikeInterface, a unified framework for spike sorting. eLife, 9:e61834. https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.61834. The Spike Sorter's amplitude cutoff and presence ratio are computed as its quality metrics compute them, except that the amplitude cutoff's smoothed counts stay real numbers.

Bulmer MG (1979). Principles of Statistics. New York: Dover. The informal |skewness| ≥ 1 rule of thumb for strong skew behind the Compare suggestion.

Burnham KP & Anderson DR (2002). Model Selection and Multimodel Inference: A Practical Information-Theoretic Approach, 2nd ed. New York: Springer. The AIC difference of 4 or more behind Dose–Response's note on what varies between data sets.

Butkevich AG & Lindegren L (2014). Rigorous treatment of barycentric stellar motion: perspective and light-time effects in astrometric and radial velocity data. Astronomy & Astrophysics, 570:A62. Moving Gaia's star positions to an image's date (Plate Solving).

Calabretta MR & Greisen EW (2002). Representations of celestial coordinates in FITS. Astronomy & Astrophysics, 395:1077–1122.

Canolty RT, Edwards E, Dalal SS, Soltani M, Nagarajan SS, Kirsch HE, Berger MS, Barbaro NM & Knight RT (2006). High gamma power is phase-locked to theta oscillations in human neocortex. Science, 313(5793):1626–1628. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1128115. Time-shift surrogates for coupling.

Carnall AC (2017). SpectRes: a fast spectral resampling tool in Python. arXiv:1705.05165. https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.05165. Resampling a spectrum with its flux kept.

Carnevali L, Barbetti M, Statello R, Williams DP, Thayer JF & Sgoifo A (2023). Sex differences in heart rate and heart rate variability in rats: implications for translational research. Frontiers in Physiology, 14:1170320. https://doi.org/10.3389/fphys.2023.1170320. The rat HRV bands recommended in ECG / HRV.

Carroll RJ & Ruppert D (1988). Transformation and Weighting in Regression. New York: Chapman & Hall. Why dose-response 1/Y² and 1/Y weights come from the fitted curve, iterated, rather than from each point's own response, which biases the fit.

Cheng Y & Prusoff WH (1973). Relationship between the inhibition constant (KI) and the concentration of inhibitor which causes 50 per cent inhibition (I50) of an enzymatic reaction. Biochemical Pharmacology, 22(23):3099–3108. https://doi.org/10.1016/0006-2952(73)90196-2. Kᵢ from IC50 in Competition Binding.

Clements JD & Bekkers JM (1997). Detection of spontaneous synaptic events with an optimally scaled template. Biophysical Journal, 73(1):220–229. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0006-3495(97)78062-7 (the Template Method in Synapse Detection).

Cleveland WS (1979). Robust locally weighted regression and smoothing scatterplots. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 74(368):829–836. https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1979.10481038. The lowess smooth on the regression diagnostic plots.

Cliff N (1993). Dominance statistics: ordinal analyses to answer ordinal questions. Psychological Bulletin, 114(3):494–509. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.114.3.494. Dominance δ.

Clopper CJ & Pearson ES (1934). The use of confidence or fiducial limits illustrated in the case of the binomial. Biometrika, 26(4):404–413. The exact interval behind the one-sample binomial CI, McNemar's odds ratio and Cohen's g CIs, and the paired dominance δ's CI.

Cochran WG (1954). Some methods for strengthening the common χ² tests. Biometrics, 10(4):417–451. https://doi.org/10.2307/3001616. The expected-count rule for the χ² test.

Cochran WG (1977). Sampling Techniques, 3rd ed. New York: Wiley. The rule of thumb n ≥ 25 × skewness² for a reliable mean, behind the Compare suggestion at large n.

Cohen J (1988). Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences, 2nd edition. Hillsdale, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum Associates. Cohen's h for a difference in proportions.

Collins KA, Kielkopf JF, Stassun KG & Hessman FV (2017). AstroImageJ: image processing and photometric extraction for ultra-precise astronomical light curves. The Astronomical Journal, 153:77.

Cook RD (1977). Detection of influential observation in linear regression. Technometrics, 19(1):15–18. https://doi.org/10.1080/00401706.1977.10489493. Cook's distance.

Cossarizza A, Chang HD, Radbruch A et al. (2021). Guidelines for the use of flow cytometry and cell sorting in immunological studies (third edition). European Journal of Immunology, 51(12):2708–3145.

Cotterill E, Charlesworth P, Thomas CW, Paulsen O & Eglen SJ (2016). A comparison of computational methods for detecting bursts in neuronal spike trains and their application to human stem cell-derived neuronal networks. Coursey JS, Schwab DJ, Tsai JJ & Dragoset RA. Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions (version 4.1). National Institute of Standards and Technology. https://www.nist.gov/pml/atomic-weights-and-isotopic-compositions-relative-atomic-masses. The isotope table.

Cox DR (1972). Regression models and life-tables. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 34(2):187–220. The proportional-hazards model behind the Kaplan-Meier hazard ratio.

Craig M, Crawford S, Seifert M et al. ccdproc, version 2.5 (an Astropy affiliated package for CCD data reduction).

Cumming G & Calin-Jageman R (2024). Introduction to the New Statistics: Estimation, Open Science, and Beyond, 2nd edition. New York: Routledge. The basis of the Estimation Plot. Estimation statistics.
